PREFACE TO THE REVISED EDITION 

New knowledge of the physiology of the brain, which has been arrived at in both America and Germany and by different types of evidence, chiefly experimental in America, chiefly clinical in Germany, must very soon modify profoundly the teaching of psychology. This book is the first attempt to make this modification.

The old brain or "brain stem" can no longer be regarded as a center merely for reflex action. It certainly presides over emotional and instinctive behavior and is more intimately a center for consciousness than the cerebral cortex itself (see quotation from Ewald, p. 29). These facts permit the psychologist to describe first the simpler and more primitive human behavior as dependent upon the brain stem, and then to show how the new brain comes to modify and direct this impulsive behavior, so that it becomes in large part intelligent action. This order of procedure has several advantages. (1) It permits us to follow the probable order of brain development. (2) It permits the description first of the simpler, then of more complex processes. (3) It brings psychology and anthropology, which have hitherto seemed to be quite independent sciences, into much closer relationship. (4) It shows how consciousness modifies and regulates behavior and how necessary the recognition of consciousness is to a description of behavior. [7]

(5) It suggests how similar the higher animals and man may be in their emotional life and in the functions of the old brain and it suggests also how widely different they are in intelligence and learning. (6) It furnishes a scientific basis for the new science of mental hygiene and character development. (7) It suggests the great antiquity (instead of recency) of the "conflict psychology" and offers a better explanation for it than the present speculative one.

In the present revision the chapter on intelligence has been extended to give place to the results of recent investigations on the relative influence of heredity and environment on intellectual ability and to note a correction necessary to be applied to the Binet Scale (Freeman's correction). A rather long chapter on learning has been added and the introduction tries to give a clear account of the functions of the old brain and the new and their relations to each other. Then behavior due to the old brain is described. A review by Albrecht Peiper of the nervous processes and actions present at birth, those which are absent at birth but rapidly added seriatim, and those which are present in the newborn but absent in prematurely born babies, has been given almost completely. It seems to the writer to be more complete and more soundly analytical than any account in English of the behavior of babes. 

Minor changes and additions to the text have been made at many points. After trial, the material included seems to be sufficient for a text-book designed for study during a semester or during two academic quarter-years. 

It is, however, a text-book; not a treatise. The writer is [8]

convinced that, despite the innumerable volumes descriptive of human nature, they must, taken altogether, fall far short of a really good account of the finer shadings of mental and emotional processes.

It is hoped that the matter selected for presentation may be satisfactory to the considerable number of teachers who used the first edition to the text. Their valuable criticisms have been observed, it is hoped, with two exceptions. 

The writer is still committed to an opinion (perhaps an erroneous one) as to the exact nature of space perception. 

It seems futile to give all the "clues" and "signs" for the perception of space and yet leave the thing itself an algebraic X. It seems better to take one position on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays and its opposite on Tuesdays,

Thursdays and Saturdays, as Bragg did for the theory of light until his dilemma was resolved, than to be vaguely non-committal or to close the mind to alternatives. Again, the opinion that any knowledge at all of the structure and development of brain and sense organs is too difficult for the modern youth to learn, and consequently the information is too definite and difficult to teach, is an opinion I cannot share. Only the elements of that knowledge will save psychology from the tendency, which it shows in some quarters, to become once more pure speculation. 

My thanks are due my colleague, Miss Henry Etta

Reynolds, for preparing the index and to the publishers named in the text for permission to reproduce figures of their publications.

BOULDER, COLORADO, AUGUST 18, 1930. 

L. W. COLE.

CHAPTER I INTRODUCTION 

Psychology has been defined as the science of human nature. But human nature is complex. On one side it presents every variety of behavior; on the other side, thoughts and feelings, plans, purposes, desires, hopes, fears, ideas and ideals, in a word, states of mind or of consciousness. 

The behavior side of life is called objective; the conscious side subjective. Some writers on psychology are inclined' to emphasize the objective side of human nature. They describe behavior almost exclusively. Other psychologists give chief attention to mental processes and subjective life. 

This is due to a difference of interests. We shall gain more reliable and useful information if we try to face both types of facts impartially. Unless we can do this we shall gain only a distorted and one-sided view of human nature. 

The child in school whose behavior suddenly changed from frankness and honesty to concealment and moroseness, because his father had been imprisoned, could not be understood unless we have a sympathetic knowledge of human emotions and their immense influence on action. They are subjective states but they changed the boy's behavior entirely and endangered his future. We must try to take both subjective and objective facts into account. Like the psychologist, the novelist must describe both behavior

and thought and feeling. The greater writers describe the nuances of the feeling, thought, passions, and motives of their characters. Knowing these, we readily imagine the behavior of the characters which the novelist creates for us. 

We may trace the development of behavior from acts which are totally unconscious and independent of conscious control, to those which come more and more under the control of mind, and finally to behavior so purposive and so fully directed by intelligence that, knowing the purpose, it would be superfluous or useless to describe the behavior which carries it into effect. In fact, when a great plan has been conceived and completed, the behavior which carries it out may be that of persons other than he who made the plan, or he may even employ automatic machines. Perhaps a simple diagram will illustrate the relationship.

BEHAVIOR CONSCIOUSNESS 

Behavior which is simple and primitive, like reflex action, is rather independent of consciousness. But as thought takes more and more control of action, the importance of the behavior is reduced. This relationship appears to be a general one. When thought devises clearing houses and international balances, the transfer of gold

17 diminishes in volume, etc. This diagram shows why we may begin our work by describing behavior at first and turn more and more to an account of mental and emotional processes as we continue. 

Types of Behavior. Without insisting on a perfectly sharp boundary between them we may distinguish three main types of behavior.

Behavior Reflex 

Impulsive or instinctive

Deliberate, considered, voluntary Each of these types is more complex and more conscious than the preceding one. We are only slightly aware of some reflex acts. Others are completely unconscious. Due to evaporation, the eyeball is becoming dry all the time. 

Yet if it ever did become dry, it would be infected and sight would be lost. Glands continually secrete the fluid tears and every few seconds the eyelids wink and spread the fluid evenly over every part of the surface. If we ever became conscious of this reflex winking it would become annoying or distracting. A fixed feature of the environment is perfectly met by this simple reflex. Breathing is also below the threshold of consciousness unless it becomes labored due to exertion or disease. The nervous impulses which control these reflexes do not reach the brain. If breathing were dependent on the mind at all, our first slumber would result in death. Consequently the vital reflexes are carried on by lower and older centers of the nervous system and are purely automatic. These reflexes go on perfectly in an animal whose brain has been destroyed or has been severed from the lower nervous centers by a delicate incision across the spinal cord and the lower cranial nerves. A simple diagram (Fig. 1) will illustrate the nervous mechanism of the winking reflex.

The drying of the eye causes impulses to course along an afferent nerve to the center. They are reflected along 

VII 

Sp.c. 

Fig. 1-Schema to show probable nervous connections for the eye lid reflex. 

More central connections indicated by dotted line. Of course many neurons, not a single series, are required for the reflex. This reflex is one of the last to be abolished in anesthesia. Hence it is used as a convenient sign. a motor nerve to the eyelid and winking results. For this kind of behavior the formula S-R, stimulus-response, seems to give an adequate explanation. A brainless or socalled decerebrate frog will crawl up a slanting board on which he has been placed. Reverse the slant and he will turn about and crawl up again. Evidently the slant of the board or gravity is the stimulus; crawling upward the response or reaction to the stimulus. The reflex is predictable. A frog with its brain intact will make all sorts of efforts to escape, none of which is predictable. When this predictability of simple reflexes was discovered it was claimed that reflex action is the type of all action and S-R is the formula for all behavior. Any one who has observed human behavior or that of the higher animals knows that this formula cannot be true of behavior above the reflex level. The claim is an instance of men believing

INTRODUCTION 

19 what they wish. This human trait was discovered long ago by Julius Caesar and set down by him in the words, Homines perfacile credunt id quod volunt. Evidently this trait has remained unchanged through the centuries. 

For the partly reflex act of eating, both hunger or appetite and the sight or smell of food must be present. 

Both an external and an internal stimulus cooperate to produce the response. Even then, if a doctor's orders forbid it, the response will not follow upon the stimuli. When a mother bird suddenly changes all her behavior, settles down upon a nestful of eggs, turns each one over each day, and finally warms them into life, she is acting partly from internal, bodily conditions, and the behavior is too complicated and prolonged to be called a simple response to a simple stimulus. It is not purely reflex but instinctive behavior. It has nothing to do with the well-being of the mother bird but it has much to do with the preservation of her race. Human beings are not devoid of these impulses. 

Why do we imitate all sorts of acts and customs and the speech we hear about us? Why do we fall in love? Why can we hardly resist following an excited crowd and so on? 

These actions cannot be explained by the simple S-R formula. We cannot afford to purchase simplicity by ignoring the facts, if psychology is to aid in understanding human nature.

When houses were lighted by candles, the little glowing flame was attractive to babes as bright things always are. The child reached for the flame and sooner or later it was burned. Every language has its proverb: "A burnt child dreads the fire," "Gebranntes Kind scheut's Feuer."

But once this dread is set up, the child no longer touches the flame but avoids it. The S is the same. The behavior is entirely different, because the child now acts from a

memory of the former sharp pain. This example gives the clue to the most important human behavior. Most adult behavior is due to memories and anticipations. Very often the success of our behavior depends upon whether we have sufficient knowledge to select the course of action which meets the situation. Psychology must give a reason for the widely differing success of different men in what appears to be the same environment. This it cannot do if every human being is supposed to react fatally to a particular stimulus. The fact is that our behavior arises from our inner organization, our emotions, memories, and desires. How otherwise could we speak of human initiative at all? If a man desires only fame he may disregard the acquisition of a fortune or even of a competency, but if he wishes above all else to acquire a fortune, he may be very contemptuous of fame. This contempt and his ambition may, indeed, drive him to deeds which result in an evil reputation, whose damaging force he never realized until he met its blow. Like the child he will dread it thereafter. Of course, there are things in the environment which we desire and these may be called the stimuli for our actions, but the simplicity of reflex action is no longer present. 

The predictability is gone and we can partly restore it only by an intimate knowledge of the individual, his tastes, his ambitions, his hopes, and his fears. He is a center of force and initiative and what is likely to be a stimulus for him we can only infer from a knowledge of mind in general and his own in particular. Very often outer stimuli are only opportunities for the exercise of our desires and determinations. This is not only observable in human behavior but it is written, as it were, in the very evolution of the human brain. Let us consider the evidence for this.

The Old Brain and the New Brain.-Anatomists have

INTRODUCTION 

21 long known that certain parts of the brain originate and develop in the animal series earlier than other parts. They also develop earlier in children. These primary reflex centers of the brain stem and cerebellum are called the paleëncephalon or old brain. The cortex, or outer gray covering of the cerebral hemispheres, along with its dependencies, is called the neëncephalon or new brain. We shall use the terms old brain and new brain rather than their Greek equivalents.

In the child it is known that nervous connections of the new brain are not complete at birth, and many of them are not complete for a long time after birth. Fig. 4 "Three sections through the cortex of the anterior central gyrus. from a child 14 years old. B, from a man 36 years old. C, from a man of 53 years.

Myelin staining. Controls have shown that the differences are essentially occasioned by age. Yet the possibility that a different amount of use of the cortical region under discussion may bave added in some degree to the difference cannot be overlooked. (After Kaes.)" 

Because of this condition, reflex and impulsive behavior continues in the child for a long time before it comes under the control or even partial control of the cortex. The babe and the young child perform innumerable spontaneous and impulsive acts which, if they were not gradually replaced by more prudent behavior, would make him incompetent in any modern social or physical environment.¹ Consequently, while spontaneous movements "The mentally retarded child is an "incompetent" in just this sense. He may cope with a very simple environment.

INTRODUCTION 

23 appear to be necessary to the development and ripening of the nervous system, they must finally be checked, recombined, and connected in new ways with other elementary movements until they become appropriate to the situations which the child finds confronting him. He is then said to have acquired new behavior patterns. This process makes up a large part of his simpler education, the formation of suitable habits. Thus behavior becomes appropriate to the environment and ministers to self-preservation and success.

The checking or suppression of some reflex or spontaneous act, contraction or secretion is called by the physiologist "inhibition." There appear to be special inhibitory centers in the nervous system at lower and higher levels. From these centers fibers arise which carry only inhibiting impulses to the part of the body or the organ affected. Other fibers carry impulses which stimulate to activity or accelerate it. The fact of inhibition and its importance are fully established.

Inhibition of Impulses.-If impulses arising from lower nerve centers can be checked or inhibited by higher centers, we have in this the means for complete modification of behavior. It can be changed so as to adapt the individual to his environment more and more perfectly as knowledge and the new brain take charge. Perhaps further illustrations are necessary to show that this is the order of development.

For a year the babe cannot control the emptying of the bladder and the bowels, though habits can be formed for him. Gradually, their time of discharge comes under the inhibition of lower nerve centers and these under the control of intelligence and the will. After showing that the physiologist can bring about inhibition by means of chemi-

cals, Howell remarks, "This experiment accords with many facts which indicate that the brain may inhibit the activities of the spinal centers. In the reflex from tickling, for instance, we know that by a voluntary act we can repress the muscular movements up to a certain point; so also the limited control of the centers of respiration and micturition is a phenomenon of the same character." Many acts are for a long time reflex and impulsive in the child, so thoughtful observers expect only impulsive behavior in the child and even in the adolescent, until higher control is established by growth of the inhibitory function in the new brain. Very gradually behavior becomes more deliberate, prudent and intelligent. Due to cortical inhibition of impulsive acts, behavior has come partly under the control of thought and plan. If, however, we wished to deny the influence (or even the existence) of thought or ideas we should still have the physiological proof that the cortex comes into control of many reflexes and impluses and that one of the primary functions of the new brain is the inhibition of impulses of the old brain and of even lower nervous centers, as illustrated above. If we keep in mind this relative antagonism between the functions of the old brain and the new and the increasing control of behavior by the latter, we can give a clearer explanation of human and animal behavior than if we overlooked this fundamental fact. Either we must accept this well-established fact which accounts for development, education, and the modifiability of behavior, or else we are driven to the conclusion that the human nervous system is like a series of telephone circuits heaped one upon another. From every sense organ there would be a nerve circuit which would allow impulses to pass to the muscles and result in a fixed reaction. This the stimulus-response formula implies. But

INTRODUCTION 

25 nervous action is not so simple as that. There is central control of behavior. It becomes more centralized and controlled as the cortex develops and as knowledge increases. 

We may turn aside for a moment to point to the fact that similar centralized control of the behavior of nations is aimed at by the establishment of the World Court, the League of Nations, and the International Bank. These all aim primarily at the inhibition of future wars. It is safe to say that society in its evolution repeats what the nervous system did long ago in its development of higher and more centralized control.

We shall regard the brain, therefore, as the organic, living mechanism for modifying behavior and for adapting us even in advance to an expected environment. In this ability to expect a change and to forecast a future situation, man differs emphatically from even the higher animals. Their adaptation to future change seems to be due to instinct and natural selection, while man's is due to thought and consideration.

If we accept the order of brain development as the order of our description, we may describe the simpler and more impulsive behavior first, as belonging predominantly to the old brain, and complex, deliberate and original behavior second. This will have the advantage of putting the simper processes and reactions first. Then, after a description of the more complex processes, the reader will have to employ his scientific imagination and sagacity to see how enormously the primitive behavior of the older brain centers has been modified and complicated by every addition of cortical control. This more primitive behavior is the theme of the whole history of civilization and its products are in quest by archeology. 

An organism, whose behavior is due to the interaction

and interinfluence of the lower centers and the cortex working together, will not exhibit the conduct which is due to either alone but behavior which is a resultant of both with now one, now the other, playing the predominant role. It is for this reason that psychologists, who are looking for the stereotyped, instinctive behavior of animals and savages in civilized man are certain never to find it in its pristine purity. It will be greatly altered and obscured by the influence of intelligence. Yet it is doubtless absurd to say that man has nothing in common with the higher animals.

Not only does the new brain obscure the pure functions of the old in the race but each human cortex has an individuality all its own which alters individual behavior. The human babe is supposed to creep at a certain time in his growth but, as we shall see (p. 142), some roll forward, some rock along to the object of their desires, some pull themselves by their heels and others may even roll backward. What is first hit upon modifies the later behavior very much. Yet in the light of all the observations it is probable that the human child is for a time a creeping creature and later a walking animal. If, therefore, we separate processes and functions in our description a little too sharply at first, we shall later see that at their borders they fuse, overlap and are transformed because impulse and intelligence have so coalesced that their respective contributions to behavior can be only partly analyzed. For the sake, then, of this perhaps too sharp discrimination we must anticipate a later page to state what the optic thalamus, an important structure of the old brain, most certainly contributes to human experience. 

Since the above statements were written there has come to hand exactly the same hypothesis made by the

INTRODUCTION 

27 2 German psychiatrist Ewald. He adduces, however, quite different evidence, namely that obtained from the behavior and symptoms of patients suffering from cerebral influenza. In such cases which came to antopsy inflammations and modifications of the brain stem were clearly visible under the microscope. For the sake of correct representation of Ewald's view I quote him in translation. It is noteworthy that, while Ewald recognizes the contribution of Freud to psychiatry, he also recognizes its abuses and feels certain that we cannot proceed reliably on the basis of what he calls the "literary psychology" of psychoanalysis and behaviorism. We must pay regard to the body and the brain and recognize the functions of the brain stem, if we would come finally to an interpretation of personality. "Since 1909, Reichardt has striven to give convincing proof that the brain stem, which psychiatry had so neglected up to that time, is of capital importance as the 'seat,' according to his expression, of the emotional, instinctive and voluntary life and as the 'seat' of psychic activity. At the same period, Kleist sought to furnish the proof that certain troubles of action and of movement, which we find particularly in the catatonic form of dementia praecox must have an anatomical foundation which can be determined. But this proof was not yet sufficient and for a time it was believed a duty to consider these two investigators as outsiders. It is what is called cephalic influenza or cerebral influenza, a disease which made terrible ravages after the war, which brought all at once the justification of the researches undertaken by these two authors. Cerebral influenza is a disease which pro- 

Ewald, G., Fortschritte und Wandlungenen der psychiatrischen Lokalisationslehre, Scientia, Vol. 47, No. 113-1, pp. 21-80, 1980.

duces profound changes in the brain stem and these changes are visible under the microscope. At the same time there appeared (in complete correspondence with the ideas of Reichardt) great troubles in the affective and instinctive life of these patients; a tendency to scratch and bite, ill-nature and spitefulness of all sorts, tendencies to torment, to pinch, and prick those about them, impulsive explosions of rage, thievery both instinctive and refined, etc. On the other hand, difficulties of movement were produced, very similar to the difficulties of movement studied by Kleist. Nature had herself given clinical experiments which were hitherto lacking. Now the intelligence of these unfortunate patients remained completely intact. The disease affected only the brain stem. Here was a new proof that we must look upon the cerebral cortex as the essential organ of intelligence, just as the early observations had led us to believe. It suffices to recall the diseases of progressive paralysis, of softening of the brain, which attack selectively the cerebral cortex and lead to a disappearance of intelligence, of judgment, of understanding, and of memory and finally result in complete imbecility. Senile dementia with its feebleness of memory and of judgment is a disease of this kind which involves the disappearance of the cerebral cortex. "Phylogenetic researches and considerations connect themselves with this type of ideas. The cerebral cortex, with its great extent, is only a relatively new possession of man along with his intelligence, while we see at the same time a life based on instincts and impulses with the lower animals which are almost devoid of a cortex. But almost all possess masses of cells (knots of ganglia) and the systems of fibers of the brain stem, almost of the same kind and in the same order as those of man in the deep parts of

INTRODUCTION 

29 the brain. These animals, with their irreflective and instinctive life are individuals with a brain stem. More and more, studies of comparative anatomy have brought proof that from the histological and the histochemical point of view, the brain stem of primitive animals is constructed in the same manner and behaves itself chemically the same as that of the ages-old brain stem of man. "But behold what is more: we penetrate even to the 'seat,' pardon the word, of consciousness. Breslauer has been able to show in an experiment that a wound made by puncture or operative intervention in the immediate neighborhood of the third ventricle, the ventricle most interior of the brain stem, leads ordinarily to immediate total loss of consciousness, while we can perform entire operations on the cerebral cortex without causing consciousness to be abolished. The experiments made by Breslauer were at first combatted by Enderlen and Knauer. But cerebral influenza came also to his help against his adversaries. 

Cephalic influenza bears, as we know, also the name, sleeping sickness, because it leads to profound somnolence and later to persistent insomnia. In this case also we find very frequently in the neighborhood of the third ventricle extended inflammatory modifications. If we cannot yet establish with certainty where the center, as it may be called, for sleep and waking is, nevertheless we cannot doubt that the environs of the third ventricle are of the first importance for maintaining consciousness in the waking state. In the clinic, the profound somnolence which we observe very frequently, and the tendency to disturbance of consciousness with hallucinations similar to dreams, are found in cases of tumors and other processes which develop in this region of the brain stem, a finding 

Not, of course, the sleeping sickness caused by the tsetse fly.

which is of considerable importance. From the point of view of clinical medicine, it is hardly possible to deny that unconsciousness, disturbances of consciousness and sleep are closely related. Naturally, I have no intention to 'localize' consciousness in some cells in the neighborhood of the third ventricle; consciousness is linked with the activity of the entire brain and even with that of the entire organism; but there must be in the environs of the third ventricle a cerebral center which regulates, in a very large measure, our consciousness during waking hours. "If, on the one hand, by observations made during an epidemic of cerebral influenza, we have obtained a point of solid support touching the cerebral regions, that we can put into relation with feelings and instincts, we have finally, on the other hand, the possibility of approaching, under some form, the foundations of the abnormal personality, as well as the foundations of character both psychopathic and normal. For to the concept of personality and to that of the character of a man are strictly linked the quality and the kind of his emotional attitude and his instinctive orientations as well as their domination by intelligence. Thus we go now from the 'antechamber of the psychic,' where the doctrine of aphasia is still held, to the domain of the truly psychic."

In his second paper Ewald derives certain types of personality from the predominance of emotion and instinct on the one hand and the predominance of the cortex on the other. We cannot doubt that he is right in principle and that we shall eventually find that many personalities are primitive and emotional in behavior because of the greater influence of the brain stem on their conduct. Thus the riddle of personality bids fair at last to be solved by an increased knowledge of brain functions.

INTRODUCTION 

31 The Optic Thalamus and Emotion.-The work of Cannon, Head, and other neurologists has shown that the optic thalamus (see pp. 83 and 98) is the seat of emotions such as fear, rage, hate, jealousy and so on. The thalamus is also the seat of bodily pain and in cases of lesion of the thalamus there is excessive emotional reaction. Every sensation is loaded with feeling or emotion. An example is given on a later page of the noise of the train, on which he was riding, being so distressing to a patient with a damaged thalamus that it was completely unbearable and he attempted suicide in order to escape it. Now a sensation of noise is not a sensation of pain but we say in this case that the noise sensation had an excessively painful emotional or affective tone. This effect of a lesion of the thalamus "is interpreted as due to the release of the inhibitory or regulatory influence of the cortex arising from the destruction of the ascending and descending fibers between the thalamus and the cortex, thus isolating the thalamus and allowing it to act to excess." (Herrick, Neurology, 1927, p. 295.) Cannon supports this in the following words: "These results clearly point to the thalamus as a region from which, in the absence of cortical government, impulses are discharged which evoke an extreme degree of 'emotional' activity, both muscular and visceral." (Cannon, W. B., The James-Lange Theory, etc., p. 116.) A cat with the cortex removed by delicate surgical means and under complete anesthesia displays spontaneously "the complete picture of intense fury." Again, "when cortical processes are abolished by anesthesia, emotional display may be most remarkable. During the early (excitement) stage of ether anesthesia, for example, there may be sobbing as in grief, or laughter as in joy, or lively and energetic actions as in rage. The surgeon may open the chest

or perform other operations of equal gravity, while the patient is pushing, pulling, shouting and muttering; a few minutes later the conscious patient will testify that he has been wholly unaware of what has happened." The patient would give very different testimony indeed had not the delicate cortical processes been completely suppressed by the ether. "It is when 'laughing gas' has set aside the cortical functions that the subjects laugh and weep. Similar release of the mechanisms for emotional expression is indicated in the depression of cortical activity during acute alcoholism." In fact it has been hinted that in certain localities banquets without wine are avoided because the jokes of the speakers are too stale to provoke amusement or hilarity unless the cortical government of the emotions is set aside by the subtle chemistry of the alcohol. 

In the light of a great mass of experimental and clinical evidence of this sort it is certain that the inhibition of activities of the old brain by impulses from the new is going on all the time in normal human beings. Perhaps the irksomeness of prolonged study, so necessary in our present social environment, is due to this continual inhibition, though irksomeness is a mild emotion and mingled with bodily sensations. Perhaps we may set it down, then, that laughing gas and alcohol make the individual more childish and primitive than he is when all his cortical abilities are alert. The old brain is under less inhibition from the cortex.

But psychologists have generally held that, while emotion is a psychic feeling, its exact counterpart in behavior is an instinctive act. The two are opposite sides of the same experience. It is significant too, that the phrase, emotional behavior, is coming to be used for instinctive performances. If emotion and instinct are so intimately

INTRODUCTION 

33 related as this, we are forced to believe that the nervous impulses leading to each may have the same or a similar origin. The motor impulses of instinctive behavior probably also originate in the old brain. In many instances the feeling and the behavior have exactly the same name. 

If a man grows pale, shrinks back, and takes flight we are quite as sure that he is afraid as we are when he later confesses that he was never so frightened in his life. Acts of courtship and the peculiar emotions accompanying them are both termed love or being in love, and similarly for rage and jealousy. Both have an emotional and an active side. All this was believed by psychologists before the old brain was known to have any psychic function at all and all conscious experience was believed to be localized in the cortex. A quotation will illustrate this belief. "Objects of rage, love, fear, etc., not only prompt a man to outward deeds but provoke characteristic alterations in his attitude and visage and affect his breathing, circulation, and other organic functions in specific ways. When the outward deeds are inhibited, these latter emotional expressions still remain, and we read the anger in the face, though the blow may not be struck and the fear betrays itself in voice and color, though we may suppress all other sign. Instinctive and emotional expressions thus shade imperceptibly into each other. Every object that excites an instinct excites an emotion as well." (James, W., Principles of Psychology, Vol. II, p. 442.) 

Unless this teaching is false we must suppose that not only emotion but instinct is localized in the old brain. 

It this be true, we must suppose that an animal with slight development of the new brain would live almost exclusively an instinctive and emotional life. This is what we do find. Herrick writes, "And certainly there is much evi-

dence in the behavior of lower animals, especially birds, that a high degree of emotional activity is possible where the basal centers (see basal ganglia, p. 84) are highly elaborated but the cerebral cortex is small and very simply organized." (Herrick, Neurology, p. 368.) So much for emotion, but turn to descriptions of instinct and see if the nest building and incubating behavior of birds are not described as the very clearest and most typical examples (above the insects) of instinctive behavior. Indeed it may be doubted whether psychologists would have arrived at the notion of instinct at all but for these two examples which are observed almost everywhere among domestic fowls and half tame birds which we delight to watch. 

As already stated, the child lives a more emotional and instinctive life than the man. If the child did not nurse or cry and later play and babble senseless sounds we should fear very much for his later development. As the cortex gains control, the sounds begin to have meaning and the child begins to speak. This slowly developing control has led psychologists to emphasize the "plasticity" of the child's nervous system. In childhood and youth we may become anything we wish within very wide limits. 

From those days onward the limits narrow and very rapidly. It is certain also that youthful criminals (so much discussed just now) have not been so trained as to develop the cortical inhibitions which are necessary to decent citizenship today. Sentimentality, indifference or ignorance on the part of parents or guardians has led to the unbridled indulgence of impulse, the complete sway of the old brain uncontrolled or uninhibited by the new. 

Once more when the new brain falls a prey to insanity the patient may become so much an emotional and instinctive creature that his appearance and behavior may be

INTRODUCTION 

35 repulsive. The inhibitions which would prevent his acting in a repulsive way are removed or broken down by the brain disorder. 

How ready civilized men are to fall back into savage behavior is often seen in panics. The crowd in a panic seeks blindly to escape the object of its terror. The members of such a crowd trample their fellows ruthlessly under foot in their blind and violent fear. Or, if the panic be on the sea, they struggle wildly to get a place in the life boats though women and children are left behind to perish. All this is the effect of terror when it is unrestrained. A similar case could be made out for the behavior actuated by blind rage or jealousy or greed and so-called "unbridled" ambition, the very term, unbridled, indicating that inhibition is felt by the observer to be both possible and necessary.

The reply to such examples of brutality in terror is that there are quite as many examples of courage as of cowardice. The crowd on shipboard stands aside until women and children are made safe. The captain stays to the last or goes down with his ship. Has he no fear? Yes, but he has it under control. The physiologist would say that his fear or the impulsive action its unbridling would lead to, are inhibited. The philosopher says perhaps, that the captain acts by reason or intelligence instead of instinct and thus he becomes one of the world's immortals. 

But the physiologist adds that an important function of the new brain, and possibly its most important function, is to inhibit and restrain the impulses of the old. The cerebral cortex is in large part an organ if inhibition of the blind impulses and appetites of the lower nervous centers. 

Some more definite evidence for this inhibitory function of the cortex may be given. Those inhibitions which

result in character seem to be a function of the frontal and prefrontal lobes of the brain. Damage to these areas alters character. "In 1848 Phineas P. Gage, a laborer, was injured by a premature explosion as a result of which a crowbar was driven directly through the left orbit and upward through the left frontal lobe of the brain. He survived this injury for years. As the lesion in his brain produced an extensive destruction of the frontal lobe upon the left side, it furnished an opportunity to note the clinical changes due to this disturbance. These changes were confined to what has been spoken of in general terms as the higher psychic faculties. The patient's judgment and reason were both impaired and his personality manifested marked alterations. His temper became fitful and he was subject to sudden, often unprovoked outbursts of rage; his moods were vacillating; he sought and filled many positions; his steady habits gave place to aimless wanderings and sometimes grandiose adventures. He carried the bar which caused his injury about with him and exhibited himself in many large cities. His social attitude was greatly altered. His transactions were often dishonest and his language became extremely profane, though it was never so before the accident. In a word, his personality was converted by the injury to his brain from that of an active, steady and alert workman to that of a restless, adventurous and unreliable member of society.

Following several severe convulsions he died in 1861, twelve and a half years after his accident." (Tilney and 

Riley, The Form and Functions of the Central Nervous 

System, p. 909.)

In this case most of the important inhibitions, due to early training and whose total result we call character (or "personality" in the quotation), were suddenly de-

INTRODUCTION 

37 stroyed by the explosion and thereafter behavior was much more restless and impulsive than it was before the accident. In medical literature this is called the "American 

Crowbar Case" and it has become deservedly famous. 

Experiments made on animals give somewhat similar results though the evidence is not so clear because the animal can express emotions and impulses only by gross bodily movements. On the other hand, man possesses language and the very modulation of his voice is due to the momentary ebb and flow of emotion.

In certain cases of tumor of the frontal lobe there were somewhat similar changes of character but the absence of inhibitions goes deeper than this. Sherrington discovered that, in order to bend the finger or the arm, nervous impulses must be supplied to the opposite extensor muscles to inhibit their contractions and permit them to relax. 

Without the latter impulses there would be only convulsive movements, such as occur in spasms. Now in many cases of tumor of the frontal lobe an important symptom is the grasping reflex. "It consists of an involuntary flexion of the fingers in response to the moving contact of an object with the palm of the hand. This phenomenon may be discovered by the patient himself, who finds that he is unable to withdraw objects from the hand on the side opposite the lesion. The harder he tries to pull away the object he is thus involuntarily grasping, the more firmly do the fingers grip it. This remarkable reflex, which appears to be a regression to the reflex grasping of the babe, is present in a proportion of cases of tumor of the frontal lobe and appears to be pathognomic of a lesion in 'See the work of Cameron in which a millimeter of frontal lobe removed from rats destroyed the ability to inhibit entrance into wrong openings in a maze, even after the maze had been almost fully relearned. This relearning showed quite a different pattern from the learning and relearning of normal animals.

that situation." (Horner, N. G., British Medical Journal, June, 1928, p. 1074.)

One patient with a damaged frontal lobe had no idea of hospital discipline. He smoked contrary to the rules of the hospital but he had no idea of wrongdoing. Previous to the onset of the tumor he had been a foreman but he promptly lost all ability to supervise others. Inhibition of impulsive behavior seems to be necessary to any substantial leadership.

Some evidence of the importance of cortical inhibition has now been given. This evidence seems ample to warrant the belief that impulses, initiative and emotion, without which there is no impulse to action, spring from the old brain and are directed and governed by the new, largely by means of its function of inhibiting many impulses and allowing others to go over into acts. Thus the act is fitted to the immediate environment or situation, no matter how rapid the changes it presents. This inhibition and selection of impulses is accompanied, and I think greatly influenced by consciousness, discrimination, knowledge, and information, in short by all sorts of remembered experience. This conception is more complex than the mere stimulus-response formula which seems altogether too simple to account for any but the simplest acts. The stimulus-response formula also gives the beginning student the idea that for every stimulus there is just one response or reaction and just one separate reflex arc (p. 90). 

This is probably never true.

Because we have spoken thus far of the conscious inhibitions of the cortex, the fact that there are numerous centers of inhibition in the lower nervous system must not be overlooked. These work automatically and reflexly. They are necessary to keep us alive and are of the greatest inter-

INTRODUCTION 

39 est in physiology. The conscious reactions and inhibitions of the cortex are predominantly of interest to psychology. 

If we recognize clearly the different functions of the old and the new brain and their relative antagonism we can explain types of behavior which seem to have been omitted from academic psychology. One physician of children believes that if a child is permitted to get what it wants by tantrums, screaming, and holding its breath, the basis is thereby laid for a case of hysteria later. Hysteria is a serious psychic disorder. Yet it may be that, if impulse is fully indulged in early childhood, the fact that we cannot later get what we want by tantrums and emotional outbreaks may have serious emotional consequences amounting to hysteria in those whose hereditary stamina is not sound at the outset of life. An excellent series of lectures by perhaps the most eminent specialist in mental hygiene might well be entitled: "The Folly of Parents in not Setting Up Reasonable Self-control and Obedience in Their Children." Evidently the cortical self-control is established only by obedience in childhood. We cannot neglect the development of character for a single season or month. The primitive emotional behavior struggles to gain complete dominance and the wrecks of life detailed in the morning paper are the result of its ever-present success. "Impulse Goods."-Business psychology furnishes this striking term. Great stores have learned what goods and novelties are bought with little consideration and to satisfy no definite need. Such goods are placed on counters which the customer will pass both on entering and leaving the store. Goods which the customer came to purchase are not so temptingly placed.

The Conflict Psychology.-In recent years we have heard

a great deal about the damaging effects of emotional conflicts, the bad effects of the conventions and decencies set up by society, which interfere with unrestrained behavior. 

The counsel has been that restraint is folly. The result of this counsel is now creeping into the anonymous answers to questionnaires. No good has come of it by these reports and we might infer this from the fact that the advice merely meant that the emotions and desires were to govern behavior as fully as they might in a completely primitive environment. Because of its rather disastrous results this phase of popular psychology is passing away. 

However, the psychology of conflict is far older than this recent gospel of unrestraint. There has always been a conflict between desire and duty, between wish and obligation. I think it is Lecky who writes that when the 

Christians taught the Romans, "This captive child which you are about to throw to the lions has an immortal soul and for that you are forever responsible," they paused in their orgy of blood. That pause, he thinks, was the beginning of civilization. This may seem to be, indeed, but a feeble beginning. Yet unquestionably the inhibitions of religion, as it grew more and more powerful with the years, were the essential factors in slowly changing savagery to civilization. The devout saw this conflict as a struggle between the flesh and the spirit and devised methods of keeping the flesh in subjection. This was an extreme view, conceived to compass the soul's salvation. It is doubtful if any less powerful motive would have set up the inhibitions necessary to change human behavior radically in the direction of humane rather than savage social arrangements. The ten commandments are inhibitions reduced to words. No wonder they are negatively stated.

This conception of a difference in function between the

INTRODUCTION 

41 old brain and the new brings anthropology and psychology into closer relation. They have heretofore seemed to be quite independent sciences though both claim to give an account of human nature. When man changed from eating such fruit and foods as could readily be plucked or dug up to the killing of animals for food, there immediately arose the need to protect his hunting grounds, and the methods used in hunting and in fighting are similar. This led to the warrior life. In such a life violent rage and fear play a great part in survival. Because of the inheritance of these traits, the modern psychologist says that all "drives" and "urges" to action come from emotions. They generate powerful impulses which very slowly come under the control of intelligence in both the race and the individual. 

Effect of Drugs.-We have seen that the effect of drugs gives one of the evidences for the inhibitory function of the cortex. Being of later structure and somehow finer texture, cortical cells or fibers seem to have a more ready chemical affinity for the toxin than the lower brain centers. 

This fact explains a certain type of behavior. With the inhibitions off, the drug user is far more ready to do some reckless or criminal deed than he would be without chemical aid. Thus the gangster or the gunman fortifies his so-called courage with drugs or liquor before his desperate undertaking. The drug leaves the lower, impulsive centers in full control of behavior. With a sufficient dose, the drug user is said to act like a madman, which means simply that all inhibitions are abolished. 

Personality.-Personality is so complex that it baffles analysis. Personal appearance is one factor, energy or health another, character another, and so on. In this dilemma we are more apt to point to types of personality

than to proceed to further attempts at analysis. The relation between impulse and inhibition certainly gives us two important types. James describes them as follows: 

"There is a normal type of character, for example, in which impulses seem to discharge so promptly into movements that inhibitions get no time to arise. These are the 'dare-devil' and 'mercurial' temperaments overflowing with animation and fizzling with talk, which are so common in the Slavic and Celtic races and with which the coldblooded and long-headed English character forms so marked a contrast. Simian these people seem to us, whilst we seem to them reptilian. It is quite impossible to judge, as between an obstructed and an explosive individual, which has the greater sum of vital energy. An explosive 

Italian with good perception and intellect will cut a figure as a perfectly tremendous fellow, on an inward capital that could be tucked away inside an obstructed Yankee and hardly let you know it was there. He will be the king of his company, sing the songs, and make the speeches, lead the parties, carry out the practical jokes, kiss the girls, fight the men, and, if need be, lead the forlorn hopes and enterprises, so that an onlooker would think he has more life in his little finger than can exist in the whole body of a correct, judicious fellow. But the judicious fellow all the while may have all these possibilities and more besides, ready to break out in the same or even a more violent way, if only the brakes were taken off. It is the absence of scruples, of consequences, of considerations, the extraordinary simplification of each moment's mental outlook, that gives to the explosive individual such motor energy; it need not be the greater intensity of any of his passions, motives, or thoughts. As mental evolution goes on, the complexity of human consciousness grows ever

INTRODUCTION 

43 greater, and with it the multiplication of the inhibitions to which every impulse is exposed. How much freedom of discourse we English folk lose because we feel obliged always to tell the truth! This predominance of inhibition has a bad as well as a good side; and if a man's impulses are in the main orderly as well as prompt, if he has courage to accept their consequences, and intellect to lead them to a successful end, he is all the better for his hair trigger organization and for not being 'sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought.' Many of the most successful military and revolutionary characters in history have belonged to this simple but quick-witted, impulsive type. 

Problems come much harder to reflective and inhibitive minds. They can, it is true, solve much vaster problems; and they can avoid many a mistake to which the men of impulse are exposed. But when the latter do not make mistakes, or when they are always able to retrieve them, theirs is one of the most engaging and indispensable of human types." Here are two types of personality based on the relation of impulse to inhibition. One might be called emotional, the other intellectual, and as the environment becomes complex the latter has the best of it. Even the military leader of modern warfare is characterized by intelligence and dogged purpose rather than by impulse and impetuousness.

Introverts and Extroverts.-Two types slightly different from those of James are called by Jung introverts and extroverts. The introvert is described as having few acquaintances, being sensitive and readily hurt, worrying over the possibility of misfortune, avoiding social leadership, preferring to work alone, expressing himself better in writing than in speech. He resents discipline, is introspective, a radical, a day-dreamer, and is unusually intelli-

gent and well informed. Miss Hinkle regards the late

President Wilson as a typical introvert. An introvert, who possessed all the traits above mentioned, would be an extreme example of the type. His personality would be considered introvert if he displayed three-fourths of them.

The extrovert is quite the opposite of the introvert. He goes into action on the slightest provocation. He meets life eagerly. He is social and sociable. As far as thought is concerned he is likely to be superficial. He is frequently a great bluffer. He may be a good salesman, a good actor, a great orator. He may become a great popular hero, the mob fancy being caught by the dramatic quality of his behavior. Hinkle cites Roosevelt as an example of the extrovert. (Nixon, H. K., Psychology for the Writer.)

It is plain that the best described types of personality are dependent on the relative contributions of the old brain and the new to their behavior. 

Summary. If we are to give an account of human or animal behavior some conception of the behaving mechanism is necessary to keep us from pure speculation unwarranted by facts. Since the early experiments of physiologists on reflex action kindled the imagination of psychologists, reflex action has been considered as the type of all action, and stimulus-response has been regarded as a formula for explaining all behavior. This is an attractive conception but too simple to account for the facts. Recent progress in neurology has shown that both the old brain and the new contribute to behavior. The former not only permits reflex behavior but is the source of emotions and probably of instinctive acts, but all these must be checked or inhibited in a complex and variable environment and this is especially the function of the cerebral cortex and its dependencies. Due to this, action is influenced by

INTRODUCTION 

45 memories, knowledge or past experience. The stimulusresponse formula must be expanded to include the contribution of the cortex. It will then become 

Stimulus-Sensation-Its Meaning-Reaction to the Mean ing.—Simple examples will show that human beings come to react to meanings. For the burnt child the sensation of a candle flame means a painful experience and his second and later responses to it are never like his first response. 

Christians long believed that a madman is possessed of devils to be exorcised only by beatings and tortures. Mohammedans, on the contrary, believed that a madman is one from whom Allah has taken the soul before its time as a mark of special favor and mercy. They, therefore, treated the insane with especial kindness and veneration. Here the opposite meanings attached to exactly the same object or situation resulted in just the opposite behavior by the two types of believers. Meaning alone enables us to understand the higher types of behavior. Further examples need not be given. They are observable on every side. We are merely trying to bring academic psychology into line with daily experience. We can no longer cross a busy street without having to decide whether the speed of an approaching car means danger if we take the next step. 

The aviator can, in fact, no longer trust his senses. He must face an instrument board and know instantly what the reading on each instrument means. Thus trained he may fly safely even in fog, provided panic does not seize him when the usual sensations are cut off. 

If intelligence discovers and responds to meanings to be found in a highly complex and variable environment, the acquisition of meanings becomes the most important human pursuit. An expert is one who is in fairly full command of the meanings in one field of knowledge.

Typical Cortical Behavior.-If we grant that the old brain responds to stimuli with fixed and stereotyped reactions, we may define the new brain as a living mechanism in which the slightest change of conditions produces the most momentous changes in behavior. Usually the change is in external conditions; more rarely within the body itself.

The clearest examples of this definition come from the new science of business psychology. One great department store found a difference of thousands of dollars when the salesgirls were instructed to ask the customers, "Will you pay for it now?" instead of "Shall I charge it?" In a similar instance the question "Will you take it with you?" was substituted for "Shall I send it?" The result was a great saving in express charges. Long ago the courts discovered that the form of a question might determine the answer and the greatest injustice result. The business house happened to be able to measure the effect of the question. The courts could not do so.

A store in the South had been sold a large number of little rubber alligators. They were supposed to be of interest to tourists, but they were hardly seen by them. For a long time they adorned the merchant's showcase. Finally it occurred to someone with a sense of humor to fasten a card to the neck of each alligator bearing the inscription, "Here is the man-eating alligator which I promised to send you during my stay in the South." This permitted mailing when the card was addressed and a stamp affixed.

Thus displayed, the alligators passed promptly into the tourists' hands and into the mails, though they had been hopeless "stickers" before. Similarly where tourists gather in great numbers a man is said to have accumulated a fortune by selling picture postcards stamped.

INTRODUCTION 

47 Probably no one uses suggestion to better advantage than national advertisers. Crisco, an onomatopoetic word, suggests subconsciously to many that food prepared with it will be crisp and palatable. Dutch Cleanser arouses widespread associations. Both terms have a value the moment they are given publicity. While business psychology reveals this definition of the mind or brain, it is no less important in other relations of life. Biologically the new brain seems to have been evolved to change the fixity of reflex action into the variability of behavior which is dependent on slight clues and changing conditions. The cortex alone gives this variability. Survival of the individual or the race seems to depend on this mutation. 

Consciousness. In the preceding pages the attempt has been made to give a general account of the brain and its action and to show how behavior is modified by the inhibition of impulses of the old brain and the lower nervous system. Even in so general an account we could not be understood without mention of the sense of pain, the emotions of rage, fear, jealousy, desire, and those of joy, love, affection, etc. Nor could modification of behavior take place as it does without memories, discriminations, decisions, etc. All these are states of consciousness and psychology must describe changing states of consciousness at even greater length than it describes behavior. The pretense that behavior can be described in any scientific fashion without reference to mind or consciousness is merely a pretense. The writer of such a description is himself conscious of the unreality of his account, if only he looks at is critically for a moment. It is a return to the method of speculative philosophy. 

By self-observation we are aware that consciousness includes sensations of sight, sound, taste, smell, etc. We

realize that memory reproduces these sensations as images and along with these are ideas of meanings and relationship. We know also that consciousness is in continual change. No state of mind remains long the same. Some of its items fade from consciousness; others remain but rearrange themselves until we say we are no longer thinking of the same thing. Because consciousness is in ceaseless change and seems to broaden and deepen from babyhood to the prime of life, it has been called the stream of consciousness or the stream of thought. The former term is the better because emotions and sensations are different from thoughts, though consciousness includes them all.

When we do not wish to emphasize the shifting and changing feature of consciousness we employ the term mind. But present usage gives the name mind to a man's total intellectual equipment, the intelligence he possesses, the way in which he can marshall his thoughts for the solution of problems and difficulties. According to his success in this he is said to have a good mind or a poor one, to be intellectually efficient or inefficient. There is also another distinction between mind and consciousness. A blow on the head or an anesthetic may abolish consciousness for a shorter or longer time, but we should not like to say that the mind is thereby destroyed. Aside from these distinctions, the terms mind and consciousness are used almost as synonyms and no confusion results. The succession of changing states of consciousness is the basis of our sense of time.

A moment's reflection shows that consciousness is complex. Each of our senses gives a different type of sensation and consequently different memories. A sensation of sight, called a visual sensation, is quite different in kind from a sensation of sound, and both from a sensation of

INTRODUCTION 

49 pain. After the sensations have died away we still have memories of the experience. These are called mental images. Sometimes they are images of particular sensations but more often the image is of the total object which gave the sensations. Since the traditional five senses have now been increased to eleven or twelve it is plain that we may experience eleven or twelve kinds of sensation and as many different types of memories. In addition to this, any image or sensation may be agreeable or disagreeable. It arouses feelings of pleasure or displeasure and these feelings, in turn, are conscious states. Beside these states, most psychologists agree that we are conscious of relations between our ideas or mental images. We may recognize two experiences as identical in kind, similar, different or equal in some respect, and so on. The result of such selfobservation is agreement by psychologists that consciousness consists of sensations, images, feelings or affective states, and some add, ideas of relations, as above described. 

Further than this they cannot analyze the mind, but combinations of these factors make up all our conscious states. 

Even if we could not learn by self-observation that consciousness is complex, the effect of drugs would give evidence of it. One drug abolishes only sensations of pain but leaves the others intact. In a similar way one drug will eliminate sweet tastes, another bitter, another sour, etc.

If consciousness is complex, it is capable of analysis and much scientific knowledge is the result of analysis. If we know the simplest factors of which a complex is composed, we deal with it more successfully than is possible without such discrimination. If only we knew, for example, why certain persons are poor spellers, we might teach them in such a way as to remove the difficulty or obviate it. It appears, however, that one fails for one rea-

son, another for another, and in others no reason can be analyzed out of their work in spelling." Hence, they baffle the educator. It appears that analysis in psychology has not gone far enough to be of practical use here. 

Not only are we aware of sensations and memories of objects but we are also conscious of most of our acts, and consciousness may check and modify them. A child may instinctively attempt to pet the first cat he sees, but if he is scratched, the impulse is likely to be completely checked on the next occasion. Since consciousness can modify behavior, we shall give much time to its description and explanation.

Definition of Psychology.-On the basis of the preceding discussion we may define psychology as the science of consciousness and behavior and their interrelations. This agrees fairly well with the statement that psychology studies the activities of the individual both mental and physical, but we must admit that physiology and other sciences study physical activities. In animal psychology the observation of the behavior is of prime importance because we can only infer, as best we can, what consciousness, if any, accompanies the actions. The opinion that the higher animals have no consciousness at all even remotely similar to our own is probably untenable. The dog seems to have intense emotions but how different from ours they may be we shall learn only after years of investigation. Adroit methods of setting crucial experiments will doubtless finally add much to our knowledge which is sadly lacking now. "This remark is based on Gates' list of twenty-two different deficiencies found in thirty poor spellers. (Psychology of Reading and Spelling, p. 104.)

He is now quoted in the press as follows: "Treatments that will cure poor spellers will soon be as common and effective as glasses that correct the defective eyesight." If this report is correct, it is a welcome and most rapid advance of science. Lapses of speech and writing are also causes of errors in spelling in addition to Gates' list of causes. (See pp. 169 ff.)

INTRODUCTION 

51 Branches of Psychology.-There are many different types of mind. For example, the human and the animal, the normal and the abnormal, the developed and the developing mind, and even the mind as influenced by various social environments give rise to different branches of psychology, because each type yields a different subject matter for study. These seem to be the truer or more fundamental divisions of the subject, but the methods and aims pursued in the study of each type yield branches which are practically important.

From the standpoint of method and aim: (1) Intro spective psychology is the study of one's own consciousness and the consciousness of others as reported by them. 

Obviously this includes a knowledge of their behavior, what ideas impelled it, and its results. When a novelist describes a state of mind, even one we have never experienced or a psychologist employs an illustration, we know at once, by a subtle introspective comparison, whether there are genuine experiences or sheer inventions. We promptly decide that the latter are not "true to nature." (2) Human experimental psychology employs experiment as an aid to introspection. (3) When a direct or indirect measurement of mental states is attempted, as part of the experiment, the investigation belongs to the realm of psychophysics. The relation of strength of stimulus to the intensity of the resulting sensation is a typical example of such measurements. (4) Comparative psychology consists in the study of all types of behavior and states of consciousness with a view to finding the relations between them. So much work in animal psychology has been done recently by the comparative method that at present the terms animal psychol-

ogy and comparative psychology are used interchangeably as synonyms. This is simply present usage. (5) Structural psychology analyzes consciousness into simpler and simpler processes. When discrimination can proceed no further the structuralist assumes that he has attained and described the simplest conscious processes, which he terms "elements" of consciousness. It is hardly necessary to add that conscious processes are not literally "separated" into elements but that the elements are discriminated within the more complex processes. (6) Functional psychology considers consciousness and behavior in relation to their usefulness to the individual, their function of furthering or hindering his biological interests. The difference between structural and functional psychology is chiefly that of selection and emphasis. 

Each method supplements the other.

Functional psychology has appeared in elaborate form recently under the name of Gestalt psychologie or "configurationism." It opposes structural psychology but the latter was never under bond to say that a pattern of experience involves no more than the sensations which are present in it. Relations and meaning both conscious and unconscious may be found. This is shown in later pages of the present book and the nature of one type of pattern with an "internal "internal structure" appears on page 171.

For points of agreement between this book and the Gestaltpsychologie see the article by Helson, "The Psychology of Gestalt," American Journal of Psychology, July, 1925, pp. 347, 348, 354, 355, etc. (7) Genetic psychology is the attempt to ascertain the origin (or genesis) and development of consciousness in the individual or in the race. Individual development is termed ontogenetic, racial phylogenetic.

INTRODUCTION 

53 Beyond these central definitions we need not go for the terms used will be sufficiently descriptive and familiar. 

Plainly psychology has applications in law, medicine, education, advertising, etc. Consideration of any such application is a branch of applied psychology.

Human psychology may use any or all of the methods mentioned, but chiefly it avails itself of the results obtained by their use. It gives little attention to applications. 

As to subject matter: (1) Normal psychology is the study of the consciousness and behavior of the typical or normal human being. (2) Abnormal psychology is the study of disorders of consciousness and consequent aberrations of behavior. (3) Animal psychology is the study of animal behavior in order to infer the states of consciousness on which the behavior depends. (4) Child psychology is the study of the consciousness and behavior of the child but especially of its differences from the adult in consciousness and behavior. (5) Social phychology is the study of the individual's consciousness and behavior as modified by his being a member of a social group, and of the behavior of the group as modified by the influence of each of its members. The most pronounced modification is in the direction of uniformity in feeling, belief and action. This uniformity may be so great in a particular organization, as a tribe, family, regiment, or religious sect that the group is said to have a mind or consciousness of its own. The influence of the social environment is surely as great as the term, group mind, would imply.

Recently attempts to determine the differing mental traits of individuals, the two sexes, and even different

races have led to the use of terms as individual, racial and sex psychology. 

The above classification distinguishes central or typical features with sufficient clearness for our purpose. No doubt at their borders the fields overlap considerably. 

Such classes are necessary because discrimination of facts is preliminary to learning the relations between them. 

Knowledge of the relations is often more valuable than acquaintance with the facts themselves, moreover one cannot consider "things in general" with much show of success. Nevertheless, when the fields of the great sciences overlap we cannot hope to make perfectly sharp distinctions between the branches of a single one. Nor perhaps is a sharp discrimination between them always desirable. 

For example the distinction between structural and functional psychology seems often too sharply drawn. 

Structural psychology finds that sensations of reds and greens are elementary color sensations. It then finds persons in whom these sensations are partially lacking or defective, and may name them red-green blind, or perhaps preferably dichromates. Functional psychology would add that such a person many confuse red and green postage stamps; could not see ripe cherries amid green leaves; could not match colors or contrast them; would be a dangerous pilot or locomotive engineer because so many signals are red or green. If he were a farmer he could not select seed corn and would be at a serious disadvantage at a husking bee.

Yet all this makes a logical body of fact. The functionalist who did not infer the cause from the symptoms, or the structuralist who did not reason from the cause to its effects, and test his reasoning to learn whether it were correct would surely be cutting things too short. Accord-

INTRODUCTION 

55 ing to our purpose we shall, therefore, enter now one and now another of the fields defined quite indifferently. 

Structural psychology is often called the psychology of elements. As Ewald remarks, "To work with the psychology of elements has the advantage of employing a method which is closely related to that of the natural sciences. 

This method consists in analyzing a given whole into the units of which it is composed, in order finally to recombine them into a whole whose laws we have penetrated by the analysis. In doing this it is certainly not necessary to fall into the error that these elements are joined by pure addition. Wundt long ago raised his voice against such a conception and had formed the concept of 'creative resultants."" 

This conception of Wundt's is a forerunner of the present theory of emergent evolution which has applications in psychology as well as in other sciences. The fact that water can be analyzed into hydrogen and oxygen leads no one to suppose that water shows no properties except those of the two elements added together. New emergents appear which cannot be predicted from the properties of the elements in chemistry, physics, biology, and physiology. Yet no one imagines that these sciences have not made progress by means of analysis; that physiology has not learned a great deal from the study of the separate organs of the body. We may add that structural psychology gives far more solid, permanent, and scientific knowledge than literary psychology, which refuses to analyze but insists on regarding the human being in toto. 

We shall see that simple sensations (elements) have meanings which are not sensations but arise in the mind as something additional to the sensations, yet are not simply added to them. They are a resultant of the sensations;

are suggested by them. An animal, which has been trained to go to the darker of two grays, will still go to the darker when a lighter gray is substituted for the former darker one. Thus he is choosing the gray which he was trained, in the first series of experiments, to reject. Thus the total situation is responded to, not a particular gray. This total situation is assumed by certain German psychologists to be a total form, pattern, configuration or Gestalt. On such experiments they have based the Gestaltpsychologie, or form psychology, which at times seems to imply that no individual could ever respond to a simple sensation, such as a particular tone or color. This is only implied and of course it is not true. But in addition to reacting to totals and to elements, every individual reacts to the meanings which sensations suggest and these may vary from one person to another. There is not a fixed set of forms to which we respond. Knowledge, previous training, and habit all modify the behavior. Unpredictable reactions result. If we wish to predict at all, the meaning attached to a situation or stimulus will be the best guide, though we can know only by the most careful observation which meaning will be effective, except that instinctive desires are the most "dependable motives." (Woodworth.)

Literary psychology may regard only the totality of the mind; may refuse all analysis. Genuine psychology can make no such refusal. It must, however, avoid the error of "pure addition," which has been mentioned above. This should not be difficult if we recognize that new emergents appear as a result of combinations of elements whether the elements are chemical, physical, or psychological in nature. As we shall see, the pure addition error is exemplified in the assumption that a human being is a multitude of reflex mechanisms, so that each specimen of behavior is

INTRODUCTION 

57 accounted for after its occurrence by the claim, "Well, there is a mechanism for that behavior." In fact, living mechanisms are no longer mechanisms. When life appears, something new has emerged with entirely new laws to be investigated. When consciousness has emerged from combinations of living matter, it too is novel and its laws are to be sought. They cannot be assumed from the nature of its elements. But this fact is seen on every side. A melody is more than the tones of which it is composed. A beautiful scene is far more than the colors of which it is combined. Yet who would deny that melodies and beautiful scenes are now best produced by those who have so long studied sounds and colors and discovered the laws of their combination?
