CHAPTER II METHODS Methods of Discovering Psychological Facts and Laws.- 

There are at least four ways of discovering psychological facts. (1) By self-observation or introspection. This may be carried on under either ordinary or experimental conditions. (2) The second method consists of observing the behavior of others (either men or animals) and again experiment may be used to make the observation more exact or it may take place under ordinary conditions. (3) Information of great value and certainty may be gained by the study of the structure or functions of the brain and nervous system. (4) Further information about the mind and its development has been obtained by the use of mental tests, the intelligence tests, for example, which have been so much discussed in recent years. They seem to have shown that our mental powers are not unlimited in number but that a man's intellectual ability may be determined by twelve to twenty carefully devised tests.

Besides these four methods, there are two others which may be employed to supplement any one of these and make it more precise. (1) Measurement may be used in many experiments in psychology. To illustrate, if the result of an intelligence test is compared with well established standard results, it becomes a measure of intelligence. 

When a science measures, it is said to have become quantitative in its methods, because it has gone beyond the mere

qualitative observation of facts and their enumeration. (2) The results of measurements of all sorts may be subjected to statistical treatment to aid in their interpretation. Thus the statistical method is applied to many quantitative results in psychology, as it is in many other sciences. Since there are many special treatises on mental measurement and on the use of statistics, we shall not be concerned with these two methods in our elementary description. Because it is the business of anatomy and physiology to investigate the nervous system, we shall simply borrow from those sciences such results as apply to psychology.

Self-Observation or Introspection.-The first step toward an understanding of others is to gain some knowledge of one's self. Hence from the gray dawn of history thoughtful men have striven to analyze their own minds and emotions and they have then used these conscious states as types whereby to decipher the mental states of other men. 

It seems evident that no other method is possible. If another person has no wants, desires, thoughts or feelings at all similar to my own, if we do not share at all the same stock of knowledge, I cannot "make him out." If there are similarities and identities in our thought, I may, after having discovered them with certainty, begin to detect the differences. In fact a man of retiring disposition will never understand the behavior of one who means to attain wide fame and believes that he has already a great measure of it, unless he can analyze out this master passion so clearly as to ask himself how he would act if driven by that pas sion alone.

Psychologists simply try to press this common sense method of self-observation further than it is carried in practical affairs. In the wonderful stream of our thought

METHODS 

61 do the ideas follow one another by chance alone? No; introspection finds that they appear in accordance with laws and further introspection must discover and state the laws. 

What effects have bodily states upon our mind and emotions? Before we can begin this quest some good self-observer must describe the emotions in detail. A dose of hasheesh is said to produce not only vivid hallucinations but a terrible fear of impending death. The former effect is general but is the latter due only to an idiosyncrasy of certain nervous systems? Only further introspective reports can decide. Do I believe emotionally certain statements based on no vestige of evidence simply because 

I heard them repeated often in my childhood's years? Do others similarly believe? They will have to report. Does repetition, then, establish belief so that it is difficult for evidence to shake it? The answer is important to the individual and to society. Plainly an outline knowledge of human psychology may be gained by intelligent self-observation and no basis of such knowledge can be formed without it. A defect of students is too blind a dependence on statements of the psychological text-books without in the least verifying them by introspection. This results in bookish knowledge not thought over enough to be applied in practical affairs. Examples of the use of introspection will appear as we proceed.

A criticism of introspection deserves to be mentioned. 

It is called morbid, as if the sick alone are introspective. 

This too has been repeated until it is believed and by a curious twist of imagination it is further believed that the introspection is a cause of the disease instead of just the opposite relation. Most diseases do produce an introspective state of mind but imagine for a moment no science of medicine, no help save from one's self. What more use-

ful, then, than self-diagnosis and a trial of this and that remedy with further introspection to note its effect. By this means many a man has changed his diet or given up coffee or tobacco with marked beneficial effect. The effect of bodily disorders in producing introspection is a biological adaptation of first-rate importance even though it has been overlooked. The mind does not adjust instantly to the latest progress in medical science. To keep a body in order one must know a little something himself, else he would never report to a physician. Introspection furnishes this little something in the way of knowledge. Yet on all sides we hear it said of ailing persons, "He waited too long;" i. e., he was too little "morbidly introspective."

In recent years some enthusiastic writers have advocated the use of only one method in psychology, namely, the observation of human and animal behavior. They express the greatest distrust of introspection and have gone so far as to deny the existence or at least the influence of consciousness. This enthusiasm for a pure and premature objectivism is bringing criticism for such psychology from scientists in other fields. "Many modern psychologists deny the validity of introspection as a method of studying our mental conduct. How otherwise than by introspection does Professor Wakeham know that he tried the experiment he describes? Shall we deny the validity of the experiment because introspection was a part of it? In rejecting introspection are not psychologists rejecting one of their most important tools?"

This quotation expresses the view of an eminent chemist (Noyes, W. A., Science, Oct., 1928). He further criticises the objectivists or mechanists for their omission of consciousness and conscious purpose from psychology, for

METHODS 

63 without these conceptions only habitual behavior can be described.

The objectivist also fails to see that he is self-contradictory. He is of the opinion that there are no opinions. 

He thinks there is no thinking. He is conscious that there is no consciousness. Thus he is forever outside of his own doctrine, for doctrine, of course, it is. Forcing psychology back into the field of speculation has delayed its advance. 

The objectivist's reliance on human and animal behavior alone as the source of information results in criticism like the following: "No psychologist believes anything any other psychologist says. Give a psychologist a rat and a graph and he will tell you everything there is to be known, for instance, about adult education." (Martin, Everett D.)

Plainly this educator finds the stretching of observations of animal behavior to cover human education quite unsatisfactory. No doubt he is impatient. Some observations, even of animal behavior, are illuminating for education but these are rare in occurrence and, as the psychologist's colleagues plainly see, he would better not give up introspection as a method. At least it will check and control some of his interpretations. Without it he could not have set his experiments on animals. Köhler offers this as a criticism of past experiments, but no way to avoid the error is suggested. We must not become so zealous in applying a single method and in generalizing its results that we neglect or disdain the use of other methods. In this matter the psychologist's colleagues are competent to criticize because every intelligent man uses introspection effectively in the conduct of his life's affairs. The following half-amusing example may be mentioned in support of its use though the selection of the example may well be

questioned, except for the fact that all will recognize the psychology involved as genuine.

In a New England bank robbery, it is reported that the robbers bound the cashier of the bank in a chair in his own home and demanded the combination of the bank's vault. 

He gave them a false combination but they wrote the numbers and in a few minutes they asked for them again. 

Of course, the cashier could not repeat them and he was thus forced to give the true combination, by means of which the thieves robbed the vault. Only by self-observation did the robbers know that we cannot repeat a series of numbers which we have given a few minutes before. 

Introspection in Practical Affairs.-There are two moods which often alternate with each other. The first may be characterized by the man who says to himself (or to others), "Now, just watch me"; the second by the phrase, "What is the matter with me?" These are quite opposite moods. When everything has gone smoothly and every endeavor has been crowned with success and applause, a confidence results which is likely to express itself in the now-watch-me mood in spite of some restraint. This mood is widespread and easily observable. When two opposing teams have been trained to a nicety so that even the least boastful member of either is willing to say to his closest friend, "You watch us win," the conditions are right for the assembling of supporters all of the same mood. 

But one team must lose the game and defeat ushers in instantly the opposite state of mind. "What was the matter with us, with our team, with our trainers?" etc. This is painful introspection of a sort. But all I am concerned to point out is that the introspective attitude sets in after every defeat, failure, disaster, mistake, social humiliation, or even crime. The criminal condemned to the gallows is

METHODS 

65 often quite sure he has introspectively analyzed out the exact psychic causes of his downfall. The point of fact which concerns us is to note that the introspective mood is common to all human beings after defeat or failure of any sort, and it is a vital means of correcting our mistakes and of avoiding failure a second time.

It has long been overlooked that introspection plays so large a part in the correction of errors. The assumption seems to have been made that we learn from our mistakes automatically and without intervening introspective thought. This is not the fact. It would be more exact to say that we learn from the introspection which inevitably follows every mistake. The automobile driver who, after a minor accident, cannot ask himself, "How could it have happened?" "Was I to blame?" will probably soon figure in a major disaster.

The event, which provokes introspection need not be as shocking as a bodily accident. A man may find that his best friend has become estranged from him. He retraces the memories of his relations with this friend and at last he discovers that a thoughtless remark of his concerning a matter on which the friend is very sensitive has caused the trouble. This is readily avoided thereafter.

The most successful comedian of the times says, "If your jokes do not 'get over,' if the audience fails to appreciate you and neither laughs nor applauds, to not 'get sore' at the audience. Ask yourself, 'What is the matter with me?" You will find there the secret."

One of the most successful trainers of salesmen writes, "You will succeed at this or anything else, if you get the habit of spending a few minutes to analyze every canvass you make. If you do not sell a man you thought was a possible customer, try to discover what you said or did not

say that lost you the sale. On the other hand, where you make a sale, try to figure out what part of what you said made the greatest impression on the man. This habit of reviewing the days work is one of the best assets a successful salesman has."

The sales manager then continues by rediscovering exactly what the comedian has learned. "Where you fail to get an order after a thorough canvass, or get what might be termed a flat turndown after you have had a chance to present your case, we would advise you to think along the line of WHAT IS THE MATTER WITH YOU OR YOUR 

CANVASS? Don't try to figure what is the matter with the man you are approaching or what is the matter with business. On the other hand, try to figure what is the matter with your work. If you will figure that way, then you will be able to overcome a similar case when it comes up, and you will be gaining constantly in ability to sell the machine." It is easy to see that this is practical self-analysis or introspection. These men have found it to be a large factor in their success.

Since business psychology is now a promising applied science it seems legitimate to mention its discovery of the usefulness of introspection. Still weightier interests must employ it. The most eminent religious teacher of our times writes as follows: "Believers must expect, and should be prepared to meet, as their forefathers always have met, antagonists who doubt the truth of religion. But when men begin doubting the usefulness, the desirability, the practical need of religion, the church should engage in anxious self-examination. [Italics mine.] To cause that, something calamitous must have happened in the current presentation of religion's meaning."

Vocational guides recommend a double introspection.

METHODS 

67 Put yourself in your employer's place and then try to imagine what you would require of your employees. Thus you may find whether you have the requisite interests and inclinations for success in this pursuit.

All this evidence might be unnecessary had not one group of psychologists implied that introspection is a method used only by psychologists and quite valueless to those untrained in its use and another group claimed that it is unnecessary or useless in psychology or in other human concerns. The facts appear to negative both these claims. Introspection is unwelcome to a man in the watch-me-win mood but it is nevertheless essential to any but a bookish knowledge of psychology. 

Observation of Others.-Very early in life we begin to take note of the behavior of the persons about us and, as we say, to "size them up." That is, we decide what we may expect of them. Many children obey one parent promptly and disobey or delay obedience to the other because they have come to observe and respond to a fixed difference in the behavior of the two parents. It is not difficult to detect the amusement, contempt or scorn of other persons, nor, after a time of practice in this kind of observation, their sincerity and honesty or the reverse. This close and discriminating observation of others is a type of psychologizing that all of us must practice. Our welfare and practical success depend upon it daily. Almost every one is early trained in its exercise, so that we often know as well what conduct to expect from others as of ourselves. In fact, regarding applicants for positions, we rely as much on the statements of others concerning them and on an inspection of the candidates as upon their promises. Many men must be skilled in this practical psychologizing. Those who are not so skilled are likely to find routine duties

rather than executive ones. While human nature is variable and mistakes are made, our conclusions concerning human beings are as often correct as any forecasts we make. 

In proportion as men are widely different from us in race, language, religion, and environment our ability to make correct inferences concerning them diminishes. 

Hence our discomfiture in a foreign country and our dif ficulty in dealing with a foreign tribe until, by long residence among them, we come, as we say, to understand them.

Animals are, of course, more remote from us in mental traits than any race of men. Hence in dealing with them it is said that this method of inference is likely to be unsuccessful. There is little or nothing in common to aid our decisions. Yet the whole success of the hunter and trapper depends upon his knowledge of the animal he pursues and this type of observation can probably be widened and deepened until it approaches scientific accuracy. So far as there is to be a psychology of animals, it must depend on this inference from behavior. The assumption that the bodily functions of the higher animals are similar to those of the human body has been of great value to physiology. In similar fashion, the assumption that animal instincts and experience are not beyond the understanding of human beings, and that important analogies between human and animal behavior can be found, has been and will continue to be of service to psychology. 

Whether by observation and ingenious experiments we can come to a well founded and accurate knowledge of animal psychology is one question. But whether we can make experiments on animals broaden and deepen our knowledge of human psychology is just the opposite prob-

69 lem. I think that the most solid information we have concerning fear, rage, and similar emotions has come from the experiments of Professor W. B. Cannon, who used cats as the subjects of his investigation. While describing the experiments, let us remember that physiologists have learned how to keep animal tissues under such conditions that they react as they would in the living animal. 

If bismuth is mixed with the food of a cat the passage of the food through the throat, the stomach, and the intestines can be seen by the aid of X-rays. By this method 

Cannon was studying the mechanical factors of digestion. 

In order to observe the cat, it was necessary to restrain it in a comfortable holder. Most cats were undisturbed by this and showed no fear of the restraint. A few did show excitement. If the animal showed disturbance by so much as the twitching of the end of its tail, all digestion stopped at once. This was so surprising an effect of emotion that 

Cannon resolved to study it further. Let us remember that the excitement must have released nervous impulses in the brain, which passed downward to sympathetic nerves and finally to the adrenal glands at the top of each kidney. 

These glands secreted adrenalin and this, in turn, produced the secretion and increased the burning of blood sugar. This would greatly increase the energy of the animal. 

Let us now consider Cannon's experiments which show that blood from an excited cat is quite different from that of an undisturbed animal and let us see whether similar conditions exist in human beings, when they are under stress of violent emotions, as fear, rage or other intense excitement. First, under conditions of perfect anesthesia, Cannon removed a small strip of intestinal muscle from a cat and suspended it in a U-tube, as shown in Figuer 5.

Thus attached it would record its contractions and relaxations, by means of the long writing-lever, on a revolving drum covered with smoked paper. (See Figure 6.) The

U-tube could be filled with any fluid, whose effect on the muscle Cannon wished to study, and this fluid could be quickly drawn off and another liquid substituted for it. 

When the muscle was surrounded by blood from an undisturbed cat, "quiet blood," or by Ringer's solution, it would beat rhythmically, as it would in the living animal.

Do the emotions have similar effects on human beings? "A refined and sensitive woman, who had digestive difficulties, came with her husband to Boston to be examined. 

They went to a hotel for the night. The next morning the woman appeared at the consultant's office an hour after having eaten a test meal. The examination of the gastric contents revealed no free acid, no digestion of the test breakfast and a considerable amount of the supper of the previous evening. The explanation of this stagnation of food in the stomach came from the family doctor, who reported that the husband had made the visit to the city an occasion for becoming uncontrollably drunk, and that he had by this behavior given his wife a night of turbulent anxiety. The second morning, after the woman had had a good rest, the gastric contents were again examined; the proper acidity was found, and the test breakfast had been normally digested and discharged."" Such cases as this agree with popular belief based on ordinary self-observation. For example, a patient of

These cases, along with the hundreds of similar ones known to physicians, show that laboratory results find their counterpart in daily human experiences. Emotions cause profound changes in the functions of the body, so that medical men now speak of a "psychic secretion," a "psychic tone" or a "psychic contraction" of the gastro-intestinal muscles, because the secretions and contractions are due to psychic conditions, and are absent when the psychic conditions are changed.

All the above examples apply to the visceral secretions and muscles. Is there any effect of emotion on the voluntary muscles? A patient presents himself to a young physician for examination as to his state of health. He then demands to be "told the truth." The truth is told him, perhaps in unguarded terms, and he instantly falls to the floor in a swoon and complete collapse. Plainly the violent emotions have profound bodily effects. Dr. Crile' says that in fear "all the bodily functions which are of no direct assistance in the effort toward self-preservation are suspended." That is, the muscles used in running or fighting, and the secretions which supply them additional energy, the increased heart beat and the more rapid breathing hold "Mueller: Deutsches Archiv. fur Klinische Medicin., 1907, 89, p. 434, quoted by Cannon, pp. 16-17.

73 133 the field. All other bodily processes stop. This is a very considerable effect of fear on the great muscles of the body and the resulting behavior consists of acts of defense or flight. These facts are again derived from the physiological laboratory.

Emotional states produce widespread bodily effects. 

Do bodily conditions produce mental states? Cannon and Washburn have demonstrated that the sensation of hunger is caused by contractions of the stomach and lower oesophagus. In this instance, a bodily change produces a sensation and of course there are thousands of others open to everyday observation. With attention fixed on the observed and experimental facts the physiologists find no difficulty in saying that bodily changes cause psychic changes and psychic conditions produce bodily effects.

It has long been taught that consciousness contributes to self-preservation. This seems to be its primary function. "Our sensations are here to attract or to deter us, our memories to warn or encourage us, our feelings to impel and our thoughts to restrain our behavior, so that on the whole we may prosper and our days be long in the land." Recently it has been shown that in crises the emotions contribute even more than thought to preserving the individual. They may in fact almost double his energy for a superhuman effort. We are just coming to know, from such experiments as Cannon's, why a man in extreme rage or fright, or an excited madman, displays almost supernatural strength.

The Study of the Brain and Nervous System. It is fairly evident that injuries to the head, which rendered the injured unconscious temporarily or damaged the mind permanently, led men to the knowledge that the brain is the organ of the mind. Prior to such observations the heart

was believed to be the seat of the feelings, probably because its beat responds so promptly and faithfully to any change in our emotions. Very gradually our knowledge of the relation between the mind and the brain grows and, with each increase of such knowledge, certain false opinions are corrected. It is evident, for example, that particular "bumps" on the exterior of the skull have nothing to do with special mental faculties, as was believed to some extent a century ago. Also the face is no certain index to character. An orthodontist may change the shape of the face entirely. Then which countenance, the original or the modified one, is an index of character?

CHAPTER III  

Most students know that the function of nerves is to conduct impulses from the eye, ear or skin inward to the brain or other nervous centers, or to conduct impulses outward from a center to muscles or glands. If the passage of impulses inward along a nerve of the first type (a sensory nerve) is blocked by drugs or otherwise, we feel no pain or touch when a stimulus is applied to the nerve end. We say we have lost the "feeling" (sensation) in that sense organ or skin area. The physician says there is local anesthesia. If the passage of impulses along the second type of nerve is blocked, there is a paralysis of the muscles to which the nerve goes. We cannot move a finger, hand or arm as long as its motor nerve is blocked to the passage of impulses. Evidently nerves or the nerve fibers composing them are conductors or pathways for nervous impulses. 

Most books on psychology (including this one) give the impression that a chain of single neurons (see pp. 86, 90), each one connected with the next in order, is capable of conducting impulses. While this is probably true it may be doubted whether such a single chain of very fine fibers could conduct sufficient energy to cause a muscle to contract or to cause an experience of sight or touch, though that amount of energy may be very slight indeed. The nerves are, however, whole cables of fibers running side by side and a bundle or tract of these fibers furnishes the pathway for impulses. The spinal cord, located within

Note: Langley calls the entire sympathetic system the autonomic system and limits the application of the term "sympathetic" to what is here called the "thoraciclumbar sympathetic." While Langley's usage seems to have been adopted by several psychologists, see Herrick's neurology for the usage here chosen. the spinal column, is made up of many tracts, columns or cables, some of which conduct impulses downward and by means of nerves which branch off from the cord, outward to muscles and glands. Other tracts within the cord conduct impulses, which they receive from sensory nerves, upward to the brain or other centers just below the cerebrum or located in its basal portion.

The nervous system thus serves as a means of quick communication between all parts of the body. It co-ordinates our acts with one another and causes us to respond properly to all sorts of objects in the world about us, thus adjusting our behavior to the environment. But because nerve centers retain impressions of past experience and reactions, our behavior is adjusted to future situations which we know will be like those which we have already experienced. While the most obvious functions of centers is to redirect impulses which come from the periphery of the body so as to co-ordinate action, some centers and nerves leading from them are capable of checking or slowing down the action of certain muscles. Others appear to

accelerate action. The result is that the action of the nervous system is much more complicated than that of a telephone system, to which it is often likened. Damage to one center or destruction of it may cause anesthesia or paralysis. Damage to another may cause loss of memory or speech, etc. Different areas of the brain have different functions but considered as a whole it is the chief center of control of behavior.

The account of the nervous system might begin with a description of the units of which it is composed and proceed to show how these are connected in series to form fiber-tracts and how these tracts have been brought together into cable-like bundles, the nerves and the columns of the spinal cord, while ganglia or knots of nerve cells have been combined into larger centers. This would be a very long account and gaps in our knowledge would have to be filled in with theory. Another method of exposition consists in describing the chief divisions of the nervous system with which psychology is concerned, in showing that they are composed of units (neurons) and in leaving it to be understood that centers are connected with many nervous paths which we may omit from consideration. We shall follow this method because it permits omissions but gives opportunity for an outline of the main features of the nervous system. The description should be regarded as the merest sketch.

Main Divisions of the Nervous System.-Figure 7, at the right (p. 77), shows the chief divisions of the nervous system as seen from its ventral aspect. (1) There is the cerebro-spinal nervous system, called also the central nervous system. This consists of the brain and spinal cord and the cranial and spinal nerves, with their end organs. 

There are twelve pairs of cranial nerves and thirty-one

pairs of spinal nerves. Of the latter those which extend from the ventral side of the spinal cord and transmit impulses chiefly to the muscles are termed efferent nerves. 

They are mainly motor in function. Those which transmit impulses from sense organs to the cord and higher centers are afferent, and chiefly sensory in function. Some of the cranial nerves, especially, have both sensory and motor fibers within the same nerve trunk. (2) On either side of the spinal cord may be seen ganglia, or knots of nerve cells, which belong to the sympathetic nervous system, sometimes less well termed the autonomic system. (See Herrick's Neurology, p. 229, note.)

Fibers extend from these ganglia to the viscera, and efferent impulses thus reach the viscera which affect the secretion of glands and especially the movements of the smooth intestinal muscles. Afferent impulses from the viscera along sympathetic fibers reach the cerebro-spinal axis. While recent researchers have shown that strong emotions have an enormous effect in releasing sympathetic impulses, which may completely suspend all visceral action, we have not space to discuss this important division of the nervous system. It is interesting to note, however, that the sympathetic system appears to be in many respects like the diffuse network which constitutes the total nervous system of certain lower creatures like the sea anemone. It thus represents a more primitive nervous system than the central one.

The brain represents the enormous enlargement at its anterior end of the primitive neural tube by the thickening of whose walls the spinal cord and brain are formed. The main divisions of the brain are shown in Figure 8. (1) 

There is the cerebrum or cerebral hemispheres which form the greatest bulk of the brain. (2) The cerebellum, whose

By means of these intermediate stations the impulses are enabled to take an entirely new direction to their appropriate end stations. Thus we see that an important function of brain centers is to distribute and re-distribute impulses. Finally the medulla has within it certain end-stations whose function is not to transmit impulses to higher centers but to reflect them to muscles or glands at once.

The Structural Unit of the Nervous System. Aside from some claims as to the continuity of neurofibrils, we may say that the structural unit of the nervous system is the neuron. (Figs. 11a and 11b.) This is the true nerve cell, highly specialized for the reception, conduction, and discharge of nervous impulses. It consists of a cell body, often loosely called the nerve cell, from which there extend numerous widely branching processes, the dendrites, and usually a single axon or neurite. The former are usually

short and widely branched. When short, they have the same structure as the cell-body but when long, the same structure as the axon. The axon is usually long for the conduction of impulses to a distance. In the greater num ber of neurons the axon springs from one pole of the cell, the dendrites from the other. (Fig. 11a.) 

The statement is found in many text-books that the dendrites conduct impulses to the cell-body, the axon from the cell-body. Parker has shown, however, that this belief rests on an early misconception that the cell-body of the neuron is the center of its nervous activity. This opinion has little evidence in its favor. Instead, the cell-body seems to be essential to the nutrition of the neuron and to the regeneration of its processes when they are injured, but it plays (at most) a minor role in conduction. Barker, Lickley, and others give evidence to support Parker's view. 

Therefore, instead of having to speak of cellulipetal and cellulifugal conduction with all the complications of such a conception, we may say simply that nervous impulses are received at one end of a neuron and discharged at the other. The direction of conduction is determined by the particular neuron's relation to others or to receptor and effector organs. It is known that a single neuron is capable of conducting impulses in either direction. A chain of neurons, however, conducts them in only one direction.

The axon usually gives off side branches, called collaterals, which ordinarily terminate by intermingling intimately with the processes of another cell, somewhat as the branches of trees might intermingle in a thick forest. 

Thus the branches of the two neurons do not form a struc-

tural union, but merely come into close contact with a "surface of separation" between them, so the elements of the nervous system form a felt-work rather than a network. Since impulses can pass from the branches of one cell to those of another there is functional connection between them and this place of functional connection is called the synapse (Fig. 12). بشكل Fig. 12-"Synapse between an ascending fiber entering the cortex of the cerebellum and the dendrites of a Purkinje cell." (After Ramon y Cajal.) (From Herrick's Neurology, W. B. Saunders and

A single nerve may be composed of many thousands of these long processes, axons, enclosed in their sheaths and extending from their cell-bodies in the central nervous sys-

tem to some peripheral organ, from which or to which they transmit impulses. The optic nerve is estimated to contain many millions of fibers. 

The fibers are usually invested, at least for a part of their course, by a sheath of thick, white, glistening substance, called myelin, a fat-like substance secreted by the fibers themselves. This is termed the myelin sheath, or the medullary sheath. Medullated fibers compose the white matter of the brain and cord and a large part of the peripheral nerves. The cell-bodies and fibers without myelin sheaths are gray in color and compose the gray matter of the brain and spinal cord. On peripheral nerves there may be, besides the myeline sheath, another outside of it called the neurilemma or sheath of Schwann. This is a continuous sheath, not interrupted by nodes as is the myelin sheath. At first the medullary sheath was supposed to act as an insulator. Evidence now appears that it has some part in the chemical processes involved in nervous conduction. Nuclei of Schwann's sheath play a part in the degeneration and regeneration of a nerve fiber, if it is severed from connection with the cell-body.

These structural units, the neurons, placed end to end and communicating across their synapses form chains or circuits or tracts for the transmission of nervous impulses. 

In these neuron chains those first to receive the excitement are called neurons of the first order. The others are designated as of the second, third, and higher orders respectively. While all have the function of conducting impulses they differ much in size and length. Some are of microscopic dimensions (for example in the retina); others may be more than a meter in length (for example, the nerves of

the posterior root going from the sole of the foot to the medulla).

As is well known, some neurons are sensory in function and conduct impulses to the cord, the medulla and the cortex. (Only when the cortex, or possibly the thalamus, is reached by the impulse is a sensation produced.) Others are motor, transmitting impulses to the muscles, while still others extend from centers to glands and their impulses stimulate the glands to secretion. Still other fibers have an inhibitory function, their impulses diminishing or repressing the action of the organs in which they end. 

Within the centers, however, there is an immense number of neurons whose function it is to coordinate impulses from lower levels and bring them under a single control. 

The highest examples of this are doubtless the association neurons of the cerebral cortex.

The fact that a particular chain or tract of neurons conducts impulses in only one direction is ascribed to the irreversibility of the synapse. This structure is supposed to offer little or no resistance to the passage of the impulse in the direction for which the tract is specialized, but to offer insurmountable resistance to its passage in the opposite direction. The function is of great importance and represents a great advance over the diffuse nerve-net type of nervous system. This has no synapses and consequently no polarity of its pathways; i. e., impulses seem to pass equally well in either direction.

Other Structures of the Nervous System.-Besides the neurons, which have a true conducting function, there are in the nervous system neuroglia cells which, with the ependyma, form a supporting framework. The brain and spinal cord are enveloped in three connective tissue membranes, the dura mater, arachnoid, and pia mater, together called

the meninges. These are protective and nutritive coverings.

The Functional Unit.-While the skillful work of neurologists has shown that the neuron is the structural unit of the nervous system and that it consists of milliards of neurons arranged consecutively in chains or tracts, it is no less certain that a series of at least two neurons is necessary for even the simplest reaction. 

The diagram of Figure 13 illustrates such a chain or simplest reflex arc. The several elements of a reflex arc are (1) a sensitive receptor or sense organ; (2) an adjustor or correlation center (or center of reflection) which is generally located within the central nervous system; (3) an effector or apparatus consisting of organs of response (muscles or glands) and the terminations of the efferent nerves upon them. To these we may add an afferent or sensory conductor from receptor to adjustor and an

efferent or motor one from the latter to the muscles or glands.

We may regard the nervous system as composed of innumerable arcs of this general pattern which conduct impulses from the periphery of the body (and from its internal organs) to centers (adjustors) within the spinal cord, the medulla or the cerebral hemispheres, whence they are reflected to the appropriate effector apparatus. Yet this conception is far too simple, for arcs of different orders are connected by association fibers in the spinal cord and the nuclei of the medulla, and centers of the cerebrum are similarly interconnected by even more complicated pathways. Thus the adjusting apparatus is very complex. cin.

Because of this almost infinite complexity, Herrick likens the task of tracing the pathways to that of a man who, though he knew nothing of electricity and had never heard of a telephone or telegraph, should nevertheless be required to make detailed maps of all the circuits of a great city, both cable and overhead, of all the stations and switchboards, with a complete explanation of their working. "His task would be simple compared with the problem of the neurologists." Yet the psychologist's task is more difficult still for he must not ignore the presence of something corresponding to the numberless subscribers and operators, without which the system would be mute indeed. 

The connections in the brain are most complex of all. 

A mere hint of the degree of complexity is given in Figure 14, in which it is seen that each convolution is connected by short association fibers with its immediate neighbor and by long association fibers with more remote centers. All the fibers of the figure run longitudinally. Imagine even more complex connections from right to left and from left to right portions of each hemisphere, and add to this that the two hemispheres are connected by a multitude of association fibers most of which pass through the corpus callosum. We thus gain some notion of the enormous complexity of the chief controlling center, the brain or cerebrum. 

Functions of the Brain. The preceding account of struc ture is necessary to an understanding of the functions of the brain and of the simplest conscious behavior. Even though the brain were damaged a hand or foot might be moved by reflex arcs through the spinal cord, but only in response to a stimulus. For voluntary movement of the toes a nervous impulse must start from uppermost portion of the precentral convolution or gyrus, which is just forward of the Rolandic fissure (the central large fissure of

Figure 15). For a movement of the arm, impulses start from the middle portion of that convolution; for the jaws and lips, from the lower portion, etc.

Just back of the Rolandic fissure is the post-central gyrus. Impulses must reach corresponding portions of this in order to give sensations from the same bodily members. For the mesial surface of the hemispheres the centers are as shown in Figure 16. Vision is represented in the occipital lobes, hearing in the superior temporal convolution. The cortex is more than a center for receiving impulses which result in sensations and for initiating impulses which result in bodily movements. Injury to one area may result in loss of ability to recognize common objects by

touch and recognition is an intellectual function. Damage to the center marked "motor speech" in Figure 15 causes loss of memory of the efforts necessary to pronounce words. 

These memories are acquired by the child in the first two or three years of life. A severe blow on the head may cause complete unconsciousness. This would suggest that the cortex is the organ of all consciousness but recent evidence indicates that the thalamus, Figure 10, presides over sensations of pain and over the primary emotions. 

Surrounding the area for visual sensations in the occipital cortex there is the visuo-psychic area, which provides knowledge of visual impressions. Such knowledge involves memory, association, and discrimination of former visual impressions and is the means of understanding or giving meaning to present visual sensations. In other words, "visual knowledge depends upon a synthesis of primary visual impressions compared and contrasted with previous visual syntheses which have entered into visual experience. These associations constitute the psychic activities of visual function." (Tilney and Riley, p. 866.) 

The audito-psychic area, which borders the center for hearing below and includes that for auditory speech, performs for hearing a function similar to that which the visuo-psychic area performs for visual sensations. In this region the interpretation of sensations of sound, rhythm, and meter takes place and, due to its posterior portion, there is understanding of articulate speech, a purely human ability.

The area extending backward from the postcentral convolution to the occipital lobe and thence forward and downward in the temporal lobe but below the audito-psychic area is the region for concrete thought. To quote once more, "this extensive area may be provisionally regarded as

a region of the cortex in which concrete ideas are formulated by the combination of visual auditory and somesthetic perceptions" (ibid., pp. 898-99). Bulb. olf.
