The authors just quoted regard the frontal lobes as a region for emotion, self-consciousness, introspection, and

the understanding of social and moral law, while Browning (Medical Record, June 18, 1921) gives evidence for the location of a "moral center" within the frontal lobes. Animal experimentation suggests that they are or include centers for self-control. 

For example, in learning a maze, rats with operativelyinjured frontal lobes will enter now one and now another blind alley, just before they complete the process of learning and give a perfect record. This suggests that they cannot restrain the impulse to enter a cul-de-sac even after the mastery of the right path is almost complete. A normal rat may show a persistent habit of entering a particular blind alley. This may be slow to be broken down. He may now and then make a random error, which is not repeated, but he does not in the latest trials enter now one and now another alley, as if he were obeying a reflex impulse.

Below are recorded the numbers of the blind alleys which one frontally injured rat entered just before giving a perfect record. Each horizontal row of figures represents one trial. 646624822 16 16 14 ∞ ∞ 10 12 2 12 14 

Final trial-no errors.

It is evident from this record that the rat with injured frontal lobes is as likely to enter one blind alley as another,

even at the close of his learning. In his first trials his learning is much more like that of the normal animal. Cameron gives an explanation of this behavior in more general terms as "a disturbance of physiological equilibrium” by destruction of the frontal cortex. I interpret this to mean disturbance of the delicate balance between impulse and inhibition. The normal rat learns to avoid wrong pathways. From this the selection of the right path emerges. The record is from Cameron's Cerebral Destruc tion in Its Relation to Maze Learning, Psychological Mono graphs, No. 177, 1928.

In a patient of Dr. Head's damage to the prefrontal lobes caused the possibility of reacting on two incompatible or contradictory ideas. This patient's mother had been dead three years yet he wrote her a long letter making specific inquiry as to numerous matters of detail. One may wonder whether the numerous frauds, who make a living by misrepresentation and falsehood, have some deficiency or abnormality of the frontal or prefrontal area.

Finally it appears more than probable that the possession of a special talent, as ability in music, is due to the hereditary superiority of a small area of the cortex. 

The Brain Activity of the Newborn.-We can learn facts of importance about the brain and its development and facts of interest and value concerning the babe if we consider the brain activity of the newborn. An example will illustrate this. Any artist who depicts a young babe, draws the very peculiar spreading apart of its fingers. It is characteristic of the first days of life. Now the reason for this spreading apart of the fingers is most interesting. 

At first the fingers spread and the babe is in almost continual movement because a very old portion of the corpus striatum (p. 83), called the paleostriatum, releases im-

pulses for this continual movement and for the spreading apart of the fingers. Then the new striatum develops. As it does so the hand is transformed into a grasping hand with the thumb and fingers opposed. The spread fingers will never appear again unless the adult has a disease of the new striatum. It can then no longer function to check and coordinate the movements due to the older portion and the fingers spread apart once more. This is called athetosis and the hand returns to its babylike condition. 

We know, therefore, that if the fingers of the newborn do ch. in-p.s inf.t.s neo. 

Fig. 17-Diagram of a vertical section across the brain to show the location of the paleostriatum or globus pallidus, which releases the impulses for the babe's random movements, and of the neostriatum which, when it develops, coordinates these movements. th., thalamus; pal., paleostriatum or older part of the corpus striatum; neo., neostriatum. III, third ventricle, which, when inflamed in cerebral influenza, is reported by Ewald to cause emotional disorders symptomatic of the disease. (See pp. 27 ff.)

not spread apart something is wrong, but if the fingers of the adult or the older child spread something is very seriously wrong. This is another example of the growing knowledge of what the old brain does for the child and the adult. Evidently development has taken the method of releasing activity from the older centers. Then the newly developed centers inhibit, direct, and control this activity. 

This can be seen in the excess of activity of babe, child, and adolescent. 

Let us now make a list of the reflexes which the babe does not have at first, then a list of the capabilities which he does possess, and let us realize that those at first absent are rapidly added by the process of growth. It has been asserted that the random and excess activity of the babe is necessary to the growth of directed activity. As some of the activities here mentioned have been disputed, I shall follow the account of Albrecht Peiper, who has recently reviewed the whole matter for the Year-Book for Child 

Hygiene or Medical Treatment for Children (Jahrbuch für Kinderheilkunde, Bd. CXI, 1926).

Careful observers have found the following reflexes absent during the first days of life: 

1. Enlargement or widening of the pupils of the eyes in response to pain. The adult's pupils widen enormously to pain stimulation and to fear, surprise, and astonishment. The babe at first lacks this reflex. 

2. Coordinated eye movements. The convergence of both eyes on a single object and their moving together as a team permits us to see a single object, though there are two retinal images. This coordinate movement of both eyes gives the expression of intelligence to the human countenance. 

3. Turning to the light.

4. Following a moving object with the eyes. Binet used this reaction as a very early test of development in the babe. 

5. The threat reflex or blinking at a threatened blow is absent in the newborn. 

6. Ashner's reflex, or slowing of the heart beat on pressure upon the eyes. 

7. Turning toward the source of a sound. 

8. Ability to scratch the face or body, though this is quickly developed in phemphigus neonatorum, a skin disease which may appear in the young babe. 

9. Ability to make synergic movements, e. g. : flexion of the back of the hand when the fingers are bent; palmar flexion when the fingers are extended; plantar flexion of the foot on extension of the hip and ankle joints and, with bending of these joints, the reverse movement. 

10. The galvanic skin reflex. 

Peiper states also that the newborn lack ability to acquire conditioned reflexes. As this is a cerebral reflex, the statement has support from the facts of brain development.

This very lack of the fundamental reflexes in the babe promises the very highest development later, as compared with the young of even the highest animals. As we go down the animal scale, we find greater and greater approach to complete maturity at birth. Young birds have a period of infancy of only a few weeks. Then they have all the adult reactions. Young mammals have a much longer period of comparative helplessness. Man has been assumed by the law to reach maturity at twenty-one years but his environment has now become so complex that a youth often spends thirty years in preparing for its responsibilities. This longer and longer period of infancy in

what appear to be nature's more precious children has been called "the lengthening of the period of infancy." 

With added complexity of the nervous system and especially of the cortex there results an added complexity of the social environment, so that a longer period of development was inevitable. The longer the preparation for life's duties, the greater the eventual achievements, seems to be the general rule. Moreover, the period of adult achievement seems to be prolonged by the longer period of early training. In extreme old age the cortical connections break down again and the cortex under the microscope appears similar to that of a young child (Fig. 4, p. 22). 

This is a period of decay and the aged man inevitably reaches his second childhood. This and the lengthening period of infancy suggest that one purpose of education is to have it act as a wedge to keep first childhood and second childhood apart as far as possible and as long as possible. This much education or the development of the cortex can accomplish.

We turn now to mention some of the capabilities which the young child does possess.

On the sensory side, the newborn gives evidence that he distinguishes light and dark but sensitiveness to any color is denied by most investigators and we find the statement that the child is color blind for the first year. This would be very difficult to establish with present methods but the statement may be true.

It was long believed that the babe cannot hear at all at birth and two reasons were assigned for this. (1) For a day or two the ear is filled with fluid. (2) The canal leading from the outer to the middle ear is so closely folded in the head of the babe that it was believed impossible for air waves to pass through it. An answer to the first reason is

that fluid is quite capable of conducting vibrations and to the second, that bone conduction of vibrations to the internal ear occurs, so the folding of the canal or meatus need not prevent all hearing. As usual, when a priori reasons conflict in this way, experiment must decide the matter and enough responses to sounds have been elicited from the newborn so that a majority of investigators now agree that hearing is present on the first day of life. The capability for hearing may be slight but it is thought to be present in some degree. The fact that a loudly slamming door is most often the stimulus for "startle" would suggest that bone conduction of the vibrations may be required. Some time after birth babes are more afraid of sounds than of sights. Peiper found the reaction time of a babe to sounds to be about one-fourth of a second. So the involuntary start of a nursling requires about the same time as the voluntary action of adults. The labyrinth or semicircular canals of the babe that is just born is certainly capable of stimulation. Stimulation of this organ produces a peculiar twitching of the eyes, called nystagmus. Nystagmus has been produced by rotating the babe and by the caloric test, i. e., filling the canal of the external ear with warm or cold water which sets up convection currents in the fluid of the labyrinth. This test produced nystagmus in the newborn and, as early as the seventh day of life, nystagmus was produced by rotation.

Sensitiveness to touch stimulation is well developed in the newborn babe. If the inner nose or the auditory canal is tickled with a feather, the babe makes a wry face or turns its head away from the stimulus. The babe also closes its eyes if the nose or the forehead is touched. The conjunctival and corneal reflexes are present at birth. A touch to the eyelash causes the eye to close. Touching the

lips or the tongue calls forth sucking movements, if the child is hungry. Localization of points on the body, touched or pricked, appears to be innate and not acquired. 

Sensitiveness to pain is present from birth, though the time of reaction to a painful stimulus may be as long as twelve to seventy seconds. According to Peiper, the child feels pain after mechanical stimulation as sensitively as the adult, but electric or galvanic shocks much stronger than the adult can bear produce no pain response. The newborn is sensitive to changes of temperature. The babe reacts to cold especially with changes in the rhythm of breathing. Taste: Sweet substances lead to sucking and swallowing movements; sour and bitter to making a wry face and spitting out the substance. The child will reject milk if it has been fed on sweetened milk. Here is rejection of the normal food of the young of mammals due to conditioning. The writer also knew of a child in whom too long feeding of soft foods led to rejection of solid foods and consequent serious damage to health. Over-anxiety by parents concerning a child's health leads to theories and the theories often to serious error. Some trying of different foods by the child is necessary, some conditioning of its tastes, and what the race has long eaten had better be tried and not too late in the child's development. 

The seeking reflex of the sucking instinct.—If touched on the cheek, the babe turns toward the stimulus and the fact that it will seek the breast of the mother is now regarded as fully established by German observers, though this was long denied. The brain center for sucking lies close to the breathing center on the floor of the fourth ventricle on both sides of the spinal cord and just within the two restiform bodies.

With prematurely born babies ability to nurse is not

present and they must be artificially fed. This agrees with the behavior of premature Airedale puppies as described on a later page (p. 127). Even after the sucking instinct has completely subsided in older babes, its reflex movements can be elicited from the sleeping child by touching his mouth or cheek but too gently to awaken him. Possibly the old brain is less affected by sleep than the cortex and, even with reference to the former, the term "deep" or "light" sleep may have a real physiological meaning.

The babe quickly adapts itself to four-hour feedings by day and to eight hour feedings at night. Once the habit is established it is as reliable as a clock. The child announces its hunger at the ends of these periods perfectly. The brainless child described by Edinger and Fischer would not do this. It would apparently have starved so far as the hunger cry is concerned. "It is not known where this time sense is localized in the brain." 

On the side of the sensory nerves we may say in summary that every sense organ appears to be excitable or stimulable. Therefore every sense nerve is capable of conducting impulses, though, according to Westphal, the only cranial nerve which has its medullary sheaths is the auditory nerve. The sensory pathways all converge on the optic thalamus. According to Peiper, "the thalamus is the great reflex center in which incoming impulses pass over to the vegetative centers." 

It has been necessary above to refer to some of the reactions of the babe because the reaction is evidence of the functioning of the sense stimulated. We may now summarize the reactions of the newborn babe and include one or two, for which the stimulus is not well known though the reaction is pronounced. The breathing reflex and that of the heartbeat which appears long before birth; the

sucking impulse and the impulse to seek the breast; turning the head away from a touch stimulus and making a wry face from the same cause; closing the eyes when touched on the face or forehead, or on touching the eyelash; the conjunctival and corneal reflexes; coughing, sneezing, yawning and stretching; nystagmus on stimulation of the semi-circular canals-these appear to make up most of the motor reactions of the newborn and the list should be compared with that of the reflexes which the babe does not at first possess.

This recital of particular responses leaves out entirely the most characteristic behavior of the very young child. 

The babe is really an active, wriggling, squirming creature during most of its waking hours. The psychologist says that the healthy babe is continually executing random movements, impulsive movements, whose stimuli are unknown but which are necessary to health and growth. 

Peiper reports that, "even though there is no outer stimulation, the babe remains motionless for only a few seconds at a time." Just before going to sleep, in sleep, and in sickness it becomes motionless. Certainly it is the corpselike immobility of the sick child, which was so restlessly active a few days before, which terrifies its parents. When the babe is angry or when it is beginning to cry, the movements become more violent still. Even an older nursling will grasp at an object with both hands and generally with both feet as well. The excitement passes from one center to another until all are simultaneously in action. These have been called "mass movements" as well as random movements, and the former term describes them well. 

Closely related to these mass movements is the spreading apart of the fingers, already described; both appear to be initiated by impulses from the older striatum and regu-

lated by the development of the new. Besides this fact, in normal development the neostriatum is believed to serve the truly human activities such as sitting, standing, walking and, due to its inhibitory function, particular directed movements result. "The chorea of children and of pregnancy appears to be due to some toxin or toxins affecting the neostriatum" (Keiller). In chorea, formerly called 

St. Vitus dance, spasmodic and impulsive movements return once more. The 'tween brain, which consists of the thalamus and the corpus striatum, governs the warmth of the body, the assimilation of food and water, and innervates the smooth muscles of the eyes, the vessels, and the glands. Since the young babe cannot maintain body warmth, it is supposed that the center for the control of body warmth is not ripe at birth.

For the behavior of newborn babes which has just been described, the cortex is not necessary nor even the cerebrum. This is partly proved by the presence of the reactions in the few cases of children born without a cerebrum. This also indicates that no articulate consciousness accompanies these reflexes. 

Many of the movements of adults are dependent on the motor cortex. Since it is quite the opposite with the newborn, it is now questioned whether in its case any impulses at all go out from the cortical motor centers. While the evidence on this question is not yet decisive, the conclusion is drawn that at birth the motor cortex is capable of some slight functioning but it has no such great influence as it acquires later. The movements of the newborn are chiefly due to subcortical centers. Aside from the senses, therefore, its behavior is dominated by the old brain. 

The Optic Thalamus and Pain.—So far as our knowledge goes at present, almost all sensations from the outer world

depend upon the cerebral cortex. Nervous impulses must pass along the optic nerves and reach the cortex before any experience of vision can occur. When the toes are touched, impulses from them must reach the topmost middle area of the cortex before we can experience the touch sensa tion, and so on for all the senses. Because of such facts, it was believed for a long time that every sensation depends upon the cortex but in recent years Dr. Head discovered that pain sensations and emotional states are aroused when nervous impulses reach the optic thalamus. This discovery is of so great importance for psychology that we have had to refer to it repeatedly. It is necessary at this point to give some of the evidence on which the discovery is based.

A man thirty-six years of age suddenly lost sensitiveness over all the right half of the body but at the same time he experienced paroxysms of pain in the same area. There was no outer cause or stimulus for the pain sensations. 

The man was also affected by spontaneous attacks of weeping and laughing, though he did not feel the emotion which these movements express. He was often wrought up by emotion, however, and made violent efforts to express the emotion in action. Horrible dreams seemed often to be the cause of the emotion. The paroxysms of pain, which affected the arm, leg, and shoulder continued until death and the agony of it forced him to cry out. He could not recognize the point of a pin if it touched the right side of the body. Nevertheless, its touch produced the most painful sensations. The left side of the body was normal. In such cases there is found at the autopsy softening or degeneration of the median and lateral nuclei of the left optic thalamus. The area damaged may be so large that impulses cannot pass beyond the injured thalamus to the

cortex. Evidently, since a great number of cases as clear as this one have now been found, we must conclude that the optic thalamus is a central station for sensations of pain. There were twenty-four such cases included in 

Head's first observations. The deep seat within the brain of pain sensations might suggest that it is the oldest sensation in the history of the race. A consideration for objective psychology occurs also in this case. Here was a man who wept and laughed and yet he said that he did not have the emotions which accompany these reactions in normal people. Is the behavior, then, all that psychology need consider? The psychiatrists say no and add that the absence of the (subjective) emotion was one of the symptoms of a mortal disease.

In another case heat produced excessive pleasure on the affected half of the body. Another patient could not tell that a warm or cold object, which touched the affected side, was warm or cold but touches with such an object produced pleasure or discomfort. This again indicates that the thalamus functioned but the cortical pathways were blocked or destroyed, so that discrimination of warmth and cold was impossible. Again, "all music that is capable of stirring her emotions excites unpleasant sensations in the right half of the body. She has always been musical and up to the time of the stroke enjoyed good music intensely but since the attack all such music excites the uncomfortable sensations in the right half of the body 

The singing of a so-called comic song leaves her cold but serious music is so intolerable, owing to the sensation it produces, . . .that she is obliged to leave the room." 

There is abundant further evidence that the optic thalamus is the center for painful sensations and probably for sensory pleasure as well. We need mention only these few • •

instances for the next topic may be discussing the same thing. Is it possible that the pain from striking one's finger with a hammer and from receiving an insult may be the same except for the suddenness and the greater immediate intensity of the former? This question of the great similarity between sensory and emotional pain should at least be raised by psychology.

The Thalamus and Emotion.-For many years psychologists asked themselves, what is the immediate cause of emotions. To answer this question, more than a dozen theories were invented. One of them, called The James-Lange 

Theory, was so brilliantly supported by James that it gained the belief of almost all psychologists. That theory is briefly stated on page 196, because of its historic interest and the brilliancy of the conception. It can no longer be believed, persuasive as it was until new facts were discovered. These facts must now be stated as evidence of the very simple theory proposed by Cannon, namely, that nervous impulses, which produce sensations of sight, touch etc., when they reach the cortex, produce the feeling tone or emotional tone of the same sensations when they reach the thalamus. It must be remembered that there are seven sensory pathways from the thalamus to the cortex. 

Almost any sensation, besides giving us information of the outer world, may be and generally is either slightly or intensely pleasant or unpleasant. A young child will tell you whether he likes or dislikes a particular color, long before he can name the color or perhaps express anything about it except his preference or feeling of like or dislike for it. Thus the feeling seems to be an earlier or more primitive acquisition than knowledge about the object. 

The evidence that these painful or pleasant emotions are due to the thalamus has been divided by Cannon into path-

ological, experimental, and pharmacological evidence or evidence from the effects of drugs. I select items from each division.

Pathological Evidence.-Paralysis of the right or left side of the body is called hemiplegia. In some cases no muscles at all of the affected side can be moved. The muscles of the other side function normally and the paralysis is due to disease of the motor centers of the opposite half of the brain, because motor fibers cross in the upper spinal cord. So motor fibers from the left half of the brain go to the right half of the body and conversely. 

In a certain number of cases of hemiplegia the patients cannot move the muscles of the face on the paralyzed side. 

But when they experience either a joyful or a sorrowful emotion, the muscles which could not be moved voluntarily "spring into action and give both sides of the face the expression of sadness or gaiety." In such cases the motor fibers leading downward from the cortex are affected by disease and consequently no act of will can move the muscles. This does not interfere with the effect of nervous impulses going from the thalamus to the muscles. Thus there may be reflex expression of emotions after the complete abolition of movement due to the cortex. 

Just the opposite of this condition is seen when the thalamus is injured. One patient could move both sides of his face at will but, when his face was contorted in pain or when he laughed, one side remained motionless. In the post-mortem examination a tumor was found in the left optic thalamus. There is evidently both thalamic and cortical control of the muscles of the face. In other cases whistling, wrinkling of the brow or making a grimace was not possible but in laughing, crying or frowning due to emotion the facial muscles worked normally.

Unprovoked fits of laughing and crying are mentioned in the first of Head's cases above. Such fits may last with few intermissions for hours. In 173 cases there were fits of both laughing and crying in 17%, crying alone in 16%, and laughing alone in 15%. The patients may not feel the emotions which their faces reflexly express. In these cases lesions of a special part of the pathway from cortex to thalamus are believed by Brissaud to set free a part of the thalamus from cortical control. 

Finally, "So-called 'frog babies,' anencephalic infants, born with almost no brain at all, still have the ability to draw down the corners of the mouth as if in distress at unpleasant stimulation. These emotional acts are performed without direction from the brain just like sneezing, breathing, and swallowing." Such examples as these seem to me to prove that one portion of the brain has to do with primitive emotional behavior and quite a different portion with thought and deliberate action. 

Experimental Evidence.-About 1887 Bechterev found that he could elicit behavior, which had every appearance of being emotional, from animals from which he had removed the cerebral hemispheres. The hemisphereless cats would snarl, the dogs would whine and show their teeth, but they would wag their tails when petted and stroking the back of such a cat caused it to purr. "Since these reactions disappeared when the optic thalamus was removed, he drew the conclusion that it plays a predominant role in emotional expression." (Cannon, W. B., The James- 

Lange Theory, p. 115.)

In 1925 a cat which Cannon and Britton decorticated under ether anaesthesia showed, after recovery, "the complete picture of intense fury." This rage was spontaneous. 

It could be made to disappear only when the lower poste-

rior portion of the thalamic region was removed. If we add to this experimental evidence that which was obtained earlier from Sherrington's spinal dogs with the vagus nerves also severed (see pages 197-198) we have very strong confirmation of the pathological evidence.

Pharmacological Evidence.-On page 31 reference was made to the fact that during the excitement stage of ether anesthesia, the patient may push, pull, shout, or mutter during a serious surgical operation and later he will report that he was unaware of his behavior or of the operation. "It is when 'laughing gas' has set aside the cortical functions that patients laugh and weep." In acute alcoholism something very similar appears, hence the phrase, “drunkard's humor." The drugs in these cases act first on the very sensitive cells of the cortex and diminish or abolish for a time their control of the lower centers. 

Much of the evidence above is from Cannon's paper on the James-Lange Theory. He then concludes as to the neural cause of emotions, "The theory which naturally presents itself is that the peculiar quality of the emotion is added to the simple sensation when thalamic processes are aroused." 

If we reflect on the early development of the old brain and how readily it may escape from wholesome control by the new, we find an explanation for the great number of maladjusted children, the great number of deviates because of emotional disorders, and the great mass of human wreckage with which social agencies so seriously concern themselves and whose chief handicap seems to be that they are able to get control of the child only long after his disordered emotional life is well established. With the work of the neurologists mental hygiene finds a scientific basis. 

When we realize that innumerable situations of life,

innumerable sensations, ideas, and memories arouse emotions of anxiety or amusement, grief or joy, that millions of people resort to the movies or the radio for pleasant emotional stimulation, we see that the old brain accounts for a large range of human behavior. When in the chapter on emotion we realize the great driving force or psychic energy of emotions, how potent they are to arouse instant and vigorous action, we see why there has been so much torture and tyranny in the world and why the growth of reasonable behavior is still so slow. The belief of many college students that the cultivation of ability to get on socially, not to offend but to please their mates, is of more value than any knowledge which they may acquire, is a recognition of the primitive psychology of the emotions, an obeisance to the past rather than a promise for the future. 

In conclusion, let the caution be repeated that, while we have used the word, "center," for the cortical area most intimately connected with a sensation or a bodily movement, all parts of the cortex are so intimately connected and associated that destruction of a considerable area is necessary for the abolition of certain acts or sensations. 

Then there is so intimate a connection with the old brain that many functions are re-represented there, as we have just seen. This complexity brings about great confusion and difference of opinion concerning the functions of the brain. There is point for point correspondence between the retina and the visual center but this exactitude is not repeated elsewhere. Almost every investigation contradicts some apparent discovery of the past but soon or late even the brain must yield the secret of its ways of working to the patient investigator. Two recent reviews of the whole literature show that injury to a considerable area of the cortex produces characteristic losses, so that we can

hardly say that it is equipotential. A much smaller area of damage in the old brain produces even graver symptoms, as we have seen. Psychology must depend on the findings of physiology and pathology to a considerable extent if it would avoid mere speculation. Note the immense literature as to the nature and cause of emotions, almost all of it in error, because the functions of the deeper parts of the brain were quite unknown. Analysis cannot be given up in any science.

Hormones. It was long supposed that different parts of the body can influence parts remote from them only by means of the nervous system and by the food and oxygen carried in the blood stream. Then it was learned that white blood corpuscles are capable of amoeboid movement and that they collect at a wound and act as scavengers to remove or consume toxic matter. But how are they able to direct their movement? Evidently by means of some chemical stimulus. In recent years it has been found that certain glands elaborate substances which are carried by the blood to other organs and stimulate them to action in some cases and in other cases to normal growth and development. The substances which do this are called hormones, chemical exciters or stimulants to action or to growth. Deficiency of the secretion of the thyroid gland is associated with a form of idiocy and dwarfism known as cretinism and with the affection called myxedema. 

Removal of the gland produces somewhat similar conditions. Increase of the secretion produces symptoms of nervous excitement and with increased secretion there may be enlargement of the gland. It was inferred from these facts that the thyroid secretion contains a hormone which is necessary to the development of intelligence and which helps to regulate the nutrition of the body and the

activity of other organs. Later this substance was not only discovered and isolated but it is now made synthetically in the laboratory. It is called 

Thyroxin.-Its structure is shown by the following formula: 

1 HO 1 COOH CH₂. CH NH₂

Only the position of the four iodine atoms is in doubt. 

The gland can elaborate thyroxin if iodine is present even in small amounts in the food or drinking water. Districts in which iodine is absent are known as goiter districts and cretinsim is common in such places. When the dried thyroids of sheep or thyroxin is administered to those who suffer from deficient action of the gland, the symptoms promptly clear up. The treatment of a cretinous child, however, must begin before it is three years of age. 

The cretin is almost always dwarfed, with a broad face, thick, wrinkled, brownish skin. His movements are sluggish and there is every appearance of stupidity. The psy chic symptoms in a majority of cretins are marked dullness and insensitiveness which makes them more or less incapable of receiving impressions or of organizing experiences and forming ideas and concepts. Many remain at the mental level of a five-year-old child and many even below that level. They are emotionally indifferent, phlegmatic and childish, but usually they are good natured. 

Most of them are incapable of productive work both be. cause of their stupidity and their muscular weakness. This mental wreckage due to deficiency of the thyroid, led a French scientist to remark: "The genesis and the exercise of man's highest faculties are conditioned by purely

chemical action; by the product of a secretion. Let the psychologists meditate on these facts." There has been ample meditation thereon by psychologists and many brilliant investigations by physiologists and biochemists. 

We need mention only the facts which apply to mental life. 

Thyroxin has more to do with mental development than other hormones, though any one of them which affects the body must indirectly affect the mind. When myxedema attacks an adult, there is mental sluggishness somewhat similar to that of a cretin. Hyperactivity of the thyroid often occurs with exophthalmic goiter, so named because the eyes appear to protrude from their sockets. It results in emotional excitability, anxiety, readiness to burst into tears, pressure of activity, increased blood pressure, rapid heart, etc. There is a possibility that when nature arrests an incipient hyperactivity at just the right point, the result is a tremendously energetic individual, who, if he gains power, electrifies the world and, if he does not shake society to its foundations, he may, at least, make it tremble. 

Pituitrin is a secretion of the pituitary body or gland.

For its position just below the floor of the cranium see Figure 10, page 83. The gland is no larger than a hazel nut, yet the secretion of its anterior lobe governs bodily growth and when it is disordered gigantism results. The youth grows rapidly and abnormally to some eight feet in height when the disease generally terminates in death. Here again nature may at any point delay or apparently cure the disease and there results the giant of the side shows. 

Probably because of an indirect effect on the mind in this case, the giant is not nearly so alert or intelligent as his siblings who have not undergone the pathological growth. 

If the disease affects the pituitary gland of an adult, the

long bones do not grow, as they do in the youth, but instead the hands, face and head are changed in shape. This condition is called acromegaly.

A secretion of the posterior lobe of the pituitary body increases blood pressure and induces vigorous contractions of the uterus. It is, therefore, frequently used in childbirth.

Progynon, the internal secretion of the sex glands, has recently been isolated in pure form by Butenandt. It has been thought to be capable of restoring the function of the reproductive organs. If one believes that the native mental and emotional traits of women are different from those of men, progynon is of psychological interest. Hens that fight and crow and in other ways behave like roosters and have the physical characteristics of the male, are produced by simple removal of the ovaries at an early age. Not infrequently a woman who has a tumor of the ovary develops a beard, changed voice, and other masculine characteristics due to the tumor. She promptly returns to feminine traits when the tumor is removed. Such experiments and observations, and they are now almost innumerable, lead to the belief that both the male and the female body possess the potentialities of both sexes. Endocrine secretions of the male sex glands inhibit the development of female potentialities in the male. Secretions of the ovaries, or rather of the corpus luteum, prevent male potentialities from developing in the female. 

Those who assert that male and female psychic traits are practically the same would say, of course, that the internal secretions of the sex glands have nothing to do with psychology. This claim of identity is probably based on a wish to deny the existence of any human instincts. The present writer believes that the intense interest and care

of the normal mother for her child has partly a chemical basis in hormones.

An endocrine or ductless gland need not be devoid of a duct which delivers its secretion to another part of the body. But, if there is a duct, the gland produces two (or more) substances, one an external secretion which the duct carries; the other an internal secretion. It is the latter hormones which have so interested physiologists in recent years. The pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroids, the adrenal glands, and the gonads or sex glands are the endocrine organs of most interest today. There are other secretions which stimulate action elsewhere than at their source, so that the body is a chemically integrated organism as well as a nervously integrated one. The chemical integration is more primitive than the nervous. A delicate equilibrium of all these chemical, physical, and psychic forces of the body is necessary. This equilibrium is called by Cannon homeostasis and disease is an interference with this balance of innumerable factors. An interesting feature of hormones is that they excite action in organs other than those of their origin, without apparently having much chemical energy themselves. This suggests catalytic action, though perhaps their chemical activity is more complex than processes produced in the laboratory. 

Not only do the secretions of certain glands affect consciousness and intelligence but consciousness causes secretions. The emotion connected with the anticipation of food causes the mouth to "water" and the stomach to secrete its fluids. Other emotions cause the secretions of other glands. So there is an intimate exchange of influences between the mind and the body. In fact, physiologists do not hesitate to put an emotion into the chain of

organic events which cause both secretions and behavior." 

They do not discuss behavior as if it were uninfluenced by conscious states.

Brain Weight.-There is a popular belief that mental ability is correlated with the weight of the brain or is even almost proportional to it. There is very little evidence for this. We have seen that a very considerable part of the brain is not related to thought or mental ability at all, but with emotions and still more primitive functions. Below a certain minimum brain weight and skull circumference normal intelligence cannot survive. Voisin placed this circumference at 13 inches but, aside from dwarfs, it is fairly certain that a skull circumference of 17 inches involves intelligence not above imbecility. In fact, the microcephalic imbecile is defined in that way. The adult whose cranial circumference is more than two inches less than normal will probably be feeble-minded.

A table of brain weights collected by Boyd shows the interesting fact that the brain is heavier between the years 14 and 20 than at any other period of life. The interesting feature of Boyd's table is that it puts the maximum brain weight at exactly the time at which Binet tests put the full maturity of intelligence and intelligence appears to decline thereafter with age. This parallelism is striking. 

It may be more than a coincidence and the relationship should be investigated further. It is certain that the body, too, reaches its greatest vigor by about twenty years of age.

Anatomists are inclined to ascribe more importance to the complexity of the secondary fissures and tertiary fissures of the cerebrum than to its weight. They believe that brains of distinguished persons show more of this com- Since the discoveries of Millikan, not even the old argument of the conservation of energy can be urged against this.

plexity. The brain of Anatole France (weight 1017 grams) was exceptionally small but "its shape and fissures were perfect. It seemed like a true piece of jeweled craftmanship in which the convolutions, long and winding, twisting back upon themselves, pressed cleanly together revealed a complexity that is rarely seen." (Report to the 

French Academy of Medicine.) 

On the basis of very recent weights it is said that the brains of one hundred superior men have been found to be about 100 grams above the average of the race. Spitzka of Cornell University is quoted to the effect that the "senile decrease in brain weight is delayed for about ten years in those persons who are considered distinguished." Herrick's remark that the neopallium is probably undergoing further differentiation in civilized races gives no ground for the common statement that the human brain and intelligence have remained unchanged for the past twenty-five thousand years.

A practical remark may be made on the basis of our general knowledge of the brain. It is the organ of adaptation par excellence and we may be sure that it will adapt the individual almost perfectly to any situation with which he is long confronted. One result of this adaptability is that every school curriculum and every method of instruction will and must succeed, no matter how poor the method is when compared with the results obtained by better ones. 

Those methods and curricula, which are in closest harmony with psychological laws, will be most economical of time and effort but others will certainly succeed quite well. 

This accounts for the enormous variety of processes by which different persons have gained an education. It also accounts for the disputes among educators. Each one has gained some desirable end by the device which he advo-

cates. This is due to the adaptability of the pupil and often not at all to the method employed. Just now the pressure of all sorts of subjects to be taught is appalling but the brain will accomplish its task more or less well. 

More thorough knowledge of fewer subjects would sooner adapt the individual to earning a living and enjoying a life.

EXERCISES 

1. What science or sciences investigate the structure of the nervous system; its functions? 

2. If a motor nerve is severed what happens to the muscles to which it extends? If a sensory nerve is cut what is the psychological result? 

3. Indicate on a sketch of the brain the result of damage to each part of the precentral convolution, the postcentral, the occipital lobes, the superior temporal convolution. 

4. If each of the above areas should be stimulated in the living individual by applying electrodes to them what would be the result? 

5. What is the result of injury to the area for visual speech? For motor speech? For auditory speech? 

6. If each neuron-path in the brain were insulated from every other one, how many mental abilities would a man possess? 

7. Is there evidence of many associative connections between such neuron-paths? 

8. Has each person as many memories as there are classes of items to be remembered, e. g., one memory for numbers, another for names, another for faces, etc., or are persons described as having poor, fair, or good memories? Give some evidence for your answer.
