CHAPTER IV INSTINCT 

Reflex, instinctive, and intelligent action represent three ascending grades of complexity of behavior. Particular examples of the second or third may be as simple or simpler as selected examples of the first or second, respectively, but the average of complexity increases in the order named. Moreover, as the nervous system in the animal series changes gradually from a diffuse network to a system centralized in great ganglia, the behavior changes from predominantly reflex to predominantly instinctive and with centralization of control in the new brain there is an increase of intelligent behavior. As an approach to the description of instinct, therefore, we may recall some typical examples of reflex action. 

We have already given examples of native reflexes in Chapter 1, because we there decided to describe the simpler types of behavior first, then the more complex ones, and finally to turn to a description of intelligence and its factors, which govern deliberate or thoughtful behavior. 

Some further examples of native reflexes will not be amiss to show their relation to instincts and to show how very naturally they led to the hypothesis that stimulus-response is a formula which accounts for all human behavior and that the meaning of a situation need not dawn on a man in order that he should react to it successfully. This theory has now become so widespread that certain sociologists speak of "behavior-forming situations," as if the sole

INSTINCT 

123 active cause of behavior were the outer stimulus or situation and the individual had no control of it at all. If this conception be true, it is certainly rather ominous and depressing. Native reflexes do depend on the stimulus. 

Acquired habits, however, can be modified or "broken" by the exercise of will and inhibition.

Further Examples of Reflex Action.-Observation shows that the pupil of the eye is continually contracting or expanding for an increase or decrease in the intensity of light. The change in intensity is the stimulus for the reflex. Again the heart beats fast or slow according to the amount of carbon dioxide in the blood which passes over the breathing center in the medulla. The CO₂ is the stimulus. A dog with the brain disconnected from the spinal cord will execute a very complicated scratch reflex if his side is irritated by a stimulus. This is purely spinal reflex. 

Decerebrate frogs give as interesting and almost as complicated examples. 2 Many more examples of typical reflexes might be found but it seems unnecessary to mention them.¹ They would all unite in showing that there are certain nervous circuits or reflex arcs, each of which, when its receptor is stimulated, conducts impulses at once to some lower center, whence they are reflected and conducted along the motor portion of the arc to the effector. Thus breathing, winking, sneezing, coughing, and many vital processes go on reflexly and without any need of direction by consciousness. In fact, consciousness seems quite unable to help the reflex processes but it may indirectly interfere with them. As we have seen, emotional states inhibit digestive reflexes completely. In the absence of the emotion the 

A list of reflexes which the newborn babe lacks but which are soon acquired appears on page 99.

reflexes go on quite automatically under the control of sympathetic nerves.

From these examples it is plain that certain nervous connections are present at birth or soon afterward and that their functioning results in reflex action. Each reflex connection is highly specialized and governs the performance of some very specific act. Almost always it governs the behavior of a restricted group of organs or muscles rather than of several co-ordinated groups or the behavior of the whole organism as an individual. 

Instinctive Behavior.—A grade higher in complexity are those connections which govern either co-ordinated groups of organs or the behavior of the whole animal. The bee builds the cells of the hive and stores honey. The solitary wasp builds as complicated a nest, kills or paralyzes prey suitable to feed the larvæ, and deposits her eggs, which will develop into offspring which she will never see. One species of wasp kills only crickets, another only grasshoppers, etc. Here is very complicated behavior, yet the wasp cannot have any foresight of the result her acts will bring about. Such activities are due to inherited nervous connections and not at all to intelligence. They are well called by Woodworth "ready-made" reactions but this would apply to reflexes as well. The carrion fly deposits her eggs on flesh, which will nourish the larvae, and never on fat, in which the larvae would die. Yet the odor of decayed cabbage will cause the deposit of the eggs quite as certainly as the odor of lean meat. Thus, instinctive action, though variable, is far more machine-like and less variable than intelligent action. On the western prairies advantage is taken of this somewhat automatic character of instinct in animals. If in a large flock of sheep a ewe 

The heart-beat reflex starts long before birth.

INSTINCT 

125 has lost her lamb and a lamb has lost its mother, the skin of the dead lamb is tied upon the living one and the bereft ewe promptly adopts and suckles it. Which lamb a ewe shall "own" thus depends entirely upon the odor. While the instinctive act is a response to a specific stimulus, it adjusts the animal to a whole situation. 

The behavior of birds is quite as interesting as that of bees and wasps. The bird builds her first nest quite as perfectly as any later one. It is like every nest of that species and unlike that of every other species. When eggs are present in the nest, the mother bird incubates them, according to Whitman, with no glimmer of the meaning or outcome of her strange behavior. Given a broody "physiological disposition" and a group of nervous connections, the instinctive behavior follows with almost the certainty of fate. Likewise chicks run to cover when a shadow approaches, which might be cast by the wings of a hawk, but now quite as probably by those of an airplane. 

Professor McDougall writes: "When, for example, a terrier comes across the trail of a rabbit, his hunting instinct is immediately aroused by the scent; he becomes blind and deaf to all other impressions as he follows the trail, and then, when he sights the quarry, he breaks out into the yapping which is peculiar to occasions of this kind. 

His wild ancestors hunted in packs, and under those conditions the characteristic bark emitted on sighting the quarry served to call his fellows to his aid; but when the excited terrier hunts alone, his excited yapping can but facilitate the escape of his quarry; yet the old social instinct operates too powerfully to be controlled by his moderate intelligence." (Social Psychology, p. 25.)

In similar fashion the raccoon usually dips his food in water before eating it, but what value this instinct could

ever have had is now lost in the dark pathways of development. Yet this "habit" causes the Germans to give the name Waschbär to the raccoon while in scientific classification he is called Procyon lotor, the latter word meaning the washer. The examples suggest that most instinctive acts are, or were at some time, of advantage to the individual or the race. Others seem to have persisted in a species because they were not harmful or damaging. Synapses have been joined in the lower nervous system. These structures have been transmitted by heredity and, when they are present, the animal exhibits a certain specific instinct.

Since, so often, instinctive acts involve more muscles or glands than reflex acts, it has been customary to call instincts chain reflexes or compound reflexes. Many writers still accept this description. Others reject it. Whatever decision is made, the average instinctive act is more complex than the average reflex one, and reflexes occur in nervous systems which are merely diffuse net-works and far too simple to serve as a basis of instinctive activity.³ Moreover the typical reflex arc, as described by the physiologists, is an association of only two neurons. (Parker, G. H., op. cit., July, 1909.) The history of the nervous system shows that reflex arcs are genetically earlier than any other nervous structures. It is difficult to avoid the conclusion, therefore, that the neural basis of an instinctive act is an association of reflex arcs. 

Instinct and Environment.—The phylogenetic develop ment of the nervous system also shows that some animals, whose environment is very simple (the sea anemone, for example), have a nervous system of diffuse nerve threads 

'Parker, G. H. The Origin of the Nervous System and Its Appropriation of Effectors. Pop. Sci. Monthly, August, 1909.

INSTINCT 

127 and exhibit only reflexes. When the environment is more complex, instinctive acts appear and with a complex and variable environment memory and intelligence are evolved. 

These are not separate stages of development. They overlap. The bees and wasps are very largely instinctive machines, probably because their air environment is very simple to deal with, yet they show the beginnings of space memory for locations on the ground. There seems to be no reason, therefore, against regarding reflexes, instincts, and intelligence as three ways of increasing complexity of reacting to the environment. With intelligence an extremely variable environment may be successfully dealt with while a mere exchange of odors may completely defeat instinct, as already shown. 

If the usual view, that instincts are dependent on specific nervous connections, is accepted, it is important to ask: "At what time is each connection formed?" The answer appears to be: "Not long before the environment makes the instinct necessary." Suckling the young is so fundamental an instinct that it gives name to the mammals. Yet three Airedale pups which were prematurely born by two or three days could not nurse the mother. 

The language of my informant, Mr. Winter, is: "They apparently did not know how to nurse." He continues: "The two did not live long enough to learn but by working with the one (which lived three days) I got him to take hold of the nipple and make a very feeble effort toward. the end of the second day. He would not do this, however, unless the nipple were placed in his mouth. A normal puppy commences nursing within five minutes of birth." Professor Avery reports the same condition for guinea pigs.

In my own experience, two little boys came to me bring-

ing two young coyotes in their arms. Perhaps the animals were two months old. They were perfectly safe to handle and quite as gentle as puppies. I bought them and began to train them in a puzzle box. On the eleventh day, though never before, they bit and snapped with the utmost ferocity. They became "wolves" within a period of twentyfour hours, possibly at just the moment when muscular strength became sufficient to make their defense effective or possibly at just the time they would have begun to leave the den and forage on their own account to some extent. 

Instincts, therefore, ripen suddenly and apparently nature does not supply a nervous connection long before it is needed. This might suggest a little closer connection between the environment and development than pure chance variation permits. Is it possible that other factors are yet to be found?

In view of the development of the nervous system in the race and the three great types of behavior, it is little wonder that the paleontologist describes man as an animal to whom in the past a curious physiological accident happened, namely, an immense hypertrophy of the forebrain, on which memory and intelligence depend, whereas other animals were protected by thick scales or strong teeth and claws. This implies also that instincts are dependent on the older portions of the brain, as pain and emotion have been found to be.

Definitions. From the examples given it should not be difficult to understand current definitions of instinct. Professor James says, "Instinct is the faculty of acting in such a way as to produce certain ends without foresight of the ends nor previous education in the performance." 

Lloyd Morgan, from the standpoint of animal psychology, gives a much longer definition. "Instinctive behavior in-

INSTINCT 

129 cludes those complex groups of co-ordinated acts which are, on their first occurrence, independent of experience; which tend to the well-being of the individual and the preservation of the race; which are due to the co-operation of external and internal stimuli; which are similarly performed by all members of the same more or less restricted group of animals; but which are subject to variation and to subsequent modification under the guidance of experience." 

We may add to this the observation already made, namely, that while the instinctive act is a response to a single stimulus, it adjusts the animal to a whole situation. 

Imitating the sounds made by one's mates brings to a human being language. Falling in love may lead to all the responsibilities of a family, a situation which, until recently, was supposed to last for at least twenty years, or until the maturity of the offspring. Professor Woodworth remarks that instinctive acts are not so prompt as reflexes. They are more persistent, as the nest building of birds. This, I think, is due to the fact that the adjustment is to a whole situation. The initial act may in certain cases be quite prompt.

Origin of Instincts.-A recent text-book of psychology says of instincts, "We may assume that the common and persistent elements in the habits of our millions of progenitors are transmitted in the progressive organization of the nervous architecture of the species through evolution from the humblest living organism to the highest man. 

Therefore, instinctive behavior is determined by the organized reflex arcs which remain intact on the ground that they represent well-worn racial paths." (Seashore, p. 208.)

Since biology asserts that no acquired characters are transmitted from parent to offspring and, since habits are acquired characters, learned reactions, we cannot interpret the quotation as meaning a direct inheritance of habits. Instead we are now taught that organisms continually present variations and mutations due to hereditary conditions or forces which we do not yet fully understand, so we still call some of the mutations chance variations. The nervous system is probably the most variable of all bodily structures. Those individuals which varied in ways profitable to the individual or the race would survive in the struggle for existence and leave offspring which inherit the favorable variation. Thus the variation would become a racial trait. In the past, for example, men who possessed no fighting instinct would either not survive or at least they would leave no offspring of their own pacific temperament. Warfare was "the gory cradle of the race."

Instinct appears as a variation of the germ plasm and, where one part of the traits comes from one parent, another from the other parent, variations must be almost infinite in number. Jennings likens the inheritance of traits to the process of stringing beads of different colors. Almost any combination might occur.

If a particular variation happened to be a set of nervous connections which resulted in imitation, for example, such behavior would enable the possessor of this trait to get on in a social environment much better than one who paid no attention to the behavior of his mates. So we find imitation to be an important instinct in man and to be rarely found in the higher animals. In fact, in flesh-eating animals imitation might result in starvation. Each must find and devour the food before his companions get scent of it, for there is almost no storing of food. In a society

INSTINCT 

131 which stores great quantities of food and accumulates property, often the quickest way to prosperity is to imitate the service rendered by another. In such a society imitation will be bred into the stock and become a racial trait, after the variation once appears. Among the carnivorous animals it will be bred out. We assume, however, that such hereditary variations in the nervous system as form the basis of instincts, occur in various individuals and species and the variation may occur repeatedly. It need not be an isolated occurrence. Once present, the variations perpetuate themselves because they lead to biological success.

From these statements the distinction between instinct and habit becomes clear. Instinct is due to inherited nervous connections and, therefore, the instinctive reactions are called native or unlearned reactions. Habit is due to acquired connections formed during the life of the individual in the course of his development. Some instincts may appear long after birth but their connections are due to inheritance, not to training.

Since even the old brain must by heredity have included many variations in its development, there is a fairly long list of human instincts. Some of them are so greatly modified by intelligence that they no longer present all the features of an instinct in sharp outline, as we find them in many animals. The more fundamental ones are clearly defined but psychologists might debate long as to whether such traits as sympathy and modesty are instinctive. 

Gifts or Special Aptitudes.—This theory of variation and natural selection is used to explain much in biology and psychology, though later it may be discovered that the environment has some influence, as yet quite unknown, on

the origin of human traits. Careful breeding experiments have as yet shown no trace of it unless Pavlov shall be able to cause the transmission of a habit in one generation as an instinct in later ones, which he believes to be possible. 

His experiment will require confirmation.

Whatever new facts may come to light, it appears that the origin of special aptitudes, intellectual gifts or emotional traits is exactly similar to that of instincts. The new brain is more variable than the old. A slight change in its structure, a new group of connections, may mean the possession of a special ability. Because of this, musical children, for example, may spring from parents who showed little talent for music, and so for painting and sculpture. One man enjoys computation while a hundred others have "a phobia for figures." Almost no mind is equally good in mathematics and linguistics. One or the other is preferred. The preference is supposed to be an evidence of the ability.

Because of this, one college advises its students to choose for a life work what they like best. Otherwise they will miss happiness. No consideration of the possible demand of society for the products of the student's work should sway his decision. This seems hardly practical. 

There is enough truth in the opinion, however, to make it imperative for the executive, the employer, and the employment manager to endeavor to detect evidence of special aptitudes, however slight, in his employes and to assign them work in the line of their special abilities. Anything else is a serious economic waste and a personal disappointment for the employe. A considerable portion of the enormous labor turnover in industry has been ascribed to the For evidence of the great influence of environment, see the little book by H. S. Jennings entitled, Prometheus. It was published after the above was in type.

INSTINCT 

133 absence of such an arrangement. Almost the whole energy of the effort toward vocational guidance should be directed to this end. No doubt the original impulse to the division of labor was due to the possession of special abilities by different individuals and special efficiency and satisfaction in their exercise. Choice was freely exercised. Under highly organized industry there may be no possibility of choice by the individual. Special ability may not find its suitable work and it is this defect of organization that vocational guidance is believed to be able to remove. 

This is an excursion into practical psychology but the topic is important. Logically, of course, the discussion of special abilities belongs with the account of intelligence. 

Biologically it belongs here, because of the similarity of their origin to that of instincts. A marked difference between them will also suggest itself. While special aptitudes are appearing all the time, no writer even suggests any present or recent addition to the list of human instincts. Apparently the books are closed and variation and selection have ceased to operate in this field. The nearest approach to even a change in instinct is represented by the enormous variability of methods of creeping in babes, which is to be mentioned later. This, however, is no more than variability in a single instinctive performance.

An Argument Against the Existence of Instinctive Beha vior.-Pavlov's discovery of conditioned reflexes (see p. 

166) has led to the claim that there are no native or unconditioned types of behavior, except simple reflexes, in higher animals or men. Conditioned reflexes are to take the place of instinctive behavior. Every act must be learned or, in the phrase of these writers, "conditioned" behavior is due to stimuli from the environment. Certain rather myste-

rious mechanisms are conditioned and thereafter there is a definite learned pattern of reactions for each situation. 

This may be a mere reaction against the claim of those who insist that "heredity is everything" and environment has little effect upon human destiny. A curiosity of the claim that there is only reflex but not instinctive behavior lies in the fact that one writer says this applies only to man and not to animals. Another applies it to both men and animals and believes that even the breast feeding of the babe is a conditioned response.

Perhaps the answer of Rexroad to such arguments is as adequate as any other. He says, "The somewhat striking fact about uterine development is that structures and sets of structures develop in one type of surroundings and are prepared to be thrown into typical and adjustive actions by another set of conditions encountered later. The muscles, the muscle attachments, and the neural connections involved in breathing are formed in the absence of air. 

The eyes as well as their neural connections mature in the absence of light. The taste bulbs grow in the absence of stimulations which in post birth days excite them

This growth which takes place under one set of conditions and which results in structures capable of reacting to other conditions is the basis of unlearned responses." 

(Rexroad, General Psychology for College Students, p. 

130.) Such examples as these lead most psychologists to the belief that the instinctive behavior of the babe in seeking the breast and in nursing has developed just as the eye and taste buds have developed. Certain instincts which appear some time after birth seem to have the same origin. 

Nervous structures mature and accompanying bodily conditions as well. Then the instinctive reactions appear.

If instinctive behavior is due to a mutation of the germ

INSTINCT 

135 plasm, we may suppose that some instincts have been bred out of each species when they became useless. But if vestiges of the behavior appear to persist for a short time in the young, such vestiges will be the strongest evidence of their instinctive basis. Moro is authority for an example which appears to have escaped the notice of Watson and others, who have observed the behavior of young babes.

If the observer lays the child upon a large pillow or cushion and strikes the pillow suddenly at both sides of the babe, a definite coordinated movement follows. Both the babe's arms draw backward and apart, says Moro. They are then moved forward toward each other "in a bow."

The fingers are first spread apart, then again closed together. The legs execute a similar but less pronounced movement. Moro sees in this a reminiscence of the embracing reflex (Umklammerungsreflex) of the nursling ape which holds itself grasped tightly against the mother's body by this strong embrace. Peiper finds that this reflex is best called forth by jarring the child. If the observer supports the babe on his arm and places his hand behind its head, then strikes the hand against a hard object like a table, the movement appears. Peiper was able, he says, to produce the embracing movement with sound, light, and pain stimuli, if they lead to fright. He concludes that "the fright reaction is nothing else but the embracing reflex. 

In fact, the jarring of the head produces the movement only if the child is frightened by the experiment." The appropriateness of the action is evident. The child apparently seeks to hold fast to the mother's body, when it is shaken or threatened with a fall. Of course, the babe can have no intention in the matter. The crouching or shrinking of the adult is regarded by Peiper as the last remnant of the fright reaction of the nursling. In his opinion, the

reaction harks back to the dawn of racial development when the act was useful.

Another reaction of the newborn has received a similar explanation. Dr. Robinson found that newborn babes would grasp a wand placed in their hands and, if the rod was slowly raised, they could sustain their weight by this firm grasp.

This he explained by reference to remote arboreal life. Watson found that "two infants in whom life was almost extinct clung tenaciously to the rod." 

This reaction tends to disappear after the third or fourth month of life.

Further evidence against the opinion that all behavior is learned or conditioned is found in the experience of poultry raisers, where thunderstorms come up quickly.

They make every effort to condition their hens to seek shelter from such storms. Nevertheless, the hens instinctively hover their broods and many chicks are drowned, though the shelter may be within a few feet. No amount of conditioning will overcome the native impulse. 

After long effort, two children trained a female dog and a cat to sleep side by side. But when the dog had a litter of puppies it would not allow the cat within fifty yards of them. All in all the evidence that conditioned reflexes may be offered as a substitute for instinctive behavior seems to be very meager.

Some Instinctive Behavior of Rats.-Morgan's definition of instinct demands the cooperation of external and internal factors in producing instinctive behavior. Richter has determined the internal factors in some of the instinctive behavior of rats. When 250 strips of crepe paper were hung on the walls of the cage of a rat, it would build a nest of them and the conditions demanded that it take only one strip at a time. If the nest was taken away, the

INSTINCT 

137 rat would build a new nest each day. A large amount of activity was required to do this and the amount of activity in nest-building was equal in the male and female rat over a period of fifty days. This activity and three other kinds of behavior Richter ascribes to an impulse to conserve body heat as shown in his outline below. 

Nest-building 

Burrowing 

Huddling into small spaces 

Huddling together-social contact

Running Climbing Jumping 

Conserve body heat 

Increase heat production

The increased activity of the female rat, which occurs every four days and coincides with the oestrus period, he attributes to some constituents of the sex hormones, for removal of the ovaries suppressed the increase completely and transplants of ovaries in the body of the castrated male rat produced the four-day cycle of increase of activity. This disappeared if the transplants were removed. 

Great increase of activity every two hours was attributed to the contractions of the stomach due to hunger. In all these cases the cause was pretty well established and back of each one lies a chemical condition of the body, though the stomach contractions themselves are physical. The internal factor mentioned in Morgan's definition is well identified in Richter's work. What causes gnawing, fighting, and migrating in rats is as yet unknown. 

Of his rats, Richter says, "Nest-building is practically independent of experience, since young rats thirty days old raised in sawdust build perfect nests out of the crepe paper the first time it is presented to them." (Richter, Curt P., Animal Behavior and Internal Drives, Quarterly

Rev. of Biol., I, 3, 1927, p. 337.) This certainly does not look as if the rat had to be conditioned or taught to build the nest. The "pattern" of the reaction was no doubt modified by the material offered. 

When a secretion is the cause of activity it "must take effect in some part of the central nervous system, either by simply increasing the irritability of the centers in the brain and spinal cord, or by actually stimulating those centers." (P. 327.) It is interesting to note that physiol. ogists universally ascribe types of behavior to particular centers of the nervous system, rather than to mysterious mechanisms, and they do this despite the mechanists' claim that there are no specialized centers in the brain but that it is "equipotential." Richter even offers an explanation for the simplicity of the brain and behavior of ordinary laboratory rats. Though this carries us over to the realm of intelligence we may quote his statements here. 

After recording mechanically the total behavior of rats in simple cages and finding it to be of simple types which I should call reflex and instinctive, Richter constructed a set of multiple cages which were very complex. In the multiple cage a record could be "obtained of the time spent each day by the rat in climbing, running, burrowing, gnawing, eating, drinking, and mating." "An individual brought up in the multiple cage is far more intelligent than one raised in the ordinary running cage. 

Within the multiple cage the animal shows all sorts of constructive and imaginative activities, rarely, if ever, seen in an ordinary laboratory rat, and on occasions when it escapes it avoids recapture with extraordinary success. 

We may note in passing that were rats of this environment used for experiments on extirpation of the different areas of the cortex of the brain, much more noticeable

INSTINCT 

139 defects in behavior might possibly be demonstrated as a result of the injuries than have appeared thus far in the rat kept under the usual laboratory conditions." (P. 341.) 

Evidently Richter cares little for the immense desirability of denying intelligence to animals (or men), and of regarding the brain as homogeneous. Instead, he believes that a very complex environment developed the intelligence of the rats far beyond that of rats reared in simple cages. His result, by the way, may be applied to education. Every method of instruction and every school curriculum must complicate the pupil's environment to some extent and, therefore, improve his intelligence to some extent. But many educators have claimed that improvement of intelligence in any general degree is quite impossible. The mentality of Richter's rats seems, therefore, to be superior to the human minds which have been invented to justify particular theories of education. Nevertheless, common sense observers still believe that a complex environment develops the intelligence of a bright boy or girl and for this reason chiefly do they support public schools.

We may now return to behavior of rats which is often called instinctive, a fear reaction, but which in this instance seems to have been wonderfully modified by memory. "The rats plug up the entrance to any of the smaller cages whenever they have been frightened on entering them. This is the only explanation that can be offered for the frequency with which adult rats closed the entrance to the running drum shortly after they were placed in the cage. In one instance the opening was plugged up so tightly with nest-building material that a knife had to be used to open it up again." (P. 342.) No doubt the rat ran from the running drum when it was hurt but plugging

the opening is far different behavior. It seems here as if fear had aroused a memory, much as it arouses first memories in children. This behavior seems too complex to call it a reflex conditioned by a single hurt and without participation of memory.

In these rats, therefore, fear or the memory of a hurt was the cause of one complicated activity. Bodily activity increased with hunger and the greatest activity seemed to coincide with the most vigorous contractions of the stomach. As we know, these contractions are the stimulus for sensations of hunger in man. Sensations, appetites, and quite possibly desires for food or sex motivated these animals. These "internal conditions" of Morgan's definition are sometimes called internal drives. It is important to know, however, exactly what we mean if we are to use the term. The specific cause of the particular act is often well known and when this is the case the exact name should be used for it. To invoke an undefined "drive" for each observable act of a man or an animal is, as already pointed out, a return to the method of the faculty psychology. 

Instinct and Intelligence.-Early writers on the subject believed that animals are guided by instinct, man by reason. This was claimed as the distinctive superiority of mankind. Nowadays we are inclined to use the more inclusive term, intelligence, rather than reason, but it is also believed that man has more instincts than any other animal. In him the operation of pure instinct is disguised and obscured by the intervention of intelligence. In man, as Professor James showed, "instincts are so numerous that they block each other's path." This blocking may be the matrix from which intelligence is born for, when there is a conflict between two instinctive impulses, a decision

INSTINCT 

141 must be made. Considerations in the light of past experience must determine the act. One stimulus or the other or neither must be acted upon and intelligence alone can deal with such a situation. In fact, Colvin is fond of saying, that consciousness is present only in a crisis of this sort. 

Thus, whether fear and flight or rage and fighting shall be the response to a particular situation depends on the imminence of the attack and the superior chances of escape by one method or the other. A child has an impulse to fondle an animal but injury at the first attempt may cause fear of such an animal to guide all his later behavior. Here memory inhibits the fondling impulse. Therefore, in higher animals the observer cannot tell which instinctive impulse will be obeyed. The behavior of some of the lower forms is much more predictable. Memory and intelligence are necessary in dealing with novel situations. Instinctive impulses may be the springs of action but our "memories are here to warn and encourage us." The curbing of instinct by intelligence is perhaps nowhere clearer than in the modern rearing of children. The young babe's crying to be nursed is answered by his mother's impulse to satisfy him and stop the outcry. But the mother is now taught that feeding at regular intervals is far better even for a babe. This knowledge soon defeats two strong impulses, one in the mother, the other in the child. Due to parental or maternal instinct, women desire to fondle or kiss a baby, but knowledge of possible infection prevents at least the kissing. Such peculiar and restrained behavior has led a witty writer to remark that "while our fathers feared sin, we fear only germs." These are examples of instinctive reactions coming under the rule of intelligence. Its biological function seems to be to inhibit or modify instinctive responses. So common is this process

that some psychologists believe instincts need no training but only to be curbed. As a maxim of practical life this statement merits the most careful consideration. So stated it is probably true. Complete suppression of certain impulses may, however, produce discouragement and lack of initiative.

Certain Human Instincts.-There is almost no agreement among psychologists as to the number of human instincts. 

Opinion ranges from about forty downward. Fortunately the dispute is of little consequence to an outline of psychology. It will be adequate for our purpose to describe a number of impulses which are quite generally regarded as instinctive and to direct attention to others which may not present so clear a picture.

Sucking and crying in the babe, later the impulse to creep, and still later the impulse to walk are probably all instinctive and due to the ripening of nervous circuits. 

In fact the Germans name the child successively "the nursling, the graspling, the speakling and the runling,” according to the instinct which is momentarily predominant. 

If creeping were always done in the usual quadrupedal way, we need not describe it. Some babes, however, do not creep in this way. Some time after being able to sit erect upon the floor, such a babe begins to pull himself forward by pressing his heels against the floor and powerfully flexing his knees. Thus, the feet being fixed in position, the body is pulled forward while still erect. If the first pull brings the body to the left of the feet, in beginning the next, the feet are placed at the left of the body. In this way the babe moves in a straight line toward its goal. In a few days the quick shifting of the feet from side to side and the quick, strong pulls are skillfully executed. Some mothers report that this trait is hereditary in the child's

INSTINCT 

143 family. In other cases it is a mere chance variation of the impulse to creep. This type of locomotion rather contradicts those who believe that a babe's creeping represents a quadrupedal stage of development of our prehuman ancestors. It shows that even the most fundamental instincts may be variable in mankind. In a large class in psychology, seventy-five persons had observed this nonquadrupedal creeping or locomotion in babes of their acquaintance. Twenty-three students had seen it in more than one child. Two, on making inquiry, found evidence that it was hereditary. Besides this somewhat common type of early locomotion, one child, though sitting in the erect position, pushed herself forward with her hands. 

Another put his feet underneath his thighs and "rocked forward." 

Imitation. Although animals have been observed a great deal in order to find evidence of imitation, very few clear cases have been found. Haggerty found only a score of instances in monkeys and Thorndike remarks that, if you give a monkey a toothpick, he will promptly put it in his mouth. This looks like imitation, but it is not. The monkey puts everything in his mouth. When the observer is competent and consequently critical, so few cases of imitation in animals have been found as to be negligible, apart from such sports of nature as the parrot. 

With children the case is quite different. At different times they seem to imitate everything both animate and inanimate. After the visit of the circus they imitate both the animals and the performers. At other times they imitate a train or a motor car. A whole school grade became adept at imitating the honk of a motor car. They imitate the penmanship of teacher, parent or companion. Fashions and manners of both action and speech are but evidence

Much of it is quite unconscious. of imitation.

A boy whose father had lost an arm in the Civil War was surprised to find himself tying certain knots with one hand in the same skillful way in which his father tied them. 

There had been no conscious attempt to "learn" the trick.

The unconscious type of imitation is common enough so that some writers would limit the instinct to the unconscious process. The instinctive urge to imitate seems to pass over to the conscious attempt at a copy, so the impulse to all imitation may be considered instinctive. 

Sooner or later almost every child finds a teacher whom he regards as an admirable person. Such a person is likely to be consciously imitated. This rapport with someone regarded as worthy of imitation may mark the beginning of voluntary education. Imitation of speech is clearest of all. In summer resorts the advent of the tourists is evidenced by the change of dialect. Each human being speaks the language he heard in his childhood. If a stammering child enters school, it may be a serious matter. 

At first there is imitation for fun or to torture the stammerer, but soon stammering is a habit of many unless strong measures are taken to prevent its spread. Somewhere I have read of a teacher who lisped. Before the close of the year all but thirteen of the forty-five pupils under her care lisped. Children who become deaf early become dumb, for apparently we at first imitate the words we hear others utter and later those we hear uttered by our own voice.

In the field of intelligent imitation, most republics on the western continent are copies of our own, of the work of 

Franklin, Hamilton, Washington and their colleagues.

The constitutions of the forty-eight states are also imitations of their work; some of them very poor imitations

INSTINCT 

145 indeed. Our federal reserve banks are an adaptation to this country of the Bank of England. The League of 

Nations hopes that the government of mandated colonies will be a model imitated in the government of all colonies.

Programs of study for schools and colleges are, in large part, imitations of other programs. The imitation of the elective system in the United States a few years ago is a notable example, as well as the insistence at the same time that our universities should be faithful copies of the German universities. This imitation was brought to a halt only by the war. This imitation of one institution by another has its good side as well as a bad one. Without it education would be overrun with ill-considered innovations. When, however, legal decisions are to be modeled only on the decisions of similar cases, it may be that justice is lost sight of. Our feelings support our imitations so powerfully that many historic innovators have been destroyed. What begins as imitation ends as tradition, the most difficult of all things to change.

Curiosity. While curiosity is found among the higher animals far more often than imitation, both have reached their culmination in man. With the animals curiosity almost always serves merely another instinct. More must be known about an animal which appears in the environment, for it may be either an enemy or a friend. If an enemy, flight or fighting must follow next. Hence we find that moving objects or animals are special stimuli for the curiosity of animals and hunters often take advantage of this animal trait to bring the game within range of their rifles.

For the intelligence of man, any and every object may be of interest and advantage. Hence his curiosity is general. While an animal may react on an object in only a

few definite and instinctive ways, intelligence may react in many ways and each reaction seems to reveal properties of the object or problem to which new, profitable reactions are possible. It may be that scientific curiosity, the interest in all sorts of objects, may be different from instinctive curiosity, but the latter appears to be the genetic forerunner of the former. We rank men very much according to the curiosity they display in all sorts of problems. The mind which is challenged by the processes of nature and society and is interested in resolving all the inconsistencies with which we are confronted, is the mind of the discoverer, the inventor, and the scientist. The progress of civilization is led by such minds. Besides these, however, there must be a multitude of other minds endowed with sufficient curiosity to catch at least an intelligent glimpse of what the leaders are doing. The leader in science must have constituents quite as much as the leader in society and politics. Intense scientific curiosity among the leaders of thought and a sufficient share of it in others to understand their discoveries theoretically are the driving forces in the advance being made today. Certain races of mankind exhibit this tendency in a high degree. Backward races show much less of it. 

The Hunting Instinct.-Primitive man is necessarily a hunter. His living at all depends on his skill in obtaining food. He has left his stone weapons strewn widely over the earth. So many generations of hunting ancestors must have left their mark on the nervous system of civilized man. As a result, there is in many men a strong passion for the chase. They find a primitive joy in lying in wait long hours for game and in engaging in the hunt to be "in at the death." Expensive guns are bought which, at most, can be used but once or twice a year. In modern times

INSTINCT 

147 

The this instinct seems to be harmful in great measure. annual slaughter of hunters is a fair proportion of the slaughter of the game. It seems that, unless a hunting habit and hunting caution have been grafted onto the instinct in youth, the gratification of the impulse is dangerous. Modern conditions give little opportunity for the acquisition of skill in this field, yet the number of men who experience intense delight in hunting is very great. Perhaps it is no greater than the number of men to whom slaughter, even of animals, is repugnant. The instinct has no real value to men who toil at desks today. If we give up our work with symbols and return to dealing with things exclusively, we shall again have need of the weapons of the chase.

The anthropoligist's account of how primitive men advanced from hunting to agriculture, throws some light on the present danger of the hunting impulse. Take the 

Mesa Verde cliff dwellers, for example. We are told that they were excelled in hunting and fighting by the plains Indians or their forbears. They were forced, therefore, to take refuge in the mountain cliff-dwellings. Here there was not sufficient game, so they must sow seed and raise maize to supplement the food obtained by hunting. The result was a race with a fixed habitation, a home of some sort, and a more abundant food supply than that of the purely hunting tribes. This gave leisure for the development of pottery-making and thus the change from hunting to agriculture was ushered in with all that the latter art implies. A higher stage of racial development was attained and a more peaceful and secure mode of living. This happened to many other tribes, outstripped in hunting, and in many different places. As a consequence when modern man turns back to the exercise of an instinct which flour-

ished before the beginnings of the art of agriculture and with modern firearms he becomes most self-destructive." 

The persistence of the instinct, however, is undeniable. 

The Fighting Instinct.-History is in large part an account of the exercise of this instinct. Moreover, the accounts of battles are far more easy to remember than those of the achievements of peace. The vivid interest bears witness to the fundamental character of the instinct and some historians would deprive children of the account of the heroism of their forefathers in battles. It may be doubted whether the impulse should be thus educationally bred out or whether it can be. The instinct is still of use. 

As we are descended from successful hunters, so we are descended from successful fighters. The result is a widespread determination to conquer, so that most games are arranged as contests. One side must be beaten that the other may feel the thrill of victory. A football game was of little interest to the Sultan of Turkey because, as he said, it was too mild for a battle, too severe for a game. For the participants it was a battle royal. This game will serve to show the instinctive nature of the fighting impulse. 

In a real battle to the death there are no rules. One combatant or the other must die, the other must survive at all costs. When this instinct is aroused in an intense struggle, the old impulse is present and he who forgets rules is most apt to win. Consequently, we always learn of violations of rules and the boast of every college is that it "cleaned up football." The very fact that the boast is repeated, often for fifteen or twenty years, shows the vigor of the impulse. As long as business is generally suspended to witness this most vigorous of contests, the "editing" of "Four hunters have been killed in New Jersey alone during two weeks of the present open season for game.

INSTINCT 

149 school histories only serves to disguise or omit the fact that this instinct served the preservation of the individual and the race in the past.

Pugnacity is now more useful in other fields than in contests. When a man overcomes difficulties and conquers obstacles alone he becomes of firmer fiber. He becomes responsible and self-reliant, rather than team-reliant. The difficulty of solution of modern problems gives ample opportunity for the exercise of pugnacity. A determination not to be defeated by obstacles and handicaps of training or environment permits of the exercise of pugnacity without resort to tooth and claw. Thus exercised, it seems one of the most valuable of human traits. Once, on entering the office of the manager of a large corporation, I saw a diploma from a correspondence school. Knowing that very few students who enroll for correspondence work ever send in a single lesson, I knew that this man must have been pugnacious in the best sense of the word and as the impulse works best in modern times. His determination, rather than intellectual ability, accounted for the position he had won. The more primitive impulse is described by 

James when he points to the admiring hordes who follow a prize fighter about "as if his glory could rub off on them."

Probably there is less real courage in such a group than in a similar number of quite unobtrusive citizens, so while pugnacity is still a valuable trait, the objects and manner of its exericse have changed with time. For the steadier, silent conflict required by modern conditions the victor is possessed rather of firm determination than of the unbridled lust of the fight. 

Difference in Blood Pressure in Native and Acquired Fear. -Fear and its bodily accompaniments are described on a later page and no mention is made as to whether the fear

reactions are native or acquired or both, though that question is of great theoretical importance. It has been claimed recently that there are no native or instinctive reactions in either men or animals. All reactions of fear, rage, love, etc., are, according to this view, learned or "conditioned" (p. 133). The very word "conditioned" seems to be regarded as having the mystical potency of a magic charm. Another writer of the same school or creed claims that fear, rage, and love (lust) are "prepotent reflexes" and the term is used to imply that they are not native or instinctive. A third claim is to the effect that there are only two original stimuli to fear in the child, (1) loss of support, proved by letting the child drop from the arms of the nurse to those of the psychologist or, (2) loud sounds, such as that produced by striking a heavy iron bar with a hammer. By presenting a rat or a rabbit along with this sound the child's fear soon spreads to the animal. This fear was thus learned by the child. Consequently it is a "conditioned" fear and the child was "conditioned" to fear the animal. Thus it was proved that only the environment influences human behavior. All fear of animals is conditioned or acquired and all the fears of children, except the two first mentioned, are acquired due to the thoughtless tales of nursemaids or other unfortunate circumstances. While this theory contradicts quite general observation and experience, it wears the halo of experiment. An eleven-month-old child was found who "A haloed or even hallowed experiment may be defined as one which is devised or quoted to prove a theory but has no power to modify it nor do its results suggest the theory. A story is current of a psychologist who admitted that he wrote his scientific paper first and did the experiments to prove it afterward. Such experiments have exactly the force of a testimonial for a yeast or a cigarette. They are entirely different from the experiments of other natural sciences and have led to the return of psychology to creeds and schools. 

Note the desire to ignore the physiology of brain and sense organs lest the facts of physiology should hamper the freedom of the soi-disant psychologists in formulating startling a priori theories.

151 could at first be frightened only by loss of support and by loud sounds. He would handle such animals as frogs and rats with apparent pleasure. Because of this experiment the theory that there are no native or instinctive impulses has flourished famously.

Despite all this, we hear continually of persons who are afraid of high places, some of them being paralyzed with fear when they look down from the top of a mountain cliff, others at the mere thought of ascending it. Other persons fear dark places, others open places, and still others fear some domestic animal which most of us care for as a pet. Having often heard of persons who have a violent fear of cats and are frightened to the point of illness if a cat enters the room, I was deeply interested when one of my students reported that she had always had this violent fear, that no experience of hers in childhood or later was the cause of the fear, and that it was so intense that, when a neighbor's cat was perched on the fence, she must close every window of her car before driving into the garage for fear the cat might leap into the car as she drove by it. 

She was perfectly aware that the fear is absurd and that many little children fondle cats and are quite unharmed. 

She had been ridiculed and upbraided for her senseless behavior. Nevertheless, the fear persisted with unabated force. The reply should have been, of course, that she was mistaken, that she must have had an experience in childhood, now repressed into the unconscious, which was appearing now as a cat complex, and that she needed the services of a psychoanalyst.

When, in my second conversation with this student, another reported that she too was very much afraid of cats but that she knew exactly the experiences of her childhood which had caused the fear, I decided to measure the blood

Acquisitiveness or the Possessive Instinct.-The hunting instinct seems to be a disadvantage under present social conditions unless its possessor is early trained in its exercise. On the contrary, modern society seems to favor the acquisitive impulse beyond all others. The normal squirrel stores nuts for winter quite as instinctively as the bee stores honey. Neither knows anything of winter or its needs. The dog which buries a bone may later dig it up if he becomes hungry.

With the addition of high intelligence this impulse is strengthened. Possibly the highest function of intelligence is to forecast the future and every forecast predicts no decrease of human needs. The invention of a medium of exchange assures the satisfaction of every need, if only one has the "means." This re-enforces the hoarding or possessive instinct enormously. Thrift is extolled and the spendthrift despised. Fear and caution are instincts which support acquisitiveness. Institutions like insurance companies are established which provide for needs which may never exist but, if they do occur, the necessity is so dire that the thoughtful provide for the mere contingency. Both intelligence and modern society support and sustain the thrift impulse. It is often deplored that such support makes of us mere money grubbers. But the reply is promptly given that capitalism has fostered progress and invention, the

INSTINCT 

155 growth of ideas, as no other system ever did. Under it, every talent is employed. It creates the need for every product and furnishes the means for satisfying the need. 

Men possess the acquisitive trait in very different degrees, but those alone who possess it in a major degree are able to foster every enterprise and no substitute for them can be found. Like pugnacity, there is a strong temptation to violate the rules of the game in the exercise of this impulse. 

This demands that the umpires be fully as intelligent as the players and this has often not been the case. Most of us possess the impulse to some degree. "The nun must have her garden, the monk his books." The impulse favors a certain type of social organization and that, in turn, reenforces the impulse. Behind it all seems to lie the rather mysterious law that yesterday's luxury becomes tomorrow's necessity.

The Mating Instinct. This impulse and its accompanying behavior should not be omitted because it fulfills so well the definition with which we began. So much has been written of it in recent years, however, that there can be no dearth of information or misinformation about it. For the natural instinct the possession of a mate is the culmination for the male, the possession of children for the female. 

Thus the impulse has different "objects" in the two sexes. 

No impulse is more modified and obscured by intelligence and the conventions than this one. Some of the modifications, such as occur in the marriages of royalty, seem to have interfered with sound heredity.

Certain teachings of literary psychology show that the writers have quite misunderstood the mating instinct. As

Dr. Fosdick remarks of this teaching: "It is utterly blind to the biological and psychological facts about sex. It represents not advance, but ignorance 

From nature's · ·

standpoint sex is only a lure to get two people to love each other deeply enough and long enough to bring up children. 

What nature wants is children, and because nature always makes attractive the road to the goal she seeks, she has allured men into family life by pleasant paths. What she was getting at, however, was not the pleasure of the path, but the goal of the children, and anybody who makes it his principle of action to steal the gratification of nature's lure without fulfilling nature's purpose is committing a psychological theft on which nature wreaks inevitable vengeance. The whipper-snappers in psychology may speak to the contrary; the seers tell the truth." Here is frank recognition of the fact that instinctive behavior, while it is a response to a particular stimulus, adjusts its possessor to a whole situation. When it does not so adjust, it is often a perversion, and perversions are dangerous to mental health. If Dr. Fosdick be correct, a school of the literary psychology has urged sex perversion, because of their shallow analysis of the instinct about which they presumed to write. However, nothing has been more profitable than such writing and persuading neurotic or semi-competent minds that they were suffering from repressed sex complexes, which should be let loose at once in the most licentious fashion. If this psychoanalysis has effected cures they have not been reported. Hamilton found two mates out of two hundred who had been unfaithful for no reason whatever except to claim their psychoanalytic freedom.

Dr. Fosdick's criticism of popular, current teaching is sound and sane psychology. It deserves further quotation. "Today loose conceptions of marriage as largely consisting in bodily gratification are defended in popular minds by a supposed psychological law to the effect that the sex-

INSTINCT 

157 instinct must not be suppressed but expressed. To let yourself go, this teaching says, to do as you please, to give your emotions gangway, abandon yourself and have your fling—this is the law of a healthy sex-life. In consequence of this supposed psychological doctrine, we have wild talk among our young people about the value of promiscuous experimentation during youth, and among our older people about marriage being a temporary arrangement for mutual gratification. "As a matter of fact, this idea that the sex-instinct must not be controlled, and, when other interests make it wise, suppressed, is psychological nonsense. "Consider the matter with reference to other instincts. 

We have, for example, the instinct of self-preservation. It is fundamental. If instincts must not be repressed, that of all others must be respected. But if with your wife and children you should be in a shipwreck and, your instinct of self-preservation becoming dominant and imperious, you should crowd into a lifeboat and leave your wife and children behind and be saved while they drowned, how would you explain the matter to your friends? Would you say, I have just been reading a book on the new psychology—I felt that if I repressed my instinct of self-preservation I would be in danger of serious mental derangement? You would not get off by any such method from being an outlaw and a pariah. "Most of the cheap, popular talk about the danger of repressing instincts is nonsense. The fact is that we repress instincts or, better yet, sublimate them, every hour of our lives, or else we would be in an asylum or a jail. 

The psychological law of life is not to say to any instinct, 'Do as you please,' but out of all our instincts to build a personality."

If we regard instincts as due to inherited nervous connections the curious fact appears that only some of these connections appear to be present at birth or soon afterward. Others are said to "ripen" later. Nursing appears some hours after birth. Curiosity and imitation much later and so on. The sex impulse appears later still and we regard the youth as approaching bodily maturity when it is present. What is meant by this ripening seriatim of the instincts? The assumption has been that the nervous connections were not made until just before the instinctive behavior appears. This may be true, but with the sex instinct we now know that its manifestation is coincident with the secretion of ductless glands. Due to this is the change of voice in a boy, the beginning of a beard, and other secondary sexual characters. The hormone is the cause of it all; I think even of the vivid imagination of adolescence. Thus in this one instance alone do we know what is meant by the ripening of the instinct. It seems hardly possible that other instincts are also due to hormones but surely our explanation of their serial appearance is vague enough so that we should be alert for the discovery of new information to support or refute the theory of the formation of new nervous connections at different periods of youth. 

Allport regards the theory as refuted. There are not instincts in man but reflexes co-ordinated by learning, i. e., habits which are acquired. The evidence for and against this hypothesis seems equally balanced except that the possession by man of no inherited connections and their very common occurrence in animals, which is admitted by Allport, seems improbable in the light of the biological evidence. One need not accept the all or none principle in this case. Trial and error may co-operate in the formation

INSTINCT 

159 and the "smoothing up" of the reaction. This is what we should expect when memory supervenes on instinctive behavior.

Possible Localization of Instinct.-Because instinct is closely associated with affective states and the thalamus seems to be the center for the latter, Drever believes that instinctive impulses originate in the thalamus. The experiments of Head give some warrant for this. There is no evidence for their localization in the midbrain, as stated in a recent textbook.

Instinct and Desire. Each instinct is a tendency to act in a certain way whenever the environment gives occasion for such action. Plainly there is an impulse to suckle, to imitate, to hunt, fight, and mate and so on. For a bystander reflecting on the behavior, all these impulses serve the two great ends of the preservation of the individual and the perpetuation of the race. But each instinct is specific and reflects no gleam of those remote ends, except that by introspection intelligence may turn onlooker and see that instinctive behavior serves these biological needs. 

Because of the impulsive force of instincts, it has been said that all the drives and urges of life come from them and that a man's or a child's instinctive drives are more important than his intellectual capacities, since they show how much energy he will put forth for the attainment of his ends. They determine temperament in large part and so are "the germs of the person." This is quite true but immediate ends are things desired, and we struggle to attain what we desire. Hence the drives and urges do not come from without, as the terms imply, but from within. 

We wish to be like our companions or superior to them and to make them acknowledge our superiority. A mate is desired and recognition from a potential mate means

much. Hence instincts generate desires as well as tendencies to action. The "germs of the person" thus come to be the strength and intensity of his desires and instinct and bodily appetites are the cause of most of our wishes. 

The repression of one of these instinctive wishes is, according to Freud, a cause of mental disorder or hysterical symptoms. But he adds that the wish itself is unconscious and that all desires spring from the sex instinct. These two claims are not widely accepted. The wish is conscious, generally very intensely conscious. Desire should therefore be described in psychology of the non-Freudian type and its relation to instinct and appetite made clear. Even our intellectual desires are linked with some instinct, as curiosity leads us to study or travel. Since desire has a clearly conceived or imagined end to be attained, it is partly an intellectual state, though it is partly an emotion as well.

I have described a few prominent impulses which are generally accepted by those psychologists who admit the existence of instincts at all. They are typical and permit an outline picture of the topic.
