CHAPTER V 

НАВІТ As connections are formed between neurons they become pathways for the conduction of nervous impulses. 

When they are conducted along motor nerves to muscles an act results. After the act has been performed a considerable number of times, there is a strong tendency to repeat it whenever an appropriate occasion arises and sometimes when the occasion is inappropriate. This is often a source of embarrassment. This tendency to repeat some action again and again is a habit. The strength of the tendency is proportional to the number of previous repetitions of the act. The tendency and its strength are explained by the fact that whenever nervous impulses cross a particular synapse it becomes more permeable to the passage of later impulses. Its resistance becomes less with each repetition. The result of this lowered resistance is the formation of a habit. Finally, the readiness of the impulse to discharge into the act becomes so great that it requires great effort of will to check or prevent the action. 

There are many examples of the formation of habits.

In learning to use a typewriter, great difficulty is experienced at first. Our touch is awkward, hesitant, and vividly conscious in the sense that we must give close attention to every stroke. But one, who uses a typewriter every day and all day, soon comes to strike each key unconsciously and to strike a hundred keys successively in the time required to depress five or ten at the beginning. A

HABIT 

163 habit of typing has been formed. The writing is now automatic and attention need be given only to what is to be written and not at all to the machine. The nervous system now does automatically what attention had to direct at the beginning of practice. An incidental but important result is that fatigue is diminished as the habit becomes more and more firmly established. Fatigue very quickly followed when the learning was first begun. This would suggest that the effort of attention in the first attempts was expended in getting the nervous impulses to cross the right synapses. After the habit is fully formed, it would be hard to get them to cross other synapses. This is shown by the fact that even an expert typist finds it very difficult to change from a keyboard with four rows of letters and characters to one with three rows. So habit determines what kind of machine is salable in this case as in many others. 

Typing, however, is an extremely difficult habit to form. The child's imitation of the speech he hears about him and his resulting habits of speech are far simpler. 

Almost unconsciously he comes to speak with a nasal twang, if he hears only nasal tones. If those about him say "idear" for "idea," he may find it impossible in later life to drop the r, no matter how much he may wish to do so. From such experiences we all become aware that most human behavior is habitual. Because such action is unaccompanied by fatigue, there is great advantage in habit and routine. Its corresponding disadvantage lies in the fact that habits are so very difficult to alter or to "break." 

Consequently many descriptions of habit consist of warnings against slavery to it and maxims for forming new habits. We cannot repeat this but it will be implied for the thoughtful reader in Ach's "associative equivalent of

determination" or habit equivalent of will, which forms our next topic.

The Habit Equivalent of Will.-To determine the strength of associations, Ach had the subjects of his experiments practise transposing pairs of syllables. The transpositions were repeated one hundred twenty times, and the repetitions distributed over eleven days. Then they were asked to give rhymes for the syllables instead of transposing them. There were always false reactions.

That is, the subject did not always do what he had determined upon, but sometimes reverted to the associations which had been practised in. "Yet on the thirteenth day (140 repetitions) an extraordinary concentration on the purpose to give rhymes instead of transpositions succeeded." The determination triumphed over the association but the effectiveness of the association showed itself in the slowing up of the response.

With one hundred repetitions an average determination of the will was able to direct the course of events. So for this person and this activity the "associative equivalent of determination" lay between 100 and 120 repetitions. This associative equivalent of determination is the "number of repetitions which must just be exceeded in order that the association established, and not the determination, shall determine the reaction." This equivalent of determination is important for when we come to more purely motor performances, some such number of repetitions is the habit equivalent of the will. 

This measure is eloquent of the power of habit. After one to two hundred repetitions of an act, the will alone is powerless to stop it, in some nervous systems. In others it may require further repetitions, while still others may come under the domination of habit with fewer repetitions

HABIT 

165 still. The difficulty of the task influences the number, of course. Perhaps other factors affect it. Yet the relatively small number of repetitions shows how readily we become organized bundles of habits. An army thoroughly drilled to go forward at the word of command, probably could not retreat of its own volition in the face of such a command. 

To this habit equivalent, we may add a sort of hypothetical physiology of the nervous system. It is regarded as more plastic in the years of youth, so that habits are more firmly formed, and perhaps with fewer repetitions during those years. It is believed that physical habits are completely formed by about twenty-five years of age and intellectual habits somewhat later. So far as I can observe, habits fully formed before seventeen years of age are never broken, unless health is seriously endangered by them, while those formed after thirty are readily discontinued for years at a time.

A Gland May Form a Habit. It is said that a certain state board of health, knowing the danger to babes of artificial feeding, sought to cause mothers to make an effort toward natural nursing. It was found that if the mother regularly pressed on her breasts in such a way as would have forced out the milk, if it had been present, the milk secretion would soon return and the babe could be naturally fed. The secretion was returned sometimes after several months of absence. This is a very important practical discovery, but psychologically it merely shows that a gland may form a habit, or that the nerves leading to glands are subject to the same laws as motor nerves. The next topic may suggest that possibly the desire of the mother as well as the repeated and regular manipulation may have had something to do with the return of the secretion. 

The Conditioned or Cerebral Reflex.-Pavlov, a Russian

physiologist, devised the method of making an incision in the "cheek" of a dog and attaching thereto the duct of a salivary gland. By keeping the incision open a permanent fistula was established and the gland thus opened on the outside, instead of on the inside of the mouth. By means of a smaller tube inserted into the fistula, a testtube could be attached to the duct and thus the number of cubic centimeters of saliva could be measured or the number of drops counted. The effect of different stimuli and different emotions or expectations on the flow of saliva could thus be studied with interesting results. The method has added to knowledge of animal psychology and probably many of the facts apply to human beings. 

Pavlov's method was to feed the dog at a given signal. 

Soon saliva would be secreted, as soon as the signal was given, when food or the odor of food was not yet present. 

Thus the secretion of the gland could be associated with almost any type of stimulus, not natively suited to produce the secretion at all. Such secretion, produced by "foreign" stimuli, Pavlov called a "conditioned" reflex. It is conditioned by training. Since it was later proved to be due to the cerebral cortex it has been better termed a cerebral reflex.¹ Subjectively, it appears to reveal the effect of memory and expectation in the dog on the salivary secretion. It would, therefore, depend upon association. Objectively, it is a habit produced by training so examples may be given here.

When a particular tone was sounded whenever the dog was fed, soon saliva was secreted for the tone alone. Tones of higher and higher pitch were then employed, until Pavlov could prove that the dog hears a note of 70,000 vibratract. "There are also unconscious reflexes involved, especially in the alimentary

HABIT 

167 tions per second, which is far beyond the range of the human ear. The reaction depends on the repetition of perceptions. It is not innate. It establishes itself progressively and increases as the habit grows stronger. In puppies which were fed for six months only on milk, the odor or the sight of milk would produce an abundant secretion, but the odor of no other food, except that of cheese and curds, would produce it. Meat or biscuit actually placed in the puppies' mouths would not cause the secretion. More interesting still, the kind of substance which the dog sees or smells, or even expects, due, say, to a bulg. ing pocket of his master, determines the kind of saliva secreted. If he is offered salt or sulfate of quinine the saliva appears immediately, is abundant, fluid, and poor in ferment. When he is offered sugar, the secretion is slow in appearing, small in amount, viscous and rich in amylase. 

It seems evident that memories of past experiences are the causes of the different reactions. On the other hand, a few critics insist that the reaction is a mere reflex connected with a stimulus and, while it is cerebral, no memory image exists in the chain of events leading to it. Perhaps both views are true, memory images being present in the early experiences and growing less and less vivid as the habit grows stronger. This is true of many of our learned reactions. They are accompanied by intense thought while being learned. But finally lower centers control the whole activity and the behavior goes on automatically. Of this later stage an objective account can be given but it is plain that the conditioned reflex is accompanied by expectation and emotion and it is quite as much a formation of associations as it is a habit. Consequently it is generally described as association and we shall take that point of view when we turn to a subjective description.

The Final Common Path.-For the further understanding of habit formation we need a physiological conception 

MUSCLE 

RCR 

Fig. 19-Diagram to illustrate the convergence of neurons of higher orders upon the final common path and to show how impulses may get "switched on” to the final common path in the wrong sequence, thus causing omissions, transpositions, etc. Any such diagram may give false as well as true impressions; e. g., many more neurons than those represented might come from a single small area. They are of microscopic dimensions. Hence no such wide area need be occupied by neurons of the higher orders. On the other hand, impulses may come from widely different cortical areas for the execution of a complex act. proposed by Sherrington and proved by his experiments.

If each habit represented a single, separate path from the sensory nerve ends, to the center, and thence to the muscles or glands, we should form fewer habits than we do and apparently each would be as invariable as the operation of a machine. Each pathway is not single and open to but one impulse. Instead, cortical centers may discharge downward into several paths of a lower order. These must discharge into a smaller number, and finally all the impulses must follow a final common path to the muscle. The process may be symbolized as in Figure 19.

HABIT 

169 Not all these impulses can be carried by the final path at once. They must be switched on successively. Thus in a complex habit one simple reflex is followed by another in a definite order in executing the series of simple acts which make up the habit. As long as the synapses open in the proper order the habit unfolds itself in a perfect sequence of steps. That it is thus perfect is assumed in all descriptions of habit, yet nothing is more common than slight slips in the order of the simple acts. These are called lapses and they deserve a word of explanation. 

Lapses. Though speech and writing are accompanied by conscious effort and imitation when they are being learned, they later become mere cerebral and motor nerve habits. We have but to think of what we wish to say or write and lips or hand automatically execute the act.

Later many of us add typewriting as a habitual act. But sometimes, instead of executing a perfect series of simple acts in the habitual order, we omit one, transpose two others, or anticipate another and insert it in the series before it should take place. Again we repeat the word we have just written. Thus we may, with a typewriter, write fi for if, or adn for and, while with a pen we are more likely to omit letters or repeat words. In a scientific journal I have just read the word "adaption," where adaptation was plainly meant. In fact, the profession of proof-reader probably exists because of our propensity for lapses in the writing habit. Speech is less fallible than writing, of course. Yet, I just now suggested that a letter be sent to 

Emporia. In a moment I was asked, "Did you say 

Peoria?" Here there is an omission and transposition of sounds in the first part of the word. The last three syllables have reached the final path in correct order. It seems evident that from the cerebral centers of speech or

writing impulses discharge downward to neurons of the next lower order. These pathways are less numerous than those above but more numerous than those below. Finally, there is convergence on the final common path. Several neurons or paths are ready to discharge into it but only one impulse can be carried by the final path at any one instant. Because of the readiness of the neurons of the second order to discharge, their impulses may be "switched on" to the final common path in the wrong order, or one impulse may be omitted altogether, as in the word "adaption," above. The necessity for impulses from higher neurons to use the final common path explains how lapses occur and why habitual action is not perfect, infallible, and machinelike, as it has always been described. These deviations from perfection in habit are just as important for psychology as the perfect sequence of simple acts in the habitual chain, at which men have wondered so long. 

Since physiology has given us the explanation we ought by all means to adopt it. Lapses are a very common type of behavior and psychologists have agreed to describe and explain behavior.

Two or three brief sentences of Sherrington's seem to give a complete explanation of these errors of habit. "The final common path must be used in succession, not simultaneously, by the higher neurons discharging into it. Its rhythm must be equal to theirs." "Before finally converging upon the motor neuron the arcs converge to some degree," and "the threshold of each succeeding reflex is lowered by the excitation just preceding its own." (Sher rington, C. S., The Integrative Action of the Nervous Sys tem, pp. 117 and 124.) 

Not only are lapses a common type of behavior which psychology should not ignore, but they have been a cause

HABIT 

171 of changes in language. Since writing is far slower than speech, lapses occur more often in the former, but any attempt to hasten either speech or writing increases the number of lapses. Philologists recognize hasty speech as one cause of phonetic changes. Is it possible that Sherrington's discovery may lead to an explanation of poor spelling? Thus far psychology has been able to throw no light on the subject.

Omissions, repetitions, transpositions, and anticipations of words or letters are apparently due to the capacity of the final common path and the necessity for its use in succession by neurons of the second order. There is a type of lapse as common as any one of these which appears to be due not to a final common path but to partly common paths of brain patterns. Above, when I wished to write "accompanied," I wrote "accomplished." The pattern followed by the nervous impulses may be symbolized thus: -ani accomp -ed -lish 

A newspaper reporter wrote, "Natural History Museum Artists Descended in a Suburban Tube in the Bahamas." He meant, of course, a submarine tube, as the article showed. Here, again, a diagram of the probable brain action shows partly common paths: marine sub- tube urban Of course, the reporter had written and spoken the words, "suburban tube," many times, but these repetitions would have had no influence had he not first written the syllable, 'See note, p. 50.

"sub." However, another cause of his error was the similarity of beginning (and perhaps of the ending) of the two phrases. Similarity, however, is partial identity. In this case the partial identity consists of the partly common paths. These, therefore, could account, not only for lapses plainly influenced by similarity, but for association by similarity as well. The latter is an important type of thinking.

There seem to be two reasons, then, why habit is not machinelike; why impulses starting from a motor center need not discharge always in the same sequence or may in part be replaced by others: (1) There is the structural necessity of using the final common path in succession, not simultaneously. (2) There are paths partly common to different brain patterns and this means that, instead of writing or speaking the habitual or intended word, we utter or write one of its similars, as in the examples above, to which thousands of others could easily be added. The idea of the common path seems to give us a clear conception of the mechanism of habit formation and association, thus permitting an objective account of habitual behavior, both when the habitual act is executed perfectly and when one or more of its elements go astray. 

Before the announcement of the neuron theory and its verification, William James wrote a chapter on habit so vivid and impressive that hardly anyone has written of it since. The practical and moral implications of habit are there stated as they never can be again. Consequently every student should read James' chapter either in his "Principles of Psychology" or in the "Briefer Course." I have merely tried to add a few facts which physiology has given us since James' chapter was written. If the student will reflect on Ach's "habit equivalent of will," he will see

HABIT how James' chapter could almost be deduced from that recent measure of "the force of habit."

An Example of Habit Formation.-Habits are observable in all human beings, so that few examples need be given. 

One instance, so common that it is often overlooked, may be mentioned to illustrate both the rapidity of habit formation and the power of a habit once formed. A bright little girl, who had learned to read eleven words, could read them when they were presented upside down with a loss of only 30 per cent. of the time required to read them in the normal position. Many an adult cannot read inverted print at all. Others can do so but it requires five or ten times as long as normal reading. When it comes to reading type, which is the mirror image of print, most of us are completely baffled. The forms are the same. They are reversed from left to right and we cannot read them in this "unnatural" order. But the order is not unnatural. It is simply not habitual. There is no reason at all why, if we had started with mirror print, we could not read it as rapidly and as easily as ordinary print. Our habit of reading makes this impossible and we are at a total loss to make a correction in type without first taking a proof. The printer may be able to read type but even his reading is much slower than his reading of print unless he has had an exceptional amount of practice. Mirror writing is equally difficult for us. Yet imbeciles learn so slowly that a symptom of their condition is mirror writing. Some of them produce it for a long time and do not notice that they have reversed the copy. A normal brain is a rapid habit former and in this is both the danger and the advantage of habit. Psychologists simplify the experiment of mirror drawing by asking students merely to trace a star as it is seen in a mirror. This too sets our habits at naught

and it is difficult to learn. The fact that ordinary writing and printing seem to be the only natural forms, shows the power of habit. Often a beginner in a foreign language is surprised to find the word order quite different from that of his native tongue. When he has formed the new associations, he reads the words in the foreign order and is quite unconscious of order at all.

Since habits are so readily formed and so hard to abandon, disadvantageous ones must be shunned. Probably a sound device is to promise a youth a reward if he will avoid beginning a practice until he is twenty-five years of age. Ten to one, he will never begin it and, if he does, he is unlikely to be enslaved by a habit begun at that age.

CHAPTER VI EMOTION 

Since instincts and emotions are simpler and more primitive than intellectual processes, and since they seem to be functions of the old brain, we have already introduced the term emotion in giving evidence that the activity of the optic thalamus is necessary to the experience of emotion and, when that organ is diseased, emotional life is profoundly altered. This procedure was justified by our plan to describe simpler psychic processes first. Moreover, we know from experience what emotions are and, if we did not, no description would make them clear to us. 

The simple theory of emotion stated on page 112 has taken the place of the James-Lange Theory. It should be read again at this point but it need not be restated here. 

Persons who concern themselves with social conditions are considerably disturbed by the fact that some seventyfive thousand individuals are entering psychopathic hospitals each year. Many of these admissions must be because of emotional instability, defective inhibitions, and a lack of proper balance between desire and duty, inclinations and obligations. Because of this apparent increased entry into institutions and because deviations from the normal often serve to make the latter clearer, we may begin our account with some examples of disturbed or unhealthy emotions.

Disorders of Emotional Life.-Perhaps of first impor tance among these disorders is the tendency of the emotions connected with dominance to become abnormally

exaggerated. Left to itself the desire to dominate others without any regard for their rights will grow, almost or quite to the point of criminality. Inhibition of this desire must be established in childhood or it may not be established at all. This ever increasing satisfaction in dominating others has influenced history perhaps more than any other emotion. Yet it may be that the dominating behavior is due no more to the satisfaction it gives than to the absence of inhibition. Emotions and inhibitions are subject to the laws of habit formation. Dr. Arthur H. Ruggles has given a case history of this growth in domination which is typical. It led to ruination and this too is a characteristic result. "A famous school boy football player of great athletic ability was a spoiled child; because of his ability, he was made of, grew to believe that he could accomplish anything and get his own way in everything that he desired. 

Later, when he went to college, still an adolescent, he became a very famous football player, but his mates realized his temperamental tendencies and his spoiled child attitude. When men were proposed for the fraternity he would say, 'No, I don't want that man! When asked his reason, he had none except an emotional reaction that he did not like that particular fellow; if some freshman had shown for the football player a little hero worship, he was bound to have him in the fraternity whether the others wanted him or not, and unfortunately, on account of his athletic prominence, even in college he usually gained his point. He married, had children, but soon tired of his responsibilities of husband and father, his attitude in the home changed and he announced one day to his wife that he couldn't bear to come home, that he must have his freedom and was going to have it, and in spite of the pro-

EMOTION 

177 tests of his friends and business associates this spoiled child and pampered adolescent again gained his point, slipped over into Mexico, and without reason, except his own immature emotional one, he obtained a divorce. Later in his career he tired of his business responsibilities, turned his back on those who had made him in a business way, and went off on a career of wild speculation that eventually led to his financial ruin."

Here there were no longer any inhibitions. The marriage contract, duty to wife and children and business associates did not check his pursuit of his own whims. So many cases similar to this one are known that the question should be asked, Is the behavior of a spoiled child very different from that of an insane person? The cause of each is different. The result seems to be the same, complete maladjustment to the environment. Mental hygiene seems to be the discovery of the folly of parents and guardians in not setting up normal inhibitions and early establishing self-control. Then there is the further discovery that divided homes produce the same result as senselessly indulgent parents. Exaggerated self-conceit and delusions of grandeur occur in certain insane persons and we are not sure that the delusions of grandeur produced by humoring every whim are different from those of the genuinely insane. It may be that "that way madness lies." The case quoted is a psychological miniature of centuries of history. The despot and the tyrant have their own way unhindered and unopposed. Thus they became despots. 

The great war was due more to this psychological cause than to any other. Despots and tyrants are sooner or later destroyed or exiled, so the result is similar to that of the athlete. Our forefathers were so well acquainted with this exaggerated growth of the will to dominate that they

limited the exercise of power to a term of years, except in the case of judges, who must be freed from another emotion, fear. When the whipper-snappers speak for longer terms of office, we may smile at their assumption of knowledge and their ignorance of human psychology. 

How early the tendency to dominate and to have one's own way may appear and how early it should be checked is shown in the opinion of a competent psychiatrist. He believes that if a child gets what it wants by tantrums, crying, and holding its breath, the habit may later develop into a true hysteria. Hysteria is a serious psychosis and often results in a being socially useless.

Repression and Conflict.-A type of popular psychology states that emotionally-toned ideas are often repressed into the unconscious. They are then, of course, forgotten though they are supposed to work the effect on consciousness of producing mental illness. The difficulty with this doctrine is that it is well-nigh impossible to forget intense emotional experiences. The struggle to do this sometimes produces so great a conflict as to interfere with intellectual work. Again let us borrow a case history from Ruggles, which shows that the very attempt at repression caused the trouble.

A college student had done two years of satisfactory work. "During the summer vacation following his sophomore year our patient went sailing with his chum and his chum's father; a severe storm came up, the boat was capsized and the three men clung to the upturned boat, unable to right it. This occurred at three o'clock in the afternoon and although they tried to hail passing boats none of them gave help. Our patient's companion was a rather delicate fellow with a diseased heart, and due to the physical and mental strain that he was under, and the exposure of

EMOTION 

179 clinging to the upturned boat many hours, he died during the night; then, the father and our patient, in addition to clinging to the boat themselves, had to hold the dead body on the boat, and they were not sighted and picked up until the afternoon of the second day. Our patient, exhausted and suffering from this tremendous emotional strain, then went to his own home, and his family, with the best intentions in the world, advised him neither to talk nor think of the experience; they would not even let him attend the funeral of his chum; and so, added to the physical strain, we have a boy endeavoring to repress his tremendous emotional trauma, and we have definitely learned that the repression of severe emotional traumata may cause serious emotional upsets. This boy spent most of his vacation trying to forget, but of course was unable to. 

He returned to his work in the fall and the reason that he did not study was because he could not. When he picked up his book it was to find that he was unable to concentrate on the page before him, because of the constantly recurring memory of his most unhappy experience. When he went to bed at night it was, again, to think of the tragedy, and if by chance he went to sleep the whole experience would come up vividly in the form of dreams. So this boy did what any of us would do in a similar experience—he tried to repress the memories with thoughts of experiences that would help him to forget. This is what we call sublimation, and so he sublimated, not as some do in alcohol or hysterical manifestations but rather in taking charge of his fraternity chinning, constantly being with groups of fellows who were discussing various problems of more or less importance, and taking part in every social activity that he could reach-so very truly he did not study, but simply because he could not."

This instance is instructive because it shows that memory of the tragic experience was not repressed, could not be so repressed and it was the attempt to get rid of these vivid memories which caused all the difficulty. Had this boy been dismissed from college he planned not to return home but to go West and make good, or else to commit suicide. Here there was continual conflict between emotion and thought or concentration on study. Because of its vividness the emotion was victorious over the efforts at study for two or three years. Finally, since the youth had a sound mind, his determination triumphed and he was able to complete his studies for graduation. Thousands of cases of shell shock, which occurred in the late war, are somewhat similar to the experience of this college student. 

Soldiers of great mental and moral stamina came through stressful experiences without deterioration. Others developed symptoms of hysteria, seemed to lose character and will and became practically useless to society or to themselves. This conflict between thought and feeling is always present in most of us. Conditions demand that thought and attention overcome our emotional propensities. Consequently, one psychologist, at least, has prescribed a little gratuitous exercise every day in doing what we do not wish to, simply because we do not wish to do it. This gratuitous effort will develop strength, if finally we should need to overcome stronger emotion than mere dislike. For the same reason, another writer makes a general command, "If you don't like it, do it." Obedience to this would go far to prevent such perverted emotional development as shown in the athlete, above described. 

Feelings of Inferiority. Every one has at times feelings of inferiority, the feeling of being inadequate. If such a feeling is allowed to grow and luxuriate, it may finally

EMOTION 

181 result in a morbid temperament. The best antidote for such a feeling is frankly to recognize that we must do the best we can with the powers we possess. There is no changing them except by development through use and exercise and this development is, indeed, considerable. Moreover, the reflection that many men with no greater ability than our own have coped successfully with life's difficulties should be very reassuring. The great thing is not to surrender to depressed feelings. A popular writer puts it well when he says, "It is not losing one's job but losing one's grip that counts." 

In recent years the "inferiority complex" of Freud and Adler has been almost deified. The suggestion of repetition has worked to convince the thoughtless that they must have an inferiority complex or, if not, they ought to have it, neatly repressed into the unconscious, working damage, and paralyzing effort and will. No one can know what is in the unconscious and, if there is a feeling of inadequacy, it will be embarrassingly conscious. Reflection and determination to dismiss it from mind and make the best of our powers will succeed in normal minds. 

How absurd the doctrine of complexes may become in the "literary psychology" may be seen from the following remarks by a psychiatrist: "Every dream, every neurosis, every hysterical reaction, every phenomenon of obsession, finally every psychosis, were reduced to sexual complexes. 

The daughter must have a secret love for her father, the son for his mother; brothers and sisters must carry within them the incestuous complex of a reciprocal love, and, if that did not occur, it was the love of self, narcissism, which caused all the evil. Nay more, under the direction of physicians and non-physicians, psychoanalysis descended even to the womb of the mother and knew how to

speak of complexes which the foetus had conceived even before it saw the light of day. By this arbitrary and unbridled interpretation, they threw discredit on valuable knowledge and they came to a grotesque development of this conception calling itself profound, into a miserable and mystic interpretation. In the individual psychology of Adler, it was the feeling of inferiority of which they made the unique trump. Everywhere one discovered feelings of inferiority and, in fact, who would not have them? But they must explain everything. The father corrects his child. That creates in the latter a feeling of inferiority. 

The mother covers him with tenderness. That re-enforces in the child a will to power and provokes over-compensations. Under these conditions one hardly dares to touch his child and yet it is precisely education which must do everything, for the sworn-in individual psychologist no longer knows inborn differences. Heredity and hereditary dispositions are the stories of nursemaids. Man arises from a sort of original mixture, a homogeneous mass, and what he becomes is only the consequence of the feelings of inferiority, produced by education, or of his desire for power of the same origin. And, if one admits a certain disposition-I quote the disposition, for example, to shed blood, it is finally education which will determine if such an individual will become a murderer, a butcher, or a surgeon. This is what we read in a recent study of individual psychology of characters, written, unfortunately, by a physician. In this sort of thing, by the desire to make a universal panacea out of a unique idea, a valuable bit of knowledge has been transformed, so to speak, into a farce, into a mythology." (Ewald, Scientia, I-I-1930.)

Normal emotional life fluctuates continually and in times of stress it may approach the somewhat extreme

EMOTION 

183 cases described above. Perhaps, therefore, the extreme examples may serve as an introduction to the description of ordinary emotions. Let us turn to a more analytical account of normal emotion.

Emotions Distinguished from Other Psychic States. There is no need to describe the experience denoted by such words as fear, terror, anger, rage, hate, disgust, love, humiliation, sympathy, amusement, and the host of other names of emotions. Those named by the first words above are often called the major or coarser emotions because they are accompanied by violent bodily expressions and have great impulsive force. We are impelled to punish or destroy the person or thing which we hate or at which we are angry. We attempt to avoid or escape from whatever arouses fear. All the major emotions and most of the milder ones impel to action, as we shall see in the description of their psychic energy. The term affection or affective state is often used to denote the characteristic element in emotion, the simple feeling apart from its intellectual accompaniments.

Emotions differ from sensations in having no specialized end-organs. Only the exterior of our bodies can be affected by specific stimuli such as vibrations of the ether or the air, heat and mechanical contact. In fact the warmth of a heavy warm meal is believed to be due to heat radiated to nerve ends in the skin and not to warmth nerve ends in the stomach. The sympathetic nervous system has no such highly specialized nerve ends as those which subserve sensation. The second difference is perhaps dependent on the fact just stated. Emotions are not well localized. They are within us and seem to pervade the whole body instead of having a specific location. These two physiological differences probably lead to the most

pronounced introspective differences between emotions and sensations. Emotions lack clearness. Sensations have it. 

Titchener holds that this is the prime difference between affective states and sensations. Now this difference does exist but I think it has been over-emphasized. If introspection is immediate retrospection, anxiety, grief, disappointment, despair, relief, etc., seem to me almost as vivid or clear as many sensations. The reply would be that the clearness is due to the associated ideas, not to the emotion, so perhaps each individual will wish to decide for himself. 

The emotions of different persons vary greatly in intensity and perhaps in clearness as well. As a fourth difference we shall find that the simple emotion has only two attributes, namely, pleasantness and unpleasantness. I shall add that they have also the character of irradiation and of psychic energy which are practically of great importance. 

As a further practical difference, emotions seem to arise and subside more slowly than sensations. We become angrier in thinking over our insult than we were when we received it. Here, again, individuals differ greatly. A stimulus or situation which arouses but slight emotion in one man may produce a violent emotional response in another.

On the neural side, emotion seems to involve chiefly the sympathetic nervous system and the old brain, while sensation, intellectual and volitional processes depend upon the central nervous system and the cortex. So emotions are more purely subjective than other psychic states. 

Perhaps this is the reason why one who broods over his griefs and injuries becomes morbidly introspective and misinterprets the people about him. His emotions warp his judgment.

To sum up, then, emotions depend on the sympathetic

EMOTION 

185 nervous system, are pervasive and poorly localized, are not dependent on specialized end-organs, are less clear than sensations, arise and subside more slowly than the latter, are more subjective, and have the quality of pleasantness and unpleasantness. They have also the power of irradiation and are especially sources of the release of psychic energy.

The Affective Qualities and Attributes.—When we come to the study of sensation, we shall learn that there are about thirty-five thousand distinguishable visual qualities; eleven thousand tonal qualities; at least four each of taste and cutaneous qualities, and so on for the list of the senses. 

In sharp contrast with this is the general agreement that emotions have but two qualities, pleasantness and unpleasantness. By this view my satisfaction at having done a good deed or at having completed my task is exactly the same as my satisfaction on eating a good dinner. Both are pleasant emotions. The same is true of unpleasant emotions. They are alike in quality. They are believed to differ in the associated ideas, the total setting of the feeling. We shall find that there are higher and lower feelings and for practical and ethical reasons it is important to make such a distinction. The feelings themselves do not differ, however, but only their intellectual causes or sensory sources. 

Feelings of pleasantness and unpleasantness differ fundamentally from other psychic states and are consequently elements of consciousness. We find that sensations, images, and emotions make up the total stream of consciouness but their combinations are infinite in number and variety. Ziehen, a psychiatrist, believed that sensations (or ideas) have a "feeling tone." Thus the emotion would be an attribute of the sensation or idea. There

is evidence that the emotion is caused by the sensation or image rather than being a mere fringe, tone, or attribute of it. Yet Ziehen's term, "feeling tone," is so convenient that it is widely used. Psychiatrists call the pleasurable emotions expansive or exalted; the painful ones depressed. 

These are valuable terms for the description of both normal and abnormal emotions. They may have been suggested only by the bodily expression of the emotions. 

Intensity. Both pleasure and pain occur in different degrees of intensity. We speak of a mild pleasure or of an ecstasy of delight. Our remorse is bitter and our sorrow deep. Words describing degrees of emotional intensity are numerous in every language.

Duration.-The varying duration of pleasure and displeasure needs no illustration. A very successful executive said he had moments of elation. He would have added that he had hours of anxiety. Apparently life permits but little contemplation of our successes and demands long concern for their achievement. When a particular emotional state becomes habitual it is called a mood or disposition. 

Clearness.-The opinion that affective states lack clearness has already been mentioned. 

Irradiation.-We come to a more practical character of emotion when we consider its power of irradiation. In this it is much like sensory pain. An intense pain in a given region may, after a time, bring a great part of the body into sympathetic suffering with it. A toothache may involve a whole side of the face; a throbbing finger the whole arm. This is more important still in the realm of emotion. "Particular feelings, as they arise, fuse with the total emotional state in widely different ways. Some appear fleetingly to touch the surface; others appear to

EMOTION 

187 fill the whole soul." When we read of a disaster in a remote city, in which there cannot possibly be a single person that we know, we have an example of the first type. 

But let us read of the same disaster in our own village or even in our own school and let names appear of persons whom we have known intimately. The emotion will fill us through and through. We are shocked much as by a galvanic current. There is a parallelism between the degree of irradiation and the more remote or more intimate relation to the self. Instinct and emotion show more clearly their immediate relation to self- and race-preservation, than to the intellect which pursues future ends. This power of irradiation has not been overlooked by the more penetrating psychologists and never by the novelists. 

James refers to the widespread "reverberation" of emotion, and de Maupassant describes fear as "a disintegration of the very soul." All exhortation, persuasion, advertising, and a great deal of salesmanship depend for their success on this human emotional trait. 

Irradiation thus far described is an individual experience. It belongs also to the psychology of the crowd. In a panic the fear spreads through the crowd like a mighty wave. In similar fashion emotion spreads at a skillfully managed revival or at a rally but most of all irradiation is evident in time of war, when our most precious interests are threatened.

In the case of an individual, we can do little with him or for him unless a radiating emotion can be produced. 

The pupil whom we cannot interest we cannot influence. 

Writing may be difficult for an hour or two, until a "head" of interest is accumulated. The "one man bank" is likely to fail because the hope or confidence of one man may radiate and influence his judgment. The bank governed

by a loan committee is far safer, because a committee offers obstacles to emotional irradiation. 

Besides the influence of emotional irradiation over the whole field of consciousness, there is spread of effect into the bodily realm. The trembling of fear and rage, the convulsion of merriment, and the physical depression of anxiety all testify to the spread of this influence. Hence the novelist writes of the "sweep" of a mighty emotion. While it may be vague with a mild emotion it is definite enough in the avalanche phenomenon of mortal fear and rage.

Finally, every one has observed that music is the most effective agent devised by man for producing emotional irradiation, in both the psychic and the bodily realms. 

Psychic Energy. The immediate effect of a widely radiating emotion is often called its psychic energy. Thus it may be a secondary attribute or an effect, as I have just stated, but we cannot deny its presence and importance. 

Emotions influence our ideas and will in the direction of self-preservation or the attainment of bodily and mental well-being. Ideas no doubt kindle emotions but the emotion stimulates the recall and the invention of ideas. Who has not found himself recalling every word of an address which he could not learn in his study because the audience aroused his emotion. When I marvelled at a woman's having solved a problem for the health of her child which had baffled her family physician, she replied, "When you get in a pinch you must think of something." The mother's emotion provoked a host of ideas of remedies and treatments until one succeeded. Innumerable ideas are suggested under stress of emotion which would not have come to consciousness at all in calmer moments. It is barely possible that the recall of one's whole past life in the face of great peril is due to this character of emotion, and surely

EMOTION 

189 the need of the writer, composer or other creative worker to be "in the mood" for his work is an example of its psychic energy.

Historians and savants have recognized this fact of psychic energy more fully than the psychologist. The 

Berlin historian, Myers, says: "War is the mother of all things," and the Frenchman, Anatole France, says: "War is the incomparable instrument of progress." Surely progress is an affair chiefly of ideas. It must be, therefore, that the emotions of war result in the inventions, or these historical deductions are untrue. It may be that just as emotion mobilizes the bodily powers to repel attack, it mobilizes our ideas as well. If consciousness is a biological adaptation as James so often claims, this might surely be an effect of emotion.

The splendid progress of the French and English in aviation during the first three years of the great war, while our own country lagged so pitiably behind, was due to the needs of war. While the invention of the airplane was made in America, peace was not a strong stimulus to the perfection of the art. We can hardly account for this aside from the influence of war's emotions in arousing original ideas. However, few men need to be persuaded that emotion is necessary to creative work. 

The psychic energy of emotions not only arouses ideas but it seems to add impulsive force to motives and the will, driving them in the direction of our welfare. Since our welfare includes much besides physical well-being, the energy of aesthetic feelings is said to discharge itself in an effect on imagination, that of ethical feelings in the formation of ideals and in the willing to attain them, and likewise religious emotion stimulates the formation of religious conceptions and adds to their force as motives.

While the energizing influence of a strong emotion is not easy to demonstrate in the laboratory it is accessible to introspection and to observation. It seems fair to say, therefore, that not only intensity, and duration are attributes of affective states but that irradiation with its resultant psychic energy must be added to our description if we are to describe emotion as it exists in living human beings. 

Not only does emotion thus arouse and stimulate thought; it also releases a great amount of energy in bodily activity. Books on psychology are full of statements that the emotions furnish the drives and urges to action. 

Our desires spur us on. Emotions are avalanche phenomena. They cause us to act hastily and impetuously. The emotions of the public must be deeply aroused before it will attempt to inaugurate a reform. Besides impelling men to acts of the highest heroism and the lowest cowardice, emotions seem also to make life worth living or not worth living. When black despair settles upon the poor in spirit they often destroy themselves. On the other hand, the enjoyment of life comes largely from the milder emotions, the satisfaction of achievement, or sharing the joys and sorrows of others, or even of those of fictitious persons, as in the novel and the drama. 

The very great bodily energy released by emotion is described in the second topic below. In contrast with that great expenditure of energy, it is estimated that "the professor absorbed in intense mental effort for one hour has an extra demand for food or for calories during the entire hour not greater than the extra needs of the maid who dusts off his desk for five minutes. The cloistered scholar at his books may be surprised to learn that the calories needed for one hour of intense mental effort would be completely met by the eating of one oyster cracker or one-

EMOTION 

191 half of a salted peanut." (Benedict, F. G. and C. G., Science, 1930, p. 567.) This contrast between the enormous energy released by emotion and that required for thought is very striking. It may be, however, that the fatigue due to intellectual work is better detected by introspection than by a test of metabolism. 

Adaptation of Feelings.-Like sensation, emotion shows the phenomenon of adaptation. People who visit the mountains for the first time find them apparently an inexhaustible source of pleasure, but after some months they no longer arouse emotion. Our first disgust at some spectacle may gradually wane if we see it repeatedly. The poet says: "Vice is a monster of so frightful mien, As to be hated needs but to be seen. 

But seen too oft, familiar with her face, We first endure, then pity, then embrace."

Our growing obtuseness to the horrors of war, after reports of them have rained down upon us for many months, may be offered as an example of emotional adaptation. 

Our capacity for sorrow, grief, and indignation seems to have been surfeited, at least so far as vigorous expression of these passions goes. We seem, however, to "flare up" again at times, as if adaptation were not complete extinction, as it is in the case of some sensations. 

Bodily Accompaniments of Emotion.-A general account of the feelings would be incomplete without some description of their bodily accompaniments, accompaniments which, I believe, are in most cases plain effects of the feeling. Let us take for example such a major emotion as fear. 

The senses of sight and hearing, i. e., the distance receptors, are instantly aroused to activity; "eyes and mouth are opened, pupils dilated and eyebrows raised." At first the

frightened man stands motionless and breathless or crouches down, i. e., at first there may be inhibition of the action of the great skeletal muscles, which a moment later may display enormous energy. The heart beats quickly and violently, yet it was early noticed that there is pallor and often faintness under the influence of fear. The flow of saliva stops and the mouth becomes dry so that the "tongue cleaves to the roof of the mouth." The hair may stand erect, especially in many fighting animals. There is trembling and twitching of the muscles, especially those of the lips. Breathing is rapid and hurried. The voice may become dry and husky or in extreme fear it may become the characteristic voice of terror. Finally, if the fear becomes paroxysmal, "the heart beats wildly or must fail to act and faintness ensues; there is death-like pallor; the breathing is labored; the wings of the nostrils are widely dilated; there is gasping and convulsive motion of the lips, a tremor on the hollow cheek, a gulping and catching of the throat; the uncovered and protruding eyeballs are fixed on the object of terror or they may roll restlessly from side to side, huc volvens oculos totumque pererrat All muscles of the body may become rigid or may be thrown into convulsive movements. The hands are alternately clenched and opened, often with a twitching movement. The arms may be protruded as if to avert some dreadful danger, or may be thrown wildly over the head In other cases there is a sudden and uncontrollable tendency to headlong flight; and so strong is this that the boldest soldiers may be seized with a sudden panic." These statements are from Darwin's famous description of the conditions of fear. The "symptoms" open to gross observation are well enumerated but it remained for modern physiological research to ascertain many more effects of emo-

EMOTION 

193 tion, namely those which occur within the bulk of the body. 

Besides stoppage of the salivary secretion that of the gastric juice is also stopped by any violent depressive emotion and this persists long after the removal of the stimulus. The movements of the stomach, by which the food is mixed with digestive fluids, are inhibited by the emotions of grief, anxiety, fear, or rage, and doubtless by others. The food then lies undigested and we have seen the result to be "a feeling of heaviness in the stomach" due to anxiety.

This may persist for hours or even for two or three days. 

The movements of almost all the alimentary canal and especially those of the intestine are stopped, along with those of the stomach. Even slight distress will affect these movements in both men and animals. This inhibition of visceral movements is apparently due to efferent impulses discharged along sympathetic nerves, the splanchnics especially. A further result of these impulses is the release of adrenalin into the blood stream. The latter probably co-operates with the sympathetic impulses so that the result of both is an actual decrease in the volume of the spleen, kidneys, intestines, etc., i. e., in the vegetative organs due to withdrawal of blood from them. Their functioning is stopped in order that response may be made to the dangerous or astonishing object. But while adrenalin has a vaso-constrictor effect on the arterioles of the vegetative organs it has a vaso-dilator effect on the arteries of the heart and skeletal muscles. It has slight or no effect on those of the brain and lungs, yet it appears to dilate the bronchioles of the lungs with the result that after a period of heavy exertion, during which we feel fatigue and half-suffocated, we suddenly get our "second wind” and are quickly recuperated, due to this better ventilation of the blood with oxygen. The adrenalin probably co-operates

with the rapid breathing to bring about this result. The blood supply of the heart and central nervous system is increased and the blood pressure of the great skeletal muscles rises so much that they actually increase in volume due to the added blood. In short, there is an enormous addition of blood to the organs necessary for the preservation of the individual by tremendous bodily exertion.

Besides the addition of adrenalin to the blood there is also an increase of "blood sugar," which, when oxidized, serves as a source of muscular energy. Because of the increase of sugar, some of it escapes from the blood and can be found in the urine. This condition is termed glycosuria. Since it has been proved to be due to emotion, the temporary condition is called "emotional glycosuria.” 

The stress of a hard examination or the excitement of a football contest may produce it. This condition is permanent in the disease diabetes. The researches of Cannon and his pupils tend strongly to confirm the clinical observations that this disease may be caused by prolonged, intense, emotional stress or anxiety. "Kleen cites the case of a 

German officer whose diabetes and whose Iron Cross for valor both came from a stressful experience in the Franco- 

Prussian War." Another case began during the bombardment of Strassburg. In the light of the splendid experimental evidence, which cannot be recounted here, there seems no reason to doubt that violent or depressed emotions may be a genuine cause of this disease. 

Not only does the increased blood pressure in the skeletal muscles promptly sweep away the waste products of the working of the muscles but the adrenalin in the blood is able to restore the ability of the muscle to respond to stimuli after that power has been greatly diminished by

EMOTION 

195 long or excessive activity. Thus adrenalin is a direct antagonist of muscular fatigue. "What rest will do only after an hour or more, adrenalin will do in five minutes or less." (Cannon.) Moreover, blood drawn during emotion will coagulate in far less time than unexcited blood. In many instances the time required is only one-fifth of the average time. This effect appears to be due to adrenalin combined with some product of the activity of the liver. 

In a sense also these results of emotion are wrought by means of the sympathetic, or partly by the whole autonomic nervous system. Discharges of nervous energy in the sympathetic system are more widespread or diffuse and seem to cause bodily effects more slowly than those of the central system. It requires perhaps sixteen seconds after stimulation for the adrenal secretion to be poured into the blood and a few minutes for the supply of blood sugar to increase. Plainly these examples of slowness of result apply to cases of glandular action due to sympathetic impulses. Only as compared with the quickness of response of stimulated muscle are they slow, but the time itself has some bearing when we consider different theories of emotion.

In a major emotion every adjustment is made for the expenditure of muscular energy and every function not connected with such expenditure is suspended. Little wonder that Sherrington says "emotion 'moves' us, hence the word itself." So far as we can judge the bodily adjustments due to emotion follow upon efferent impulses, especially those transmitted along the splanchnic nerves; not afferent impulses. This evidence for an effect of the mind on the body is sufficiently definite to make it rather absurd to endeavor to use the periphrases of the doctrine of parallelism in this topic. Hence I have adopted "the language

of common sense," and this the more readily because physiology seems to give license, if not warrant, for this usage. 

The James-Lange Theory of Emotion.-One who looks up theories of emotion will find at least thirteen types of explanation. About half of them are physiological and regard the emotion as caused by nerve impulses from the organs of the body. The others are psychological. 

One of the physiological theories has had so enormous an influence that we must consider it at some length. It was suggested by reflecting on the widespread bodily accompaniments of emotion. James announced the opinion that the perception of an exciting object, for example, immediately causes reflex bodily adjustments. The consciousness of these reflex adjustments is the emotion. 

Lange regarded the vaso-motor changes alone as the causal factor. Sergi agrees closely with Lange. Because these two theories are so nearly identical in principle, they are frequently regarded as one, under the title of the James-Lange theory in America, the Lange-James theory in Germany. 

James writes as follows: "Our natural way of thinking about these coarser emotions is that the mental perception of some fact excites the mental affection called the emotion, and that this latter state of mind gives rise to the bodily expression. My theory, on the contrary, is that the bodily changes follow directly the perception of the exciting fact, and that our feeling of the same changes as they occur is the emotion. Common sense says, we lose our fortune, are sorry and weep; we meet a bear, are frightened and run; we are insulted by a rival, are angry and strike. 

The hypothesis here to be defended says that this order of sequence is incorrect, that the one mental state is not immediately induced by the other, that the bodily manifesta-

EMOTION 

197 tions must first be interposed between, and that the more rational statement is that we feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble, and not that we cry, strike, or tremble, because we are sorry, angry, or fearful, as the case may be." In other words, the bodily conditions which I have detailed at length are for James the cause of the emotion (instead of being caused by it) very much as sensations are the cause of perception. 

Hence he believes that a "disembodied spirit" or a person or animal whose body was entirely anaesthetic could have no emotions, but only coldly intellectual states; judgments and decisions but no feelings. The very audacity of this conception commended it to the imagination of some psychologists, while others as warmly disputed it. One sophomore student asked: "Why not say we go into the water because we get wet?" and no doubt similar counter arguments occurred to the minds of the critics of the theory. 

The strongest evidence against the opinion seems to me to come from researches on the higher animals. 

If dogs show any evidence of psychic states, they show evidence of emotions, though of course we are cut off from any introspective evidence and can only infer from the animals' behavior. Sherrington had in his laboratory a dog which showed every evidence of affection toward the laboratory attendants, and of fear or depression at the threatening tones of their voices. She also gave every evidence of rage at the presence of a cat or of one of the laboratory monkeys. Transection of the spinal cord and of the vagus nerves "removes completely and immediately the sensations of the viscera and of all the skin and muscles behind the shoulder." (P. 260.) Yet when the cord and vagus were thus transected in this dog, her fear, anger, and affection were as evident as ever save that the brist-

ling of the hair along the back could no longer occur. "No doubt was left in our minds that sudden attacks of violent anger were still easily excited." Here then is the experiment of complete bodily anaesthesia, suggested by James as a test of his theory, neatly performed (except for the area forward of the shoulder) and yet the expression of emotion still remained. When the attendant scolded this dog her "head sank, her gaze turned away from her advancing master, and her face seemed to betray dejection and anxiety." The respiration became unquiet but the pulse never changed its rate. This seems to dispose of 

Lange's contribution to the theory that vaso-motor changes alone cause the emotion.

Some critics give great weight to this evidence against the James-Lange theory. Others refuse it consideration. 

We now have some evidence that the optic thalamus is a center for pain and affective states. Why should not an emotion be aroused, then, when an impulse spreads from a perceptual, cortical center to the thalamus, exactly as sensory pain is believed to be aroused?¹ Brain action would be the same in both cases and we should not have to suppose a different type of nervous action for emotions and sensations. That bodily adjustments would later be felt in consciousness is not denied, but the effect of this would be to intensify the emotion and give knowledge of its irradiation rather than to be its sole cause. 

The above paragraph was written six years ago. Since that time the evidence that the optic thalamus is the center for emotions has become conclusive. On the basis of this evidence I have assigned emotional and instinctive behavior to the old brain. It is now certain that, when nervous impulses reach the thalamus, emotion is aroused 'Presumably the nervous impulse goes directly to the thalamus in the case of sensory pain.

EMOTION 

199 just as when nervous impulses reach the cortex, perceptions are aroused. This frees us from the necessity of assuming two entirely different kinds of nervous action, as required by the James-Lange theory. It must be remembered that none of this new knowledge of the action of the old brain had been discovered when James formulated his theory.

The Utility of Emotions.-A few generations ago the coarser emotions were regarded only as worthy to be curbed and as leading only to impulsive behavior. A rereading of the physiological results of emotions (pp. 193 ff.) shows their tremendous utility. A major emotion, like rage, seems to mobilize every ounce of the energy of the body to resist or initiate attack. All its energy is placed at the disposal of the great muscles of the limbs and the trunk. New "levels" of energy are supplied by the blood sugar, if adrenalin also is present. The rapid breathing soon brings with it the "second wind," again probably due in part to the action of adrenalin. Even the reflex facial and bodily expression of the emotion is regarded as anticipatory and mimetic of those in actual struggle, ancestral vestiges of the movements of conflict. Is it any wonder that the present world warfare, with its scientific methods of dealing death to an unseen enemy, has seemed peculiarly cold, intellectual, and cruel, in the absence of the instinctive stimuli to immediate rage. In the bayonet attack "the blood is up," and in case of a wound then, it coagulates much more quickly. Many of nature's ancestral protective devices are partly set at naught by the scientific warfare of the "new brain." This seems to suggest in all quarters that the chief function of such a brain should be to invent social conditions which will make warfare impossible.

Classes of Feelings.-There is almost no agreement as to a basis of classification of feelings. Whether they are simple or complex, their relation to sensations or ideas, and their connection with bodily or other psychic processes have all been used as standards of classification. 

For our purposes the classification into (a) sense feelings, (b) instinctive feelings, (c) aesthetic, (d) intellectual, (e) ethical, and (f) religious feelings, is most satisfactory. 

Sense Feelings.-The very close connection between sensations and feelings is indicated by the wide use of Ziehen's term, the "feeling tone" of sensations. It is believed in some quarters that, aside from the fact of adaptation (p. 295), no neutral or indifferent sensation is ever experienced. It is thought that all will be found either pleasant or unpleasant, at least to some slight degree. 

If the intensity of any sensation is increased beyond a certain point the feeling tone becomes first disagreeable, then with further increase, painful. Tones are pleasant over a wide range of intensities and pitches, but finally the feeling tone changes. Only very slight intensities of bitter tastes are pleasant, while a sweet taste does not become, as we say, "sickening" until we reach almost a saturated solution. Perfumers find that a small amount of certain odors, which would be disagreeable in greater strengths, may be used in their mixtures, though no doubt contrast effects complicate matters in this case. The different optimal intensities of different sense qualities seem to depend on the relation of the stimuli to the possible welfare or injury of the individual. Painful sensations are warnings of possible injury. James remarks that an animal which found pleasure in the feeling of suffocation "would enjoy a longevity of two or three minutes." No great quantity of bitter, salt, or sour, can be of benefit to

EMOTION 

201 the organism, while most sweets are foods. Hence the latter are agreeable in far larger amounts than the former. 

If the feeling tone changes from pleasant to painful with an increase in the intensity of the sensation, so it does with a change in the condition of the subject. In fact the feeling tone depends upon the temporary psychological condition. Every one knows how even sensory enjoyment palls on one who is surfeited; how food which we accept with eagerness when hungry is repugnant if "forced down,” etc. In the case of convalescents with fickle appetite, Cannon thinks, "the degree of daintiness with which nourishment is served, the little attentions to aesthetic details the arrangement of the dishes, the small portions of food, the flower beside the plate-all may help to render food pleasing to the eye and savory to the nostrils and may be deciding factors in determining whether the restoration of strength is to begin or not." These statements give to sense feelings an importance far beyond that usually accorded to them.

Each sense quality varies in feeling tone. "Evil odors" disgust us through and through and repel us instantly, no matter if the stimulus be slight. Agreeable odors have no such widespread effects. Sensations of taste are likewise so well endowed with feeling that the affective tone seems almost to eclipse the sensation. We might have difficulty in describing a certain taste but none whatever in stating our like or dislike for it. Sensations of touch² or sight, whose business it is to give us information concerning the environment, have far slighter emotional effect. In fact their information-giving power would be diminished had they also to be burdened with feeling. Yet, a gray day is "Bain somewhere remarks that "touch is the alpha and omega of sexual love," and it is no less a source of the love of young children for their mother. 

This is an exception to the remarks above, due to the instinctive character of the emotion.

"gloomy" a bright day "cheerful," while the touch of something soft and moist, like a bit of mashed potato, is peculiarly repulsive, especially if we do not know what it is. 

Black seems to be gloomy like a "gloomy day," but whether white has the opposite effect on every one, may be questioned.

Goethe believes that, if the whole visual field is filled with a given color, its emotional effect may be determined. "Yellow, orange, and yellowish red are active, lively striving. In yellowish red this active side mounts to its highest energy, and it is no wonder that energetic, vigorous, savage men enjoy this color especially." Other colors have, he thinks, an equally definite affective tone, and people usually agree that for wall decoration certain colors are "restful," others stimulating or even irritating. Whether wide agreement for single colors can be reached, even when the color fills the visual field, may well be doubted, but combinations of colors are almost always pleasing or displeasing to all the members of a given social group and on this fact are based the arts of decoration and painting. 

Sensations of touch or pressure often do not become painful until their stimuli almost reach the point of doing injury. The senses of taste and smell preside over the admission of food and air-the two "life elements"-to the body and are consequently accompanied by intense feelings, which have great power of irradiation. Organic sensations are likewise accompanied by organic feelings which have the greatest strength as motives to action, since organic sensations give the most immediate forecast of threatened injury.

Instinctive Feelings. It is generally agreed that instinctive feelings include two subordinate classes, self-feelings and social feelings. By self-feelings we mean the value

EMOTION 

203 which each individual ascribes to himself and his own activities. Self-appreciation is another term having the same meaning. It varies enormously in different individuals, "Pride, conceit, vanity, self-esteem, arrogance, vain-glory, on the one hand; and on the other modesty, humility, confusion, diffidence, shame, mortification, contrition, the sense of obloquy, and personal despair . seem to be direct and elementary endowments of our nature." That is, they are instinctive endowments of the individual. Some persons are uniformly self-satisfied or egotistical, others self-abased, and no human trait will be more quickly detected by our companions than these two. 

James sets down the brilliant equation

Self-esteem: 

Success

Pretentions but the self-esteem may be increased by either increasing the numerator or diminishing the denominator. In other words the amount of one's self-esteem is a more or less constant quantity which he carries with him throughout life.

In popular language this is his "disposition." More strictly it is the most conspicuous factor of his disposition, and achievement has little to do with the amount of his egotism. As James points out, we see the most exaggerated examples of self-esteem and self-abasement among the insane. Among them instinct appears but little cloaked by their impaired intelligence.

If anything can change these feelings of self-appreciation it is the environment of childhood and youth. It seems hardly possible that the children who lived for years in constant fear of shell-fire between the two armies in France can ever feel any great sweep of self-aggrandizement in later life, while in the children of despots, whose

every nod is a command instantly obeyed, feelings of selfabasement, or humility can hardly appear. 

The social feelings find their basis in the pleasure or displeasure which we derive from association with other persons. The plainest examples have been put down as sexual love, the love of parents for children and children for parents. Enmity, hate, and revenge are social feelings at the other extreme of the scale. 

But self-feelings and social feelings modify each other indefinitely. Our pride or vanity demands the praise or flattery of others and in our regard for others self-feeling is not entirely absent. In anger or hatred there mingles dislike of its cause, while shame, a self-feeling, could hardly exist save as a feeling of the esteem in which we are held by others.

Individual and social feelings fuse most completely in sympathy. We imagine or conceive clearly another's pitiable plight, his misfortune or good fortune, and we share his sorrow or his joy. No doubt this begins with the family and extends to the tribe. The evidence is almost universal that it is absent in all animals. Hence the disgust we feel toward a man or a tribe that is devoid of it. As long as sympathy is limited to one's tribe it may be called the tribal instinct par excellence. But as civilization advances and intercommunication increases the widest human sympathy seems essential to universal peace. By imagination we must share the joys and sorrows of a race we never saw. Obviously one of the bases of society lies in the social feelings. The most peculiar fusion of all exists perhaps in malice and envy, where another's sorrow gives us joy or his joy gives us chagrin. 

Professor James, who considered chiefly the "coarser emotions," seemed to regard instinct and emotion as hav-

EMOTION 

205 ing the same limits, or rather as being inner and outer aspects of the same thing. The reactions provoked by certain classes of stimuli belonged to instinct; the feelings accompanying them were emotions. While instinctive feelings are unquestionably the basis of higher feelings, the latter seem to accompany other reactions than merely instinctive ones. "From the feeling of self the sense of honor cannot be separated." Yet society must reach a certain stage of complexity before this higher feeling can arise and be effective as a motive. Finally, our hatred or desire for revenge may direct themselves toward the disturber of society rather than toward our personal enemy, while respect or veneration coupled with love add feelings of self-satisfaction to the respected personality, though both types of emotion have the highest ethical value. 

Hence, while we may point to the preservation of the individual and the race as the result of instinctive feelings and instinctive reactions, the feelings go far beyond those objects in civilized races and form the emotional counterpart of intelligent acts and intellectual processes. Or feeling is quite as much the inner aspect of intelligent behavior as of instinctive behavior, though perhaps "the coarser emotions" belong exclusively to the latter. Instinct, unable to adapt the individual to a varying environment, had to be supplemented or even replaced by something of a new and different nature, namely, intelligence. 

Feeling, less rigid in its limitations, could extend itself to accompany the higher processes. This gives ground for 

Titchener's opinion that there is no difference in quality between the satisfaction of a good dinner and that of a good action.

Aesthetic Feelings.-Like sense feelings, these are the immediate accompaniment of sensations. But, unlike

sense feelings and instinctive feelings, the aesthetic feelings are not connected with the preservation or welfare of the individual. They may be called the luxuries rather than the necessities of emotional experience. And again, unlike sense feelings, they are almost never aroused by a simple stimulus but by colors, tones, and forms in certain relations. The stimulus, therefore, is complex. Aesthetic feelings also depend chiefly upon the "higher" senses of sight and hearing. Wundt believes that the touch and temperature sensations of the fresh, cold air contribute to our enjoyment of a winter landscape. But the share of the "lower" senses in the appreciation of beauty is in dispute. 

Perhaps in this instance the air gives rise to an organic tone which contributes satisfaction but this seems quite distinct from the appreciation of beauty. Helen Keller's statements testify to a touch-sense of beauty and here it cannot be a mere supplement to the impressions gained through higher senses, yet in general the latter are the chief sources of aesthetic pleasure, and sometimes the intrusion of touch sensations diminishes the satisfaction gained through sight and hearing.

The aesthetic effect of sensations depends upon their qualitative relations or upon space-time relations, so that Elsenhans, whose account I am following in this discussion, gives this suggestive outline: 

Harmony feelings color-harmony klang-harmony 

Feelings of proportion feelings of form feelings of rhythm

He believes that "it is the task of aesthetics to ascertain the relations of stimuli under which aesthetic pleasure

EMOTION 

207 reaches a maximum. Thus a wide realm is opened to experimental procedure. Psychology has only to point out the psychic factors which thereby become effective.
