In color harmony the feeling tones of the particular colors fuse in a total feeling whose intensity of pleasure (or unpleasantness) is determined by the qualitative relation of the partial feelings entering therein. . . . . The question, why we prefer definite, melodious series of klangs and definite, harmonious-in the narrower sense of the wordsimultaneous klangs to others, psychology now furnishes to musical aesthetics in the more definite form. Under what musical conditions does the feeling of klang harmony arise? But at the same time it is conscious that this question can be answered psychologically only for a definite time and for a definite race and grade of culture. In general the beginning of part-music occurs first in the ninth century A. D. The major third, displeasing in earlier times, is now regarded as pleasing. The progression in fifths, not unpleasant to ancient ears, is now interdicted. 

Of the most modern development of the harmony feeling it may probably be said that it follows more and more in the direction of a pleasure in disharmony itself or in klang series and simultaneous klangs approximating a disharmony. A klang which was displeasing a short time before, is first endured, then preferred, and even for the conscientious musical critic it is not always quite easy to say, in the case of a crying offense (lit. contradiction) against the momentarily existing harmony feeling, whether it is a case of missing standards of good taste by the composer, or whether it is a matter of a new form which in due time may achieve wide acceptance as a factor of a distinguished work of art. In general the increasing differentiation of civilization brings with it also a development of the aes-

thetic feelings, which no longer satisfies itself with the lucid, 'given' relationship of stimuli, but in forms complicated and deviating from the ordinary, seeks to create a reflection of the innumerable shades of the moods of modern life and the possibility of ever new nervous stimulation."

Elsenhans thinks that to a certain degree the above observations hold true of the appreciation of forms. Both the arrangement of forms and the course of their lines affect us more pleasingly according as they deviate from mere regularity without excluding clear comprehension into a unity. Certain "normal" forms practically fulfill this demand. In opposition to mere symmetry in the arrangement of forms, Zeising (1854) advocated the arrangement according to the golden section or ratio. This ratio appears in the relation of the divisions of the human body and everywhere in the proportions of windows, book and magazine pages, photographs, visiting cards, etc. Fechner found a clear preference in favor of this form in an experimental investigation.

As well for the outlines of forms as for their arrangement certain standards have been proposed. Hogarth, the 

English painter, regarded the wave line as the line of absolute beauty and Wundt points out that the slightly curved line is the one described by free eye movements. 

Yet there is probably no absolute standard of beauty for either form or arrangement. As Elsenhans says, these proposed standards apply to but a limited realm of art and the power of form or arrangement to give pleasure is partly dependent on the nature of the material. The same may 

Elsenhans regards the golden section of, e. g., a line, as a division in which the whole line is related to the longer division as the latter to the shorter division. Some of our own writers deviate somewhat from this relationship in their descriptions of the golden ratio.

EMOTION 

209 perhaps be said of colors. If the golden ratio appears in the proportions of the human form it does not appear in the form of birds. Yet to an unprejudiced observer many birds are as gracefully proportioned as human beings. 

Somewhat as forms must have certain spatial proportions in order to give us pleasure so sounds must have certain temporal proportions and relations. We then experience feelings of rhythm. These feelings may also be aroused by successive touches, successive visual stimuli and by motor experiences. Every one has noticed how we break series of uniform sounds into rhythmic measures. The click or clatter of the railway wheels, as they pass from rail to rail, seems to beat out a measure because we emphasize one element of the series of sounds more than another. 

The poet writes of "the song of the Yankee reaper" and perhaps this unconscious breaking of noises into measures first suggested the anvil chorus. It is believed that sensations of tension and joint sensations accompany this weaker and stronger emphasis of different members of a series of sounds. The feelings which accompany all these sensations are termed feelings of rhythm. Obviously the successive elements of the series must follow each other neither too slowly nor too rapidly if the series is to be broken into rhythm. They must not be too rapid to be discriminated nor so slow that a lively impression of preceding elements no longer exists. For the optimal pleasure effect the time span of the rhythm is supposed to be about one second. Riemann says a tone appears long to us if it continues more than a second, short when it endures less than a second, and this is supposed to be due to our unconscious measuring by heart beats or pulse beats. "Just as we estimate the pitch of tones by the human organs of song, we measure tone duration by the innate metronome

of the heart beat, which regulates all our life functions."

So far as I can judge, something almost the reverse of this occurs. We enjoy certain rapid rhythms because they stimulate us to more rapid pulse beats, as they stimulate us to "beat time" or to "catch step" with the music. It is not so much measurement as stimulation of muscular and circulatory processes which gives us aesthetic pleasure in rhythm. Various opinions, however, are advocated in this field. One writer maintains that trochaic rhythm, which stresses the first of two syllables, is most natural, another, the iambic, which stresses the second syllable, etc. As already noted, the sense of rhythm affects joint and muscle sensations and the pleasure of dancing is found when these sensations unite in rhythm with those of sound. Koffka finds that even the sense of vision is influenced by rhythm. 

With uniform stimuli subjective rhythm appeared with intervals of from 115 sigma to 2400 sigma, "the length of the groups fluctuated between about 650 sigma and 5600 sigma." If Koffka's findings are correct the information should be of value to operators of moving pictures. 

Since the feeling of rhythm seems to be dependent on no single sense the attempt has been made to correlate it with the tension and release of energy. It is the satisfaction of a need for periodic change of the bodily and psychic life, and, indeed, it does seem to be related to the alternate flexion and extension of our muscles. However well -or ill-satisfied we may be with this explanation, it is certain that the rhythm of music and poetry has much to do with determining our mood, and, conversely, we learn to detect the mood of others by the inflection and "phrasing" of their ordinary speech, and to express our own feelings by the same means. 

Thus far we have found aesthetic pleasure to lie chiefly

EMOTION 

211 in the form, proportion, and arrangement of sensations, or, better perhaps, of stimuli. In a word, the relations of stimuli seem to minister more to our pleasure than their quality. Can we, however, find an intellectual content in our pleasure, a factor of content as well as of relation? 

To return to music, as an example and to speak only of my own introspection, music which I like arouses very promptly a train of pleasurable ideas. It is no doubt an example of association by emotional congruity. This would give an ideational content to the experience as well as a sensational and emotional one. I may add that mechanical music in any of its varieties fails to arouse a train of pleasurable ideas, though the same selections executed by a fine orchestra would do so. Also music which I dislike arouses displeasing ideas (and cynical comment). The most important factor of content in aesthetic pleasure seems to me, therefore, to be the train of pleasurable images and ideas which arise in harmony with our mood.

A vast and silent chapel brings mildly pleasurable feelings of awe, and reverence and a train of ideas in harmony with them. To find one's self unexpectedly on an ancient battlefield brings a leap of the heart, then a host of ideas of self-sacrifice and the victory achieved there. It may be that shell-scarred Verdun and the mutilated cathedral of Rheims will in the future give this type of pleasure to the traveler and that it will be a deeper pleasure than that of the beauty of the landscape or the architecture. 

Obviously the pleasure will come in this case from memories of the deeds of heroism and self-sacrifice "for France.” 

Lipps regards this type of pleasure as due to feeling ourselves in the scenes and objects which give the pleasure. 

Meumann adds that this identification of self with the ob-

jects is really a return to the subjective, personifying perception so common in young children, i. e., the aesthetic perception of adults is like all of childish perception. 

The appropriateness of many objects for the uses for which they were designed forms another factor of content. 

Great buildings, bridges and similar works of architecture furnish examples. No doubt there are other factors of content in aesthetic pleasure.

As a fundamental principle of aesthetic enjoyment it was early demanded that we must perceive unity in the object, scene or composition. While this may be true of paintings and works of architecture there seems to be far less ground to insist upon it in the case of music, else our enjoyment could begin only when the unit were complete. 

We probably find pleasure quite as much in variety and surprise as in unity. It is doubtful whether we shall insist on "the perception of unity in a manifold" as the ground of pleasure so much as we did in former years. The desire for this may be produced largely by tradition and education. If we include the enjoyment of wit, humor, and the comic as a type of aesthetic pleasure we must regard variety, contrast, and surprise as more vital factors of it than unity. Nor need we demand that the variety "must be comprehended into a unity." In the management of vaudeville it has been carefully worked out just how much of one kind of stimulation we will stand before requiring a change. He who asserts that such stimulation appeals only to vulgar minds is urging merely a cult or tradition and he must at least exclude enjoyment of the comic from the aesthetic, whereas it is always admitted. 

The nature of aesthetic enjoyment has been defined as a "heightening of our mood in pure perception," and by "heightening" is meant "the increase in ideal pleasure

EMOTION 

213 which the aesthetic impression brings." Since this serious attempt at definition by a skillful writer says no more than enjoyment is heightened pleasure, or "argues in a circle," we see how primitive a trait of our nature is pleasure (or displeasure) in the objects we perceive. 

Intellectual Feelings. Obviously feelings are connected not only with sensations and instinctive reactions but with ideas and thought processes. The strictly intellectual feelings are connected with those trains of thought whose object is the acquisition of knowledge. Interest, the feeling of familiarity in recognition, the feelings aroused by the neatness and adequacy of a demonstration or by an original discovery, belief and doubt may be mentioned as examples. All but the last may be regarded as feelings of satisfaction which accompany successful thought. Doubt is distinctly a feeling of dissatisfaction due to baffled intellectual processes.

Interest is doubtless the same emotion whether it accompanies the delight of a child in learning about some new thing or in mastering a problem or even in the spelling of a difficult word, or whether it accompanies some brilliant new discovery in the mind of a scientist and forces his shout of Eureka. The objects which arouse interest vary from person to person. One finds the keenest interest in unearthing the broken jars and implements of the forerunners of our Indians, and he will suffer hardships to be at his excavations. Another regards the fruit of all this toil as so much "junk," but he is equally interested in some pursuit. For most of us, however, our interest is not determined by talent alone. We are interested in a variety of intellectual pursuits, yet our interest is heightened very much when we select from these the one we wish to expend our efforts upon to the exclusion of the rest. Intellectual

manhood may be said to be reached in most youths when they begin to study with a fixed purpose instead of with desultory and intermittent impulses. Interest has been defined as "pleasure in intellectual occupation with objects of a particular kind," and in the teacher's task, to awaken interest, his purpose is best attained when the topic chosen is of value to the pupil and the method of treatment lets him find intellectual satisfaction in it. 

When a student has been taught the truth and respect for it by such a method there is no keener dissatisfaction than his when, instead of such teaching, ill-grounded opinion is offered him for truth and he knows the opinion will not be changed no matter what the experiments show. We may add, therefore, that genuine intellectual interest can have no other object, be aroused by no other thing, than the truth.* Unconscious error may creep in but the conscious substitution of error for truth arouses not only doubt but intellectual contempt, which should perhaps be added to our list of intellectual feelings. Intellectual interest may and often does attach itself to objects of no use to the individual as in solving riddles or playing chess or even in the solution of problems which seem to have no useful applications. It may be worth while to point to a contrast between interest and voluntary attention. The latter never fails to arouse a sturdy purpose, while the former may or may not do so. Along with other emotions it is often the fate of interest to "evaporate" with no result.

Attention partakes of the nature of an act of will. 

The feeling of familiarity will be described in a later chapter (p. 433). In certain cases one may thrill with it though it is usually a mild feeling. It probably precedes "Of course this statement is not meant to deny an interest in brilliant fiction but even this must be "true to nature."

EMOTION 

215 intellectual recognition more often than it follows it and is closely akin to the feeling we have that the answer to our problem is almost at hand, as we see the last few relations fulfilled.

The logical feelings come next. These are feelings of pleasure which accompany clear concepts and correctly drawn conclusions. Different men prefer different forms of thought because each finds pleasure in the type of reasoning or judging which he prefers. It is thought that many disputes arise from this fact. The facts may be recognized by both contestants but they receive a different interpretation according as each one prefers a different form of thought. One man delights in deductive reasoning and consequently enjoys mathematics or philosophy. Another would find himself unhappy with such endeavors. He finds satisfaction in observation and induction, but the feeling of truth is the same in both. 

The satisfaction may accompany processes of thought based on hypotheses which are not questioned or the processes may be based on facts and objective truth. In the latter case the feeling of familiarity is present as well as the feeling of evidence or truth. "The investigator who with a new hypothesis is able to illuminate some realm always dark before is guided less by detailed conclusions and proofs than by an immediate feeling of the truth." 

Later he verifies his flash of insight with explicit analysis or experiment. This ability to feel the truth is regarded as the vital factor in the advance of science. Where evidence must be weighed and there is no clear balance for one conclusion more than another the feeling of doubt occurs and it is too familiar to most mortals to need description.

The feeling of truth need not depend upon objective

conditions but only on the subject himself. It is then mere belief or conviction. It is due usually to the influence of others. We believe what they tell us or we rely upon authority. The child's belief in the infallibility of its parents or teachers is an example of this but it appears that citizens of a whole nation may exhibit this "authoritybelief" in their monarch, quite as blindly as children do, if they have been properly educated in the doctrine of the divine right of kings. Political mistakes have been made by diplomats in underrating the power of this subjective feeling of the truth. The more subjective it is the less is such feeling accessible to influence by facts or evidence. "The authority of teacher, church or state appears as a power to which the individual is in duty bound to render obedience through inner assent and outer acknowledgment of the doctrines announced by them."

But not only does the feeling of truth attach to doctrines taught by authority; we also tend to believe what agrees with our own opinions and wishes. "Homines perfacile credunt id quod volunt," and "The wish is father to the thought," are classic expressions of this fact. The steady resistance to subjective influences in forming opinions and the steady subordination of his thought to objective factors by the man of science is regarded as the most valuable contribution of scientific training to the formation of character. 

Moral or Ethical Feelings.-Since moral feelings and judgments have the whole discipline of ethics devoted to them we may be brief in the discussion of them here. The prevalence of such words as "ought," "duty," "right," and "wrong," testifies that civilized men approve certain acts and disapprove others. Moreover the approval or disapproval extends to the actor as the cause of his deeds, and

EMOTION 

217 even further to his intent or purpose in doing the deed. 

If there was a plain intention to injure a fellow-being or even the absence of an intention to be reasonably thoughtful of his safety or welfare, as in "criminal carelessness,” condemnation or disapproval follows promptly. The satisfaction or dissatisfaction of approval or disapproval are the ethical feelings. These feelings seem to be the same in all men, savage or civilized, but the deeds which are judged right or wrong may be very different according to race, training, education, and tradition, and certainly the deeds which are adjudged wrong or right change in the same race from generation to generation. In time of war also many acts are wrong which would be approved as right in time of peace. Even as I write, profits and patriotism are announced as incompatible when our nation is at war, while in peace, only certain kinds and amounts of profits are wrong. Fortunately it is not our task to trace the varying intellectual basis of judgments of right and wrong, though a race or nation is regarded as civilized or barbarous according to such judgments and the deeds it permits itself to do. It is easy to see, then, that moral acts are those which have an effect on the weal or woe of our fellow-beings. Acts which have no such effect have no ethical character. Consequently, ethical feelings are social feelings. Robinson Crusoe could have no occasion to experience such feelings before the advent of his man, Friday. 

That they are social feelings is further shown by the wide acceptance of Bentham's principle that the justification of a measure should be whether it attains "the greatest good for the greatest number."

It is probable that the social feelings most valued in our own times come indirectly from instinctive social feelings, as the love of parents, of children, of brothers and

sisters or even of one's "own people," or tribe. To every child there comes early a conflict between individual instinctive feelings and social instinctive feelings and soon we find him defining the acts of himself and his playmates as "fair" or "unfair." Thus he shows a "sense of justice" which is perhaps the most important ethical feeling, and far less instinctive than sympathy or love. Its importance is shown by the vast structure of law reared to satisfy it in civilized lands.

The quality of ethical feelings is the pleasure or displeasure corresponding with judgments of right and wrong. But these feelings exist in all grades of intensity, and it is taught that "the intensity of ethical feelings increases with the strength as motives of the temptations by which they are tested." This seems to be a very indirect measure and from the standpoint of the laboratory very "unscientific," yet the more we consider it the more it seems to describe a prime fact of human nature. Kant gives the example of a man who would not yield to the demand made upon him to slander an innocent person even though he suffered, first, loss of property, then persecution and sickness, then threats against his freedom and his life, and was finally forced to witness the dire need of his family. By such an example Kant supposed the youthful listener would pass from mere approval to a feeling of the highest honor for such a man. Unfortunately the Great

War has given us finer than academic examples. The 

German policy of "frightfulness" only increased the spirit of self-sacrifice and patriotism. It is said that, when the 

Belgians were deported in great numbers, it was demanded that they sign a contract "that would bind them to stay in Germany and would make it appear that they went voluntarily." In order to force them to sign they were sub-

EMOTION 

219 jected to the most intense and prolonged tortures added to starvation, yet when the agreement was offered them again, they replied simply "I will not sign." One of these men, who died of frostbite, starvation and hardship, was just at his last gasp. The priest had administered extreme unction; his hands were folded on his breast. The doctor, by accident, jogged his elbow. His eyes opened. "No; I will not sign-I will not sign!" he muttered-and died. This example illustrates well that the intensity of a moral feeling is proportional to the strength of the stimuli which it resists. Thousands of other examples will occur to the reader familiar with the incidents of the war which tapped the very deepest levels of men's moral emotions. It may surely be said that love of country and posterity is the most intense and profound emotion which stirs the human heart. 

Turning from intensity to the psychic energy (p. 188) of ethical feelings, or their power to arouse and "consolidate" thoughts and ideas in harmony with themselves, we find it dependent on the closeness or remoteness of the feelings to the needs and demands of life, both the life of the individual and that of society. If a feeling is closely related to my personal welfare it arouses train after train of thought in harmony with it, but my own thought would be paltry compared with the vast literature of maxims, proverbs, laws, rules, and commandments which spring from ethical feelings. The Ten Commandments are no doubt the most striking example of this, yet most of them are immediately related to the demands of social life. 

When the psychic energy of ethical feelings is strong, the thought related to them is likely to "consolidate" into some general notion which we call an ideal, a sort of precipitate of the total wisdom of the race and the individual

relative to certain types of conduct. No doubt the ethical feeling of greatest psychic energy is conscience, which is the feeling accompanying approval or disapproval of our own acts. 

Perhaps ethical feelings, more than any others, are likely to be mixed feelings. When certain rules of action find their sanction in authority the feeling inspired by the authority is likely to enter the ethical feeling as its chief component. Thus public opinion, the church, the state, the law, or even respect for parents or teachers may give color to our ethical feelings. Sometimes, too, the feelings inspired by these agencies conflict with ethical feelings. 

Professor Stratton gives the example of a murderer released, because the indictment did not recite that his victim was dead! Respect for law thus became respect for the verbiage of law, and justice was defeated. 

Finally ethical development has been defined as "the raising of instinctive feelings to ethical feelings under the guidance of the more refined social feelings." 

Religious Feelings. Of late years psychologists have been more inclined to write and lecture on the psychology of advertising than on the psychology of religion. Yet there is no doubt that religious feelings form a definite group of experiences which are capable of psychological investigation and description. Elsenhans has given so excellent an account of these feelings that I shall give a brief abstract of it. His analysis seems to embody the best features of James' extensive work on this subject. "The religious feelings are complex and the psychologist's task consists in finding their components. Their chief factor is the self-feeling of the individual. In its commerce with the outer world this feeling suffers checks and difficulties of numerous kinds and these in turn bring

EMOTION 

221 about emotional effects. A part of these difficulties is overcome by thought and deliberation; a part by will and action. But another part overwhelms his nature according to the strength of the individual and gives him the humiliating feeling of his own insufficiency. His bodily life is subjected to sickness and death. The longing for good fortune remains unfulfilled. Fate carries on its incomprehensible play with him, and in the enrichment of his selffeeling by civilized society, in which he enters, he still feels the narrow limits of his own powers. Knowledge, in comparison with the infinitely great and the infinitely small of the universe, appears paltry and unsatisfying. But morality as opposed to his own passions and the reality thwarting his success, and the forms of beauty in comparison with the resistance of matter and the striven-for perfection are even more disheartening." The reader will recognize this as having much in common with James' description of the "sick soul." "But it is characteristic of the psychic organization of man that it strives to overcome in some way every condition of dissatisfaction. Where immediate help is impossible it happens that by virtue of the effect of ideas of the present emotional state, the image of a better condition arises in which those imperfections are overcome. This image is accompanied also by anticipatory feelings of pleasure. So far as the idea of such a condition is thought of as real, we name it an ideal. We may, therefore, designate the conviction of the possibility of such a perfect condition or the belief in ideals as the chief mark of religion." 

The result is that the anticipatory feelings of pleasure, "Were one asked to characterize the life of religion in the broadest and most general terms possible, one might say that it consists of the belief that there is an unseen order, and that our supreme good lies in harmoniously adjusting ourselves thereto." (James, Varieties of Religious Experience, p. 53.) ܙܪ

connected with the idea of such perfect condition, displace the unpleasant feelings arising out of the hindrances of self-feeling. But, since such hindrances always appear again, a victory for that belief in ideals would be impossible were there not some sort of pledge for its realization. 

In the ordinary conditions of life, this pledge is not to be found, since, indeed, the hindrances spring out of them. 

It must, therefore, be sought in powers which stand above this world, but whose activities must be thought of after the analogy of human activities, the only example available to men, i. e., they must be thought of anthropomorphically. Thus there is joined to the belief in ideals the belief in their realization through God. This is the second mark of religion. With this there enter, as elements, into religious feelings all the emotional factors which link themselves to ideas of God or gods."

In these statements I think Elsenhans has given the psychological basis of religion though there are innumerable other conceptions. The devoted belief in dogma, the belief by finite minds of their nature as that of the infinite mind, "the recognition of all our duties as God's commands," etc., are all examples of notions with which philosophies of religion begin, but they have little to do with its psychology.

This psychology underlies all religion from the fetishism of the savage, who believes that charms and amulets protect him from disaster, to the Christian belief in man's unworthiness and his salvation by God's mercy. "The coloring of religious feeling is thus dependent upon what is expected of God: material advantages (fruitful weather, health, the destruction of enemies), blessing-bringing, guidance for the whole people, sanctions for law, strength

EMOTION 

223 for a righteous life and for the manifestation of brotherly love, salvation from sorrow and guilt."

The religious feelings may be ushered in in many ways. 

Fastings, ceremonies, the majestic tones of the organ, the quiet of the chapel, the subdued light of stained glass windows are all sensory means of arousing these feelings. 

When the mood of devotion is heightened to the limits of the abnormal, it may reach the degree of trance or ecstasy, "in which every sense perception, all consciousness of time and space and all idea of self are lost in the blissful feeling of union with the All-one. The irradiation of the religious feeling through the whole of consciousness is here so complete that it crowds all else out of consciousness. This process is furthered by pantheistic ideas of the identity of the I with the All, as it is found especially with the civilized races of Asia, in the Tao of the Lao-tse, in the Indian esoteric doctrines of the Upanishads, but also in Neo-Platonism and in German Mysticism. In part this is connected with self-hypnosis as is evident from the Hindoo methods of withdrawal from all sense stimuli and concentration on inner contemplation (Yoga), perhaps also in the symbol of the light which is to be found almost everywhere." 

Such exercise of the emotions is of course unhealthy, since normally they should discharge themselves in expression or action and not end in mystic contemplation. But no one will doubt that such exercise is characteristic of a whole type of religions and that it is practised even in modern times.

Influence of Emotion on Memory.-In the psychology of learning, all sorts of methods of memorizing are described but the influence of emotion on memory has been overlooked because ordinary laboratory experiments do not arouse vivid and effective emotions. Nevertheless there is

some evidence to the effect that our first permanent memories are due to emotion. For some years I have asked large numbers of students to report the first incident of their past lives which they can remember. Was emotion present? Was the event remembered the beginning of consecutive memory or a disconnected "island" of experience which preceded consecutive personal memory by a considerable period of time? Perhaps one or two examples of these early memories may be given: First year. Fear. Seeing a huge black snake winding in and out of the spokes of a buggy wheel.

Permanent memory of an event of the first year is rare. 

This fear could hardly have been "conditioned." 

Second year. 

Pain and terror. Mastoid operation without an anesthetic. Acute pain of operation and terror at seeing the physician bring out more instruments. Memory very clear. 

Third year. Strangeness. "Island." "Island." Bewilderment and strangeness on finding the face of a nurse instead of her mother's face when she awoke in illness. "In all the memories of about that time the thing I remember seems to be not so much external circumstances as inner feelings and states of mind." This emotion of "strangeness" in young children is almost always aroused in them by their moving into a new house. We have a surprising number of reports of this event being stamped in the first memory. 

We discovered one student who could recall no event before her sixth year and a German psychologist gives eight years as the time of the first memory of another girl. 

This may mean no more than that nothing happened during these years to arouse an intense emotion.

By the Freudian psychology each of the fearful experiences should have produced a suppressed complex but the subject of the experience should not have been able to recall the event nor any slightest trace of it without the aid of a psychoanalyst. This forgotten complex should have resulted in disturbed emotions every day thereafter until the advent of the psychoanalyst. Our reports show that this is not the order of events at all. These shaking experiences are remembered vividly and no other events are remembered at all for months or even for a year afterward. In this sense our reports are fully controlled. 

Since emotion releases an avalanche of bodily energy, we may surmise that it also stamps into the cortex the substratum of the first permanent memory. This it does if hundreds of recalls may be believed. If emotion is the cause of the first permanent memory, is it not also the cause of every permanent memory? There is much evidence for an affirmative answer to this question. 

Wonder is expressed that hundreds of students have no scholarly purpose in attending college but delight in college "activities.” The activities enlist their emotions. 

Science, literature, and art do not. Wonder is also expressed that the apparent duffer at his books often succeeds well in after life. The problems of after life aroused his feelings so that he started to work. Of course he may have been aided by fortune but his feelings were the chief factor if mental effort was required. With about one-third of present students the fear of failure to pass examinations and consequently dismissal from college is the single emotion which prompts to enough study to make "a pass."

The fact that fear is the motive employed only confirms our thesis that there is no thought without emotion. 

A further example may be added. We forget most of

EMOTION 

227 the names of persons to whom we are introduced. But let one of them be a person who will have charge of, or affect seriously, one of our most vital interests. His name is indelibly stamped upon our memory and that without necessity for repetition. The books on psychology neglect this instantaneous learning, yet it occurs very often. A memory which required repetition for matters of vital importance would have no survival value at all. Perhaps, therefore, the most important condition of learning is an aroused emotion. As long as this emotion is native curiosity the child delights in his lessons. When we must learn for a remote object the absence of emotion demands continual effort of attention and will. 

Emotion in Deception.-A very successful method of detecting guilt consists in testing the associations of the suspected person for words which have no connection with the deed of which he is suspected and for words which do have reference to it. The latter may be called significant words, the former non-significant words. The significant words suggest the deed to the suspect and do not suggest it to an innocent person or to one ignorant of the details of the crime. The best method is to read to the suspect one hundred common nouns of which twenty are significant. 

The innocent suspect responds with associated words at about the same rate for all the nouns. The person who is guilty and is trying to conceal his guilt responds in quite a different manner. (1) He is slower on the significant words. (2) He is slower on the non-significant and semi-significant words. (3) The excess of time on significant words as compared with non-significant words is greater in guilty suspects.

(4) The times for words immediately following significant words are longer for the guilty. (5) Suspects (who later confessed guilt) gave more guilt-revealing replies than the innocent. (6) Suspects failed to respond six times as often as the innocent. (7) Guilty persons more often asked that the significant word be repeated. As they confess, the mind becomes a blank when the significant word is pronounced. 

Crosland, who has recently repeated this word-association experiment gives these and many other symptoms of guilt elicited by the test. He employed the test seven times and secured a confession by means of it in six of the cases. This is a high percentage of success. The guilty person was probably selected by the test in the case which failed but he did not confess. As employed, the experiment is an application of the word-association test or method and it might perhaps be described under association. But why does the guilty person's mind so often "become a blank" when he hears a significant word? Why is his time of response longer on these words and longer also on the words next following significant words? Why does he so often ask to have the word repeated, etc.? The answer appears to be that his disturbed behavior is due to the emotion of guilt and the fear of detection. The emotional shocks inhibit prompt replies and disconcert the guilty subject. If so, the success of the experiment is dependent on emotion. The evidence for this comes largely from the following extension of the test.

We have seen that emotion has widespread bodily effects. In principle any one of these effects is capable of measurement and in practice one of them can be measured, namely, the changes of blood pressure due to emotion.

EMOTION 

229 Marston has employed this measurement along with the word - association test, though he substituted questions at times for the single word. By his method the systolic blood pressure of the subject or suspect was registered on a sphygmomanometer and recorded at each response to a stimulus-word. Marston usually separated himself from the witness by means of a screen and judged as to his guilt or innocence by changes of blood pressure alone. In his researches he employed a jury of six persons and compared his findings with theirs. As a total his decisions as to guilt were correct in more than 95% of the cases. The jury's decisions were correct in 48%. It is evident, therefore, that a witness cannot control reflex rises of blood pressure which are due to emotion. The significant words aroused fear, embarrassment or anger and the result was an increase of blood pressure. The curve of increase for fear was found to be distinguishably different from that for anger. Marston secured confessions by this method when the guilt was genuine and admissions of mere laboratory guilt. The attempt to deceive arouses emotion whose reflex effects can be measured. These methods of detection will doubtless be very slowly accepted and given practical applications. Meanwhile every advance in delicacy and precision of measurement increases applicable and useful knowledge. Possibly a photoelectric cell could even now measure the change of color of a blush. In that event 

Mark Twain's remark that "man is the only animal which blushes, or needs to" could perhaps be employed to some social purpose. In any event, we must continue to make a list of the bodily effects of emotion until we have learned to measure most or all of them.

Leaving blood pressure aside and returning for a moment to the word-association test, Hull and Lugoff

found various signs of deception or guilt effective in the following order: (1) "greatly lengthened reaction time, (2) repeated use of the same response word, (3) defective reproduction, (4) repetition of the stimulus-word, (5) wrong comprehension of the stimulus-word, (6) strange or senseless reply, (7) no response at all, and (8) obvious perseveration or recurrence of idea or meaning. Delay of response, beyond a point represented by the mean of the reaction times, is a far more dependable criterion than is reaction time foreshortened to a point under the mean. A group of indicators is far more diagnostic than any one indicator alone." It is evident from this list and that of 

Crosland above that the mental signs of confusion are numerous. The fact that measurements of the bodily symptoms are impersonal and objective gives them an advantage. When Lincoln proved the absence of moonlight on a certain night by reference to the almanac, he confounded the opposing witnesses and saved his client from conviction. So little was objective evidence used in those times that his thoughtfulness was little less than a stroke of genius.

According to the Freudian theory the above tests of emotion should fail completely in cases in which the disagreeable complex has been repressed into the unconscious. 

Griffiths reports on this as follows: "Very little evidence was afforded to prove that the subject inclined unintentionally to repress the unpleasant associations (therefore, the subject tested for guilt very likely calls up the response -fatal to his chances of being found innocent-and refuses to reply or substitutes another reply, and in doing so consumes additional time)." Here theory and experiment seem to be in conflict. Not the extension of the Freudian

EMOTION 

231 theory to normal personalities but its limitation to hysterical patients seems to be warranted by the evidence. 

Enthusiasm.-Enthusiasm for some one object, idea or pursuit is peculiar in the vast amount of psychic energy which it releases and in the frequent spread of the contagion to all the members of a group. It is not so contagious as fear, perhaps, but it is next to fear in social irradiation. This quality of enthusiasm has both a good and a bad side. Probably the best recent example of its stimulating to progress is the event of Lindbergh's flight to France. At once the feelings of Americans were electrified. Now there is hardly a youth who does not aspire to fly. There is no logic but only psychology in this for two 

Englishmen had flown from Newfoundland to Ireland years before and created hardly a ripple of excitement. 

That Lindbergh crossed alone cannot have made much of the difference in effect. Enthusiasm irradiated because one of our own countrymen had done something which we ignorantly supposed was almost impossible of achievement and far more likely to end in disaster than success. 

Since this enthusiasm was not permitted to subside at once, the result was an impetus to progress in aviation. 

Examples less valuable, if not actually harmful, lie in the enthusiasm for applying some novel idea or conception far beyond its reasonable limits. We may note how, for some writers in psychology, any human or animal behavior which the single word, conditioning, will not explain is either ignored or its existence denied. Other psychologists and educators are as devoted to the words adjustment and maladjustment. A few years ago feeble-mindedness was regarded as the cause of all crime. That enthusiasm subsided but now we read that all the inmates of one state prison have glandular defect. All this illus-

trates the enthusiasm for finding a single unitary cause for every type of phenomenon. The feeling seems to attach itself so often to the new that the maxim has been coined, "Not everything that is new is true."

The history of education reveals many methods of instruction, theories, and administrative devices which were proclaimed as nothing less than revolutionary of the whole educational process. They have disappeared along with the enthusiasm which they aroused. Blind enthusiasm can be aroused for any object desired, a crusade, mental healing, rejuvenation, fiat money, socialism, Mississippi bubbles or tulip crazes, to mention no recent examples. Salesmen of stocks or bonds are young men because their enthusiasm for their work can be made to blind them to the fact that some of their offerings must result in loss to the purchaser; in fact show every promise of it. Enthusiasm is a useful emotion when it stimulates to earnest effort toward a well considered aim. When it paralyzes all critical judgment, it serves only to illustrate the psychic energy of emotion and its irradiation. 

Random Observations Concerning Emotions. We have found that unpleasant emotions seem to be more effective than pleasant ones in establishing first memories. A playwright regards the former as far more widely understood and appreciated. "A man making a joke is less widely understood than a man shedding tears, and a tragedy, even if it be an old one, will appeal to a greater variety of peoples than a comedy, even if it be a new one. Humor is local and ephemeral but sorrow and grief are lasting and universal. We do not all laugh at the same things but we nearly all cry in the same way and for the same causes." 

Again, "the greatest documents in history are more poetic than practical, more visionary than judicial, more roman-

EMOTION 

233 tic than real. The Declaration of Independence reads like a soliloquy from some great play. The four gospels ring with an epic rhythm."

The almost universal feeling that a gray day is gloomy in an emotional sense, is matched by the observation that very often clerks show little interest in making a sale on such days. One chairman of a board of directors is unwilling to call meetings of the board on such days because pessimism seems then to reign supreme. Business psychology seems to be very largely the psychology of emotion. Very intelligent clerks grow bored to death after selling trifles for a department store for some months.

Clerks who have had a higher education are more restless than those who have attended grammar school. The taxicab driver who is brooding over his troubles is more liable to accident, etc. Business seems to discover these trifles daily and in business they cease to be trifles. 

Up to this point we have discussed reflex and instinctive behavior and emotional experience or emotional states of mind. This behavior and experience is predominantly dependent on the old brain. An animal or a very primitive man might have intense emotions and might act instinctively in many simple situations but such a creature need have little intelligence, almost no memory, and no knowledge of the outer world save that brought to him by the senses. He would have almost no ideas. He could not forecast the future from the lessons of the past even in simple situations. He could discriminate food, foes, and mates, and but little else. He would have only emotional language, which would give evidence of pain or excitement. Having practically no words, he would have no abstract terms and could not make even the simplest general-

izations. In this absence of general terms he would resemble certain Indian tribes of today. Many animals about us exhibit this simple behavior and only certain simple types of memory. In primitive man the cerebrum or new brain is present and it must function more and more as instinctive behavior fails to adjust its possessor to his environment. Neverthless, the brain of primitive men seems to have for each tribe a specific limit beyond which it cannot go in development." 

G. Elliott Smith thinks that the development of the cerebrum in man has been due to the struggle for supremacy between the sense of smell and vision and the final victory of vision. Animals with a highly developed sense of smell have greater development of the midbrain which serves the olfactory sense. With the development of the camera eye and the human type of vision, whose center is the occipital lobes, there comes great development of the cortex with the possibility of visual images, visual memory, visual discrimination, adequate space perception, etc. 

The sense of smell seems to have declined as vision developed, so man is called microsmatic as compared with animals which have a keen sense of smell and are called macrosmatic. It is fairly probable that the cortex has developed partly as a dependency of the visual center but we may suspect that there are still other causes for the great development of this organ in man. "In evidence of the slow growth of "cortical government" the following striking description of the men of Charlemagne's time should be read: "Children they were, the adults of that day, primitive, unreasoning, impulsive, sensual, stuffing themselves on a narrow choice of coarse dietary, satisfying appetite at whatever cost, dying young, usually incapable of moral reflection or of introspection, playing like uniformed children at such costly games as war and banditry, living for the hour, careless about tomorrow in this world, occasionally trying to propitiate it in another, uninformed, superstitious, fond of unprofitable amusements, coming back from them to run amuck, sometimes as half-mad beserkers, sometimes revenging with senseless cruelties the emptiness of life.

One turning the blood-soaked pages of their record would wish to do so with tongs, a gloved hand, and handkerchief at the nose." 

Russel, C. E., "Charlemagne, First of the Moderns.”

235 It is certain that because of the great growth of the new brain, man is endowed with high intelligence. We must next consider this general ability and its factors or the special abilities on which the operation of intelligence depends. 

EXERCISES

2. Describe the probable behavior of a person in whom these rates were reversed. Are these rates quite different in different personalities?

4. "A man becomes angrier in thinking over an insult than he was when he received it." Give a bodily reason for the truth of this statement.

6. Why may a man be thoroughly frightened and tremble after the danger is passed? 

7. Discuss the effect of attempted deception on blood pressure.

CHAPTER VII INTELLIGENCE 

It is an everyday observation that one person is more intelligent than another, more alert, more efficient; that one child is brighter than another of the same age; that older children are, on the average, more intelligent than younger children. Woodworth adds that man acts more intelligently than the dog partly because man makes more use of his past experiences. He certainly appears, therefore, to use memory and we may profitably consider whether memory is not a factor of intelligence. Persons of ready and retentive memory, who are unintelligent even to the point of stupidity, are found, of course, but persons of high intelligence and very poor memory have never been discovered by the present writer, except among the aged. 

Also a natively good but partly undeveloped memory may co-exist with fairly high intelligence, which also remains poorly developed for lack of information. Remembering exactly the fact which will solve a problem and remembering it at the critical moment seems to be an important element of intellectual efficiency.

Woodworth also seems inclined to banish all general terms from psychology at present. "Intelligence is thought of as a general characteristic of the individual and one individual is said to be more intelligent than another. 

This form of expression is likely to mislead us into conceiving of intelligence as a sort of substance of which one individual possesses more than another. . . The concrete fact is that one individual pulls more strongly, or moves

INTELLIGENCE 

237 more rapidly, or acts more intelligently, than another. To say that man possesses more intelligence than the dog really means that man acts more intelligently than the dog." (W., p. 24.) This, of course, is a plea for a purely behavioristic terminology and somehow suggests the predicament of the Indians who have twenty names for particular kinds of oak tree but no name for oak in general. 

The practical question to ask is, If this man or student has always acted more intelligently than his fellows may we not expect him to do so again? If we do, we probably believe that some permanent quality of his nature gives him this ability. We, therefore, expect intelligent action of him and we are not disappointed in the expectation. We also expect him to lose alertness in extreme old age. We also imagine that he did not act so intelligently when he was a young child. This assumption we can verify also.

When we compare further various grades of intelligence, we shall be driven, I think, to believe that intelligence does depend on some quality, condition or character of brain substance and this will lead us to ask, Can this quality be changed or influenced in any way? With the cretin, yes. 

He acts like an imbecile but if supplied with thyroxin at an early age he changes and acts intelligently. It may be there are other ways in which intelligence can be influenced. An open mind in this matter has led to progress. I believe that we cannot give up thinking from effect to cause and the reverse and general terms are an aid to this. 

Intelligence is not only a characteristic of behavior but of thinking as well. If a man thinks more intelligently than his fellows they will carry his ideas into action quite willingly. They will act more intelligently because they are carrying out his plans, not their own. We would then be justified in assuming the existence of intelligence and even

in asking whose intelligence dictates this behavior. Should we believe that because certain "behavers" are "acting intelligently" now they will also make intelligent plans of their own and act on them we should often be seriously mistaken. By inferring that intelligence is evidenced by thought as well as action we shall look for it in the products of thought, and very often the opinion, decision, or diagnosis of an expert is what we most need to know. 

Their advice often directs our action. Even machines (an automatic substation, for example) may behave as if intelligent, if great intelligence has gone into their design and manufacture. Consequently we say mechanical progress is dependent on intelligence and the statement seems to be accepted as true. We cannot do without general terms in psychology without distorting and mutilating our descriptions of human nature. To ascribe intelligence only to behavior and not to thinking is such a mutilation. The student must then learn about thought and thinking piecemeal in experimental sciences, which are quite untroubled by the thought that there is no thinking. Certain general characteristics of the thinking process should be taught in psychology. With this apology for believing that evidence of intelligence may be found in thinking as well as in action, we may, for a moment, turn to the thought and language of Alfred Binet, for it is chiefly through his discoveries that we are able to determine approximately different grades of intelligence. "If you interest yourself really and deeply in a child, you cannot put to yourself a question in regard to him more interesting, more important for his future and for his education, more agonizing for the heart of a father or a mother, than the following question: 'Is this child intelligent or is he not?" When a child succeeds in his

INTELLIGENCE 

239 studies, has good marks for diligence and reading, a good rank in composition, there is no doubt. The child proves his intelligence by what he does. It is the same for adults. 

In order to know their worth in intelligence and character observe their achievement. But it often happens that the child does not succeed in his studies. He does not profit by instruction. He is in the lowest ranks. There is an obstacle to instruction. To what must we impute it? We must seek the answer always without prejudice and with sincere desire in order that the explanation which we find may suggest (lit. contain) a remedy."

Binet then points to the importance of considering health and regularity of school attendance. "We can tolerate, indeed, twenty days of absence each year. It is the average number." He then takes a typical case of poor work in school and insists that we know whether the child tries or is merely lazy. "Shall we indict his intelligence or his character?" "Teachers and parents seem to imagine that when they have declared that a pupil lacks intelligence they have said everything and nothing further remains to be investigated. This is too summary a judgment. If we hold to it we shall not go far. Questions remain to be solved. What is the degree of defect of intelligence? Is it great or small?

If it is great, is it so great that the educator must despair? 

Is it real or apparent? Is it increasing, exaggerated by exceptional circumstances? In what does it consist? In what particular function, in what kind of work does it manifest itself the most? And finally what are its causes?

Are they of such a nature that we can modify them? It is necessary to have an idea on each of these different points, to consider them, to bring them to light."

Binet then recites case after case of mismanagement of

the child, wrong classification, disorientation due to a change of schools and so on to illustrate causes of apparent lack of intelligence but I have quoted him at length to show his sympathetic attitude toward the child and child training. This did not obstruct his pathway to the most important practical discoveries which have been made in psychology. His recital of instances shows also that these discoveries were not made without years of sympathetic interest in children. The coldly scientific attitude which some psychologists unconsciously assume by analogy with dealing with a physical science may be an error which could prevent discovery. The material with which we are dealing could very well modify our methods. We must quote a little further to show that preconceived opinions may also stand in the way of dealing successfully with human nature. "I have often determined, and with great regret, that there exists a widespread prejudice against the educability of intelligence. The familiar proverb, 'When one is stupid it is for a long time,' seems to be taken literally and uncritically by educators. They drop all interest in pupils who lack intelligence. They have no sympathy for them nor even respect, for their intemperance of language makes them utter before children such words as these: "This is a child who will never do anything. He is poorly endowed. 

He is not intelligent at all.' I have heard these imprudent words too often. They are repeated daily in the primary grades and even the secondary school is not exempt. I often remember that in my examination for the bachelor of letters an examiner, indignant at one of my replies (by confusion of words I had given to a Greek philosopher a name borrowed from a personage of the characters of La Bruyere), declared to me that I would never have a philo-

INTELLIGENCE 

241 sophic mind. Never! What a momentous word! Some recent philosophers seem to have given their moral support to these deplorable verdicts by affirming that the intelligence of an individual is a fixed quantity, a quantity that cannot be increased. We ought to protest and react against this brutal pessimism. We shall try to show that it has no basis at all."

Binet then proceeds to give excellent evidence that intelligence can be developed up to a certain limit in each individual and recently Freeman has further proved the educability of intelligence. The quotation from Binet will show why his general conception of intelligence led him to succeed in its measurement while other conceptions of intelligence led to failure.

The Binet Tests.-Binet saw the importance of an examination of achievement in studies and of a health examination. But he also saw that not only what the child had accomplished should be tested but his ability to learn must also be ascertained. A child sixteen years old in the first grade might know the studies of that grade but be unable ever to master those of the second grade. Not achievement alone but the development of ability to achieve must be measured.

In this practical situation and because of his long investigation of child psychology Binet assumed the existence of intelligence and began to invent a measure of it. 

He simply turned his back on the academic disputes and adopted the earlier opinion that mankind is possessed of intelligence. Binet spent years on his investigation but in 1908 he published tests which measure the mental ability of children with some accuracy. He published a revision in 1911 and the Binet scale for the measurement of intelligence soon became known in America, due to

Goddard's revision, under that title. Binet's title was "La Mesure du devellopement de l'intelligence chez les jeunes enfants."

Had this title been adhered to the public would have understood better the nature and purpose of the tests. In 

America Lewis M. Terman again revised the tests. This is called the Stanford revision and it is the form most widely used at present. After years of experimentation, therefore, Binet's hypothesis that something which may be called intelligence exists and its development may be measured has been fully verified. Much mystery has been made by schoolmen as to what this intelligence is. Much dispute has raged over its nature, but the working hypothesis has been proved and accepted. 

Examples of Binet's Questions.-The child of three years is asked to (1) point to the nose, eyes, mouth, (2) repeat three digits, (3) enumerate objects in a picture, (4) give his family name, (5) repeat a sentence of six syllables.

To this the Stanford revision adds the naming of three out of five familiar objects, such as a key, penny, knife, watch, pencil. The revision also asks, “Are you a little boy or a little girl?" if a boy is being tested, and the order of sex is reversed for a little girl. This is because the three-yearold tends very strongly to repeat the last word of a question rather than to answer it. This is a part of his language learning impulse and helps him to acquire language but interferes with an intelligent answer to your question.

It appears that dull children are slow to observe any difference between the sexes and to classify themselves as boys or girls.

The three-year-old who can answer these questions correctly has normally developed intelligence for his age or he may fail on one or more of them but answer some of

INTELLIGENCE 

243 those for four-year-olds, and still attain a score normal for his age.

A moment's attention shows that even a three-year-old child must have discriminated prominent features of the face, have developed some immediate memory, be capable in simple and interesting observation, must have picked up a name not often used in the family and must exhibit immediate memory once more.

If we consider the questions or tests of the Stanford revision we find that later questions require the use of these powers over and over again in somewhat more difficult situations. Knowledge acquired is tested by about seventeen questions. Much of this knowledge is of a kind acquired in the natural environment rather than in school. 

Some of it is school knowledge. Immediate memory is tested fourteen times though in five of these times visual imagination is coupled with the memory. Discrimination appears ten times, observation or perception several times. 

Perception and memory of time, judgment, the interpretation of meaning, inductive observation and arithmetical problems appear in the tests.

It must be observed that no child, youth or adult, needs to have answered all these questions in order to have his grade of intelligence determined. Twelve to eighteen questions are often quite adequate. Apparently twelve to eighteen or twenty samples of ability being present in normal development other abilities are present in normal or nearly normal development or the Binet tests would not work so well as they do. Since the tests have worked satisfactorily in literally millions of cases the conclusion is forced upon us that immediate verbal-auditory memory, permanent logical memory, or the ability to learn, discrimination, perception of time, and the ability to under-

stand meanings loom very large as samples of intelligence. 

It should be observed that most of the questions or tests are such that information must not only be known but used in dealing with a situation or problem. So "common sense" or the practical ability to use knowledge in a somewhat novel situation must be present if there is to be a high intelligence score. Apparently, also, each type of situation can be made so complex or abstract that the average intelligence cannot deal with it successfully in the time allowed. If "intelligence is what the tests test" it seems evident that the abilities described in human psychology are large factors of intelligence. Not every one of them need be present in a high degree. One may compensate for the partial absence of another. A man completely devoid of visual imagery finds it difficult or impossible to spell a long word backward, so he might not get a high score on repeating a large number of digits backward. He might do exceptionally well on other tests and prove to be high in intelligence. It must be admitted that special aptitudes cannot be excluded entirely from the tests. A gifted computer scores high on arithmetical questions; a gifted linguist will be able to give many words, etc.

We may enumerate briefly the qualities of Binet's questions which seem to contribute to their success. (1) 

Questions which test knowledge "picked up" in the child's daily environment are often used. The intelligent child makes ordinary observations and discriminations early which the less intelligent child makes only much later. He also understands language and gives better attention than the latter. (2) Knowledge is tested but more often the use or application of such knowledge in some simple situation is required. (3) The tests become more difficult at each age level. (4) A perfect score on the questions for a

INTELLIGENCE 

245 particular age is not required if the child answers one or more questions at the next age level, so the tests are (5) a process of sampling. (6) Binet arrived at the entirely novel conception of mental age. (Entirely novel in the science of psychology.)

Mental Age.-At first Binet selected some thirty questions, increasing in difficulty, and employed them in testing his two daughters and other children. No doubt they formed a fairly satisfactory test for a given range of intelligence. Tests for adults, or more usually group tests, follow exactly this pattern. At some point in his research, however, Binet conceived the idea that normal children may increase in the ability called intelligence by a certain amount or a certain degree each year. He then endeavored to get a few questions which would test the intelligence of the normal three-year-old, four-year-old, twelve-year-old, etc. If sixty-five per cent. of the children of a certain age answered a question it was retained as normal for that age. Thus an age scale was built up and Binet found that he could measure the development of intelligence in children. As already mentioned, some "scattering” of answers was permitted. A child might not answer all the questions of the five-year level but he might succeed with two of the six-year level. Then it appeard in giving the test that some seven-year-old children could pass the test for nineyear-olds and some ten-year-olds could pass only the tests for the seven-year level. Such discoveries led Binet to the conception of mental age. The seven-year-old who passed the tests for age nine years was assigned a mental age of nine years. All those who could pass only the tests for seven years had a mental age of seven years, no matter what their chronological or life age might happen to be. 

This permits the measure of the development of intelli-

gence in terms of a unit of a normal or average year's growth in that ability. It is evident also that children can be ranked in mental age and that this is partly independent of chronological age.

This concept of mental age is probably the most important practical discovery in psychology, for it has been shown again and again that the most reliable single criterion for assigning a child to a grade or class in school is his mental age. His health, previous years in school, etc., may be considered but the best single standard is his mental age.

This has been proved true for normal children. It is even more important for subnormal and retarded children. 

In 1921 Massachusetts passed a law requiring that every child three, four, or more years retarded shall be given a mental examination and special training. The result has been the psychological examination of thousands of retarded children. As a result the school grade possible for such children at each mental age is as follows: 

Mental Age 4-5 10-11 

School Grade Possible 

Kindergarten 

First grade 

Second grade 

Third grade

Fourth grade 

Fifth grade except arithmetic

The mental age, universally abbreviated now as the M. A., is thus shown to be of great practical importance. 

Binet also discovered that his standard mental ages were not attained so early by the children of a poor district or neighborhood as by those of an average or superior so-

INTELLIGENCE 

247 cial environment. Some of this retardation was permanent for it appeared that the high average level of the better neighborhood would never be attained by the poorer one. Others have confirmed this finding. Psychologists who believed in the almost exclusive influence of heredity on human destiny were sure that the character of the neighborhood is determined by the grade of intelligence of its people. We need only look to heredity for the reason. 

Some even claimed that intelligence is transmitted as a unit character and is uninfluenced by training. We have seen that Binet himself shared neither of these opinions but regarded intelligence as educable. Many other psychologists also held judgment in suspense as to the purely hereditary character of intelligence. In poor homes especially the younger children learn to talk earlier and progress in speech acquisition more rapidly than the first born because of the presence and influence of the latter. 

Here there seems to be an environmental influence. Terman found the number of words known, the vocabulary test, to be an excellent test of intelligence.

Since Binet's discovery of age grades of intelligence it is beginning to dawn upon us that we can hardly set a child a task which does not test his intelligence. If the thing involves more than habit, intelligence is required. 

As a result Goodenough is able to determine intelligence or mental age by the child's drawings. Accuracy and detail of the child's drawing of the human figure increase with each year of age and with sufficient investigation the grade of drawing is made to determine the child's mental age. Such a test of ability is called a performance test. 

The Intelligence Quotient or I. Q.-Another important concept was suggested by William Stern and called by him the mental quotient. It is now called the intelligence quo-

tient. It is obtained by dividing the mental age by the chronological age. In the Stanford revision every attempt was made to devise tests and so arrange them that the normal intelligence would have an I. Q. of around 100. This is average intelligence or rather average intelligence ranges from 90 to 110. Terman gives the following classification for the various I. Q.'s. I. Q. Above 140 120-140 110-120 90-110 80-90 70-80 Below 70 Classification

Dullness, rarely classifiable as feeble-mindedness 

Border line deficiency, sometimes classifiable as dullness, often as feeblemindedness 

Definite feeble-mindedness

The concept of the I. Q. has been of great value though at first its significance was misunderstood. It does not indicate what should be the present classification of the child in school, but for retarded children at least it permits the prediction of the final attainable school grade. On the basis of the Massachusetts experience the following predictions are made:
