It has been found that these subnormal pupils can complete certain grades but they require three or four years to do so. 

If the teacher and the principal understand this there is no difficulty. A further discovery stated by Dr. 

Fernald as a result of the Massachusetts tests is that "there is no special pedagogy of the feeble-minded." If kept where they belong in ordinary schools, they accomplish quite as much as in the most expensive private schools with special devices and methods.

While the Stanford revision of Binet's tests is doubtless the most reliable test in use today, it is now probable that a correction should be applied when this test is employed. Freeman, toward the close of his investigation of foster children, found that the I. Q. instead of remaining constant dropped with increase in age. As a result, the original standardization of the test was thoroughly investigated. With the original 905 unselected children, on which the revision was standardized, the average I. Q.'s for ages 5 to 14 years dropped from 111 points to 98. This is an average decline of more than one point a year due to the tests themselves. Terman appears to grant this discrepancy. Hence Freeman corrects for it and a similar correction should always be made between these ages. 

Group Tests of Intelligence.-Dr. Arthur S. Otis, a stu dent in Terman's laboratory was first to see that intelligence tests might be devised which could be given to a large group of persons at once. He devised the first group intelligence test and invented stencils for the very rapid marking of such tests. With the entrance of the United 

States into the World War a committee of psychologists

under the direction of Dr. Yerkes devised group tests for determining the intelligence of army recruits. After a year or so of investigation and experimentation, tests were devised which were eminently practical and valuable. The most famous of these were the Army Alpha for literate recruits and the Army Beta for illiterates. Since then a legion of group tests has been devised and for their uses the special books must be consulted. We may, however, state briefly their general character.

Each page of the group test begins with very easy questions or problems and proceeds by degrees to very difficult ones of the same general kind. One widely used test, for example, employs a form of the Ebbinghaus completion test, i. e., there are thirty sentences with essential words omitted. The blanks are to be filled by the examinee. Next there are twenty problems involving arithmetical reasoning. These are followed by twenty tests in artificial language. A code is supplied and sentences must be translated into the code and from the code into ordinary language. In two lists of twenty proverbs each, the pairs having the same meaning must be selected. In the next test synonyms and antonyms must be selected and paired. Sentences containing errors must be marked minus and correct statements plus. A test in estimating, which proved to be a poor test, was followed by a test in non-arithmetical reasoning. 

If any considerable number of persons could complete any one of these tests the result would be damaged or spoiled, consequently every test of the series is rigidly timed, so that except in the case of one or two tests, no one can complete them all. The score for each person is the number of questions correctly answered. The scores are then arranged from highest to lowest and the individual

INTELLIGENCE 

251 who has the highest score is rated as the most intelligent member of the class or group tested. Such tests are useful in predicting success in studies provided the intelligent student is also reasonably industrious. This is not always the case. Then the test leads to a knowledge of the cause of the student's failure in school.

Performance Tests. Many writers have objected that intelligence can be expressed in manual performances quite as well as in the so-called intellectual way. Others reply that manual dexterity and skill are a special gift. 

Whatever be the merits of the dispute many performance tests have been devised and sold. The form board, long in use for the feeble-minded, is an example. The subject of the experiment must rapidly fit blocks into mortised openings exactly fitted to receive them. They may be asked to draw the pathway through a series of mazes each one more difficult than the one immediately preceding it. For the great variety of performance tests the special manuals must be consulted.

Results of Intelligence Tests.—As several million intelli gence tests have now been given to a very wide range of persons we may draw some approximate conclusions in regard to the relative intelligence of different classes and different races. The army tests showed that illiterate enlisted men made the lowest scores, then followed enlisted men, corporals, sergeants, members of the officers' training corps and officers, in order. Perhaps the difference between the last two classes was not great enough to be significant. The intelligence ratings of men of different occupations was determined. The list is long. Laborers, tailors, cobblers and miners were at the foot of the list in the order named, while stenographers, accountants, civil

engineers, medical officers, army chaplains and engineering officers were at the top, each profession making a slightly higher score than the one just preceding. It may be, therefore, that grade of intelligence determines what profession one enters or is a factor in such determination, though other interpretations of the results are possible. 

It was found by Goodenough that very young children of professional men had an intelligence quotient of 116, those of managers and proprietors 112, of clerks 108, of farmers, bakers, painters, etc., 105, of semi-skilled laborers 

104, of laborers 96. There is evidently a correlation between occupation and intelligence. The median score of drafted men on the Army Alpha test was 65 points; of college freshmen 150.

For different races Professor Garth found in a community, which included whites, Indians and mixed bloods, that the Indians stood lowest on an intelligence test, the whites highest, and the mixed bloods between the two.

Porteus has found somewhat similar conditions with oriental stocks. Tests made by white men would probably be somewhat in favor of that stock. Yet, after allowance is made for that probability the rank in intelligence is, no doubt, approximately as stated. Average scores, must be interpreted with caution, of course. Yet, if intelligence is inherited as a unit character, as is sometimes claimed, a certain number of mixed bloods should have had the grade of intelligence of their white progenitors and others of their Indian ancestors, instead of standing between the two as in blended inheritance. Again, after due allowance for the character of the tests used, the intelligence scores of immigrants from the south of Europe average lower than those of north European countries.

Is the Intelligence Quotient Constant?-This question has aroused most heated and prolonged discussion. If the intelligence quotient were almost exactly constant, no matter what the child's environment may be, we should have to decide that intelligence is a matter of heredity only and is uninfluenced by environment. Many records of children tested by the Binet scale on successive years have shown intelligence quotients which varied by only a few points. 

A difference of only five points was common. One of twenty points was rare.

On the other hand, Mrs. Woolley tested children who had entered a nursery school and those on the waiting list who could not be admitted but were of the same social status as the entrants. The average scores of the two groups were alike. Six months later both groups were

again tested and those who had been in school showed a superiority of eight points over the average intelligence quotient of those who had not been admitted. Mrs. Woolley thinks that a part of this gain will remain permanent. In a similar research Miss Goodenough found a superiority of three points in I. Q. of children in a nursery school over those not in school. Cyril Burt offered evidence to show that 53 per cent. of what intelligence tests test is due to training or education. These results found little favor among those who believed that intelligence can be influenced only by heredity.

On pages 240-241 we find that Binet protested against the idea that "the intelligence of an individual is a fixed quantity that cannot be increased or decreased. We ought to protest and react against this brutal pessimism. We shall try to show that it has no basis at all." 

One of Binet's arguments depends, however, on his views of the nature of intelligence and the reply would be that intelligence is not what Binet thought it is. Considering Binet's long study of intelligence and his pre-eminent success in that field this would be a startling rejoinder. 

We may, however, accept it for a moment and return to the matter in the next topic.

The most crucial evidence as to whether the intelligence quotient remains constant and whether intelligence is influenced at all by environment has been obtained by 

Freeman in testing foster children. Does a change to a better environment result in an increase in the intelligence quotient? Freeman tested seventy-four children who had been placed in foster homes at the average age of eight years and had remained in these homes for an average period of four years. "Their average I. Q. at the time of adoption was 95. The average I. Q. after four years, when

INTELLIGENCE 

257 we made allowance for the fact that the standard score gives a drop of five points between the ages of eight and twelve, was 1022, a gain of seven and one-half points.” 

One-half of these children had been adopted into superior homes, one-half into poorer homes. The former half had made a gain of over ten points in I. Q. in the four years. 

Their average I. Q. was 105. The half in poorer homes had gained only five points. This gain of ten points by foster children of the better homes seems to be very important evidence. "The gain is greater than that of one-third of children in general."

For convenience of speech children of the same parents are called siblings. Siblings reared in the same home resemble each other more in intelligence score than foster siblings who were reared in different homes. The foster siblings who were separated early in life were less alike than those which were separated late. Those who had been separated for a long period were less alike in intelligence than those who had been separated for a short time. Those who had been placed in similar homes were more alike than those of dissimilar homes. The average I. Q. of the foster children in better homes was 95; of their siblings in poorer homes, 85.7. Finally of a group of 401 foster children, those in superior homes had an average I. Q. of 106.8, those in inferior homes averaged 88.9. This is a difference of 18 points. No factor of selection of foster children for adoption was found which would account for these differences. 

These striking results of Freeman's work can hardly be ignored. It would seem fair to conclude that, while the 

I. Q. of a child in an unchanging environment may remain approximately constant, a change to a superior environment may raise the I. Q. and change to an inferior environment may stop this improvement of intelligence or, after a

considerable time, the child may have even a lower I. Q. than he attained on an earlier test. The I. Q. is not unchangeable and determined solely by heredity. Either this conclusion must be drawn or we must turn upon the tests and say they are unreliable measures but they have shown themselves to be by far the most reliable measurements obtainable. The Stanford revision, made by Terman, is also the most reliable test and this Freeman used in his investigation. Having now what attorneys call a preponderance of evidence based on intelligence tests, we may ask whether the mind or brain could develop without exercise or stimulation, by inner growth alone. This is hardly probable. Nothing we know about the brain or body suggests its independence of the environment. The intelligence quotient is not unchangeable. Intelligence is educable as Binet believed it to be.

Character. The child's home influences the development of his intelligence. It influences his character much more or at least more disastrously when the home is evil. 

It may not be amiss to point to this influence even in a section on intelligence, for the child's character may be influenced through and by his intelligence. In one year in a juvenile court, "16.2% of the delinquent children were orphans or half orphans, 18.5% were from homes where one or both parents were addicted to the excessive use of intoxicating liquors or narcotic drugs, and 26.5% were from homes broken up by desertion and divorce.”¹ 

Pierce Bailey found that 12% of the boys and more than 50% of the girls put on probation in the state of New York were brought into court in the first place on account of improper guardianship. "Many normal children be- 

¹A wit has interpreted such figures as follows: "From the child's point of view it is better to allow his parents to drink than to divorce, and better to destroy them than to permit either." One seeks the error in this logic.

INTELLIGENCE 

259 come deviates under this condition." Mrs. Wembridge, who has much knowledge of delinquent girls, is of the opinion that girls acquire ideals of chastity about the time that they acquire speech or they do not acquire them at all. An observant and experienced business man states practically the same thing when he says, "If you want to make a man honest, you must begin before he is eight years of age." The influence of the home on character appears to be far greater than its influence on intelligence but we know very little as yet concerning the inter-relations of these two traits.

The Nature of Intelligence.-Just as physicists and chemists have always tried to conceive more and more correctly and exactly the nature of matter and, with every advance in the correctness of their conceptions, have been able to solve new problems and to make new applications in their sciences, so most psychologists have tried to conceive more correctly and exactly the nature of mind and intelligence. Since Binet solved a very important problem, insoluble before, the present writer would have no hesitancy in saying that the conception of intelligence with which he started and which yielded so superior results, is the most correct conception. This test of results is accepted in other sciences. However, other conceptions of intelligence must be stated and perhaps compared with that of Binet. 

(1) The Conception of the Faculty Psychology.—The spiritualists in psychology were accustomed to say for every mental ability or performance, "The soul has a 'faculty' for doing that." Then they listed a limited number of faculties as sensibility or sensation, intelligence, memory, imagination, understanding, attention, reason, etc. But they unconsciously fell into the habit of speaking

of the imagination, the memory, etc., as if these faculties were identical in different persons. This, of course, was a gross error, for Galton showed that some persons imagined scenes and situations in vivid visual images, while others thought of them only in words. Their thought material was verbal. Charcot, also in his study of aphasia insisted on different types of memory based on different types of imagery. His teachings had enormous influence. 

It was immediately evident that anything which could be called "the imagination," "the memory" did not exist but that different persons had predominantly different types of memory and imagination. This does not deny, however, that every intelligent person has an ability to remember or imagine in some sort of terms and we now see the term mental abilities returning in educational psychology, for such abilities certainly exist.

Another defect of the faculty psychology was its invention of a particular faculty for every performance of the individual, whether such performance was mental or physical. There was a faculty invoked for each. We have seen that this error has been returned to us by the mechanists in psychology. For every act of an animal or a human being there is a mechanism and a drive and the mechanism can be "conditioned." These mechanisms are often very mysterious and we are told to wait until their nature is discovered. But there is really no difference in method between invoking a mysterious faculty on the one hand or a mysterious mechanism on the other. Neither term may name anything real.

Another influence served to aid in the overthrow of the faculty psychology. Psychologists discovered that instead of five senses there are at least eleven, each one having different receptors or sense organs at the surface of the body,

INTELLIGENCE 

261 different pathways to the central nervous system and to the brain and different centers or adjustors in the brain. 

Each one might, when stimulated, lead, however, to the same movement. They were thus not exactly different abilities but each of the senses was independent of all the others. This independence of the senses and of different types of imagery and consequently of memory, was bound to destroy the fixed faculty hypothesis but it was also bound to lead to overemphasis on independence and to the consequent invention of a multitude of very minute or little faculties, now called independent functions. 

(2) The Theory of Independent Functions.-This theory really implies that there are as many minute, independent, mental functions as there are reflex arcs with adjustors in the cortex. Any complex intellectual performance is due to the average result of minute functions. 

This conception was taught for a long time with great vigor and authority. It is still taught by inventing and diagramming particular bonds or connections between stimulus and reaction. Even the beginner in psychology feels that these inventions are artificial and non-existent in nature. This conception may be called the reflex arc theory of mind. But the reflex arc cannot be isolated even in the brain of the simplest fishes. The interconnections of nerve fibers are enormously complex even in so low a brain. The idea that fiber paths are insulated from one another as they lead through the brain is not true. We must remember that the conception of the reflex arc is derived from experiments on the lower nervous system of animals. Generally the brain is destroyed or completely separated from the spinal cord in such experiments. 

Association rather than insulation is the fact, especially in the brain.

The theory of independent mental functions is sufficiently sketched for our purpose in the following quotation: "The mind must be regarded not as a functional unit, nor even as a collection of a few general faculties which work irrespective of particular material, but rather as a multitude of functions each of which involves content as well as form and so is related closely to only a few of its fellows." There is thus almost complete independence of mental functions, since each one is closely related to only a few others. "There is no one power of sense discrimination to be delicate or coarse, no capacity for uniform accuracy in judging the physical stimuli of the outside world. There are only the connections between the sense stimuli and our separate sensations and judgments thereof, some resulting in delicate judgments of difference, some resulting in coarse judgments. There is no one memory to hold in a uniformly tight or loose grip all the experiences of the past. There are only particular connections between particular mental events, and others, sometimes resulting in great surety of revival, sometimes in little. 

And so on through the list. Good reasoning power is but a general name for a host of particular capacities and incapacities, the general average of which seems to the namer to be above the general average in other individuals" (1910). 

Since these minute functions were conceived as almost completely independent, each function must be tested separately with a minute and specific test and thousands of such tests were made. The test of intelligence, by this conception, must be of the nature of an invoice of all the specific functions. Binet's tests are "samplings," not invoices of minute items. Thus we see that the conception of intelligence dictates the type of experiments which are

INTELLIGENCE 

263 devised to test it. Binet turned his back on this conception of intelligence and on its extreme opposite when he began his quest for a practical test of intelligence. His words have both practical and theoretical value. "If ever a question was in controversy it is that of the value of correlations. There are two opinions, absolutely contradictory and both claim the force of proofs. According to one, which has been sustained with ardor by the American, Thorndike, the mind is only a collection, absolutely heterogeneous, of capacities which are juxtaposed but remain rigorously independent. The opposite opinion, sustained by Spearman, is that intelligence is one; that there exists in each of us an ability meriting the name of general intelligence, and that we discover a correspondence between the degree of all our activities even the most remote. This is exactly the counterpoise of the opinion of 

Thorndike... all in all these are extreme theses and rightly enough it is the truths of the golden mean which they leave standing." (Binet, Les Idées Modernes sur les Enfants.) Binet then gives evidence for his opinion but the best evidence is the success of his tests. 

The Two-Factor Theory of Spearman.-Having de scribed the multiple function theory of Thorndike at length less space will be required to state Spearman's conception. There are special abilities but their activities are permeated and all are influenced by a single general factor which he names G to avoid describing it further in the present state of our knowledge. This general factor brings all special abilities into relation to one another so that their output may be named poor, average or superior for different individuals. Spearman's theory, like Thorndike's, is derived from correlations so a word must be said about the method of correlation later.

Binet's Conception of Intelligence.-Binet has hinted above that his view of intelligence represents a golden mean between that of Thorndike and that of Spearman.

Then, in speaking of the educability of intelligence, he adds: "Now if one considers that intelligence is not one function, indivisible and of a particular substance, but that it is formed by the concert of all these little functions of discrimination,² of observation, of retention, etc., whose plasticity and development we have established, it appears incontestable that the same law governs the total and its elements and that consequently the intelligence of any one is capable of development. By exercise, by training, and especially by the method used, one succeeds in augmenting his attention, his memory, his judgment, and literally in becoming more intelligent than he was before and this progresses to the moment when he reaches his limit." (Binet, ibid., p. 143.) Binet then decides that it is highly probable that we have the power to develop intelligence. 

This hypothesis of Binet's seems to have received strong support from the work of Freeman on foster children. 

By "function" in the above quotation Binet plainly does not mean the minute, independent functions of Thorndike's theory. He mentions some of the special abilities which he regards as factors or elements of intelligence. 

We may now turn to the tests themselves. Does not the character of these successful tests give the best evidence as to the nature of intelligence? I think it does. 

Attention is in evidence throughout every intelligence test. 

It functions with special importance in timed tests. Out of a total of ninety particular Binet tests of the Stanford revision, memory or knowledge acquired is tested 26 It is a curious fact that among a dozen recent text-books on psychology only incidental mention is made of discrimination.

INTELLIGENCE 

265 times, immediate memory 18 times, discrimination or comparison 10 times, comprehension of meaning 13 times. 

Thus 67 tests are accounted for. Visual imagination is surely tested several times, perception of time at least once, and so on. If we turn to other tests than the Binet, computation and the solution of arithmetical problems appear in most of them, as does also the perception of relations. These are tests of ability to use abstract ideas and the situations, relations, and problems grow more abstract as we go up the age scale. A passage from Adam 

Smith is more abstract and complex than one of Aesop's 

Fables. 

To the unprejudiced observer of the best intelligence tests it appears that the list of abilities tested is exactly the same as that discussed in text-books of psychology for many years. The intelligent person possesses these abilities in a marked degree. Consequently he learns readily; so intelligence has been defined as (1) ability to learn or to profit by experience, and (2) the ability to adapt readily to novel situations. Both these definitions are widely accepted. The present writer believes that the presence in high degree of just the score or so of abilities which common sense has always ascribed to human beings constitutes intelligence. If my view should prove to be correct a large part of the present text is given to an attempt to describe the nature of intelligence, and it seems reasonable to expect this of a text-book of psychology. 

It must not be supposed, however, that many psychologists accept Binet's theory of intelligence though they accept his tests as of the very greatest value and importance. 

Freeman (Mental Tests, pp. 486-487) does accept Binet's conception, if I interpret his words correctly. He further points out that intelligence depends upon association

areas of the cortex; "upon the rearrangement of association, patterns among the neurons." There seems to be ample evidence for this hypothesis. 

The Correlation Method of Studying Intelligence.-We may wish to know whether intelligence is the chief factor in success in study. A rough way to estimate this would be to set opposite each person's name his score on a reliable intelligence test and the average of all his grades or marks in his studies. If we arranged the intelligence scores in a column from highest to lowest and then found the averages in school work taking exactly the same order, we should decide at once that intelligence is the chief factor in success in study. If both the order and relative size of the scores in both the intelligence test and the record of success in study were the same we should say there was perfect positive correlation. When the degree of relationship between two sets of scores cannot be determined by inspection, it may be obtained by calculating the coefficient of correlation designated by r. The formula commonly used for this calculation is Σ xy nσ1 02 The number of persons or the number of scores on each test is symbolized by n of the formula. The meaning of the other symbols can be learned from the following illustrative table and the explanatory remarks. For the sake of simplicity I have chosen scores that are in perfect positive correlation. (See table on page 267.)

If the order of the school marks were changed to 24, 20, 28, 16, 4, 8, 12, r would be .75. r may vary, therefore, through all values from 1 to -1.

When r=0 the two abilities tested are assumed to be totally unrelated or perfectly independent of each other. 

Such a value for r is rarely found.

If a correlation of .75 between intelligence and success in studies were found, it would be assumed that intelligence is a large factor of success in school work and high correlations were so interpreted for a long time. There are, however, many pitfalls in the interpretations of correlations. It is not the infallible instrument for measuring relationships which it was at first supposed to be. 

Only three of a great many precautions can be mentioned. 

1. There must be a large number of measures or persons sharing in both tests. Some writers think the number should be at least 75. Our example is illustrative only. 

2. There should be a great number of measures of each individual in each test, otherwise the r must he corrected for attenuation. Thorndike gives an example of an r of .38, based on an ordinary number of measures, which would become .70 or .80 when corrected for attenuation.

Yet many uncorrected coefficients are still published. 

3. The correlation coefficients are not reliable unless they are two or three times the probable error and preferably four or five times the probable error. This error is often computed by the formula .67449×(1—r²) Vn in which the r and n are those of the Pearson formula. 

A simpler device for calculating correlations is called the rank difference method. The formula for this is r=16Xsum of D² 

n(n²-1) Here D is the difference in the rank of each individual on the two tests, Σ is the sum, and n the number of persons tested.

It requires great sagacity, however, to interpret what a coefficient of correlation means. Thorndike says, "Until the work of Spearman in 1904, it was not known that any relation calculated from other than complete measurements of the divergences to be related would be reduced from its true amount toward 0. Wissler, for example, found the relation between drawing a line equal a 100 mm. line and accuracy in bisecting it, to be only .38, because he had as measures of the two traits to be related only the results with a single line. 

If each individual had been tested with hundreds of lines at different times so as to get his real total abilities the result would have an r of .7 or .8. Since this fact of the

'attenuation' of the r's obtained from imperfect original data was not realized at all until 1904, and is not realized by many students even now, the majority of the r's that have been calculated are of doubtful meaning" (Thorndike, 1910, pp. 188-189).

Another difficulty involved in constructing psychology and educational theory from statistical conclusions lies in the fact that we do not learn from statistics anything at all about the particular person, pupil or student. By an individual intelligence test we ascertain a fact of the greatest importance about him and we can at once classify him with his equals in intelligence. Many correlations have proved to be disappointing and not applicable to practical affairs.

Just now, however, a startlingly high correlation has been found between what appeared to be unrelated functions. If the tendon, which extends to the foot, is struck a light blow just below the knee cap the foot thrusts forward with a reflex kick, if the center in the spinal cord is in sound health. This is called the knee jerk. Now Travis and Hunter have found a correlation of .87 between the reflex time of the knee jerk and scores on an intelligence test. The experiment was repeated and the same high correlation found. This is surprising. The conclusion is drawn that the same quality of the nervous system underlies quickness of this reflex action and the elementary processes of the nervous system which constitute intelligence. This interpretation is a return to the function theory of intelligence. It is interesting, if true, that the quality of the brain can be ascertained from an involuntary reflex of the spinal cord. It is possible, of course, that mental alertness and quickness of the knee jerk may be the same thing but, if so, we should expect quickness

INTELLIGENCE 

271 of reflexes in general to go with alertness and this is not often the case. However, this high correlation has been found and it will be interesting if it is found to be an index of intelligence.³

CHAPTER VIII SENSATION 

An account of particular mental processes must begin with sensation, for not only does consciousness appear to be awakened into activity by impressions from the external world but memories of such impressions make up much of the data of thought, the so-called "contents" of consciousness. "The mind can frame unto itself no one new simple idea." Without sensations due to light there is neither vision nor visual memories, nor thought of hue, nor tint, nor shade, nor black, nor white. 

Sensations are, therefore, the first states of consciousness which we experience, or, more strictly defined, a sensation is a state of consciousness produced by an impression on an afferent nerve.

The Stimulus for a Sensation. We have learned that by means of reflex arcs stimuli initiate acts and that they may at the same time arouse sensations by means of conducting paths to the cortex. The analysis of our incoming experiences into simple sensations has been aided by the discovery of qualities and movements in the objects which cause such experiences. When I see a tree I no longer say I "sense" it, as was done in Berkeley's time. Instead I say I "perceive" it and the tree is the "object" of my perception. This object, however, has certain qualities, as colors, form and extent. Its rustling leaves set the air into certain rates of vibration. Consequently, the stimulus for a sensation is some quality of an object or a movement (often vibratory) of matter.

SENSATION 

273 A rate of 256 vibrations per second in the air, gives the sensation of the pure tone middle C. Ether wave lengths of 656.2µµ¹ give a sensation of pure red, of 492.4μμ of bluegreen. When, however, these two wave lengths, or their physiological effects, are mixed in proper proportions the resulting sensation is a pure gray. Thus the psychologically simple corresponds to the physically, or at least to the physiologically, complex stimulus. But aside from complexities of this kind, it is probable that if the world about us were divided and subdivided, until analysis could go no further, it would consist of the stimuli which produce our sensations directly and indirectly. If it includes qualities and motions which affect us neither directly nor indirectly we can of course have no knowledge of them at all, because of the law that the data of consciousness are, or are derived from, sensations.

Some of the stimuli which affect our senses only indirectly are of especial interest. A swift flying bullet gives no sensation of pain, because such impact came into our environment but yesterday. Ultra-violet light and X-rays are likewise beyond the range of our senses, but we translate them into that range by artificial means, so that their effects are visible. Wireless waves are made to affect our ears by means of a Morse key, etc. Since these are not direct stimuli it appears evident that the receptors (p. 90) for each type of sensation have developed under the influence of the stimuli long present in the environment. 

This is evidenced also by other facts. The brain (except perhaps the thalamus) may be operated upon, rubbed, cut or burned without any sensation whatever. The stomach, liver edge, kidneys, etc., may likewise be handled without a sensation of pain, or touch (though later inflamma- 'Millionths of a millimeter in length.

tion may produce acute pain) while the exterior of the body is supplied with two to four million pain points.

Stimuli, therefore, seem first to have produced appropriate receptors and, where the latter are present, the stimulus produces a sensation and usually an appropriate reaction. 

The stimulus which normally and usually causes the sensation is called the adequate stimulus. When, however, we see flashes of light from nudging the eyeball or from a blow on the back of the head, or when quinine produces a "ringing" of the ears we have examples of what is called the "inadequate" stimulus. This is surely a misnomer, yet the term has come to be used in both psychology and physiology. 

Projection of Sensations.-There is ample evidence to show that sensations are aroused only when the nervous impulse reaches the cortex. Yet we are never conscious of this fact. Instead, experience seems to have taught us to locate sensations either outside the limits of the body, at various distances, or within its bulk. Thus the eye, the ear and the nose are termed distance receptors, because the sensation is localized at a distance in the environment. 

Taste sensations are located within the mouth while touch and temperature sensations are located now at the surface of the body, now in the object which furnishes the stimulus. Sensations of dizziness and nausea seem to have their location in the head and the body respectively. This so-called "projection" of the sensations thus furnishes the basis for a rough classification of them as exterior, at the limits of the body or within it.

The Threshold or Limen of Sensation.-Lights may be too faint or too distant to be seen, touches too light to be felt, sounds both too low and too high or too faint to be heard, and so on for the whole list of sensations. The

SENSATION 

275 smallest amount or lowest intensity of a stimulus which gives a sensation at all is called the limen or threshold of stimulation of that sense. It must be determined for each sense by the average of a sufficient number of experiments. 

Because of fluctuations of attention and other changes, a single experiment will not exactly determine the threshold. 

Sounds too high in pitch to be heard by human ears are said to be above the upper limen of the auditory sense. The series of sensations which we get between the lower and the upper thresholds is called the range of that sense. At the upper threshold of most senses the sensation changes into pain. It is often said that pain in turn, if too intense, may produce unconsciousness.

If we represent the intensity of the stimulus by a line, equal distances along which stand for units of intensity, thus, 0 1 2 3 4 5 the threshold of stimulation will stand at some point, "a", according to the size of the units of stimulus chosen. It is a matter of common observation that the various sense thresholds are different for animals and man, that different individuals are differently sensitive to stimuli of about threshold value, and in the case of some senses the liminal stimuli are different for men, for women and for children. 

Finally practice changes the threshold value. By practice we become sensitive to stimuli which were quite imperceptible before.

The Threshold of Difference and Weber's Law. When it is once above the threshold of sensation how much must the stimulus be increased in order to produce a just perceptible increase in the intensity of the sensation? The physiologist Weber found that when a weight of thirty

ounces was placed on the supported hand it could just be distinguished from one of twenty-nine ounces. The same result was obtained when dram weights were used. Hence by his determination the difference threshold for pressure is one-thirtieth² of the original stimulus. For the intensity of sounds the difference limen has been shown to be one-third of the original stimulus, for light intensities one one-hundredth.

The remarkable fact is that for each sense the increase in the stimulus necessary to produce a just perceptible increase in the sensation bears a constant ratio to the original stimulus. This is called from its discoverer Weber's 

Law. It must be mentioned further in the account of discrimination. The law appears to hold true of medium intensities of sensation, though now and then an investigator remarks that its validity is "still an open question." 

That we do not see even the brightest stars when the eye is already stimulated by sunlight, that in the quiet of night we detect sounds which would be unnoticed if other sounds were present, and that when the snow muffles most noises the remaining ones are far more distinct, seem to be ordinary applications of this law. Again, while a natural scene in brightest sunlight may be a "millionfold" as bright as a twilight scene, the skilled artist can represent them to us truly though his brightest white pigment is only a hundred times as bright as his darkest black. It is evidently the amount of difference, the relationship between tints which affects us. If this is correct the absolute intensities are not essential for creating the correct impression. Within medium intensities music seems to depend almost altogether on the relations between tones, rather than on their absolute intensities, and Ebbinghaus Strictly, 1/29.

SENSATION 

277 adds that because of Weber's Law a great number of the seats at a concert can be sold at the same price, while those which are very near and very distant from the music are less valuable.

Discrimination of different qualities is far more important than distinguishing different degrees of intensity. 

This is shown by the fact that hundreds of instruments have been devised to assist our senses in such discrimination. There is a difference threshold of quality which these instruments lower. But aside from such instruments, discrimination is improved only by practice. 

Practice. The term practice is usually applied to motor performances and vocal training as in singing and speaking. In those fields skill and habit are the results of the training. It is sometimes overlooked that our sensory equipment is capable of improvement by practice and the result is greater and greater refinement of discrimination. 

Practice, therefore, must lower both the threshold of sensation and the threshold of difference. The unpracticed observer requires a change of one-sixtieth of the original illumination in order to detect a difference, the average observer one one-hundredth, while the practised experimenter's difference threshold is only one two-hundredth. 

In the field of touch sensations most of us can distinguish silk from woolen. The expert can grade silks and woolens. Flour is graded partly by the sense of touch. 

The quality of flour a sample of wheat will make is often learned by taste. A wool grower in Colorado washed a sample of his wool and sent it to Ohio, whence it was forwarded to buyers in Philadelphia. A prompt reply said, "The sample you sent us is western wool. We think it is from Montana." Presumably this fine discrimination was made by, touch. I once led a blind friend along a city

street. He reported every tree we passed in the parking beside the walk. Then he said, "I think this must be a small tree." It was in fact a post. His delicate sense of the pressure of air between himself and such objects was, he thought, the cause of his perception. Bats, which fly in darkness, have this sensitiveness to air pressures or temperatures in a high degree. Hence they rarely collide with objects when flying. In them the delicate sense hairs over the wings and body are said to be the receptors for this "telaesthetic" touch. Helen Keller "hears" the applause of her audiences, as she says, "through my feet," i. e., by means of vibrations communicated along the floor. 

This again is typical of ants and other creatures which live in continual contact with the ground. It conducts vibrations more rapidly than the air. In a great estab lishment for canning salmon the slightest opening in a can is detected by the sound it gives forth when struck with a light mallet. Certain buyers of milk can tell by taste whether milk will become sour in the 12 to 20 hours required to send it to market.

In the visual and motor realm, the doors of the Baptistry at Florence are said to have perfect figures carved within one thirty-second of a square inch. We might continue with examples of detecting counterfeit paper money by touch and with the wonderful discrimination of tasters of wine and tea.

Sense discrimination may go so far as to produce socalled "mind-reading." One professional player of baseball made a reflex motion of his knee before delivering the ball. 

The base runners learned to watch for this motion and profit by it. Another glanced longer at the object of a real throw than at that of a feigned one; still another unconsciously looked at the ball in his hands when he purposed

SENSATION 

279 to pitch a "curve," and forgot to do so when it was to be a "fake curve." A still more famous pitcher formed the habit of raising his eyebrows before delivering a difficult ball. "This made the peak of his cap go up and down," and the opposing batsmen detected this unconscious signal. It was exactly in this way that the famous horse, Clever Hans, made his master believe that he could count and calculate. 

The master wore a broad-brimmed hat and gave a very slight but unconscious nod when the horse's tapping reached the right number. This is called "muscle reading" in psychology but in the instances mentioned it is also perfectly successful "mind reading." Animals which watch the movements of their trainers give the most frequent examples of it. In conclusion, it is probably true that any one who will train a single sense to its maximum of discrimination may depend upon that sense alone for a livelihood.

Adaptation.-Adaptation seems at first to be just the reverse of practice. We pay no attention to differences and they vanish from consciousness. We wear several pounds of clothing but we do not feel its pressure upon our bodies. The ring, which was felt as tight at first, is now unnoticed though it may even constrict the bloodvessels. Those who work in heat and cold become, as we say, "accustomed" to it. The more interesting fact, however, is, that once we are adapted to a particular condition, we are extremely sensitive to a very slight change from it. 

Nansen felt that a temperature of -20° (-4°F) was "delightfully mild and springlike" after he had been exposed for weeks to arctic temperatures of -40° (-40°F). Psychology had to wait long for a similar experiment to be made in the antarctic regions but finally there came the expedition of Sir Ernest Shackleton. After describing

the stupendous ice barriers of that terra incognita he pauses to tell how very uncomfortable all of his party were when the thermometer rose to 29 degrees Fahrenheit on a spring day, after they had become accustomed to temperatures well below zero. The experience leads him to comment on the ease and rapidity with which the human body accustoms itself to any sort of conditions. The result of a battle or a whole military campaign has more than once been decided by the adaptation of an army to severe temperatures. Its effects are not limited to the nervous system alone. Miners who have lived for years below ground suffer from rheumatism when subjected to the great changes of a surface climate. Persons who live for only a few months in a mountainous district report that they "miss the mountains" when they remove to level country and it is said that Swiss boys have been known to die of homesickness. Possibly Byron's lines, "My very chains and I grew friends,

So much a long communion tends 

To make us what we are," are psychologically true.

If this is but poetry, however, then truth is again far stranger than fiction for Barbusse writes the following as plain fact of his experience in the trenches. "Crack! 

Crack! Boom!-rifle fire and cannonade. Above us and all around, it crackles and rolls, in long gusts or separate explosions. The flaming and melancholy storm never, never, ends. For more than fifteen months, for five hundred days in this part of the world where we are, the rifles and the big guns have gone on from morning to night and from night to morning. We are buried deep in an everlasting battlefield; but like the ticking of the clocks at home in the days gone by-in the now almost legendary past-you

SENSATION 

281 only hear the noise when you listen." (Under Fire, p. 6.)

Such an extreme of adaptation is far stranger than becoming endeared to one's chains.

Social adaptation is no less prominent and important than physical, though in the former it is more than sensory adaptation. At almost regular intervals we read of some man who has struggled for a lifetime to have a mansion on Riverside Drive or on some Capitol Hill, only to find when he had succeeded that he and his are the most unhappy of mortals. Soon a "For Sale" sign appears on the lawn and the family has returned to the old environment and the old friends. So far as we have social classes in America they are based entirely on the psychological fact of adaptation. 

Other division lines may be readily swept away.

Dr. Crile defends the thesis "that environment has been the actual creator of the man." If this is true of race history it is hardly more important than the enormous modification of the individual due to his adaptation to various environments.

Difference Between Practice and Adaptation. The effects of practice are wrought under the influence of strict attention. Pay attention to stimuli and you can sense finer and finer grades of difference between them until your power of discrimination is marvelous, if not, as the maxim says, "perfect." But refuse to pay attention to stimuli and they cease to exist for you. Thus, being partly due to inattention, adaptation differs in that particular from practice. 

But since we are sensitive to a slight change from the usual stimuli or environment, both adaptation and practice appear to lower the difference threshold. Moreover adaptation is the quicker process, apparently because the environment operates constantly, attention only intermittently. For this reason a favorable new environment is

usually far more effective than a good resolution in breaking off a bad habit.

Summation of Stimuli.-A better phrase is "summation of the effects of stimuli." Let us take an analogy from the stimulation of a reflex circuit. Sherrington found that the "scratch reflex" in a spinal dog could not be elicited by a single induction shock however intense. In many cases the muscle contracted only after the fortieth shock and nearly four seconds after the application of the first shock. 

Thus the effects of successive shocks summed themselves together and produced the reaction. This summing of effects is not due to the nerve trunk or fiber but to the cell or synapse.

In a similar way a stimulus may be too slight to produce a sensation and yet, after several repetitions of the same stimulus, the sensation may arise. Or a single stimulus may produce only a slight sensation, its continued repetition a very intense sensation. This is called re-enforcement of stimuli and apparently it may be either temporal or spatial, i. e., repeated applications of a stimulus to the same nerve ends or the stimulation of a greater number of nerve ends increase the effect. For example if the finger alone be plunged in warm water it may feel only warm. If the forearm be thrust in the same water, it may feel agonizingly hot. Part of this increase in effect is due to summation, part of it to a difference in adaptation to warmth. 

When the higher functions are considered, "nagging" is nothing but summation. Animals in captivity pine away and die partly from the continual or repeated presence of stimuli to fear. Similar statements may be made of human beings. When already depressed a singly gloomy word added may produce despair. Or, on the side of pleasure, people who are not hungry eat because the food is

SENSATION 

attractively served, etc. All this is summation or re-enforcement of the effects of stimuli. A stimulus just intense enough to produce a sensation is called the liminal stimulus. Those which are less intense are subliminal. 

Fusion and Interference of Sensations.-Sherrington has shown beyond question that two similar sensations coming from the right and the left retinas, respectively, fuse into a single sensation. This is not a fusion of nerve impulses but of fully developed sensations. It is "psychic fusion." 

Again right and left eye images fuse into a single image of one object. Closing first one eye, then the other, shows that the two images are different in position and in the portion of the object seen. Because of this continual fusion of retinal images persons have become blind in one eye without knowing it. Sherrington (p. 383) has shown further that simultaneity suffices to produce sensual fusion. Apparently, therefore, James' statement, "Any number of impressions from any number of sensory sources, falling simultaneously on a mind which has not yet experienced them separately, will yield a single undivided object to that mind” (B. C., p. 245), has been proved to be true by the most refined experiments. Flash, snap, and sting are not distinguished. They are the one thing, "electric spark,” etc.

This law of sensual fusion is of so great importance that we shall later ask whether an idea and a sensation may not fuse so completely that we cannot tell where one leaves off and the other begins. If so, many illusions and human misunderstandings will be thoroughly explained. 

Seeing is believing, but such belief need by no means be the truth. It is so often untrue that this may be called the chief "fallacy of testimony." One says "of course," and instantly belief and perception are inextricably mixed.

But sensations also interfere with each other. Close one eye and there is no sensation of darkness. Close them both and darkness is instantly experienced. Here one sensation, that of light, eclipses the other and interference is complete (Sherrington, p. 367). This inhibition of one sensation by another is the usual experience. More rarely one sensation reduces another in amount or intensity. 

This is notably true of two flicker sensations. These laws of fusion, reduction and complete interference of sensations go to show once more that consciousness is "like a delicate optical instrument" adjusted for just one stimulus, situation or thought at any one moment. This has been called the "unity of consciousness" and fusion, reduction, or inhibition of one higher mental process by another is so common that it is more important in that field than in the realm of sensations.

The Attributes of Sensations. According to Titchener any sensation combines at least four attributes-quality, intensity, clearness, and duration. In some sensations even a greater number of attributes may be distinguished. 

Quality is the attribute which determines the kind or class to which a sensation belongs, gives it a special name and distinguishes it from all other sensations. Less exactly quality is the kind of sensation. Sour, salt, green and gray are different sense qualities. As already shown, there is a somewhat close, but not perfect, correspondence between the qualities of sensations and the classes of receptors stimulated. The term quality is used in both a narrower and a wider sense. In the narrower sense all sensations of green have the same color quality, and sour tastes differ in quality from sweet. In the wider sense we speak of the visual qualities, the taste qualities, etc., in-

SENSATION 

285 cluding thereby the whole list of optic or gustatory sensations.

Sensations of the same quality may be compared in intensity. One is stronger or weaker, heavier or lighter, more or less painful than another. In this way sensations of the same quality are referred to a scale of intensities. 

Intensity is dependent on the energy of the stimulus. 

Clearness.-In any given state of consciousness certain items may be clear, others more obscure. The clearness of a sensation is, therefore, its degree of definiteness and vividness as compared with other items present in consciousness at the same moment. Or its clearness is the degree to which it absorbs consciousness at any moment; the degree to which it obscures other conscious states. 

The clearness of a sensation is quite different from its intensity. (1) Clearness is due to a subjective process, the condition of consciousness itself, its continued adjustment to the stimulus. The intensity of a sensation depends upon the intensity of the stimulus and changes when the latter changes. (2) In the case of intensity we compare sensations of the same quality and to be compared they must occur or be given attention in immediate succession, while in clearness we compare the items of consciousness present at any one moment and they may be very different in character or kind. (3) It is claimed that there are but two grades of clearness while there are many different degrees of intensity.

If a sensation is clear it is said to be in the "focus" or "foreground" of consciousness, if obscure in the "margin" or "background." The metaphors contained in the words "foreground" and "background" "focus" and "margin" must not be overlooked. By the first pair of terms consciousness is regarded as a painting or other perspective

view which has foreground and background; by the second pair, consciousness is analogous to the field of vision having a small field or "focus" surrounded by a more obscure "margin." Thus the notion of consciousness as a field or as having a certain extent is implied, while in other connections we speak of consciousness as a process, a stream of thought, or train of thought, by which is implied that one of the fields or states of consciousness has gradually or rapidly changed into another.

Assuming the spatial metaphors implied by the above terms, clearness has been defined as "the attribute which gives a sensation its particular place in consciousness," i. e., focal or marginal. This agrees with our own definition in the fact that both imply a comparison of momentary contents of consciousness. We wish to imply, however, that clearness does not merely happen to a sensation or other state of consciousness. Sometimes by effort we make the obscure clear and conversely, the clear obscure. 

Consciousness seems able to shift focus and margin or exchange them. At other times we cannot make the clear obscure. One idea possesses and absorbs consciousness though we make a great effort to banish it. It seems true, therefore, to say that perfect clearness of a sensation means the occupation of consciousness with it to the exclusion of everything else. Less clearness means the distribution of consciousness to more than a single item of experience, or, more strictly, consciousness of more than one thing. The analogy here is with high or low illumination, brilliant or diffused light, and it is implied that consciousness by adjustment often determines what shall be focal and what shall be marginal in its field. Often the adjustment is accompanied by effort. This seems to agree with the definition of consciousness as a process and yet it does

SENSATION 

287 not rob us of the notion of fields of consciousness with focus and margin. The matter is of importance for according to the definition given of clearness we must write the remaining chapters of psychology in the passive voice only, or we may include activity and effort in our description. 

Introspection often testifies to the presence of conscious effort and, after long periods of such effort, the cortical cells present a picture different from that of their unfatigued state. If the testimony of introspection is not illusory, consciousness may be concentrated on any one object or small field which thus becomes clear, or it may be distributed to many objects and the clearness of any one is thereby diminished.

Duration.-All sensations differ in the time during which they continue. This attribute is called their duration and we can often distinguish the phases, rise, full presence, and decline, as we can, indeed, of all other mental states. This duration and change may be the source of our sense of time. 

Extensity. Finally, some sensations are said to have the attribute of extensity, but it is added that "odors and tones show no trace of it." It seems to me that extensity is not a simple attribute but rather a fairly complex perception. The sensational attribute seems instead to be what Lotze called "local sign," namely, we not only know that we are touched but where we are touched. Each nerve end from the skin has its own "local sign." Even the man who has lost a leg still feels the instep or the toes. Obviously, therefore, a number of neighboring nerve ends pressed upon at once will give the consciousness of extensity and, stimulated in succession, will give the consciousness of motion and its direction. Since no one regards motion and direction of motion as attributes of sensation

neither should extensity be so regarded. It seems even more complex than linear motion. Once more, the eye makes us conscious of the direction along which an object lies and skilled marksmanship shows how very accurate is this localization by retinal nerve ends. They not only respond to light but to the direction from which it comes. 

They are endowed with "local sign" as the cutaneous nerve ends are, and a patch of retinal nerve ends stimulated together gives the consciousness of extensity; while neighboring ones stimulated consecutively again give movement and direction. I think this fact has been overlooked because of the influence of Weber's experiment, which showed that the localization of two points on the skin is inexact. But so is our judgment of the intensity, pitch, and duration of sounds. The localization of objects by the well-practiced eye is wonderfully exact but its perception of extensity is often at fault. 

It should be added to our enumeration of the attributes of sensation that clearness and duration are attributes of every mental state whether it is sensational or not, and they have long been so described. They should be regarded as no more fundamentally attributes of sensations than of ideas, images and other thought processes. These attributes seem to belong to emotional states as well and, if so, the writers were correct who described clearness and duration as characters of the total stream of consciousness. In fact clearness and duration were first noted in connection with thoughts and, later, introspection showed that they are attributes of sensations as well. Quality, intensity and extensity (or local sign) are more distinctively attributes of sensations and appear to be closely correlated with the external stimuli.

Finally, quality and intensity of sensations lead to the

SENSATION 

289 perception of things, direction and extensity to the perception of space, and duration to the perception of time. 

CUTANEOUS SENSATIONS The Skin as a Sense Organ. Before we consider the special cutaneous sensations it is necessary to know something of the sense organs in the skin. An outline will indicate its chief layers from the outermost horny one to the innermost connective tissue.

Sensory nerves have their endings in all but the first or horny layer. The endings are either free or surrounded by a specialized organ whose function seems to be that of emphasizing the sensation somewhat "like a crumb in a glove." (1) The richly branched free nerve endings are very numerous in the Malpighian layer, and most numerous in the palm of the hand and the sole of the foot. They are found in other areas and are believed to exist over the entire surface of the body.

(2) A wreath of nerve ends surrounds each hair below the mouths of its oil glands. (3) Again in the Malpighian layer at the bottom of the sack-shaped folds of the papillae there are, especially on the body, round cells called Merkel's cells or touchcells. They are not over 1/100 mm. in diameter. On their under surface, nerves end in a disk or plate. (4) Ten times as large as these are the Meissner's corpuscles or tactile corpuscles which end in the papillae of the cutis and are of spindle shape and complicated structure. They are especially numerous where hairs and Merkel's cells are lacking, as in the palm and on the soles; most numerous of all on the finger ends where 23 to a square mm. have been found while in the first phalanx of the same index finger there were but 3 to a square mm. 

As a rule these have two nerve fibers running to them.

First the fibers wind about the outside then branch richly within the corpuscle. (5) In the neighboring mucous membrane as the lips, the conjunctiva of the eye and the genital organs the end bulbs of Krause are to be found. These structures, closely related to the Meissner's corpuscles, are similar to them but less highly developed. (6) Twenty times as large as the Meissner's corpuscles, and therefore easily visible to the unaided eye, are the 

Pacinian corpuscles. They are whitish in appearance, eggshaped or pear-shaped and, because of the fine nerve bundle which enters them, they look like berries on their stems.

These occur in the deepest layer of the skin, the connective tissue, but are found in other organs than the skin, as in the intestines and in all the joints. Six hundred of these have been counted on the inner surface of

The Pacinian corpuscles are onion-like in structure. 

They consist of a great number of white coverings encapsuled one in another which enclose finally a central sheath through which the nerve runs and ends singly or branched in a small swelling or enlargement.

Cutaneous Sensations. Of the impressions coming from skin senses distance and size are perceptions and will be discussed later. Then we have impressions of touch, pressure, temperature, tickling, itching, cutting, burning, pricking, tingling, etc. We locate these sensations in the body but impressions of pointed or dull, smooth, rough, hard, soft, wet, dry, etc., we objectify as qualities of the object.

All the sensations named above are not elementary ones. "Touch is nothing but a sensation of weak pressure.

The sensation of a cut is simply a line of pricking sensations. In smoothness, roughness, hard and soft, pressure sensations combine with those of movement and resistance. 

Wet is a combination of smooth and cool."

Because of the law stated on page 283, we do not ordinarily observe that these sensations are compounds but we realize it at once when the fact is pointed out. The elementary components are found to be sensations of pressure, pain, and temperature. Perhaps the sensations of tickling and itching must later be added to this list, but as yet there is no agreement in regard to them. The sen-

SENSATION 

293 sation of tickling appears to be a compound of pressure and movement. These elementary sensations are as distinct from one another as sensations of sight and hearing. 

Even cold and warmth appear to be different sense qualities, perhaps mediated by different neural paths, so that pressure, pain, cold, and warmth are the four cutaneous sensations usually named.

Introspection recognizes these four sensations as different from one another in quality. There is other evidence pointing to the same conclusion. In the beginning of ether and chloroform narcosis pain is completely abolished while sensitiveness to pressure and temperature remains in normal or almost normal strength. Local application of cocaine abolishes pain first. In some diseases of the spinal cord there is marked loss of sensitiveness to temperature, in others to pressure.

Finally we shall see that certain points on the skin, when stimulated, give only sensations of pressure, others only pain, others only warmth and still others only cold, while still other small areas have no sensitiveness at all. 

This seems to indicate the presence of highly specialized receptors. Possibly, therefore, there is a separate end organ, a special nerve path, and a special cortical center for each of these sense qualities. At any rate, there is ample evidence to show that they are distinct.

The Temperature Sensations.-In 1884 Blix, a Norwe gian, Goldscheider, a German, and Donaldson, an American, discovered cold and warmth points by exploring the skin with a metal point, either cooled or warmed. 

At certain points only pressure is felt, at others cold flashes out, and on still others warmth alone is felt. The warm points are more difficult to find than cold points, chiefly because the metal point used becomes cooled

quickly, but partly because warmth is less penetrating than cold, and partly because warmth points are fewer in number than the cold. On the average there are thirteen cold points and but two warmth points to a square cm. 

The points are arranged irregularly, and between them will be found insensitive areas and areas which contain only now and then an isolated point. Some of the points are very sensitive, others far less so even when an intense stimulus is used. Moreover a cold point will give the characteristic sensation of cold when stimulated mechanically or with an electric current. When the stimulus is warmed up to 45°C. the cold points give sensations of cold, though not so marked as with cooler stimuli. Because this sensation of cold is produced by a stimulus warmer than the body temperature it is sometimes called the "paradoxical cold sensation."

Thresholds and Range of Temperature Sensations.-The temperature at which an area of the skin feels neither warm nor cold is called the physiological zero. This is different for different areas so that the physiological zero ranges from 31°-35°C. (87.8°-95°F.). The average is about 33°C. This indifference point may be regarded as the lower threshold for warmth. The upper threshold for warmth is about 70°C. (158°F.), the lower threshold for cold about 10°C. (50°F.). In a moderately warm room in which one feels neither warm nor cold, different parts of the body have different temperatures. The end of the nose, the ears, fingers and backs of the hands are relatively cool; the palms of the hands, the temples, clothed parts of the body, and the interior of the mouth cavity relatively warm. 

At the extremes of the range of heat and cold sensa-

SENSATION 

295 tions they change into pain. At physiological zero the sensations cease to exist.

At any point within the range, the intensity of the sensation depends upon the particular area of the skin, its temperature, the size of the area stimulated, the duration of the stimulus, etc. When the stimulated area is fairly large and the temperature somewhere near physiological zero a difference of 1/10°-1/20° C. can be felt. Under less favorable conditions the difference threshold is much larger. 

Source of the Stimulus. It is indifferent whether the temperature stimulus strikes the nerve ends from without or whether it springs from the interior of the organism, as in fever or feelings of shame, embarrassment or fear. Menthol applied to the skin gives a cold sensation, the electric current and many acids a feeling of warmth. Pepper, alcohol and peppermint, when applied to the mucous membrane of the mouth, give a burning sensation. 

Adaptation.—A cellar or cave feels cool in summer but warm in winter because of our different adaptation in the two seasons. The average summer temperature of our rooms is felt as unpleasantly warm in winter, while the temperature, which is unnoticed in winter, would be felt as cool in summer. I have already mentioned Nansen's feeling a temperature of 4° F. below zero as delightfully mild and "springlike" after he had lived for a long time at 40° below zero. The wind is not tempered to the shorn lamb but the skin of the lamb is tempered to the wind.

Particular points for cold and warmth cease to respond after repeated stimulation. Hence, as might be inferred, fatigue and adaptation apply to points as well as to areas of the skin. Closely related to the temperature adaptation of the skin is the question of taking cold. Subjecting an

area of the skin to a lower temperature than that for which it is adapted seldom fails to cause a cold, while perhaps the best preventive of colds is to adapt the skin in advance to lower temperatures than that to which it is likely to be subjected.

Pressure Sensations.-Besides points sensitive to warmth and to cold there are, in the skin, points sensitive only to pressures. These are most easily found by using a horse hair as the stimulus. Pressure points will be found near the root of every hair especially on its "windward" side.

They are also found on the hairless portions of the body. 

As a general rule, they are most thickly set on the more mobile parts such as the tip of the tongue and the finger ends. There are, on the average, 25 pressure points to a square cm. over the body, exclusive of the scalp, which may have 300 points per square cm. The results of some experiments seemed to show that there are no pressure points on the conjunctiva and the cornea of the eye but the matter is undecided. 

The Stimuli.-Pressure and touch sensations are produced by pressure on the skin from without or from within as in a boil or other swelling, by stretching the skin as in bending the finger or wrinkling the brow. Finally the contraction of the smooth muscles attached to hair bulbs produces the touch sensations which we term "goose flesh.”

By the pressure sense alone, therefore, we cannot tell whether the skin is stretched or depressed. This shows that the stimulus for pressure sensations is a deformation of the skin. This may be proved by Meissner's experiment. 

If you immerse the hand or forearm in water you feel a ring of pressure sensation at the surface of the water. Below the surface the pressure is equal in all directions. The skin is not indented and no pressure is felt. The same

SENSATION 

297 thing is true if the heavy liquid, mercury, is used instead of water. This is just the reverse of the temperature senses. The hand plunged in hot or cold water feels the heat or cold below the surface. We may add to these normal stimuli, pressure and stretching of the skin, the abnormal cases. For example, the patient affected by delirium tremens sometimes feels that ants are crawling over his body. Here the cause must be a diseased condition of the cortical center, for there is no stimulus to the end organs. 

Localizing of Pressure Sensations or Local Sign. When we experience a pressure stimulus we know not only that we are touched but where we are touched. In fact it appears that if two neighboring pressure points are stimulated in succession, but with an interval of about 2/3 of a second between stimulations, the two points can be distinguished. This accurate localization of successive stimuli led us to name "local sign" as a most important attribute of touch sensations.

However, not the accuracy with which successive stimuli are localized but the inaccuracy in the case of simultaneous ones was first known. If the blunted points of a pair of compasses, or so-called aesthesiometer, are applied simultaneously to the tip of the tongue they must be in round numbers 1 mm. apart to be felt as two points, on the volar side of the last joint of the finger 2 mm., on the second joint 4.5 mm., and so on, until on the middle of the back they must be separated by 68 mm., almost 234 inches.

Obviously these apparently contradictory facts of simultaneous and successive stimulation must somehow be harmonized. The hypothesis of Bernstein is one of the most satisfactory. He regards the cutaneous sensory cortex as a geometrical projection of the cutaneous sensory area or of its nerve ends. He also believes that the cor-

tical center offers resistance to the spread of the nervous excitement. Ja le 1 2 P. 1 2 

Fig. 24-Diagram to illustrate Bernstein's theory of the localization of two simultaneous touches on the skin as at a single point. See text.

(From Nagel's Handbuch d. Physiologie des Menschen.) 

If we regard the short parallel lines as nerve fibers, the periphery as PP, and the stimuli as applied at 1 and 2 the cortical excitement due to 1 is represented by the curve cbd, that of 2 by the curve gfh. By irradiation the excitements have spread, as indicated by the curves, and the two overlap. Their combined excitements fuse into a single one, which is represented by the curve kil, with the maximum excitement at i. So long as the two irradiation curves have a common maximum the two stimulated points are felt not as two but as one. When the points are separated far enough to produce two distinct maxima they will be felt as two. Or again, if two adjacent pressure points are stimulated successively their maximal excitements occur at different times and the point of stimulation is felt to have shifted its position. 

The fact that receptors are so much more numerous on

SENSATION 

299 the more mobile parts of the body and that simultaneous stimuli are more delicately discriminated there, is a beautiful example of adaptation to environment.

Thresholds.—The threshold of pressure depends upon the weight or mass of the stimulus, the suddenness with which it is applied, and the size of the area stimulated. A threshold of less than 0.4 gm. per square mm. has been found for a small surface, 0.5 gm. per square mm. for a single pressure spot, though the average for pressure spots is 1.28 gm. per square mm. The difference threshold averages about 1/30 of the original stimulus, as already stated. 

Feeling Tone of Pressure Sensations.—Almost every sensation is either agreeable or disagreeable. Hence it is said to have a feeling tone. The purpose of pressure sensations is to make us aware of mechanical stimuli. In ordinary intensities such stimuli are neither advantageous nor injurious to the body. Consequently the feeling tone of the sensations they produce is practically indifferent, i. e., these sensations seem almost neutral while others are promptly classified as either pleasant or unpleasant. 

Adaptation to Pressure Sensations.—When an area of the skin is subjected to a constant uniform pressure we become adapted to it and cease to feel it. The presence of spectacles, rings, or necklaces is no longer felt, nor even a plate of false teeth. We are not conscious of the pressure of our clothing upon our bodies, though in winter it may weigh several pounds.

On the other hand pressure sensations often persist when the stimulus is no longer present. We still feel the hat we have just been wearing and a coin pressed against the forehead may be felt for several seconds. These "after sensations" are explained as due to a deformation of the

skin after the deforming object has been removed. This "after sensation" disappears somewhat slowly.

Skin Sensations of Pain.-The office of these sensations is to warn us against injury so they make their disagreeable character felt at once. Like temperature and pressure they abide in points stippled over the skin. These points average 200 per square cm. or pain points are 8 times as numerous as pressure points. 

The sensation of pain arises more slowly than pressure, warmth, or cold. If the finger be put in warm or cold water the above three sensations appear almost together (strictly in the order pressure, cold, warmth), the pain part of a second later. So one may press on his foot with a cane and observe that touch is felt first and pain appreciably later. Just as the pain sensation arises more slowly than the others it dies away more slowly.

The other skin sensations when intense change into pain. Only with a weak electric current can the pain sensations be produced without an accompanying pressure sensation.
