The Nerve Ends for Each Sensation-At least we are certain that the nerve ends about the hair bulbs correspond to pressure points and Meissner's corpuscles are also nerve ends of pressure.

Some or all free nerve ends are organs of the pain sensation and perhaps Merkel's cells have the same function.

301 The end-bulbs of Krause are organs of cold, while those called Ruffini's endings may subserve warmth sensations. 

KINAESTHETIC SENSATIONS 

Professor Strumpell once had a patient so anesthetic that "his only sources of feeling were the right eye and the left ear." When his eye was bandaged his body could be placed in the most grotesque positions without his being in the least aware of them. "Passively holding still his fingers did not affect him. He thought constantly that he opened and shut his hand whereas it was really fixed.” 

This boy, if his eyes were closed, could not put his one arm or leg in the position in which the other had been passively placed. Normal persons can do this perfectly. On what sense or senses does this power depend? Experiment has shown that cutaneous sensation has nothing to do with it. The sense organs located in the muscles or tendons contribute little or nothing. It has been proved, however, that each joint of our bodies contains delicate sense organs and these chiefly make us conscious of the movement of our limbs, its direction and amount. Even when the arm is passively moved and the eyes of the subject are closed, the sensation of movement comes instantly to consciousness, and a moment later the amount and direction of the movement are perceived. Therefore, while this articular sensation is somewhat vague, the perception to which it gives rise is extremely delicate and accurate. It is this power that swordsmen, billiard players, and tennis players train to the nicest accuracy. The sense is tested in laboratories with a piece of apparatus called a joint sense board, or a kinematometer. With this, even passive movements of the hand and shoulder joints as small as 4/10 of a degree can be readily detected. The delicacy of this sense

for active movements, as in fencing is much greater than for passive ones. Its chief organs are probably the Pacinian corpuscles in the tissues of the joints. (Herrick, p. 88.) 

Perhaps the sense of strain, derived from nerve endings in the tendons, and the muscle sense contribute something to our perception of movement but the articular or joint sense is apparently its chief source. These senses, whose receptors lie in the deep tissues of the body and regulate bodily movements and their coordination, are called proprioceptive senses. The nerve terminals in the semi-circular canals, which govern the poise and balance of the body, are also proprioceptors. The kinaesthetic senses thus give us sensations of the position of the body and its members. 

Miss Thompson states that men execute movements more accurately than women but women are superior in the co-ordination of fine movements, a fact which may account for women being better in penmanship than men and perhaps for their wide employment in stenography and type- Semicircular

EQUILIBRATION AND HEARING 

The Sense of Equilibration.-The ear is a double sense organ, or better, it includes two different sense organs, one exteroceptive, the other proprioceptive. The cochlea gives us sensations of hearing, the semi-circular canals are instrumental in making us aware of the position of the head, even when our eyes are closed, and to them are due the sensations of dizziness induced by whirling or the deck of a tossing ship. hz hz 

Fig. 26 

The three semi-circular canals lie almost at right angles to each other and each has an enlargement at one end called the ampulla. In the latter are hairs which project into the endolymph or fluid contained in the canals. The hair cells are connected with fibers of the vestibular branch (Fig. 

26) of the eighth nerve, hence they are delicate end organs for this branch. 

Any movement of the head will cause a flow of the fluid into one or more of the ampullae thus stimulating the hair cells and initiating impulses in the nerve. When these impulses reach the centers, the appropriate reaction to the movement, which has stimulated the canals, is released. So far the action is reflex and almost entirely unconscious. Hence we might say that the function of the canals is not to arouse sensations but merely to cause these reflex adjustments. This is no doubt their chief function. Diagram of hair cells in the semi-circular canals and a nerve fiber of the vestibular branch of the VIII nerve for which the hair cells are sensitive receptors. A movement of the endolymph stimulates these cells. fz, non-nervous support- ing cell; hz, hair cell; sn, axon of the vestibular neuron. (From 

Herrick's Neurology.)

Yet if one reclines on a horizontal rotating table with eyes closed it may be turned through any number of degrees if the rotation is very slow and uniform. If it be increased ever so slightly the subject reports an experience of movement mediated by the canals, for vision and the articular sense are excluded. Very slow rotation does not drive the fluid into an ampulla. More rapid rotation does so.

Besides this sensation of movement, the canals give rise to the sensation of dizziness or vertigo. A very simple experiment proves that the seat of the sensation is in the head. If with the head erect one whirls upon his heels, then stops suddenly, the walls of the room appear to move in the direction opposite to the whirling. If the test is repeated with the head bent it is the floor which appears to revolve. Consequently the seat of the sensation of dizziness is in the head and not in the body, however nauseatingly it may affect the latter. The dizziness is accompanied by jerky movements of the eyes, called nystagmus.

Both the dizziness and nystagmus can be produced by flooding the ear with very warm or cold water, which changes the pressure of the fluid in the canals, or by an electric current which stimulates the nerve more directly. 

These processes are used to detect disease of the canals. 

The canals, therefore, by reflex adjustments provide for the poise and balance of the head and body. They make us aware of all but the slowest and steadiest movements, and they give the sensation of dizziness. The power to keep the head and body erect seems, therefore, to belong primarily to the canals. The best evidence for this comes from the birds and fishes which must balance accurately in air and water. Operations on the canals of these animals leave no doubt of the facts. If the canals of a fish are injured it swims in all sorts of positions, generally in

SENSATION 

305 circles with the body tipped far to one side and the pupils drawn far toward the edges of the eyes. A pigeon with injured canals may stand with the back of the head on the ground and the beak pointing straight upward. 

The evidence for the sense of dizziness must come, of course, from human experience. That it is due to stimulation of the canals is shown by the following facts: (1) 

Commonly occurring accompaniments of diseases of the ear are uncertainty of gait, difficulty in standing erect, and attacks of dizziness. The patients feel themselves suddenly and violently whirled about or thrown to the ground and nausea and vomiting occur. The feelings of movement and dizziness are due to the canals directly, the nausea and vomiting to their effect on other organs. One "patient who lost one labyrinth by disease and, to escape unendurable vertigo, had the other removed by operation, was quite unable to guide his movements or realize his position in the dark. Rising from bed one night, he collapsed on the floor and remained there helpless till succor arrived." (2) A certain per cent. of the deaf and dumb cannot be made dizzy. If these persons are whirled about the long axis of the body they can, after the whirling ceases, walk erect without staggering. Again, if such persons are placed on a rotating device, like a merry-goround, they do not incline the body toward the centre of the circle, as normal persons do. Further, if these persons are asked to stand or walk with closed eyes they are very unsteady. Evidently sensations are now lacking which usually guide their movements. Finally when those who can swim are put in deep water they no longer know, when their eyes are closed, the directions up or down, nor their position in the water. 

Hill, Leonard, Pop. Sci. Mo., Vol. 81, No. 4, 1912, p. 375.

From all this it seems plain that the semi-circular canals have not only a reflex function but a conscious one, that they are organs which give us sensations of the position of the body and of dizziness. But other kinaesthetic senses, and vision as well, may also serve the function of equilibration. Hence the semi-circular canal function seems to be degenerate in man but of the highest importance in some animals.

The canals have still another reflex function which is of interest. They stand in close relation to the musculature of the body. Excitements going out from them keep up the general tonus or steady tension of the muscles. A severe blow on the point of the jaw may be communicated by the rigid bone directly to the canals and interrupt this function. A man so struck falls in a flabby heap because the muscular tonus is gone. For this reason the point of the jaw is a favorite target for a "knockout" blow with prizefighters.

Another discovery not devoid of interest has been made. 

Persons subject to seasickness may become adapted to the toss of the vessel and recover. But when they embark on a smaller or a larger vessel, which consequently is tossed by the sea at a different rate, the nausea returns. This appears to be a sort of adaptation of the canals to a given rate of the ship's movement.

The Sense of Hearing. From the semi-circular canal function the sense of hearing seems to have developed. 

Fishes exhibit the former function in perfection while they have developed only the most rudimentary sense of hearing. In order to understand auditory sensations a clear notion of the structure of the ear is necessary. This can be gained by the study of the following outline and figures.

Surely everyone knows that sound is due to vibrations of air, and the wide use of the telephone and the micro-

SENSATION 

309 phone should teach us that a stretched membrane (or a very thin metal plate) responds with the utmost nicety to these vibrations and can consequently transmit them. A stretched membrane or a metal plate, which transmits impulses, is called a diaphragm. While telephone engineers use the transmitting diaphragm only to change electrical resistance, and the current causes the receiving diaphragm to duplicate the movements of the transmitting one, nature has not resorted to the use of electricity for hearing. Instead, the ear is a mechanical receiver (receptor) of air vibrations and a transmuter of them into liquid vibrations. 

The first diaphragm of the ear is the tympanic membrane or head of the so-called eardrum. Attached to this membrane is a small bone, the hammer, which is jointed to another, the anvil, which, in turn, articulates with a third, the stirrup. The hammer and the anvil are levers whose lengths are exactly suited to convert air vibrations into liquid vibrations and this they do. To an inward thrust of the tympanic membrane an inward thrust of the stirrup corresponds. But its inward thrust sets the fluid, endolymph, of the cochlea into vibration. These liquid vibrations correspond in every particular with the air vibrations. In the cochlea another membrane, called the basilar membrane, takes up the vibrations of the endolymph. 

Probably both the membranous and the lymph vibrations stimulate the hair cells which are mounted on the basilar membrane. Fibers of the auditory nerve end on the hair cells so that their stimulation results in nerve impulses to the cortex and the latter result in sensations of sound. 

We find in the ear, therefore, (1) a canal, the meatus for conducting air waves to the sensitive diaphragm, the tympanic membrane, (2) an apparatus for converting its vibrations into liquid vibrations, and (3) the basilar mem-

brane for responding to liquid vibrations. The hair-cells located within the organ of Corti are the immediate receptors of the stimulus to the nerve ends. The above are merely the most essential features of the ear. The curiously folded cartilage, called the concha or shell, appears as if it might be a collector of air waves but there is little damage to hearing in cases where this external portion of the ear has been removed.

It may be remarked that the liquid in the cochlea is not "water," as a recent text-book states it to be, but a fluid secreted by the brain and whose pressure is kept constant. 

It is the fluid within the central membranous canal of the cochlea, the ductus cochlearis, which is called endolymph. 

That in the other two divisions, the scala vestibuli and the scala tympani, is called perilymph. The Eustachian tube extending from the middle ear to the pharynx (the back part of the mouth cavity) permits the air pressure on each side of the drum membrane to be equalized, except when we go to great altitudes or when we have a cold which closes the tube.

The Stimulus for Auditory Sensations. While the outer cause of sensations of sound is vibrations of air, they differ in tones and noises. In noises a chaos of vibrations and parts of vibrations reaches the ear at the same instant, so noise is a compound of short irregular tones only slightly different in vibration-number and changing quickly in pitch. In a tone the vibrations occur at a definite uniform rate and give rise to sounds which we regard as smooth and restful, as distinguished from noises. From the point of view of the sensation, tones and noises are quite distinct. From the point of view of the stimulus they are similar.

The vibrations which form the stimulus for a tone may

SENSATION 

311 vary: (1) In amplitude or extent of swing of the air particles. This depends, of course, on the energy of vibration of the body which sets the air in motion. (2) They may vary in the rate of vibration. For the tone, middle C, there are 256 vibrations per second. (3) They may vary in the number of impulses which affect the vibrating particle at the same instant, thus giving it a new path of vibration. 

Thus, if the three keys of a piano which vibrate at the rate of 256, 512, and 1024 per second, are struck simultaneously, the form of the vibration must be different from that caused by one of the strings alone. Yet the tone is a pure tone because the last two rates are multiples of the first. 

In fact, if only the string for middle C (256 vibs.) had, been struck it would vibrate as a whole, giving the tone, middle C, but it would also vibrate in halves, giving the octave of middle C, and it would vibrate in fourths, giving the second octave. The tone produced by the string vibrating as a whole is called the fundamental tone. The simultaneous vibrations of its parts give overtones, first, second, etc. Thus, while the stimulus is complex, the tone is simple except for those highly trained ears which can discriminate the overtones separately. Since vibrations vary in amplitude, rate, and form, we have next to ask whether the ear responds to each of these differences. 

Auditory Sensations and Their Attributes.-Each tone that we hear has a certain pitch or place on the musical scale. This is due to the rate of vibration. It has a certain loudness or intensity, which is due to the amplitude of vi. bation, and a certain quality or timbre, which is due to the form of the vibration. Each musical instrument has a sounding board or resonance chamber, like the voice-box or larynx of the human voice. These sounding boards or resonance chambers suppress some of the overtones and

reflect the others to our ears. This gives the difference in quality of the tone. By means of it we can distinguish two voices which are singing the same note or two musical instruments. "The tones of reed instruments have a sharp klang; those of trumpets a crashing timbre. An old, wornout piano sounds empty and thin; a new grand piano, full and rich; the clarinet nasal and hollow and so on." A very old, well made violin enriches its quality with age, due to reflecting more overtones, hence the desire for a Stradivarius or a Cremona. A highly trained ear is able to analyze out of the compound tone the various simple ones which compose it. Hence for trained ears, timbre seems not to be a simple attribute of tones but a complex one. 

The untrained ear is like the eye and gives the simple attribute of timbre when the stimulus is complex. 

We thus see that to each property of the air vibrations an attribute of the tone corresponds. Vibration rate amplitude form pitch Sensation loudness or intensity timbre or quality

This omits a property of air vibrations. Very powerful sources of sound must set a great volume of air into vibration. Consequently some psychologists assert that tones have volume. Others say that the low, deep tones simply remind us of something large. A reminder that is always present may be, of course, a meaning, knowledge about the sound. This would be supplied by the mind and not a direct, mechanical result of the stimulus. The loudness of the tone would suggest volume or bigness. Since, after experience, we supply meanings for stimuli and react to them, the "reminder" theory may be correct.

SENSATION 

313 Noises are rough, unclear, and disturbing in character, even when they continue uniform. We feel that noises differ in intensity and pitch as tones do, though the pitch of a noise is not so clear and definite as that of a tone. We are sure, however, that "a pistol shot is higher in pitch than the report of a cannon." Having admitted the two attributes, loudness and pitch as belonging to noises, we can say little more, except that noises are momentary, as a snap or crack, or continuous, as in hissing, grating or roaring noises. That is, like all sensations, they have the attribute of duration. Most sounds in nature are compounds of tones and noises. "Human speech, for example, regarded purely as sound, is a mixture of manifold noises, the consonants, with tones of different timbre, the vowels." 

Thresholds. The briefest time during which a tone may last and yet be heard as a tone is called its duration threshold. Pfäundler found this to be two complete vibrations for the range 16 to 3000 vibrations. This would make a duration of only 1/128th of a second for middle C. If the vibrations were of weak intensity, more were required, as we should imagine from the summation of stimuli. One strong vibration gives rise to the sensation of a snap or stroke. From the quickness with which tones in music follow one another we might infer that the ear has a very brief duration threshold. Unlike the eye, the ear does not give after-sensations. If it did so, music would be either impossible or much changed from its present character. 

The rods of Corti have been supposed to be instant dampers of the vibrations of the basilar membrane. Thus sounds may follow one another at very short intervals and yet be individually distinguished.

The threshold of loudness or intensity is usually determined by the distance at which a watch-tick can be heard.

As watches differ greatly, such measurement is only a rough comparison of one person's hearing with another's, provided the same watch is used. It would detect any considerable degree of deafness. Professor Seashore remedied this by the invention of the audiometer, in which a telephone diaphragm is set in vibration with less and less energy as the resistance in the electric circuit is increased. 

It is possible that this instrument may be superseded by the audometer, devised by the engineers of the Western Electric Company. This is said to measure the degree of deafness with the greatest accuracy all along the scale of tones. Measuring deafness is determining the loudness thresholds of a particular person throughout the whole range of his hearing. The bones of the head conduct vibrations readily. Therefore, persons whose middle ear is damaged may hear sounds by means of a head set. In this way persons quite deaf to air conduction may enjoy the radio by means of bone conduction. Plainly an instrument should be devised for them which can transmute even gentle air vibrations into an amount of energy transmissible by the bones of the skull and it must be adapted for each particular type of deafness. Because of the recent great advances in radio and telephony, this will undoubtedly soon be done. Thresholds of intensity will then have to be determined for both air conduction and bone conduction. All this suggests that we shall need to know more concerning auditory thresholds rather than to ignore them. Because knowledge of hearing is now commercially very valuable it is increasing in scope every day. It is interesting to note that the telephone was originally meant to remedy deafness. This it at first failed to do but now that its applications have been extended it is partly meeting its inventor's first aim, to lower the threshold of hear-

SENSATION 

315 ing for the deaf. The professions based upon the sense of hearing are now grouped under one head, telephone engineers. They should be grouped under the title, "auditory engineers." Instead of "illuminating engineers" and their colleagues, we should have the general name, visual or vision engineers. The raison d'etre of both these large groups of professions is to extend the range and delicacy of hearing and vision.

Any measurement of great value and importance appears to be very difficult to make. So different investigators have worked for years to ascertain the threshold of loudness of the ear. How much energy must be applied to the membrane of the eardrum to result in a just perceptible sensation of tone? Wien found this to be the energy necessary to raise 1/200 of a milligram one-millionth of a millimeter. Two later investigators found the weight to be 1/20 of a milligram. For noises, the energy required is much greater. This great sensitiveness of the normal ear may arouse little interest, thus stated as an abstract measurement. Yet it is interesting to reflect that by amplify. ing vibrations of something like this strength, radio inventors and engineers have made us hear the human voice almost around the world. In this way they have delighted many people who understand neither the ear nor the instrument which translates electric impulses into air vibrations or bone vibrations and the reverse.

The threshold of intensity is but one measurement. 

The determination of the lowest and the highest tones which we can hear is quite another. These are called the lower and upper thresholds of pitch. The lowest audible tone is perhaps 16 vibrations per second. But since overtones are present, it is more often the tone of 24, 32, 48, or 96 vibrations which is heard. The upper limit for most

persons is 15,000 to 20,000 vibrations per second and this lowers steadily and rather rapidly with age. 

The difference threshold of pitch varies as we go through the octave. A tone and its octave are relatively hard to distinguish, so with a tone and its third and fifth, because they harmonize or the vibration-number of the second is a multiple of the first. Two adjacent tones, as 

C and D, are readily discriminated. If, between two such tones, we interpolate others, until the difference is but 8/10 of a vibration, that difference is detected by those only fairly trained in music and one writer puts the difference threshold of pitch at only 2/10 of a vibration. Of course, on difference in pitch harmony and discord in music depend.

Turning to the intensity of noises, a difference of 1/3 or 1/4 of the original stimulus is given as the difference threshold but this is for slight noises. 

Beats and Beat Tones. When two tuning forks both give exactly the same tone, they have the same vibrationnumber. If the prongs of one are loaded with wax, their vibration rate is slowed down. Thus, one of the forks may have a rate of 260 vibrations per second, while the rate of the other may be decreased to 240. Then every twentieth vibration of the latter fork will re-enforce the vibration of the first and there will be "swelling" of the sound. At intermediate points the two tones will interfere and the sound be diminished. The resulting "billowy recurrence" of strength and weakness is called "beats," and in the case mentioned there will be 20 beats per second, or the number of beats is equal to the difference between the vibration-numbers of the two forks. When the mistuning of one fork is sufficiently great, the beats occur rapidly enough to form a tone, called the beat tone or intermedi-

SENSATION 

317 ate tone. Evidently almost any two tones of different vibration-numbers will give beats. But beats do not roughen the smooth tones perceptibly if they are very rapid, say above 150 per second. A theory of hearing must be to explain beat tones as well as ordinary pure tones. 

Combination Tones.-Besides the beat tone, which was first mentioned by Mersenne in the 17th century, we have to describe much more peculiar tones, called combination tones. If two whistles of different pitch are sounded simultaneously a low, deep tone will be heard whose pitch corresponds to the difference between the vibration numbers of the two generating tones. This is called the first difference tone and by means of it and the original tones still other difference tones are produced. Besides the difference tones "summation tones," which are supposed to correspond to the sum of the rates of vibrations of the two whistles, may be heard. The summation tone is faint and difficult to distinguish. The peculiarity of combination tones is that there appears to be no stimulus of air vibrations for them. They are, instead, ear tones, or the two objective tones combine their effects in the ear, but not in the air, to produce a third tone.

There are, it is true, a few instruments besides the ear which produce combination tones. These are the double siren, the harmonium, the tongued box devised by Appun, and certain membranes, among which is the diaphragm of the loud-toned telephone. The tones produced by these instruments are called objective combination tones. Those produced in the ear are called subjective ones, because even with the most refined methods of research no vibrations of air corresponding to them have been discovered. They do not excite a resonator as objective tones do. Because dia-

phragms like that of the telephone produce objective combination tones, it is believed that subjective ones are due to the action of the membrane of the tympanum or, in its absence, to the membrane of the round window. Others insist that the effect of the generating tones is wrought on the basilar membrane.

The Action of the Ear in Hearing. This is, of course, a matter of theory so our topic may be better named the theory of hearing. I sketch only one of several theories, that of Helmholtz, because all other conceptions have thus far had to yield to this one. Since, from the structure of the ear, it seems plain that in order that different notes be heard, different hair cells must be stimulated the question is how are the different hair cells stimulated? The answer appears to be by the action of basilar membrane fibers. These fibers are, like the strings of a harp, of different lengths. We suppose then that when vibrations occur in the lymph of the cochlea the shorter fibers of the basilar membrane respond to rapid vibrations and make us aware of high notes, the longer fibers respond to slow vibrations and make us conscious of low notes. The fibers of the basilar membrane are, therefore, resonators and little groups of them pick out the rate of vibration to which their length and consequently their own rate corresponds exactly as a piano string takes up sympathetically a tone sung near it. "To account for the sensation of noise, we need only assume that a broader strip or perhaps that several broad strips of the basilar membrane at the same time are thrown into brief vibration. The sensation of a compound tone will be produced by the simultaneous vibration, at different amplitudes, of a number of narrow strips, each one of

SENSATION 

319 which, if it vibrated alone, would give us the sensation of a simple tone." 

To account for beats let us suppose that two tones of 300 and 306 vibrations strike the basilar membrane at once. The parts of the membrane set in motion by these will overlap and a tone of nearly 303 vibrations will be heard. But this tone will fluctuate or beat because the two original tones will at one instant re-enforce each other, and at another instant interfere with each other, making the beat tone alternately weak and strong. These fluctuations are "beats" and in the supposed case there will be six of them per second.

When the two tones differ more widely as 300 and 320 vibrations per second, respectively, we hear both tones and the intermediate tone. In the first case we hear only the beat tone. Hence beats and intermediate tones are due to the overlapping of parts of the basilar membrane set in vibration by the two stimulus tones. Besides accounting for beats, a theory of hearing ought also to give a reason for combination tones, but since there is still discussion as to whether these tones arise from the drum membrane or the basilar membrane I shall omit the arguments for each opinion. 

There are objections to the Helmholtz theory. For example, the internal ear is little larger than a grain of corn and in a tube so small as the cochlea friction would stop any movement of the fluid, according to the laws of physics which we now know. Yet the Helmholtz theory is so far the most satisfactory one. 

Reaction Time for Sensations of Sound. The stimulus for a sensation is also a stimulus to action. In fact the chief function of consciousness seems to be to make the Titchener, Text-Book of Psychology, Macmillan & Co., N. Y. Hereafter referred to by the initials T. B.

action appropriate when, because the situation is complex, deliberation, comparison, and decision are required. When the situation is not complicated but simple, action follows at once upon stimulation, and hence it is termed a "reaction" to the stimulus. How quickly one can react to a given stimulus is termed his "reaction time” for that sense. 

It has been found also that one reacts more quickly if he keeps in mind the movement to be executed rather than the stimulus which is to be given. In other words muscular reaction time is shorter than sensorial. The times are recorded in sigmas, i. e., thousandths of a second. This fact must have value for the preservation of the individual. We all realize how "startling" noises are in comparison with objects seen. The biological reason for this is that when an approaching object can be heard it is already time to adjust one's self to it, to make ready for flight or defense.

321 Finally, hearing is called the most accurate sense because of the fine discriminations it makes. The Great 

War had gone on but a few months before the men in the trenches could name the type of gun from the noise of its projectile, had observed that the noise or tone changed for each part of the arc described, and could distinguish the shell about to fall dangerously near them from one which would pass harmlessly beyond them.

THE SENSE OF VISION The Organ of Vision. By this term I shall mean the whole mechanism for seeing. This includes the eye, the optic nerve, the optic tract, and the occipital cortex. A complete description of the eye would include an account of (1) its protective parts, (2) its refracting or focusing mechanism, and (3) the sensory mechanism or retina. I shall describe only the second and third divisions. 

The eyeball is enclosed in two coats or covering tissues. 

The outer one is the tough, resistant sclerotic coat or sclera, which continues in front into the transparent cornea. 

Next within the sclera is the choroid coat which bears blood vessels and a dark brown pigment which diminishes the reflection of light within the eye and lessens the amount of light which would otherwise pass thru the sclera. In its forward part the inner side of the choroid ends in numerous folds, the ciliary processes. Just outside of these and attached to them are the ciliary muscles which control the focus of the lens. But the choroid continues forward into its foremost part, the iris, which is pierced in its center by the pupil of the eye. Inside the choroid coat and lining the posterior two-thirds of the eyeball is the retina or nervous lining of the eye, composed of nerve ends called rods and cones. The fibers which

enter the eye in the optic nerve bend backward after entering so that the rods and cones point toward the choroid. 

This is said to be a defect of the human eye.

The ciliary processes, and muscles, and the lens form a partition which divides the globe of the eye into two chambers, the anterior one, in front of the lens, which is filled with aqueous humor, and the posterior one which is filled with a vitreous or glassy body or humor, called the vitreous body. The cornea, the aqueous humor, the lens and the vitreous body are all transparent refracting media which serve to bring the rays of light to a focus or true point upon the retina. The iris of the eye, which is a circular muscle, contracts and expands the pupil which it sur-

SENSATION 

323 rounds, thus admitting more light when the outer illumination is dim, less light when it is intense. This enables us to see objects by a wide range of illuminations. When the eye is treated with atropin the iris is temporarily paralyzed Ch Ch Nop Ch Ch and relaxed.

Hence the patient must remain in dim light or his eyes will be injured. The power of the iris enables us also to focus the light from near and distant objects on the retina at the same time. Thus we have a clear image of both. No other optical instrument is able to do this. If the image of the nearer object is clear, that of the further one is dim and shadowy, and conversely. The first adjustment of the eye is thus the pupillary reflex. 

Convergence. The second adjustment is also a reflex performance, but it is acquired in the first few weeks of babyhood and is not automatic like the pupillary reaction. 

This adjustment is termed convergence and the name means no more than that the two eyes work as one organ and both together turn toward the object to be seen; in doing that they converge or turn toward each other when

looking at a single object. The degree of convergence is greater for near objects, less for distant ones. If it were not for convergence we should probably be conscious of two images of each object instead of one. There are always two images but by convergence they fuse into a single one. 

The young babe which has not yet formed the habit of converging the eyes, can be seen with them rolling in quite opposite or diverging directions, a species of staring which gives it an idiotic appearance. Soon objects and light call forth the reflex and the two eyes move as one. This con- tinues unless the person becomes blind, when the reflex is again promptly lost.

Accommodation. The third adjustment of the eye is its true focusing process, accommodation. The lens is held somewhat flat by a circular ligament which rests upon it like a weight. When the ciliary muscles contract, this weight is lifted, and, since the lens is elastic, it springs at once into more spherical form. Thus the effort we feel in looking at a near object is the effort of contraction of the ciliary muscles when they lessen the pressure of the ligament upon the lens. For a clear image of a near object the lens must be more spherical, for a clear image of a distant object it must be more flat. We get this effect in a camera by moving the back of it forward or backward. As we cannot move the back of the eyeball, the focus is brought about by thickening or thinning the lens, i. e., by making it more or less convex. 

By these three adjustments (1) just enough light is thrown on the retina, (2) the rays from a single object are thrown on geometrically similar parts of both retinas, (3) the rays focus or come to a point on the retina. In other words, normal eyes are stigmatic and not astigmatic. (The term stigma means here a point.)

SENSATION 

325 The Retina. From this it is evident that the retina is the true organ of vision. It is composed of highly specialized nerve ends, or receptors, called rods and cones, which a b 

Fig. 32-Diagrammatic representation of the structure of the retina (Cajal). 

A, layer of rods and cones; a, rods; b, cones; E, layer of bipolar cells; G, layer of large ganglion cells; H, layer of nerve fibres. point toward the choroid and away from the geometrical center of the eyeball. At their outer ends the rods are in contact with a layer of pigment cells, which produce a black pigment. This migrates inward along and between the rods when the retina is exposed to light. It migrates to the outer ends of the rods when the eyes are closed or in darkness. The pigment cells also renew the visual purple of the rods. It is not renewed in rods which are torn from the layer of pigment cells.

We may say, indeed, that the retinal elements are capable of three reactions to illumination. (1) When exposed to light a black pigment migrates along and between the rods and theory has supposed that this pigment prevents a leakage of light from one rod to its neighbor, though this theory is questioned. When light is withdrawn the pigment migrates in the opposite direction, or from the bases to the outer ends of the rods. (2) When light is excluded from the eye the rods become suffused somewhat slowly with visual purple, so that they appear to "blush." When strong light is admitted once more the visual purple is bleached. The visual purple plays some part in the adaptation of the eye to dim light. It, therefore, aids in twilight vision. Finally (3), the cones, which are shorter than the rods, extend and shorten under the influence of light. They have a true phototropic reaction, but what part this may play in vision is not known. 

Where the nerve enters the eye there are no rods or cones, so that spot is blind and is always referred to as the blind spot. The edges of the retina or, as we say, the periphery of the retina, is color blind, and there are no cones in the periphery. Thus even in the normal eye there is a totally blind area, the blind spot, and a color blind area, the periphery of the retina.

The most important area of the retina, however, is a small spot almost directly back of the pupil of the eye. 

This is called the fovea or pit, because the optic nerve fibers bend apart a trifle there and thus are heaped up so as to form the sides of the pit. Thus the cones are especially well exposed to light in the fovea. This little area is important because it is the spot of keenest and most discriminating color vision, but it is blind in twilight vision. It contains only cones. Hence at the fovea there are only

SENSATION 

327 cones, which grow fewer in number as we pass to the periphery of the retina where there are only rods. 

The Stimulus for Vision.-Plainly light or, more exactly, vibrations of the ether are the stimulus for vision. But the fact is that all the vibrations taken together give us sensations of brightness, i. e., the various whites, blacks and grays. A single rate of vibration or wave length gives a sensation of one color, another wave length, a sensation of another color, etc. I shall call that light which gives a sensation of a pure, single color, homogeneous or monochromatic light. Homogeneous light of low intensity gives a sensation of brightness, not of color, i. e., in twilight all colors become a uniform gray. Finally there are pairs of colors which, when mixed, give only a sensation of gray or white. It will be seen, therefore, that we have a somewhat tangled array of facts to explain with our theories of vision. Those stated above may be summarized in a list as follows:

Two colors such as R and BG or B and Y which, when mixed, give white or gray are termed complementary colors. The seven colors which, when combined give white, are called the spectral colors. "All wave lengths excite brightness and the quality of the brightness depends upon the amplitude of the wave, not at all upon the length. 

Each of the waves at a given intensity excites brightness "The initial letters of the color names may be used to designate them if Bk be used for black; thus BG-blue-green.

in a very slight degree, color in larger amount. A faint red light appears black because it affects the brightness organ only; as it grows brighter it grows first dark brown, then dark red, then red, and pink in order, and with very great intensities approaches white." From this it appears that the stimulus for a color sensation is homogeneous light. The brightness of a color or a gray is due to the amplitude of the vibrations and every color has a certain brightness, or will match in brightness a certain gray of the black to white series, because homogeneous light waves have a certain amplitude, as well as a certain length. 

There are at least two inadequate stimuli for the sense of vision. A blow on the back of the head causes us to see flashes of light, apparently because the blow stimulates the visual center directly. Santonin powder makes everything in the field of view appear yellow, apparently by some peculiar selective action which affects the visual apparatus.

Thresholds. It appears from what has been stated above that there are two distinct thresholds for visual sensations, one for sensations of brightness, the other for sensations of color. As shown by the experiment just mentioned in which a red stimulus at first appears black, i. e., dark gray, the brightness threshold is lower than the threshold of stimulation for color. Or a less intense stimulus is required to produce a sensation of brightness than of color.

So far the facts appear simple, but they grow more complicated. The condition of the eye changes from moment to moment by adaptation. We have seen in the case of Nansen that the threshold for cold was raised, and that for warmth lowered by a stay of months in the arctic regions. But while the nerve ends for temperature require

SENSATION 

329 a long time for adaptation the retina appears to adapt in a few minutes. After a few minutes in darkness we see objects clearly which we could not distinguish at all on coming out of a lighted room. In other words, the eye is adapted to darkness, and an amount of light which would not affect the light-adapted eye at all strongly, affects the dark-adapted retina. The threshold of stimulation is lowered to meet the condition of dim light. If we prolong our stay in darkness this adaptation will go on slowly for eight hours, and people who have lived long in darkness are said to see by the faint light almost as well as nightseeing animals. So the eye has a quick and a slower adaptation. Since the visual purple bleaches quickly in light and is generated again in darkness, it seems to be either the cause of adaptation to dim light or to be closely associated with the cause. As a result of these facts, it is evident that in stating the threshold of stimulation we must state it for the dark-adapted eye, as that limen will be far lower than that for daylight vision.

Again the area of the retina most sensitive to dim light is a circular band lying about ten to fifteen degrees from the fovea. Astronomers, when gazing at very dim stars, find that they see them best, not by looking at them directly, but obliquely to the amount of about fifteen degrees. 

This circular band of the retina is, therefore, most sensitive in dim light.

The lowest perceptible brightness is about that of black velvet illuminated by a single candle at 8-10 meters distance from it. Langley determined the threshold of stimulation for light rays of middle wave length in terms of energy. After fairly long adaptation to darkness he looked at a narrow slit at a distance of one meter which was illuminated repeatedly for half a second. The energy which

reached the eye during that half second would raise a weight of 1/35 of a mg. one millionth part of a millimeter, or it would raise a 15th part of a milligram of H₂O a billionth of a degree C (15-'¹x10-¹² calories). This is as much as to say that the stimulus for vision is almost inconceivably slight, or that the eye is marvelously sensitive. 

Even when the eyes are closed, the retina is still stimulated so that one who observes closely still sees a play of streaming colors and brightnesses. This is called idioretinal light. (Eigenschwarz.) The eye, however, is not too sensitive for the uses to which it is put. An astronomer who wishes to observe a distant star gets almost no light from it.

The difference thresholds would have to be stated separately for every part of the retina and for every color and brightness but let us take the most sensitive area of the retina and the most favorable grade of brightness, about that of white paper in an ordinarily light room. Practiced observers will detect a change of 1/120-1/200 of the original brightness. Ordinary eyes could not detect a change less than 1/60 of the original brightness. Hence we find the average statement of 1/100 given in discussing Weber's law. (See p. 276.) Since effects in painting are wrought partly by differences in light and shade, we see how delicate the means of stimulation with which the artist works. 

While the fovea is not most sensitive to brightness it is the retinal area most sensitive to color and to color differences. As already stated there are only cones in the fovea. 

The Qualities and Attributes of Visual Sensations.-The visual qualities, or qualities of visual sensations, fall into two great groups, the brightnesses (grays) or grades of light from the most intense black to the most intense white,

Beginning with the lights or brightnesses, if we say that the sun's disk gives the most intense brightness there are between that and the deepest black "between six and seven hundred light sensations" (T. B., p. 60), or blacks, whites and grays.

and white. The colors of middle brightness and greatest purity lie around the margin of the color square at the base of the double pyramid. Those of greater brightness lie above the base and toward white. These are called the lighter tints of each color. The darker tints lie below the base toward black. Each tint matches in brightness the gray of the axis which lies at the point at which a line from the tint and parallel to the base intersects the axis. The colors along this parallel are of the same hue or color tone and of the same tint. They would differ in another attribute, however, that of purity of the color or saturation or, as Titchener calls it, chroma. That is, as you approach the gray of the axis the color will appear more and more like that gray and consequently be less a pure color. The other introspective facts shown by the pyramid are readily seen. Reading from it we see that psychologists ascribe three attributes to every color: (1) every color has a certain hue or color tone, (2) it has a certain tint or place on the scale from light to dark, (3) it has a certain grade of purity or saturation or chroma. The pure circumference colors have no suggestion of gray in them. The colors close to the axis appear more suffused with gray than with the color. Hence, in short, every color has the attributes of hue, tint and chroma. 

I have one objection to the color pyramid, as I have drawn it. There are about 600 or 700 whites, grays and blacks. Unless a part of the spectrum, say red, can give as many sensations as the whole of it, it cannot have all the tints from white to black in a single grade of saturation. 

Hence the white-black axis should extend above and below the apexes of the pyramid where the colors end. In other words, I have never seen a red or yellow as bright as snow and yet still red or yellow.

333 In the spectrum physicists find that there are about 

150 distinguishable colors. Adding all distinguishable tints and chromas to these Titchener puts the full number of color sensations at 35,000. The workmen who laid the mosaic of the Vatican must have discriminated 30,000 different colors.

Complementary or Antagonistic Colors.-Referring once more to the color pyramid it will be seen that lines in the basal plane drawn through the W to Bk axis connect R and G, B and Y, etc. When two colors joined by such a line are mixed in proper proportions the resulting sensation is white or, if their intensity is not great, gray. Two such colors, as thus give white or gray, are called complementary colors. When two disks of colored paper are rapidly rotated on a color wheel they are evenly mixed, apparently on the retina itself, because it requires about 1/10 of a second for the nerve impulses and consequently for the sensations to die away. If a second stimulus is added before the effect of the first dies away the sensation is the result of the two impressions combined or added. This result for complementaries is white. A mixture of two non-complementary colors gives one whose wave length is intermediate between those of the two colors mixed. Mixing pigments is subtracting colors, and of course, no statement about getting colors by addition applies to getting them by subtraction. The chief pairs of complementary colors are shown by the pyramid. Lines drawn parallel to those in the basal plane but higher or lower along the axis also terminate in complementary colors but of a different intensity or tint.

The double pyramid is, thus, a convenient way of portraying the whole list of visual sensations and the relations between them.

Color Blindness.—In normal eyes only the outermost zone or periphery of the retina is color blind. There are a few persons, however, whose retinas are color blind throughout. Even by central or direct vision they see only grays. Such persons if asked to sort a lot of different colored worsteds will pile each colored skein with the gray one which it matches in brightness. He does not see the colors at all but only the grades of brightness. Such a person is said to be totally color blind and the defect is

rare. Partial color blindness is more common, especially red-green color blindness. Persons who are red-green blind see blue and yellow correctly but the reds and greens all look like different shades of gray. The English physiologist Dalton was the first to call scientific attention to this type of blindness. He was himself so completely redgreen blind that he could not distinguish his red academic gown from the green grass of the lawn at Oxford. Both must have been of about the same brightness. The Oxford gown is of a rather bright red hue. Thus there are (1) total color blindness, (2) red-green color blindness," and possibly (3) blue-yellow color blindness, which is due to injury, if it ever occurs. The red-green type is the one which causes railroad disasters. However, since the threshold of color is higher than that of light, an engineer on a foggy night might see a light and yet be quite unable to tell its color. In such cases there is a strong tendency to supply out of the imagination an image of the usual color or the one expected. Generally the color supplied would be correct but in rare cases it would be wrong and an accident might follow. The colored lights are often too dim.

About 4% of men are color blind and very few women. 

Yet the defect is inherited predominantly through daughters, not through sons.

Contrast. As we have seen, the retina is composed of some millions of nerve ends called rods and cones. 

These are extremely sensitive to light and are somehow so related that a stimulus applied to one area or "patch" of "Whittier's trouble-an unfortunate one for a poet-was color blindness.

He could not distinguish between red and green. The red apple and the leaves of the tree looked to him exactly the same. His mother discovered the defect when Whittier was six years old. He was in the fields picking wild strawberries and could see no difference between the color of the berry and the leaf. 'I have always thought the rainbow beautiful,' he once said, 'but they tell me 

I have never seen it. Its only color to me is yellow.'

SENSATION 

337 the retina has an effect on the surrounding rods and cones, and even on those at some little distance from the stimulated area.

If a small box is painted dead black, both inside and outside, and lined with black velvet we find on looking at a hole through its front that the former dead black surrounding the opening becomes distinctly grayish. That is, the opening in the velvet-lined box is so much darker than the black paint that when we look at the former the latter becomes gray by contrast. This is brightness contrast.

There is also color contrast. If in a darkened room we hold two plates of ruby glass before a stereopticon very pure red light is projected on the screen. If we hold a book or a broad ruler in the path of this light its shadow will be green. If the glass used is blue, the shadow is yellow, or in general the shadow is the complementary of the background. Withdraw the glass. The background is light and the shadow dark gray or black. The same relations hold true if a piece of gray paper is placed on a colored background and both are covered with tissue paper. The gray is suffused with the complementary of the ground.

Such experiments led Hering to the opinion that, if one area of the retina is stimulated with a color, a reaction is set up in the surrounding area which gives rise to the sensation of the complementary color. Both reactions were believed to be chemical in nature.

In color decoration contrast is taken into account in the phrase that complementary colors re-enforce each other and neighboring colors in the spectrum subdue or "kill" each other. To represent white marble as seen by moonlight it must be painted many times brighter than the

real moonlit marble would be in order to keep the contrast the same, for in a painting it must be viewed by daylight.

Adaptation.-Contrast depends upon the space relations of the stimulus and background. The facts now to be stated depend upon time relations. I have already described adaptation to brightness in the discussion of the thresholds. (P. 328.) There is also adaptation to color.

Anyone who has worn blue or yellow glasses has been astonished to find that after a few minutes all objects appeared in their natural colors and had lost all trace of the color in which they at first appeared. Ebbinghaus says, "When at evening with increasing twilight the lamps are lighted we see at first with perfect definiteness that their light has a marked yellow color. After they have burned a while this consciousness is lost. Their light appears white and objects which appear white to us by day, now make undoubtedly the same impression. The predominant yellow in the visual field has, as a result of the longer continuance of the objective stimulation, lost its specific color character and given place to the impression of a neutral color. It has, as we may say, shifted in the direction of its complementary color. This behavior is general." The general law of adaptation may be stated thus: With somewhat long continuance of the same visual stimuli the color impressions produced by them do not keep their original character but change rather rapidly. 

Their brightness recedes from the extremes and approaches a middle brightness and their various colors gradually become dulled and approach neutrality, i. e., a neutral gray.

So far our remarks apply to stimulation of the whole retina but there is also adaptation when only a part of the

SENSATION 

339 retina is stimulated. This is called local adaptation. Perhaps the most striking example of this is our complete unconsciousness of the shadows cast upon the retina by the blood vessels within the eyeball. When, however, we enter a dark room and allow light from a candle to enter one side of the eye through the sclera the branching blood vessels appear on the opposite wall like a branching tree. The oblique direction from which the light enters has cast the shadows on rods and cones unadapted to their presence and they at once become visible. The effects of local adaptation are also seen in 

Negative After Images. If you look for 40 or 50 seconds at a bright object like the window and then turn your eyes upon the gray walls, after a moment the image of the window will appear on the wall but with all its parts reversed. What was bright in the stimulus will appear dark in the after image and conversely. Each color will be changed into its complementary, except that contrast comes in so that instead of a gray field on a red ground giving a red field on a gray ground it gives a red field on a greenish ground in the after image. These images with brightnesses and colors just the reverse of those in the stimulus are called negative after images. Each part is the negative of the corresponding part in the stimulus. 

Positive After Images.-Soon after a stimulus is withdrawn the retinal image dies away but if you wait with fixated eyes for a moment the image returns just as it was when the stimulus was present, only in much weaker intensity of color and brightness. This is the positive after image. It often requires a rather good observer to detect it. 

Since an image requires a tenth of a second to die away sparks just extinguished still appear before the eye. 

Hence a rocket leaves a luminous trail and a spark

whirled around gives an impression of a circle of light. 

Moving pictures depend on this fact of vision. 

Purkinje's Phenomenon.—With moderate changes in the illumination of the spectrum the colors and their relative brightness remain practically unchanged. When, however, the illumination is considerably diminished red, green, and blue-violet tend to spread and displace the other colors, and they themselves become darker and grayer. But the most striking change is the shifting of the relative brightness of the colors. By daylight, yellow is the brightest spectral color, but with continued decrease of illumination the spot of greatest brightness shifts more and more toward the green until it becomes the brightest part of the spectrum. The long-waved end of the spectrum (red and yellow) becomes darker than the short-waved end under this decrease of intensity, so that in dim light the brightness relations of the spectrum are as follows: Darkest Red

Orange Yellow Brightest Green 

Less Dark

Blue Indigo Violet This change with decrease of illumination was first noticed by the physiologist Purkinje and color theories must take account of it. Probably this darkening of the yellow under dim light and the corresponding brightening of the green is the fact most influential in leading to the decision that we possess two types of vision, namely, twilight vision and daylight vision, with separate end organs for each. It seemed impossible that the same end organs should respond to the spectrum with yellow as the brightest color in daylight, and green in twilight. 

Decrease the illumination still more and the spectrum becomes merely a gray band. This is apparently its ap-

SENSATION 

341 pearance for the totally color blind eye, even when the intensity of illumination is great. The Purkinje phenomenon does not occur when only the fovea is stimulated. 

Hence the area of keenest color vision seems to be insensitive in dim light. As already remarked, the fovea is used only in daylight but then it is the most sensitive part of the retina for color vision. 

Theories of Vision.-If we understood perfectly the action of the retina it would be easy to account for all the facts of vision and we should know them, as it were, from the center outward. Conceivably all the facts might be explained in a single formula. Unfortunately we are in no such happy position. We must assemble the facts and in the light of all of them we must try to formulate a theory which will account for them. The difficulty of the problem will be seen if we enumerate three theories of vision or, as they are sometimes called, "color theories," for until recently at least color vision seemed to be the chief fact of vision to be accounted for.

The Young-Helmholtz theory of vision, named from its two inventors, assumed that there are three types of nerve ends in the retina. One type responds to long-waved ether vibrations and gives the sensation of red, the second responds to vibrations of medium length and gives the sensation of green, and the third type, the sensation of blue-violet in the same way. A light of any color stimulates all three types of nerve ends in some degree but predominantly red, green, or blue-violet. When all three types are stimulated at once we have the sensation of white light. Hence this theory explains color mixing because any two of these types of nerve ends stimulated together in the proper intensity would give the sensation of gray. The three reactions of the retina were called its "elementary excitements" of

which all other sensations were compounds. Contrast was explained as an error of judgment. The fact that all colors and brightnesses tend to middle grades by adaptation was ascribed to fatigue of the retina. The other facts of vision were not explained and were little known when the theory was formulated. This theory is followed chiefly by medical men and appears in the text books of physics. For years it was the only theory of vision. 

The second theory is that of the physiologist Hering. 

He says the retina contains three photo-chemical substances as follows: Dissimilation

White-Black 

White

Red-Green 

Red Yellow-Blue Yellow

Assimilation Black Green

Blue If assimilation and dissimilation are equal the result is a sensation of gray. Hence color mixture and complementary colors are readily explained. If there is much dissimilation of the red-green substance on one spot of the retina all around it there will be assimilation of this substance. Hence the red is bordered with green and contrast is explained. After images are accounted for in a similar way. The spot of the retina just now exposed to red light has the red-green substance dissimilated or decomposed in a high degree. Close the eyes and this substance begins in a moment to assimilate or build itself up once more. 

Hence the very spot which gave us a sensation of red now gives us one of green and this is bordered by red by virtue of contrast.

The black-white substance extends all over the retina. 

There are no color substances in the periphery hence that part of the retina is color blind. Persons who are red-

SENSATION 

343 green blind lack the red-green substance. The totally color blind eye has only the black-white substance. Other facts are explained in a similar way. 

The Hering theory cannot explain the difference between the two different types of red-green color blindness which have been found to occur. It cannot explain the 

Purkinje phenomenon, and finally two grays, produced by mixing colored lights, which match perfectly by daylight illumination do not match in twilight, as they should do if there were only one kind of black-white substance and this was present all over the retina. By the time the facts had undermined this theory it began to dawn on the investigators that what we possess is two distinct kinds of vision, twilight vision and daylight vision, and that the nerve ends which function chiefly in twilight vision are not those which give us color sensations. This is called the 

Dual Theory of Vision.-The rods are the organs of twilight or dim light vision, the cones of bright light vision. 

The cones give us the whole variety of color vision, the rods a dim white in different degrees of intensity or rather a sort of bluish white as seen in a landscape by moonlight. 

The rods are, therefore, affected by the spectral rays of middle wave length and perhaps a trifle by shorter wave lengths. The long waves affect only the cones. Dim light does not affect the cones at all but it does affect the rods, so dim light vision is rod vision. On the other hand, in strong light the visual purple is very quickly bleached and then the rods cease to function.

A very strong evidence of the truth of this theory is the fact that in a dim light spectrum the intensity of the chemical effects of the different colors on the visual purple agrees with their brightnesses, i. e., the brightest light waves bleach the visual purple most rapidly.

Again this theory accounts for the Purkinje phenomenon. In intense or strong light the cones alone function and yellow is the brightest color. As the light grows dim the rods begin to function and the cones gradually cease to do so. 

When they no longer function the bright region is in the green. Since there are no rods in the fovea this change in brightness does not occur when only the fovea is stimulated, or, as we say, in central vision. On this theory totally color blind persons are those who either lack cones or whose cones are diseased and therefore do not function. 

They are "rod seers." The birds which cannot see at night possess only cones. We have thus gone far in the solution of the problem but by what process in the cones we are able to see color we do not know nor do we understand the facts of contrast, etc. It seems apparent, therefore, that to this dual theory we must add a chemical theory somewhat like that of Hering, save that we must suppose that all vision is accomplished at the expense of dissimilation of the photo-chemical substances of the retina. 

Chemical Senses.-The senses of taste and smell are stimulated chemically. A great deal is known concerning the former but it cannot find place in an elementary description chiefly because some knowledge of physical chemistry is necessary for understanding it. Suffice it to say that the elementary taste sensations are sweet, salt, sour, bitter, and possibly a metallic taste. On p. 73 it was stated that the sensation of hunger is due to contractions of the stomach and lower oesophagus. While the stimulus is, therefore, mechanical the sensation appears to be one of pain, the hunger "pangs," so-called.

Synaesthesia. In the year 1873 a young philologist, Nusbaumer by name, reported to the Vienna physicians' Verein certain peculiar self-observations. He and his

SENSATION 

345 oldest brother had, since their earliest youth, connected a definite color sensation with every normal tone sensation. 

If a tone was sounded on the organ he gave for that tone always the same color sensation whether he was able to recognize the tone correctly or not. In childhood these color sensations were so vivid and surprising that on hearing a tone he often broke out in raptures, not over the beauty of the tone but because of the beauty of the secondarily felt color sensation, and thus he brought ridicule upon himself from his parents and brothers and sisters. As the tone was sounded on this or that instrument, so that the quality was different, a new tint of the color appeared. A 

Vienna alienist thought his behavior was psychopathic and warned Nusbaumer to be careful. His fears, however, proved groundless.

Fig. 36-Number form showing the arrangement of the numbers 1-100 in the imagery of one individual. A three-dimensional number form is apparently very unusual. 

Since that time many persons have been found who have this "colored hearing." For the sounds of the letters a, b, i, o, and u, one person reported the visual sensations of yellow, white, blue, red and black, respectively. Another associated similar color sensations with the sounds of the spoken numbers 3, 4, 5, and 9.

The following example of synaesthesia in a boy of eleven years indicates both the native, the sensory, and the individual nature of the experience. As it came to me in a letter I will quote it exactly: "My son eleven years old has taken violin lessons for about three years and he is very good for one of his age. Now the first time I ever heard of sounds having colors was through him. He needed a new violin, so we brought one home on approval that he liked better than any of the others, which a certain music house had. He kept it for a few days. It had just the tone that he liked but we returned it on account of defects of material. Then he tried out some from another music house, but none seemed to satisfy him like the one he had in the first place. Now, I know but little about music or tones, so I asked him why he liked the violin from the first place the best, and he replied, 'Because the Astring has an orange sound.' That sounded strange to me; in fact I didn't know what to think of such an answer.

I just thought he was trying to explain something and didn't know how to go about it. But within a few days I read your article, so I began to test him out a little myself. 

In the meantime he found another violin that suited him with an orange-colored tone A-string. Here is the way he said three violins that we had here sounded in the test, all being tuned together:

Closely related with these sensory experiences, are the so-called number forms. When numbers are thought of they are mentally seen in certain definite arrangements, e. g., in an ascended zigzag with ten and its multiples at the angles. 

These facts of synaesthesia and number forms belong strictly to individual psychology since most persons are quite devoid of these interesting experiences.

CHAPTER IX PERCEPTION 

Elementary sensations are the raw material of consciousness. This is evident from the fact that if a single sense is lacking a certain type of consciousness is absent. 

A blind man, for example, thought scarlet must be like the sound of a trumpet. Yet, apart from such examples, we are rarely aware of single sensations. We are instead conscious of the thing which causes or gives the sensation. 

Hence most of perception might be described under the heading "perception of things." Knowledge of sensations comes only by a careful analysis of experience such as we have made in the preceding chapter. It is the result of abstraction. This analysis is necessary, however, if we wish to learn the source of consciousness. Henceforth analysis need not be carried so far though it cannot be dispensed with.

During a lecture to a large class in psychology there was a sudden, deep, roaring, ominous noise directly over the heads of the students. For part of a minute they showed a sudden, startled surprise and even fear. Notetaking stopped and instinctively everyone straightened up. 

Then just as suddenly these expressions ceased, tension relaxed and the noise was recognized as snow sliding from the roof. The first moment was one of sensation and strange, surprising sensation, the second moment was one of perception of the object, snow. Yet only because this experience is unusual and because snow is rarely perceived by the ear were there two distinct moments of different

PERCEPTION 

351 experience. Under ordinary circumstances we know the object as present the instant we get a sensation or sensations from it. The sensation is quite eclipsed by our knowledge about it. The noise is the street car, or the postman, or a motor car, or the wind. This at least is the experience of adults. Young children, perhaps, get pure sensations which are not instantly submerged in knowledge of their causes.

If we consider the illustration of the sliding snow we can get an accurate notion of perception. From the outer world there came only the single sensation of the heavy, grating noise. From the minds of the hearers was supplied the knowledge "snow-sliding-from-the-roof." This gave the sensation a meaning. So perception consists of one or more sensations plus the knowledge which gives them a meaning. Obviously we often get more than one sensation from an object, e. g., we both see and hear it, but that is a minor detail. The moment we have supplied a meaning for the sensation or sensations we understand them. Hence most of every perception comes "from out our own heads," or most of every perception is the imagery aroused by the sensation. Meaning then is a fundamental factor of perception. Usually we supply the correct meaning. When we supply a false meaning the result is an illusion. Because perception is composed of both sensations and images or knowledge some have used the phrase "mixed perception" for the ordinary type of perception and "pure perception" for an extraordinary or unusual type. The latter is so rare that we are justified in saying that every perception is a mixed perception. When the knowledge which supplies the meaning does not come to our aid we have only sensations and a groping for their import. In this sense too every perception is an acquired

perception because we have had to gain the knowledge necessary to interpret sensations. 

The fact to be emphasized is that in almost all cases the mind supplies the meaning of the sensations instantly. 

One must wait long before he finds a case, like the illustration of the snow, in which an appreciable time elapses between the coming of the sensation and the recognition of its cause and import. I hear a voice in the hall, only a word or two, but I say, "My friend is here." The knowledge about the sensation so eclipses the latter that we are almost unconscious of it. In ordinary life, therefore, sensations are chiefly signs for which we supply appropriate meanings. As we shall see, a large part of human progress is due to attenuating or making more abstract the signs but causing them to suggest more and more meaning. In the history of the race there are first objects, then picture writing to represent the objects, then hand writing instead of picture writing and finally stenography instead of hand writing. The history of mathematics furnishes similar examples. Apparently the more abstract we make our symbols the more meaning they are able to suggest. We shall consider the matter once more on a later page. 

While I have defined perception as consisting of one or more sensations plus the knowledge which gives them a meaning, we must remember that ordinarily sensations mean the object from which they come and whatever can be done with it or with regard to it. Hence Professor 

James defines perception as "the consciousness of a particular material object immediately present to sense." 

This includes a large and important part of our perceptions. We live in a world of material objects with which we must deal. We become acquainted with objects in our childhood and thereafter we are in daily contact with them.

PERCEPTION 

353 Even the persons about us are objects in the sense that they must be perceived materially by their voices or appearance. It is because objects have so much meaning and practical importance for us that we do not observe our experience of them, so far as it comes from without, to be made up of sensations. As already remarked, memory supplies an image of the object at the slightest sensational hint. This is seen in the following figure. 

Fig. 37-The duck-rabbit illusion. (After Harper's from Warren's Human Psychology.) 

One sees this sketch either as a duck or a rabbit according to the anticipatory image supplied by memory. The sensations coming from the sketch remain fixed. The imagery which interprets the sensations may be changed at will. To illustrate further how much imagery contributes to perception Warren also gives the following figure.

Hold the book at a distance and the outline of the letters appears complete. The missing lines are supplied in perception. 

(From Warren's Human Psychology.) 

The mind readily supplies the lines suggested and reads the word correctly.

Conversely, it is not difficult to defeat memory in this process, i. e., to delay the coming of the supplied meaning though the sensations are already present. If we invert the newspaper we are reading its page becomes an irregular blotch of curiously running black lines, in which we recognize nothing. Yet children and the savages taught by missionaries for a time read the few words they know as readily when the page is inverted as when it is upright This shows how much of our lives is given to acquiring a stock of meanings with which to interpret the objects and symbols with which we have to deal. If the photograph of a landscape is inverted in a similar way it is quite unintelligible, and again most people stare for some time quite helplessly at the French words, Gui n'a beau dit qui sabot dit nid a beau dit elle? before the sounds suggest a familiar line of the song. "Coming Through the Rye."

Finally Seashore gives a picture of a dog comfortably curled up but very few people can see it so until they are told what to look for. (Figure 39.)

These facts are important in the matter of education. 

We do not understand the world about us because we do not know what to look for. But an expert appears and gives us a stock of anticipatory images whereby we readily
