What is it?

Fig. 39 

interpret the minerals, or crystals or the microscope slide of a stained tissue or malignant germs or what not. Education is, therefore, largely the process of acquiring anticipatory images which will enable us to interpret our sensations successfully. A certain color in a test tube means that a precious metal has been discovered. A certain symptom may mean a malignant disease. Those who object to the storing of memory with meanings should entrust their health to a physician of like beliefs who consequently doesn't possess an enormous stock of anticipatory images of symptoms to use in diagnosis and prognosis. 

When we have acquired a stock of meanings it is difficult or impossible to see objects as we saw them before, not because the outer world has changed but because we are changed. Hence someone has wisely said: "We see things not as they are but as we are." This is entirely true and incidentally it accounts for an enormous amount of

disagreement, even with regard to the same outer objects. 

The birth of a genius means the later founding of many laboratories in order that the young may be taught to see things, not so much through his eyes as through the meanings he discovered in the objects and then to find new meanings of which even the genius did not dream. It is evident, therefore, that both recognition and memory images are present in an act of perceiving. 

Children's Perceptions.-Plainly children must spend much time in acquiring a stock of meanings, and what makes the remarks of children so interesting is the peculiarly false meanings they attach to new impressions.

For example, one three-year-old child, who had learned the alphabet but not Arabic figures, asked, "What does e, z, i spell?" She was looking at the figures 1, 2, 3 and reading them from right to left. The correction of false meanings must constitute a large portion of the teacher's work, a fact often overlooked in theoretical pedagogy. 

Very soon false meanings obstruct the acquisition of true ones. This is especially shown in the drawings of children. The constant injunction of the teacher of drawing must be, "Draw what you see, not what you know." One boy in sketching a landscape actually drew into the picture the house on whose porch he was sitting when making the sketch.

A five-year-old girl drew a table as shown on the next page. Yet the psychology books are full of statements that such an object never appears twice the same. Now it has two acute, and now two obtuse angles. From another point of view these interchange, etc., but we ignore all these changes and see the table top as rectangular. This the child has done. It is generally important to ignore false appearances but not in drawing.

PERCEPTION 

357 

Fig. 40 

The very young child has been assumed, when looking at objects, to get only sensations since he has no images with which to "meet and greet" them. No doubt this is true for a time.

Certainly the behavior of young children seems to warrant the belief. They appear to try to learn all the qualities of anything which is given them. When they see an object, they at once want to handle it. But even that is not enough. They explore it with the mouth and tongue. A baby's mouth is much more than a feeding organ. It is also an exploring organ for learning the properties of things.¹

Hence someone has said that the child learns more in the first two years of life than in any later two years. This is probably true. When these two years are past, we know most of the world about us in its ordinary aspects, most of the common objects and their qualities. If, after that age, we desire another novel perception it is best to turn to the microscope or the telescope to get it, or else resort to some psychological experiment, so that the object shall show us new qualities. 

One of my friends, a specialist in diseases of the throat, thinks that the tonsils are useful at this time in getting rid of bacteria which must enter the mouth while it is used as an exploring organ.

Recognition in Perception.-Whoever returns to his childhood's home after an absence of ten or twenty years will find a host of memories returning to him which, he will be sure, would never have revived had he not returned to the old surroundings. Houses, trees, locations, and the faces of persons long vanished from his consciousness will be recognized the instant they appear to his senses, though they could never have been recalled without the aid of their physical presence. The feeling of familiarity which accompanies the return of such objects to the environment may be regarded as the last vestige of a fading memory. Anything less would not be memory nor any part of memory, but a perception of a novel object. 

Thus in every second and later perception of an object, recognition is present and even in first perceptions we sometimes recognize the class to which an object belongs, the use for which it is designed or the elements of which it is composed. For these reasons recognition is regarded as commonly a factor in perception and in many cases perception is said to be more than half memory, because so many memory images are supplied while so few sensations are received from the object.

Perception of Symbols.-The cause of ordinary perception is an object or thing. But ordinary objects can be sketched and it was early discovered that a sketch, which is understood at all, will suggest as many memory images and consequently as correct a meaning as the thing itself. 

Had development stopped here we should all have become artists and our letters to one another would have been filled with accurate, trustworthy sketches of objects. This, of course, is picture writing but our power of memory destroyed it. No complete sketch proved necessary but only the barest hint. Therefore the pictures became less and

PERCEPTION 

359 less like the objects they were designed to represent. They became attenuated into mere symbols and now we must learn by memory what object of thought each symbol represents. Memory has never flagged in this enormous task. 

We now have symbols for almost every object of thought. 

Whether it be an idea of a concrete thing, an abstract quality, a class or a relation, there are symbols for each of them. Because of the slightness of the hint required by memory, symbols have grown less and less like the objects they represent until no trace of resemblance is left. Any arbitrary sign will serve to suggest the necessary meaning. 

Such signs are now so widely used that we may be said to live amid a world of symbols rather than of natural objects, and this must modify the account of perception. 

Youths give years to learning linguistic, mathematical or other symbols that they may perceive these foreign or technical meanings. Stenographers repeat this process of abstraction and make symbols to represent symbols, thus economizing time once more. Credit likewise represents money, while money in turn is a symbol of tangible value. 

Consequently barter of actual goods rarely occurs in modern society. Apparently the more abstract the symbol which we must perceive and the further it is removed from similarity with the object it represents the greater is the saving of time and effort afforded by it. This saving seems at first sight to be clear gain but it is not, for we must now spend years in learning system after system of symbols and learning to judge their validity, not only languages and mathematics but credits and foreign exchange, and symptoms of disease (which are after all natural symbols of diseased conditions). Apparently one need only master an important system of symbols in order to have the most necessary tools of a profession. Since symbols become

more and more abstract, it is difficult to see how all instruction can be made concrete and objective. Records of schools seem to show that each student's education ends at the point at which the knowledge offered becomes too abstract for his mastery and intelligence tests indicate the same condition.

Great surprise has often been expressed at the growing equality of women in industry and other pursuits and subjective explanations have been offered. In an environment of crude weapons and other things woman's disabilities were physical. As the change to an environment of symbols took place, woman after woman found herself well suited to deal with symbols and her so-called emancipation gradually took place. Her disabilities were removed and equality gained by this slow, unnoticed change in the environment; not by any consent or edict at all. Now that this process has gone on for many decades the surprise expressed because of the number of women in all sorts of pursuits seems ludicrous. A changed environment means, of course, new opportunities. Why seek any sort of personal explanation at all? A mutation of the environment has caused all the mischief.

Perception of Situations.-If, because of the increasing complexity of civilization, symbols are largely replacing things as objects of perception, it is for a similar reason that much of our time and training must be devoted to perceiving correctly complex situations of a physical, social, business, political or financial nature. A large and valuable building on fire seems to furnish a simple but exciting physical situation. Yet experience in only two such cases taught me that from one such building property can be saved with little risk of life. Attempt it from another and suffocation is certain. Expert firemen probably know

PERCEPTION 

361 many classes of fires at each of which their behavior must be different for successfully dealing with the situation. 

Different persons are gifted with the ability to detect and respond to the essential features of varied situations. 

But such persons add to their gifts by acquiring more and more knowledge which gives each situation its true meaning. One knows how to deal with strained situations. He is the "great pacificator." Another manages better those situations in which decisive and irrevocable action brings results which are later justified. Success depends always on how well the action is suited to the essential rather than the collateral features of the situation. Plainly years of training and experience are necessary for any noteworthy success, even though there be great ability to start with. 

Coming up from the ranks is regarded as essential to competent leadership in many a great industrial establishment. 

In many cases of dispute probably the perception of exactly the proportion of justice in each claim is the most valuable and the most difficult to attain, yet sufficient knowledge, if uncolored by feeling, gives the situation its true meaning. After experience, therefore, what was originally decided by reflection and analysis comes for the executive to be a ready perception of situations. This constitutes his great value.

Closely connected with all this, detecting human character and predicting human behavior are so imperatively necessary that men have always tried to reduce them to immediate perception. Personal appearance or style of dress has been claimed as significant. Physiognomy, whether a man is "dish-faced" or convex of countenance, blond or brunette, and so on have all been selected as essential to prediction and each theory in recent years has been "sold." Phrenologists thought they could detect character

perceptually, etc. We have seen that less than a certain minimum circumference of skull indicates imbecility and perhaps the same is true of a countenance which shows nothing but vacancy and a lack luster eye. Further than this, however, neither character nor intelligence can be detected perceptually nor otherwise, save by actual trial. 

Prompt determination is a problem at which psychology is working and with little hope of immediate success. A claim of solution at the present time is, of course, fraudulent.

Reactions to Institutions.-Recognizing that the perception of things, though fundamental, is now relatively unimportant, one psychologist believes social psychology to be an account of reactions to social institutions. "Education should train the young to react properly to our complex social institutions." Another replies that an institution is merely a stimulus like any other stimulus. Any other features it may have can and will be ignored. By our view, an institution differs from an ordinary stimulus in that an informed mind supplies for it many meanings, to any one of which the individual may react to his lasting advantage. Without these meanings, a human being may be within the sphere of influence of a beneficent institution for a lifetime and never react to it at all. Such rather pathetic instances are often observed. Really our environment consists of what we understand, of the things whose meanings we know. It is absurd to say that two men who live in the same place have the same environment, as we might if it were perfectly primitive. Now we may directly train the young to react to social institutions by sheer imitation. For a time they will behave as we do. But in the end they must be taught the meanings of institutions and how to discover new meanings, for to these alone will they

PERCEPTION 

363 finally respond. Schools do endeavor to teach the meanings of those institutions which are of vital importance and proved usefulness. If they go further than this they meet great difficulties, because the meanings of an institution are no more discovered by theorizing than the way in which mercury will behave in a boiler. The latter discovery required years.

Illusions. We have seen that in perception knowledge due to earlier sensations fuses indistinguishably and unconsciously with present sensations. But often the wrong interpretation may be aroused by the object and a false perception occur. This is called an illusion and false images may be supplied either (1) because those images are the usual associates of the sensation, or (2) because the mind is occupied with those images to the exclusion of others. The first is called the habit illusion, the second the expectation illusion.

Examples of the habit illusion are common. In the lowlands an object which is seen in sharp outline and clearly is near. In the mountains such an object may still be miles distant, and the newcomer is surprised, if not disappointed, if he tries to traverse the intervening space. 

Stereoscopic views give another illusion of this type. 

Every object gives us two retinal pictures viewed from points about three inches apart. Now set two cameras about three inches apart and take two pictures of one object. These two flat pictures, when we look at them through the stereoscope, give us the impression of a solid or three dimensional object because our habits of seeing are fulfilled by the method. Separate the cameras three feet and the view will be distorted by having too much depth; its third dimension appears enormous.

Again, a woman who occupied a dimly lighted room

opened and closed the transom daily to supply fresh air and she felt the air grow purer, as she thought. After two months of this a glazier appeared to set a glass in the transom. When the woman had done what she thought was necessary she was satisfied. In this case both expectation and habit played a part, so the behavior was due to both types of illusion working together. Generally one factor or the other is distinctly predominant. 

It is of interest to ask, "How long a time would one need in order to train himself out of his habits of perceiving things in certain ways?" Apparently about one week will overcome any set of them. Professor Stratton wore a pair of reversing lenses on his eyes for a time. These made all the objects at his left appear as if they were on the right and conversely. At the end of a week he experienced little difficulty in dealing with the objects about him. 

The association between an object's position and the movements necessary to go to it were formed in that time. It is little wonder, then, that we are unconscious that the retinal image is inverted.

Illusions due to anticipation or expectation are quite as common. We read the words we expect to see, so we notice no misprints. When we turn to reading proof with care we have an intensely conscious and attentive experience, and the reading must be repeated or we read only what we expect to see. "How heavy it is," said Parson, as he estimated a small piece of the new metal potassium placed upon his finger. 

Yet potassium will float upon water or even upon olive oil. 

Having expected the metal to be heavy, he felt it to be so. 

Suppose, however, the expectation idea instead of being commonplace is deeply tinged with emotion and interest, the idea of our health, for example. One physician says

PERCEPTION 

365 that sixty per cent. of patients are cured if they have confidence in the physician's statement that they will recover. 

This confident expectation and nature effect the cure. But suppose instead that this confidence attaches to some lurid advertisement descriptive of symptoms. The patient buys the drug. The most recent case is that of a man who was influenced by quacks to pay $35 for a drug worth $3.50. 

Yet the man was not afflicted with the disease described at all, nor, in fact, by any other illness. Some of the most noted characters in history have had this illusion of illhealth. The rule of the expectation idea is this. Any idea may become an expectation idea and fill the mind and control the will unless we can bring it under criticism by means of another idea.

The most common illustration of this type of illusion is that of the hunter who mistakes some domestic animal for the wild game he is hunting. The illusion does often occur, but less often than one hunter mistakes another for the game. Of two young men hunting for foxes, one had red hair. They separated and presently the other fired, as he supposed, at a fox, but killed his friend who was seated and had for a moment removed his cap.

This expectation illusion has its good side as well as its disadvantages. Under the influence of an ideal which fully possesses the mind men have brought about results which to cooler observers appeared impossible. Most men have this illusion of expectation about themselves. We rate ourselves at least a little stronger or a trifle weaker than we are. The tests of life surprise some of us by revealing unsuspected sources of strength, others by revealing great sources of weakness. Finally the middle-aged man may find that the courage and endurance he was sure he had in his youth were really never within him.

Practically this illusion works its worst effects in the case of indulged children. Kept from the touch of the actual world and with every whim pampered, they cannot form a true expectation idea of the world about them. 

Eventually it turns out to be so much harsher than their anticipations that they fail ignominiously to meet its demands.2 

Recently experimental psychology has shown that there are types of mind especially subject to this kind of illusion. 

Nothing is taken literally. Every experience is filled out with expectation ideas, every stimulus seems richer than it really is. A child with this fanciful type of mind needs quite different training from that given the literal-minded child.

Closely related to the expectation illusion is the tendency to fill gaps in perception. A great many persons when asked to state whether the figure six on their own watch is Roman or Arabic will give a wrong reply because they have filled a gap in perception with an image. When you have shown a group of persons a picture, then removed it from view and asked, "Was the cupboard open or closed?" some will try to answer the question though no cupboard appeared in the picture.

Testimony. The facts stated above show some of the reasons for the weakness of human testimony. It has more defects than mere inaccuracy of memory. Stern found in 

Aussage experiments that 6% of all statements were false in free recital and 33% of all statements were false under cross-examination. Such facts deserve consideration.

The story is told of Sir Walter Raleigh that while imprisoned in the Tower he was engaged in writing his 

History of the World. One morning he heard hot words 'Recent intelligence tests of college freshmen show that different environments of early life produce real differences in character and industry.

PERCEPTION 

367 below his window and looking out he witnessed an altercation. At breakfast he gave an account of the incident and was surprised to learn that almost every statement he made was in error or inaccurate. It is said that on returning to his cell he cast the manuscript of the History of the 

World into the fire saying: "If one cannot see and report correctly what happens before his eyes it is hopeless to attempt to describe truthfully the most remote events." 

Those alive to the difficulties of giving accurate testimony will regard his decision as wise.

The expectation illusion has frequently operated to identify an innocent man as a wrongdoer. In order to be relied upon the witness should be able to pick out the man he identifies from a group of men similarly dressed and of similar height and weight. 

Suggestion. We hear much nowadays concerning the psychology of suggestion. Suggestion is really little more than the planned implanting of the expectation idea on which it is desired that the person shall act. The chief difference, therefore, between suggestion and the expectation type of illusion is that suggestion applies to acts and to the immediate future. The illusion refers to facts and can usually be proved an illusion at once. Of course suggestion will work best if there is some basis of fact beneath the expectation. One must not expect imagination to build the whole picture but rather to fill in the gaps. Facts are most potent of all in suggestion. The pioneers in the commercial manufacture of nitrogen from the air found that they could safely employ only young chemists. The older men knew too many reasons why the plan must fail. 

Hence they could have no faith in the outcome of their work. This is negative suggestion due to an interpretation of facts. Positive suggestion is often just as potent. Sug-

gestible persons can be made to buy articles for which they have no need and no use and actually no desire except the momentary one aroused by some artificial expectation idea. 

Hallucinations. An illusion is an expectation idea quite out of proportion to the stimulus which caused it. Can the disproportion be greater still and no stimulus at all be present, though it is firmly believed to be there? This happens often enough but, in spite of statements to the contrary, it is rare except in disordered minds, unless the reader is willing to call some dreams hallucinations. I shall not do this. In many dreams there is a stimulus but it causes a false consciousness of itself. We dream we are being suffocated because the heartbeat has actually slowed down in sleep, etc. The stimulus is thus really within the body, not outside of it as the dream consciousness reports it to us. There are also pure thought or fancy dreams, composed of memory images alone. But even in such dreams the images rarely take on the intense sensory vividness of hallucinations. Moreover, dreams belong to the sleeping, hallucinations to the waking consciousness. 

As there are illusions of all the senses so there are hallucinations of all the senses, and as auditory illusions are most common so auditory hallucinations are more frequent than those of any other sense. Let us take one or two typical pathological cases. First the patient hears inarticulate noises-"the roaring of beasts, ringing of bells, crying of distressed children." A little later the sounds become articulate. The patients are "taunted by passing crowds, threatened with death, are cursed, called traitors, thieves, and murderers. Paraesthesias of the skin lead to the ideas that ants are crawling over them, that bullets have entered the body, and even the absence of wounds does not deter them from exposing limbs which have been

PERCEPTION 

369 shot full of missiles. Hot irons are being applied to their backs and dust thrown in their faces. They can detect the odor of gas; sulphur fumes are being forced through the keyhole. Real objects about the room assume life; the tufts on the bedding become creeping things, and the bedposts demon guards. The content of the hallucinations is not always of a terrifying nature. Sometimes angels are seen; beautiful music is heard. God appears to them announcing that they are Christs, and empowered to cast out devils; they are commanded to go to confession and to proclaim the gospel message; they are in beautiful surroundings, are richly dressed, in palatial quarters," etc. (Kraepelin, Psychiatry, pp. 175-176.) "The patient firmly believes in the actual presence of these objects. He fears them, flees from them, resists them or begs to be protected from them. This belief sometimes leads to an 'occupation delirium' when the patient is busy gathering up the gold lying about him, driving a flock of sheep, leading an orchestra, or addressing an audience." (Diefendorf's Kraepelin, p. 176.) "The hallucinations in a few cases, and especially after the height of the disease has been passed, are nothing more than a passing show for the patients; they then gaze at the hideous forms and listen to the various noises quite unconcerned." When the patient thus realizes that the visions and objects are unreal they are called pseudohallucinations.

So far as we know at present hallucinations are due to brain processes and not at all to nerve processes, notwithstanding their sensational vividness. "Hallucinations seen through a colored glass are not similarly colored," and you can make the hallucination reappear in the patient merely by directing his attention to his former

visions and voices. The delirium due to prolonged use of alcohol appears to give the most vivid and varied hallucinations.

CHAPTER X  

Thus far we have discussed the perception of objects. 

We have now to consider the perception of what is not an object, if we may use that form of expression. Because, when objects are perceived, they must be perceived as in certain places and as having certain dimensions, these accompanying space perceptions have often been regarded as innate, “necessary forms" of perception. This is a nativistic doctrine. An opposing school insists that space perception is an acquisition due to experience. Such a doctrine is called empiricism. Interesting as this dispute has been to its participants, our task is the psychological one of attempting to find the sensational source of space perception and of trying to ascertain once more how much of this perception is sensation and how much is supplied imagery. 

We have, therefore, two topics for consideration: (1) perception of space in two dimensions, i. e., the perception of surfaces, and (2) perception of third dimension or depth or, as the Germans say, perception of the "depth-dimension."

At least two senses give us perceptions of two-dimensional space, namely, touch (and perhaps in less degree the temperature and pain senses) and sight. While the functioning of these two senses appears to be fundamentally similar, the eye is much more delicately discriminating, partly due to the greater number of nerve ends per

unit area of the retina. Because of this difference it will be clearer to discuss first touch and then vision. 

Touch.-On page 287 it was stated that when we experience a touch sensation we are aware of its location on our body. This was called its "local sign" or local characteristic. Local sign appears to be an elementary factor of cutaneous sensations for one who has lost a limb "still feels the instep or the toes." Others feel the presence of the whole "phantom limb." Localization seems thus to be a result of the functioning of an afferent nerve and its centers quite as much as touch or pain sensations are results of such functioning. Because localization is characteristic of several sensations it seems to have been regarded as secondary to the special sense quality. It is hardly secondary in importance. By means of local sign we are able to distinguish spatially the excitement of every nerve and every pressure point from every other when the stimulations are successive. When two neighboring pressure points are stimulated in succession the observer seems to feel the stimulus shift from one to the other. When the two stimulations are simultaneous, localization is inexact, as was shown on page 297.

This power to locate the position of cutaneous stimuli is the sensational basis of cutaneous space perception. 

Acquaintance with points on the surface of the body is given by means of it and ideas of the size and form of objects touched or handled. Passive touch does not enable us to tell with certainty whether an object laid on the palm is square or triangular, etc. Active touch permits this and the more delicate perception of form such as is seen in the blind who read raised letters by moving the fingers over the page. Muscle and joint sensations co-operate in the perception of size and form and, when the hand can

grasp opposite sides of the object with thumb and fingers, form perception is greatly refined. Cutaneous sensation permits, therefore, clear perception of the size and form of surfaces. It gives poor orientation in space. This too is shown in the case of the blind.¹

That cutaneous perception of form is due to localized points is beautifully shown by the invention of Braille characters. From about 1800-1830 letters composed of raised or depressed lines were used and with no great success. Between 1830 and 1840 the punctiform letters were invented and now the skilled blind reader can read as rapidly as the seeing child of twelve years who is well practiced in reading. Points in their relation to one another, therefore, lead to cutaneous perception of size and form. 

It seems evident, therefore, that an area or "patch" of nerve ends, when stimulated simultaneously, gives the perception of a surface or extent. This is so simple an experience that it might be called a sensation but probably there is some meaning added due to past experiences and this, we have agreed, shall differentiate perception from sensation. When, not an area, but lines of nerve ends are stimulated, our experience is one of an open pattern. A moving point stimulates the nerve ends in succession and the patterns traced are perceived very clearly. When, instead of a single point tracing a pattern, a pattern of points is supplied over which the fingers move, the pattern gives meaning and enables the blind to read. The tongue is not available for this experiment. If it were, the blind could read smaller characters with equal facility, for its "space threshold" is only about one-half that of the fingertips. A sample of Braille at my disposal has characters 'In space orientation the blind are helped by their delicate sense of the air pressure reflected to them from nearby objects and by their sense of hearing which enables them to distinguish approaching and receding footsteps and the echoes of similar sounds reflected from nearby walls.

two and one-half millimeters high. Compare these very large characters with the smallest visible print. 

By virtue of local sign the cutaneous nerve ends enable us to perceive both surfaces and patterns. We must not overlook the fact that the delicate joint sense and the muscle sense contribute much to this type of perception and refine its discriminations. 

Sight. If, in cutaneous space perception, each stimulated nerve end gives a characteristic local sign is there any similar condition for the retina? Here the just perceptible distance between the ends or other limits of a single surface is regarded as the space threshold. This distance can best be stated in angular degrees. The average of many experiments gives 40" to 60" as the amount of such angle or space threshold for direct vision. This corresponds to a distance on the retina of 0.004 to 0.006 mm., and this distance, in turn, is almost identical with the diameter of a retinal cone. Consequently it has been assumed that for two points to be seen as two at least two retinal elements must be stimulated." In the case of very distant objects like the fixed stars the angle must be smaller than that stated above. In such cases it is believed that there is dispersion of light within the eye ball. Obviously with near objects a whole "patch" or area of adjoining cones is stimulated. The result is an experience of a surface extending in two directions. This seems to be the nature of the visual perception of extent. Two retinal elements stimulated simultaneously give the minimal sensation of extent, or the space threshold. At the same time each retinal element responds with a sense of the direction from which the stimulus comes. This is a retinal local sign 

If this account is the true one the attribute of extensity is "Another theory holds that one unstimulated element must intervene between two stimulated ones.

Other due to the stimulation of contiguous nerve ends. accounts assume that extensity is a native and original attribute of visual and cutaneous sensations and analyze it no further because the simplicity of the attribute is also assumed. By either account the completely resting eye would give us sensations of extent. Perception of space in two dimensions would thus be due to a sensation from either the retina or the cutaneous end organs. By movement of the eyes or head our vision sweeps along lines in various directions. By the aid of memory we link the points just seen with those now present, and thus the visual field is enormously enlarged. 

Here again we must recognize the importance of the muscle sense. Amount of movement up or down, to right or left, or obliquely, enables us to estimate the size of surfaces over which our eyes sweep by the amount of muscular tension and effort involved. 

The Third Dimension, Distance or Depth.-To gain a clear conception of the perception of depth one must really collect facts and weigh evidence. Vagueness here will make matters seem simple, while there is a real problem and a difference from the types of perception already discussd. 

Heretofore we have always found a sensational core as the basis of every perception. Can we find it here? I think we can, but instead of appearing in all our perceptions of depth as a sensation it appears only in one of them as such, and in the others as an idea, a meaning, an interpretation of sensations which are not depth sensations at all, often not even space sensations.

Psychologists say that depth or distance is of two kinds: (1) distance of an object from me, the observer; (2) distance of objects from each other. I wish to re-write this as follows: Depth or distance is of three kinds: (1)

the three dimensions of my own body and its members, any one of which is third dimension to the other two; (2) distance of objects from the observer, me; and (3) distance of objects from each other. Since the existence of the last two is granted, let us try to give evidence for the first. 

The following case from Dr. Head's practice seems to me clear and decisive. He writes, "A patient of mine had received a gun-shot injury, which had disorganized the elbow-joint and completely destroyed the ulnar nerve. 

For five months we hoped to be able to save the limb, but were at last compelled to amputate through the lower third of the arm. From the time he was wounded, there were the usual changes, both motor and sensory, associated with complete ulnar paralysis; but the little finger alone was devoid of all forms of sensibility, superficial and deep. 

So long as he retained his limb, the finger seemed to him a dead object attached to the hand. But the phantom hand, which appeared after the amputation, had four digits only.

During the five months of total insensibility the schemata associated with the little finger, no longer reinforced from the periphery, had gradually died away and, when the actual hand was removed, this digit was absent from consciousness. A portion of the body, cut off from the central nervous system, but endowed with sensibility and movement, may continue to exist as a 'dead' part of ourselves. 

Like a dental plate in the mouth, it occupies a certain place in our spacial conceptions. But as soon as the structures on which it is based are removed, it disappears from consciousness, whilst the normal parts of the amputated limb are represented in phantom form." Head, Henry,

The Conception of Nervous and Mental Energy, British 

Journal of Psychology, XIV, Pt. 2, pp. 136-137, October, 1923.)

This example alone ought to convince us that there is a deep sensibility which gives a direct and steady sensation of the bulk of our body and its parts. Phantom limbs have the same bulk as their normal predecessors. This indicates special nerve fibers and centers for deep sensibility. A further evidence of deep sensibility, if one is needed, lies in the fact that, like other sensations, it may be disordered in disease. One patient reports, "I had the feeling of being without weight." However, probably no one needs to be convinced that we feel the total bulk of our bodies at every moment of our waking lives. If we have deep sensibility at all, it includes sensations of depth or the three dimensions of one's own body. If other experiences suggest a third dimension, the knowledge acquired from this sensation could readily give meaning to the hint. 

We do move and grope through three directions and, while sensations of movement are not depth sensations, the experience demands a third dimension in order to be intelligible. Karl Pearson suggests that a fish in an aquarium so narrow that it could move only to and fro, up and down, even though endowed with intelligence, would live only in a two-dimensional world, and would be as ignorant of a third dimension as we are of a fourth.

Turning now to the distance of objects from us and their distances from one another, we find that these distances appear to be given by both sight and touch, muscle sensations cooperating with both. But sight, touch, and muscle-sense give only sensations of sight, touch, and strain. They do not give distance sensations. Therefore in my belief depth or distance is an idea which serves to give meaning to certain experiences of sight and touch. 

The original source of this idea is, I think, the deep sensibility already described.

There are two views opposed to this: (1) It has been assumed that sight and touch can give sensations of depth. (2) Ebbinghaus believes that we have no sensation whatever of depth; that our consciousness of third dimension is entirely ideational. He opposes the first view with well considered arguments and we shall summarize them, because the matter is of great theoretical importance. Let us imagine someone to have said that we surely have visual and tactual sensations of depth or third dimension. 

Ebbinghaus would reply: 

1. Skin and retina are surfaces, two-dimensional structures. Two-dimensional objects could, therefore, affect these organs sensationally, as already described, but it is hard to conceive how the third dimension or depth could affect an organ without depth. In fact it does not do so. 

Our consciousness of the corporeality of objects is not a sensational consciousness at all. 

2. It has been said that we get the sensation of depth by both eyes working together. If depth could be sensed by the eyes, one eye alone must be able to give the sensation. Otherwise the impression of depth would vanish when one eye is closed, but this is not the case. We cannot regard a sensation of depth as due to both eyes working together if neither alone gives such sensations. Both working together result in the development and strengthening of depth perception, but that is all. People have become almost blind in one eye without noticing the fact. 

3. Accommodation cannot give depth sensations for it is simply the sensation of accommodation, and what have such sensations originally to do with space? By experience a relation is set up between them, but primitively they are two different experiences which occur together. 

Neither does convergence give a sensation of distance. A

small object which is near subtends the same visual angle as a larger, similar object when more remote. The sensations of muscular effort are not sensations of distance. 

What would we say if it were asserted that when a tone is sung with great muscular effort it is nearer, with less muscular effort it is farther away? 

4. The distances which we believe we see are of two kinds, distances of things from us, or distances of things from one another along the line of sight. For the first, since the eye does not see itself, how can it see a distance from itself? The living eye exists for our consciousness as a thing thought of, but the distance of a thing seen from a thing thought of can evidently not be seen. 

For the second, we believe that we see things as distant according to their distance from one another, e. g., the house across the street as more remote than the window through which we view it. But what we really see is the brick-work of the house exactly beside the window frame. 

The brick-work lies sharply beside the wood of the window. 

We know of course that in reality space lies between the two, and in such knowledge lies the consciousness of distance and third dimension. But we see nothing of this intervening space. Apart from this knowledge the objects lie side by side without a gap.

In the real sense of the words distances in the third dimension are not seen, but thought or imagined, generally of course with an extraordinary and illusory vividness. 

We see such distances in much the same way as a hundred pound weight looks heavy; an empty pasteboard box, light; steaming soup, hot; a roof covered with frost, cold, etc. 

Similarly we see two contiguous objects which also present certain peculiarities. But in a thousand cases we have learned that such contiguous objects would separate them-

selves by a considerable distance if we changed our point of view; or two things which appear contiguous to vision would not appear contiguous to touch, etc. Such ideas are aroused, but they inter-penetrate the visual impressions until with the mind's eye we see distances between objects which are not existent for the bodily eye at all. But these ideas have proved true so uniformly that they cannot seem so pale and schematic as ideas which have not had this regular support of experience. 

5. Apart from this rich imagery of depth we actually see a two-dimensional world, but we must take care to understand what is meant by the words. With our developed consciousness of depth all the surfaces we see have a nearer and a remote side. There is distance beyond them and between them and our eyes, etc. But the primitive surface which we experience is more like that which we see when we look into darkness, or into a thick fog, or at the flames of a great conflagration. Here the secondary criteria are partly withdrawn from our gaze. The surrounding mist appears quite different from a sheet of gray paper. 

6. What holds true of the visual sense holds true of touch. The skin, like the retina, has two dimensions. 

What is perpendicular to its surface is not felt by it in the sense that it can distinguish a rod of 2 cm. in length from one of 2 m. placed endwise on the palm. The greater pressure of the latter is a sensation of pressure, not of depth or length. 

7. Nor should it be said that because the hand can be curved in the third dimension it is fitted to give a sensation of that dimension. This bending of the fingers is brought about by movements of the joints. The sensation which comes to consciousness from it is, therefore, the sensation of joint movements. Moreover the retina is curved, but

this does not result in curving the color field at which we look, nor does the curved basilar membrane give a third dimension to tones. Just as little as the sensations of eye and ear return the form of their organs, just so little do skin sensations return the momentary form of the touched surface. 

8. Perhaps there should be added to these arguments the statement that a good painting or a mirror gives us quite as satisfactory an impression of depth as an actual scene. 

Ebbinghaus then gives the usual account of two-dimensional space perception. From two-dimensional space perception he then derives the ever-present idea of a third dimension which is not sensed but indicated or suggested by thousands of daily experiences. His remark that "our consciousness of the corporeality of objects is not a sensational consciousness at all" gives his meaning clearly. In conformity with his view he should not speak of the perception of distance at all, but of the ideation, conception, or thought of it. 

I think this is in error. Given deep sensibility of our own bodies we have a depth sensation. This gives meaning to impressions of vision and touch. An object may look distant or bulky exactly as a weight looks heavy, a pasteboard box light, or a snow-covered roof cold, because we have had each of these sensations from another sense than sight. Our point of agreement is in the claim that neither sight, touch, nor the muscle sense gives a sensation of depth.

What are the visual impressions which we interpret as signs of distance? (1) Change of Color.-Distant mountains appear blue because of the low intensity of the light we receive from

them. The greater the distance the lighter is the tint of blue. When near they appear reddish brown or brown because of the increase of light intensity. 

(2) Definiteness of Outline.-If distinct in outline objects are believed to be near, though in a dry, clear atmosphere they may be miles away. Conversely, because of the dimness of light in a fog, objects must be near to be seen at all, therefore, when seen they appear enormous because they still have the vague outline indicative of distance under usual conditions. Before the days of large scales farmers found that cattle buyers overestimated the weight (size) of cattle if they judged them in the dim light of a heavily wooded enclosure. 

A large part of our perception of size and distance is due to unconscious inference. Because this inference is wrong in hundreds of cases we suffer many space illusions. 

The sagging telephone wire a few hundred yards distant is taken to be a path up the mountain a mile distant. A projecting rafter of a house nearby is believed to be a large truck backed up at a house farther distant and farther up the slope. An area smoked black at the base of a cliff appears to be the mouth of a cave. Examples are found frequently if only one cares to look for them. These illusions are of the expectation type. (3) Inference Due to Knowledge.-We often know two of the three factors and infer the third. Known apparent size

Known real size distance real size apparent size distance Inferred distance real size apparent size, i. e., what the apparent size should be if drawn in a picture

These inferences as to the size and distance of objects are made continually. The sun or moon on the horizon appears much larger than at the zenith partly because with many intervening objects we unconsciously judge the distance to be great, so the object appears large. In the case of the sun and moon, however, the atmosphere probably bends the oblique rays of light more than the vertical (perpendicular) ones, so the physical magnification is added to the psychological one. (4) Superposition.-If two objects are in the line of sight the nearer hides part or all of the one more remote. (5) Shading.-If shadows are drawn on a plane surface as they would be cast by a solid object, we get the illusion of depth or solidity. (6) Relative Motion.-When we are moving, distant objects seem to move with the eye, or remain stationary, while near objects move rapidly in the reverse direction. (7) Accommodation.-In focusing light from a very near object on the retina, the lens must become very convex. The muscular strain for this accommodation becomes a sign of nearness; the absence of strain, a sign of distance. 

All the factors thus far mentioned apply to vision with one eye as well as with both. The next two factors apply to both eyes working as a single organ. (8) Convergence. For near objects the eyes must be greatly converged; for distant objects they may be less converged or their axes may be parallel. Again the degree of muscular effort is indicative of the distance. 

(9) Difference of Images of the Two Eyes.—When we view a solid object like a house from not too great a distance, the right eye sees it from a point a little to the right, the left eye from a point a little to the left of the median plane of the body. When these slightly different images

fuse there arises the perception of a solid object having depth or third dimension. Within certain limits the difference between these two images is less the greater the distance of the object from the eye. Consequently the shifting of similar points of the object toward each other may be taken as the sign of a distance of the object from the eyes.

If two pictures are taken of one object with two cameras about as far apart as the two eyes and such pictures placed in a stereoscope, we see but one object and that possessed of depth or solidity. If the cameras are separated by a distance greater than that between the pupils of the eyes, objects appear to have depth which in ordinary vision show no trace of it. The moon, for example, appears as an enormous sphere instead of as a disc. When the cameras are still more widely separated ordinary objects are distorted; the picture has too much depth. Evidently the slight dissimilarity of the two retinal images of a single object is a sign of the depth of the object and of its distance from the eyes. The stereoscope thus satisfies our habits of seeing objects though its pictures are, of course, perfectly flat. The illusion is made to correspond with reality. 

Fig. 41 

The experiment may be performed without a stereo-

scope by looking through the two drawings at some vividly imagined object, say a mile distant. Thus the two figures can be made to "float" together into an image of a single solid object. Often three images appear, but an ordinary blotter (used as a stereoscope partition) will reduce them again to one.

Plainly most of the visual impressions which we get from objects are hints from which we infer depth and distance from the eyes. There is no visual, tactual nor muscular sensation of depth, but there is the deep sensibility of our bodies and limbs. Because of this, we cannot agree with Ebbinghaus that depth perception is all ideation and inference. If this were so it could not come under the head of perception at all, though it is uniformly so classified. 

Auditory Perception of Distance. We have already noted (p. 373) that the blind can tell with some accuracy the distance of walls and similar obstacles by the echo of their footfalls. Normal persons, however, depend so little on the ear for perception of distance that their errors would probably more than equal their successes in such judgment. 

Since ships have been sunk because pilots thought they could tell the direction of sounding fog-horns, we surely do not depend upon the ear for perception of distance, aside from inference based on the loudness of sounds. 

Space Illusions.-Geometrical-optical illusions in two dimensions are entirely different from the illusions of ordinary perception already described. They are uniform for normal eyes and seem to me to depend on the geometry of the eye and not yet to have been satisfactorily explained. 

Some writers explain these uniform two-dimensional illusions as due to eye movements. It seems to me that they are just as pronounced when the eyes are held as motionless as possible, and I think they would be experienced by

anyone with immovable eyes, if such an individual could be found. There are many such illusions. Three are given as examples:

Not only do associated lines change two-dimensional space perceptions, but surrounding forms are capable of changing the intensity of colors. There are many interesting examples of these changes. They have given rise to a new form of investigation in psychology called by the Germans die Gestaltpsychologie. Since their experiments are most interesting and instructive, advanced students of psychology will hear much of them. Here we can only say that they seem to belong to the same species as these twodimensional illusions. But according to the Gestaltpsy-

Third-dimensional illusions are called illusions of reversible perspective. They are illustrated by Schröder's steps and the reversible cube. By first imagining the steps as a cornice projecting in the opposite direction from the steps, the figure promptly fulfills our imagination of it. 

The cube (or the parallelepiped) projects as a cube from a point of view at the right and slightly below the level of the figure, or it projects as a cube from a point of view at the left and on a level with the figure. These illusions appear to be of the expectation type already described. 

The lines remain constant, the meaning changes. This is not the case with the two-dimensional illusions.

CHAPTER XI PERCEPTION OF TIME 

It was stated on p. 287 that sensations have the attribute of extent and this attribute or local sign we found to lie at the basis of two-dimensional space perception. But we found also (p. 288), that not only have sensations the attribute of duration, but all other conscious processes as well. 

Thus the sense of time applies to all events, both external and internal, while space applies to outer objects, and some psychologists are fond of saying that "the thought of a triangle is not triangular,” i. e., thoughts are not spatial.

We find thus one difference between experiences of space and of time. Another lies in the fact that time seems to have but one dimension while space has three. Still more important for our purpose, our experience of time seems almost perfectly continuous or, as we say, "time flows"; more rarely it "beats" or "throbs." The feeling of discrete "stride" or "transition" is much more emphatic in the case of spatial experiences. 

Besides these differences a certain likeness between the sources of the two perceptions should be mentioned. We found that even a punctiform stimulus applied to skin or retina gives a sensation of a certain vague extent. The senses give us no hint of the geometrical point which has no extent. It is in fact a metaphysical conception. Similarly in considering the perception of time we need pay no attention to that "thread without thickness" which separates past from future. The present which "has melted within our grasp, fled ere we could touch it, gone in the

instant of becoming" has no place in psychology. It too is a metaphysical assumption out of which neither past nor future can ever be built. The briefest mental process is not limited to a point of time in this strict sense. It includes a certain duration or temporal extent which James calls the "specious present" and Stern the "psychic present." This "psychic present" is the duration unit (if a flowing process can be said to have a unit) of our experience of time. In other words, sensations, thoughts, feelings, and decisions have a certain duration, and it is this duration of processes which is directly felt and remembered. The change in consciousness from one process to the next or from one to another phase of the same process gives time its discrete flow instead of the smooth flow during which no change occurs. It follows from this that "we have no sense for empty time." The cause of our perception is change or succession of events. This is always present in some form. Our thoughts and feelings go on in a procession nor can we empty our consciousness of them completely. If we could do so time would collapse, as it actually does in anæsthesia and sometimes does in deep sleep. It is the failure to recognize this fact which breeds the intellectual fear of death. It is really fear of duration after death, a purely metaphysical notion of time. Psychologically duration may be supposed to be as completely extinguished by death as by anesthesia. Psychological time ceases with the one as with the other.

When we pay attention to the passing of a process we have an experience of duration. If, on the contrary, we attend to the beginning and end of a process we experience a time interval. As a continuous process slows down to one of intervals there is for a time a consciousness of

PERCEPTION OF TIME 

391 "roughness" where previously we said the sensation was smooth and unbroken.

The Shortest Perceptible Intervals.-The ear is the most delicate organ for the perception of intervals. Exner found that by hearing he could distinguish two electric discharges when they were separated by 0.002 of a second. 

With light stimuli an interval 22 times as long was required. These numbers do not represent the time threshold, however, but the advent of roughness or brokenness in the sensation. Only when two sensations follow each other at an interval of from one-eightieth to one-fiftieth of a second can the interval be detected and with visual sensations, which die away much more slowly, one-twentieth of a second is necessary in order to tell which impression came first and which second. Even this "time threshold" holds good only under experimental conditions. When we reflect that in a dream lasting no more than one second a whole act of drama may unfold itself with no loss of the sense of succession we realize that we cannot safely generalize these "time thresholds" which were determined under the simplest conditions obtainable. The fact that visual and tactual sensations die away much more slowly than auditory ones probably accounts for Titchener's observation that we can perceive a considerably shorter interval between the sensations noise-spark, than between spark-noise, and between noise-touch than between touchnoise. Again when two such stimuli occur simultaneously we always perceive them in succession with now one and now the other coming first. Hence "young surgeons sometimes see the intently expected blood flow before they hear the click of the cupping instrument, though both must occur at the same moment." Here the sensation expe-

rienced first is determined by attention and the "expectation idea." 

Perception of Duration.-With what degree of exactness can two durations be compared and on what conditions does the perception depend? With times of from one-half to two seconds a difference of from one-twentieth to onetenth of their objective value permits them to be recognized as different, and the judgment is most accurate with a duration of about one second. The estimate of durations seems to depend chiefly upon the degree to which they are filled with events of any type. This "filling out" also affects differently small, medium and greater stretches of time. "When two durations, one of them filled with stimuli, the other empty, are compared the filled time seems greater than the empty one with brief durations. With longer durations the very reverse is the case. The stimulus-filled time appears shorter than the empty one. Between the briefer and longer times there appears an indifference zone in which equal objective times appear approximately equal whether they are filled or unfilled. As a rule there is neither over- nor under-estimation of the period." This law may be compared with that of filled and unfilled space. 

Time Perceived Versus Time Remembered.-In ordinary life, time filled with events is short in passing, long in retrospect. Empty time is long in passing, short in retrospect. 

Apparently this is because we recall few events in the latter case but many in the former. Because of this relationship the novelist says truthfully of space of twenty years, "The years followed each other slowly, monotonous and short because they were empty." He had both passing time and time remembered in view when he penned the apparent contradiction. When, however, George Eliot says:

PERCEPTION OF TIME 

393 "Time-what a word to fling to charity 

Bland, neutral word for slow, dull beating pain,— 

Days, months and years," it is only the passing time which is being considered. This slow passing of eventless time makes isolation and solitary confinement the most acute of tortures, while the dread of empty time teaches the story teller that he must have his recitals "filled with action," especially if his auditors are children.

We can find, however, the psychological ground for the dragging of eventless and the flying of eventful hours. 

Empty time gets attention centered upon itself. The moment that occurs its passing seems interminable. Eventful time receives attention only now and then. The events themselves engage our interest and we are surprised to find so much time has passed. In remembering the time, however, many events are recalled and we consequently estimate the time itself to have been long. 

Finally the years of adult life and old age seem shorter than those of childhood, and it has been humorously claimed that each successive year is shorter because it is a smaller fraction of our past life; a sort of application of 

Weber's law to the memory of the past. The fact is, however, in childhood all sorts of events are interesting and impressive, hence the child's past is eventful and obeys the laws of "filled time." In adult life most events are of familiar sorts, hence they are not impressive and are quickly forgotten.

Finally anyone who is looking forward to a painful experience at a certain time or even to the ending of a joyous time finds the time pass rapidly whether it is filled or empty of events. This may be called the factor of emotion in the estimation of passing time. We seem unconsciously

to compare the actual flight of time with the slow rate at which we wish it to pass and thus the actual time elapsed seems brief indeed.

Perhaps the absence of a sense for empty time is shown in our memory of past time. Not years but events are remembered and primitive men catalogue the reigns of kings, the generations of men, or the number of "moons" as their best means of recording time. 

In the fact that hearing gives an accurate perception of time and almost no perception of space, while vision gives accurate space perceptions and inaccurate time perceptions, we have an example of the division of labor among our senses.
