CHAPTER XII  

The physiology of the eye shows that it is a camera and the retina a photographic plate of living, nervous tissue which is capable of receiving separate impressions in color at a rate of ten per second. At this rate successive impressions are kept distinct. Several chemical reactions have been found to take place in the active retina and it seems probable that its photographic action may, at some future time, be well understood due to increasing knowledge of photo-chemistry. 

By means of the optic nerves and optic tracts every point of the retina is projected on the occipital cortex. By the study of head injuries during the war Holmes and

Lister (Brain, 1915) have shown what part of the field of view is lost by injury to any part of the occipital cortex. 

A pattern of cortical cells receives nervous impulses when light from any object falls upon the retina. As a photographic plate the retina clears itself of the image as soon as the eyes are turned away from the object. Apparently the occipital cortex clears itself as quickly. Nevertheless, if attention has been given to the object, an image of it can be recalled later, when the object is no longer present. 

This process is called reproductive imagination and sometimes memory. It is one of the most important functions of the mind because so many mental processes are based upon it. In a similar way we recall past experience of melodies and tones, of touches and tastes, of dizziness and nausea, etc. Besides recalling mere sensations, we recall

perceptions of objects, symbols, and situations, our past successes and failures, etc., so that the brain's power of "registering" impressions and reacting to later images of them is enormous. This registering ability frees human beings from the necessity of reacting to present stimuli alone and permits them to anticipate situations which may occur in the future and prepare suitable responses beforehand. With this ability, the formula of human behavior is not stimulus-reaction, nor stimulus-sensation-reaction, but is instead stimulus-sensation-image or idea-reaction. 

Prompt reaction to the stimulus alone is very often the proverbial jump from the frying pan into the fire. All our memory images have meaning for the guidance of our behavior and he who searches out their meanings and implications is most successful when any test of truth or correctness is applied to his responses. When no such test is applied, the vividness, the plausibility, or the agreement of statements with one's own opinions or prejudices may cause them to be accepted temporarily. However, we call theories and beliefs "academic" which have not been subjected to a test for their truth. Consequently, while behavior follows the formula, stimulus-sensation-idea-reaction, one of the chief purposes of the reaction is to find the meaning or degree of truth of the idea, and so to modify it until the reaction produced by it shall be perfectly correct and successful.¹ Consequently we find much trial and error behavior which finally becomes trial and success. 

The presence of mental images, however, permits much of this "behavior" to be mental. An eminent French psychologist defines reasoning as "doing the experiment in one's It is this modification of our ideas by actual trial that causes "experience" in practical pursuits to be so highly valued, and the almost universal condemnation of changing, say, municipal employes with each change of administration. 

This it is also which renders the principle of promotion so valuable in business and the principle (if so it may be called) of favoritism so disastrous.

mind." This is an excellent definition, but it leads to the reflection that a great deal of thought, some of which might not be called reasoning at all, consists of doing the experiment in one's mind. Due to the presence of mental images, therefore, many thoughtful people first do the experiment mentally, then subject their results to actual test. This type of thinking may be a prime difference between man and most animals. The animal does nothing at all until confronted by an actual situation, except so far as he is driven to it by instinct alone, e. g., the storing of food by animals and the beaver's building his dam for winter are instinctive procedures. Yerkes has found some evidence that the chimpanzee may sometimes do the experiment first mentally. Instead of merely making many random attempts, he seems to stop and consider and then he succeeds with one trial.

To sum up the discussion thus far, the retina has a truly photographic action which is probably duplicated in the occipital cortex. While these photographs disappear promptly with the removal of the object causing them, mental images of them reappear later in consciousness without the presence of the object, due to memory processes. By perfectly similar action we have images of other sensations, and perceptions. Often we call these images memories without emphasizing their image character, and we often call them ideas without emphasizing their memory character. But certain it is that these ideas have the most profound and important influence on behavior. The retentiveness of memory and the readiness with which we summon images to our aid to deal with an actual or an expected situation often determine our practical success. To fail to recall a single item which applies may result not only in failure, but sometimes in actual disaster.

It is said that the members of the Scott expedition to the South Pole lost their lives because it was overlooked that tin crystallizes at low temperatures. As a result the petrol leaked away. This fact was not summoned to mind when they were preparing for the expedition. The mentally done experiment was not complete. It is usually not complete, but under ordinary circumstances the actual trial permits correction and supplementation. Behavior due to memory and knowledge is of very great importance. While reflex and instinctive reactions are fundamental, they assist our progress only a little way.

Images Compared with Sensations and Perceptions.-We may define mental images as impressions of sensations and perceptions recalled in the absence of the stimuli or objects which originally produced them. Being images, they are more or less faithful copies of the original sensations or perceptions, so that one writer describes them as centrally aroused sensations. Since normal persons almost never confuse images with sensations, the points of difference are more important than the likenesses. (1) Images recur when the stimulus or stimulus-object is absent, while sensations depend for their occurrence upon stimuli. (2) Images suggest or recall one another. Sensations do not.

Thus images belong to an inner, subjective world of one's own consciousness. They obey laws of association and recall yet to be stated. (3) Sensations are now of sight, now of sound, and again of smell or touch or taste. The imagery of any given person is more homogeneous than this. His thought goes on chiefly in one or two types of images, not in images derived almost equally from every sense. As we shall see, normal persons differ from one another in the imagery which they employ in thinking, but persons with normal sense organs do not differ in their kinds of sensa-

tions. (4) David Hume, who was one of the first to consider the difference between sensations and images, thought that they differ only in degree of intensity and vividness. This is the first distinction which occurs to anyone who is asked to state the difference between the two. The images are only weaker and less vivid. But his critics reply that, if you let the image mount to the very highest intensity, it does not become a sensation nor when you think of a sensation as very much weakened, it by no means becomes an image. "Is the sugar we imagine only less sweet than that we have tasted?" These critics conclude that the difference between sensation and image is not merely one of degree but of kind. As Lotze said, "The idea of the brightest sheen does not shine, that of the loudest sound does not sound, nor that of the greatest torment give pain." While this statement of Lotze's has been criticised, it has also found strong advocates who argue further that while an intense sensation causes greater activity and more widespread nervous and mental excitement than a less intense sensation, no more activity is required to imagine an intense brightness than a pale shimmer, no more effort to recall the thunder than a slight noise. In short, it seems probable that a nervous impulse coming from a sense organ causes greater activity in the cortical center than an impulse coming merely from another part of the cortex, and the consciousness corresponds with the brain action. In a diseased brain this may not be the case and the subject of hallucinations believes the objects they represent to him to be actually present. Surely this is exactly the kind of exception which proves the rule and shows disease of the brain rather than identity of sensation and image in normal experience. (5) The image is more fleeting and its content less steadfast than that of

sensations. Every student knows that he must compel the return of images by repeated efforts of attention and that the features of the image essential to his problem may fade unless they are specifically attended to. (6) The image is not always of the same quality as the sensation. Fechner reported of himself that, even with the greatest effort, he could not reproduce colors at all in recalling colored objects or he imagined only fleeting traces of color, and he never dreamed of colors. While this was a personal peculiarity of Fechner's shared by no great number of others, it reminds us that we recall many objects by their names and merely a vestigial image of the object. The image fades more, the more we use the name, so the "translation" of object-images into verbal images is quite common. (7) 

Finally, peripheral nerves and the sense organ are always active in sensation but, since persons blinded after seven years of age think and dream for many years in visual images, it is probable that the brain alone is active in imagery. The conclusion is drawn by psychologists that images and sensations are different in kind, though a few prefer to mention neither sensation nor image but describe only stimulus and reaction. By the latter word they mean sometimes a bodily reaction and sometimes a mental one, so that confusion results as to their meaning. This confusion is due to the attempt to give an account of behavior as due to the stimulus only and as if memory and knowledge had nothing to do with it. 

Types of Images.-Probably no one would deny that every sense may contribute images which may be recalled. 

Some persons have so vivid and distressing an image of the sensation caused by the sudden downward start of an elevator that they would like to avoid the experience altogether. This is important for self-preservation and the

avoidance of discomfort but such an image would not occur often in ordinary thought. Our question is, therefore, What images predominate in our thinking? Do they vary from person to person? Are there other identifiable contents of thought which cannot be called images? As the answers to these questions can be gained only by very careful introspection we must examine some personal reports.

As early as 1860 Fechner described imagery of his own which would be recognized at once as individual and different in some details from that of almost any one who might read his account. We have seen (p. 400) that he could not recall the colors of colored objects. Twenty years later Francis Galton, who was already much interested in individual differences, sent to a large number of persons the following inquiries: "Think of some definite object-suppose it is your breakfast table as you sat down to it this morning—and consider carefully the image which rises before your mind's eye. Is the image dim or fairly clear? Is the brightness comparable with the actual scene? Are the colors distinct and natural?"

Verbal-Motor Imagery. The first result which appeared was the astonishing one, that many of his correspondents possessed nothing which they could properly call visual imagery. One wrote, "It is only by a figure of speech that 

I can describe my recollection of a scene as a 'mental image' which I can see with my mind's eye-I do not see it any more than a man sees the thousand lines of Sophocles which under due pressure he is ready to repeat." (Galton, Human Faculty, p. 59.) Here was a man who evidently did not think in visual images but either in auditory ones, as of words sounding on his mental ear, or in verbal-motor ones, images (?) of uttering words. From

what we now know, it is probable that the verbal-motor images served him far more than auditory ones. He seemed, to his own introspection at least never to have visual images. This result is astonishing to those possessed of clear, accurate, and stable visual images and, if hundreds of students who have reported to me can be credited, a great majority of us do think in visual images in many of the situations of ordinary life.

Perhaps verbal-motor imagery will be best understood if we realize that all movements tend to become habits and all habits tend to become unconscious, most of all, our habits of speech which are mechanized very early in life. 

Vocal performances tend, therefore, to leave a disposition or tendency to be repeated rather than an image to be recalled. Sometimes we find a person who insists that he has no images at all. One is tempted to believe that such persons think with some motor portion of the nervous arc. 

If you insist that they introspect their imagery, their attempt to do so merely produces movements of the lips and glottis, which, because of their habit character, leave no imagery. Everyone knows that in reciting even very familiar poetry or prose, if he tries to imagine the words he is to say next, the reciting ceases with embarrassing abruptness. We must trust our habits, not inspect them or try to interfere with them in action. The mechanism for motor performances functions reflexly and is independent of consciousness. These persons, if they happen to be psychologists, insist that thought is the re-instatement of incipient movements of lips and glottis, with perhaps some auditory images. The result is that these persons distrust or suspect the visualizer's account of his imagery and the visualizer cannot understand their descriptions. 

How common lip movements are in reading and learn-

ing may be seen from the following observation of two high school classes made by Professor Avery. In learning a poem twenty-two out of thirty-two pupils were seen to move their lips. In learning an outline, eight showed decided lip movement, nine slight lip movement, and in four no movement could be detected by the observer. There were but twenty-one students in this class. Thus movement of the lips is far more common than we should suppose in view of the fact that teachers discourage the practice from the very first year in school. Incipient vocal movements may have been present in all these students. 

In that case they would be as prevalent as we have found visual images to be. This valuable objective evidence, is supported by the following excellent introspective description by one of my students whose thought is chiefly verbal motor: "In Miss Fernald's classification of subjects according to their imagery, I would be placed under 2b, 'Dependence on vocal-motor; absence of auditory imagery; deficiency in visual both verbal and concrete.' I depend entirely upon motor imagery; and I feel certain that if, in some way, this motor imagery could be interfered with, I would be unable to memorize. When I am memorizing I always feel movement in my throat. When I have studied hard for two or three hours my throat feels tired just as if I had talked incessantly during these two or three hours. I do not think that I ever had a visual image of a word until the second half of this year at which time I began to have visual images of a few words when I memorized by visual presentation. "On the other hand, I have visual imagery of concrete objects, but it is not clearly defined, and I have fairly strong color imagery. One of my chief sources of enjoy-

2 ment in poetry is the color imagery which is aroused. My thought is decidedly speech motor. I always feel myself saying anything that I am thinking. There may be a little auditory imagery in my silent speech, because I inflect the words just as if I were really talking. It is said that people who are completely deaf do not modulate their voices but speak in a monotone. This absence of inflection in the deaf is explained by the fact that they do not hear themselves speaking. Therefore, since I inflect my silent speech, there may be slight auditory imagery connected with it. The important part of my dreams is speech. 

I am always talking as fast as I can in dreams, and although there are visual images present, these do not remain so distinctly in my memory as do the words I have spoken in the dream." Almost all investigators of imagery insist that the imaginal type has almost no effect on learning or the pursuit of a profession. My student has a very different opinion relative to at least one type of learning. 

She continues, "A good example of the mistakes made by teachers who do not understand individual differences in ideational types is furnished by my own experience in music. I could read music quickly but I memorized it with great difficulty. My music teacher told me that I must memorize more music but I always became extremely discouraged when I tried to memorize a long selection. I then read, one day, in a musical magazine an account of the way in which the great musician, Leschetitsky, required his pupils to commit music to memory. They were seated away from the piano and instructed to memorize the sheet or sheets of music until, so said the article, they could read "No doubt the speech of Helen Keller is chiefly in mind here. Children who become deaf even after a year or more of speech become dumb very soon afterward.

pages off from memory, having a visual image of every note in mind. I tried this plan when next my music teacher imposed upon me the task of learning an eleven-page piece of music; but, to my sorrow I could make no more headway than before. I could not see a single note before me unless the page were there, and I had to resort to my old method of playing the piece over and over until I remembered it mechanically. Not until last summer, when I became interested in the experiments in memory and the imagery concerned, did I discover that my imagery was purely motor, a fact which explained my inability to memorize music easily. And not until then did I realize that most people experience a type of imagery which I do not know, namely, visual images of words, musical notes, etc." 

Evidently here is an example in which the predominant type of imagery made a certain method of learning impossible. On the other hand, teachers of typewriting prescribe that the machine must not have letters on the keys and the student must learn "touch typewriting" (a plain misnomer for the keys are all alike), by which is meant that typewriting must be a motor performance from the first, and come to be a habit devoid of all imagery. If the teachers are not mistaken, the presence of imagery in this art is a positive disadvantage.

In addition to these practical examples of the effect of imagery I feel sure that certain books are not read because they are devoid of all visual imagery and, therefore, are almost as difficult for a visualizer to read as if they were written in a foreign language. Among psychologists individual differences of imagery have led to misunderstandings of each other's meaning and it can hardly be claimed that such misunderstandings are limited to psychologists alone. Finally, the memorizing of prose or poetry is accom-

plished in less time when lip movements accompany the process, whether the learner is a visualizer or not. This has been tried by a considerable number of students with somewhat remarkable uniformity of results for individual tests and a well established average. 

Besides the above practical differences due to differences of imagery Professor Titchener believes there are others to be found in the attitude of attention, the mode of recitation, and the literary style of a writer. It is certainly desirable to ascertain all the practical differences arising from differences of imagery. 

Visual Imagery. While this verbal-motor type of imagery has been described at length, it is not nearly so common as thought in fairly clear, accurate, stable, visual imagery. Probably the most extreme case of this is the patient, "Mr. X" of Charcot, described by him in 1883. 

Before the onset of his malady he had a remarkable visual memory. "He no sooner thought of persons or things, but features, forms and colors arose with the same clearness, sharpness, and accuracy as if the objects stood before him. 

When he tried to recall a fact or a figure in his voluminous, polyglot correspondence, the letters themselves appeared before him with their entire content, irregularities, erasures and all. At school he recited from a mentally seen page which he read off line by line and letter by letter. In making computations he ran his mental eye down imaginary columns of figures and performed in this way the most varied operations of arithmetic. He could never think of a passage in a play without the entire scene, stage, actors and audience appearing to him... Being a good draughtsman he used to sketch views which pleased him; and his memory always brought back the entire landscape exactly. 

If he thought of a conversation, a saying, an engagement,

the place, the people, the entire scene rose before his mind. 

His auditory memory was always deficient, or at least secondary. He had no taste for music."

Due to his malady this patient lost apparently every vestige of his visual memory, could not recall the appearance of his home, the faces of his wife and children, etc. "Figures which he adds he must now whisper to himself.

He realizes clearly that he must help his memory out with auditory images, which he does with effort. The words and expressions which he recalls seem now to echo in his ear, an altogether novel sensation for him. If he wishes to learn by heart anything, a series of phrases for example, he must read them several times aloud, so as to impress his mental ear," etc. This patient was changed from a visualizer to an "auditory-vocal-motor" type of imaginer, to use the descriptive term employed by Miss Fernald. 3 

Motor or Mimetic Imagery.—An example of this kind of imagery (along with verbal-motor imagery) is given by 

Colvin, "Such a sentence as this comes to mind: 'Infinity broods over all things,' Immediately with the words themselves, arises in consciousness a general motor symbolism. 

The symbolism for the word infinity is found in the tendency to prolong the word in imagination, this prolongation being accompanied by the distinct impression of projecting the word from the mouth, and then following this projected word, as it seems to float out in space, with the body. There is an image of a forcible and continued ejection by the speech-motor apparatus and a bending forward of the entire body, setting itself for flight. There is no visual symbol here as, for example, of extended space or the limitless vault of the heavens on a starlit night. The whole suggestion of unending space comes as an image of 'Colvin, S. S., The Learning Process, pp. 109-110.

motor-adjustment. The word broods brings an entirely different suggestion. Here the ideation centers in a distinct picture (motor, not visual) of outstretched hands, with the body bending forward and downward. All is symbolized by a sensation or image of roundness in the oral cavity, and by an extensive gesture (not actually executed, but merely represented) of an inclusive movement with both hands sweeping around and joining in front of the body. The symbol for things is the mental representation of a direct and sudden gesture with the hand extended and index finger pointing outward and downward."

This gesture-thought of Colvin's consists either of muscle-sense images, memories of how the gesture would feel in limbs and body if it were executed or else it consists of incipient movements which suggest the complete movements. They are tendencies to movement. If they are the former they are sensory and exactly like any other sensory images. In that case we should have no right whatever to speak of motor imagery and it probably is a misnomer. But such thought has been regarded by psychologists as due to tendencies to movement and sometimes as actual movement. In that case thought may go on in motor terms. In a similar fashion tendencies to lip and tongue movements would make up the so-called verbalmotor imagery. This gesture-thinking and bodily-attitudethinking would then consist of what Miss Washburn terms, in another connection, "remnants of remotely ancestral motor attitudes."

A Neural Theory of Motor Thinking.-If Miss Wash burn's term is a correct description of the phenomena, thought is a wider process than the recall and rearrangement of sensory images. Some thought is motor and we

are confronted by the fact that motor centers of the brain give no images, not even images of the words we so slowly learned to utter during our early childhood. They give memories but nothing which can be called images. Can we account for this?

Motor impulses are impulses to acts. Such impulses repeated become habits and habits are unconscious. When an act has been executed a few times, there is a strong tendency to repeat it but this tendency is unconscious in almost all cases. We say, it is true, that we "remember" how to perform a complicated act. But we mean that we have often performed the act successfully and that we feel sure that our motor disposition to perform it can be trusted. It is a motor memory not a sensory, imaginal or ideational one. It seems just as desirable to divide memory into sensory memory and motor memory as to divide original experience into sensation and act. Now if the thought of some persons consists of tendencies to action, incipient efforts, or actual acts, they would describe their thought as verbal-motor, or motor and mimetic exactly as they have done above. They would have no very vivid images and might well report that they have none at all. 

As psychologists they would be pure behaviorists. Because speech is motor, we should find that it is dependent on "memories of the efforts necessary to pronounce words," as aphasia shows it to be. Let us consider memory as consisting of sensory memory, imaginal or ideational memory whose thought stuff is images, and motor memory consisting of incipient or overt efforts toward the acts. 

The physiology of the brain gives evidence for this division. In fact, motor dispositions for the performance of complicated acts, including those of speech and writing, and sensory images are functions of quite different areas

of the cortex. Tilney and Riley (pp. 898-899) say, “In general this extensive area situated between the temporal, postcentral" (sensory area), "and occipital areas may be provisionally regarded as a region of the cortex in which concrete ideas" (images) "are formulated by the combination of visual, auditory, and somesthetic perceptions." 

The area just forward of the motor area is called "the intermediate precentral area." "The intermediate precentral area may be regarded as the portion of the cerebral cortex which controls skilled movements through proper correlation of their motor formulae." (Ibid., p. 845.) By "their motor formulae" the authors mean the patterns of cortical connections made by practice, the connections which underlie the skilled habit, say of speech, writing or other highly skilled performance. The psychic correlatives of these patterns are memories of the efforts necessary to perform the acts. These are motor memories or habits and not images in any exact sense at all. 

Besides the extensive parietal area for images, there is a visuo-psychic area surrounding almost completely the area for visual sensations and an audito-psychic area beside and below the sensory speech area. This audito-psychic area is necessary for the understanding of words. In general, then, injury to the parietal, the visuo-psychic and the audito-psychic areas abolishes images, and injuries just forward of the motor zone abolish habits of speech, writing, etc. If a man thinks of things in terms of the incipient efforts he would make overtly in actual dealing with them he would be a motor thinker, very much as Colvin describes himself. With others, more purely verbalmotor thought predominates. In these cases the brain activity would probably be in the frontal region of the cortex at least in the act of forming the habit. The imaginal

thinker has images and, unless the authors above quoted are in error, such images are due to activity in the parietal, the audito-psychic, and the visuo-psychic areas. The physiology of the brain seems to localize imagery and memories of efforts (which, I think, should not be called images) in quite different parts of the cortex. Having found the distinction between motor and sensory functions indispensable at the outset of our study, should we not keep it as far as brain physiology warrants?

It is also important to educational psychology and to teaching to distinguish between motor and sensory learning. The one leads to habits, the other to knowledge and information. Yet we have descriptions of learning which do not mention the latter and speak of learning only as responses to stimuli with trial and error acts which result in the formation of habits. Thus all learning is habit formation. This is tacitly to deny that human beings can gain information from one another or from reading and study, which they can use in situations of later life. It has the apparent advantage of reducing all learning to what we can observe of animal learning, namely, the animal's acts and final habits. Yet the conditioned reflex experiment (p. 166) indicates something more than this even in animal learning. The implication that we learn only to perform acts is surely misleading. It is contradicted both by experience and by brain physiology. 

Are There Types of Imaginers?—We have seen that there is probably a type of imagery for every sense and this is supplemented by motor memories which, we believe, should not be called images at all. It was long supposed or assumed that different persons think almost exclusively in one or other of these types, so some were called visualizers, others motiles, etc. Now we know that this is not the fact.

The task to be performed has an influence on the imagery. 

My student had a few visual-verbal images when they were forced upon her by a laboratory experiment, but she had never visualized words before. Charcot's patient developed a type of imagery unknown to him before. On the other hand, the sister of my student reports the same kind of verbal-motor imagery (or memory) and the weariness in the throat after prolonged study. There appears to be, therefore, an hereditary predisposition for one type of imagery in the ordinary pursuits of life. This imagery may be used predominantly but not exclusively and most persons use several kinds of imagery with almost equal facility, but no doubt for different intellectual tasks. So 

Woodworth believes "the 'mixed type' is the only real type" though he grants that "nearly every one gets visual images more easily and frequently than those of any other sense." (P. 370.)

Imageless Thought.-Discussion has raged as to whether there can be periods of thought without images. On our view, that motor memory supplements the imaginal variety, the discussion could not arise. It springs from an insistence that consciousness consists only of sensations, images and feelings. Woodworth, the ablest exponent of imageless thought, sums up the conclusion thus, "The best indications are to the effect, first, that vague fleeting images" (we should say, memories), "especially of the kinesthetic" (motor or verbal-motor) "sort are often present without being detected except by very fine introspection, some image being pretty sure to come up every few seconds when we are engaged in silent thought or recall; but, second, that images are not present every second of the time, and that at the instant when a non-sensory fact is

recalled it is apt to be alone." (Woodworth, Psychology, pp. 374-375.)

On our view, psychologists committed to the conviction that images must be present have believed they found vague fleeting traces of them where none existed. They have simply suffered the expectation illusion (p. 364) in their introspective observation. We have chosen instead to use the terms of those who operate on the brain successfully, the terms of brain physiology. 

Relations and Meaning. The mere chance return to consciousness of images and memories would produce a disconnected type of thought which does not occur in normal minds nor probably in diseased ones. Laws of the mind itself determine the order of our ideas. They come and go in obedience to the relations between them, subtle and delicate relations in some minds, gross, side by side relations in others. In the following quotation James* describes the process. "As we take in fact a general view of the wonderful stream of our consciousness, what strikes us first is this different pace of its parts. Like a bird's life it seems to be made of an alternation of flights and perchings. The rhythm of language expresses this, where every thought is expressed in a sentence and every sentence closed by a period. The resting places are usually occupied by sensorial imaginings of some sort, whose peculiarity is that they can be held before the mind for an indefinite time and contemplated without changing; the places of flight are filled with thoughts of relation, static or dynamic, that for the most part obtain between the matters contemplated in the periods of comparative rest." "Let us call the resting-places the 'substantive parts,' and the places of flight the transitive parts of the stream 'James, W., Principles of Psychology, 1899, p. 243.

of thought. It then appears that the main end of our thinking is at all times the attainment of some other substantive part than the one from which we have just been dislodged. And we may say that the main use of the transitive parts is to lead us from one substantive conclusion to another."

Professor James then shows how difficult it is to detect these "transitive states" by introspection. To attempt to stop a transitive state to examine it destroys it completely, while if we try to examine it after conclusion is reached it seems to be swallowed up by the stability and vividness of the latter. The attempt to introspect the "transitive states” is “like seizing a spinning top to catch its motion, or trying to turn up the gas quickly enough to see how the darkness looks. And the challenge to produce these psychoses, which is sure to be thrown by doubting psychologists at any one who contends for their existence is as unfair as Zeno's treatment of the advocates of motion, when, asking them to point out in what place an arrow is when it moves, he argues the falsity of their thesis from their inability to make to so preposterous a question an immediate reply." (Ibid., p. 244.)

Calling the transitive states feelings James says, “We ought to say a feeling of and, and a feeling of if, a feeling of but, and a feeling of by, quite as readily as we say a feeling of blue or a feeling of cold." (Pp. 245-246.) Besides these relations we all recognize equality, likeness, difference, varying together or the reverse, and all sorts of spatial, temporal, quantitative and qualitative relations between the members of pairs of objects and, while some of the relationships seem capable of being imaged others cannot be, further than that we know they are carried by transitive states of consciousness. Many of the words of

our language besides certain verbs, are "transitive" and get their full meaning only when their relations are recognized. Moreover, in a half-mastered foreign language we can often infer correctly the meanings of substantive words from the relations in which they stand. Conversely we must still plod in a language until relations come with the words. When leuchten suggests feuchten, or pioche, mioche, though their meanings are so different, we feel at last that we are "getting a vocabulary." 

Perhaps the best single experiment to show the importance of relations is to learn a foreign language in the academic, bookish way. For a long time words must be translated and the meanings transposed into the English order. Then rather suddenly one finds himself reading in the foreign order and not translating at all because at last he "feels the relations" of the foreign words, the meaning to which they are tending before the meaning is complete. 

Some psychologists have doubted or denied Professor

James' addition of relations to the substantive images, perhaps because transitive states did not lend themselves readily to laboratory demonstration. Yet images embedded in their context by relations are surely the material or contents of the thought of most of us.

In discussing the term "feeling," as used above by 

James, Miss Washburn" writes: "Take the feeling of 'but,' for example: the sense of contradiction between two ideas present when we say, 'I should like to do so, but-here is an objection.' If we trace this back, what can it have been originally but the experience of primitive organisms called upon by simultaneous stimuli to make two incompatible reactions at once, and what can that experience have been "Washburn, M. F., The Term Feeling, Jour. Phil., Psych., and Sci. Methods 

III, pp. 62-63, 1906.

but a certain suspended, baffled motor attitude? Similarly with the feeling of 'if'-'I would like to do so, if a certain condition favors.' The primitive representative of this must have been the experience of an animal called upon to suspend all reaction until a definite added stimulus was given."

These are motor attitudes and some motor thinkers have claimed that such motor attitudes alone give meaning to ideas. While the meaning of many a thing or situation is, "What am I going to do with it, or about it?" other meanings are due to thoughts of relation. We understand a thing or a statement when we discover its relation to something else. After long experimental study the terms used for meaning were "relation," "relationship," and "connection." Dürr says in summary, "Along with our sensations there is a consciousness of time and space, of identity and similarity, etc. They might all be classed under the expression 'consciousness of relationship' and this it is that will prove to be the ultimate analysis of thought." (Moore, T. V., The Process of Abstraction.) 

Thus we see that James' account is confirmed by later careful work. Meaning may, perhaps often, be due to motor attitudes. It is also due to the discovery of relations.

Image, Memory, Idea, Concept.-We have found it best to use the terms image and memory, the latter when the recall seems to be motor and due to a motor portion of the cortex. But images often lose much of their image character. They become schematic, very much as picture-writing lost its picture character and gradually became reduced to symbols. These schematic, modified images are often called ideas and it is a useful term. When an idea becomes more abstract still, as a notion of a class of objects

or of a quality apart from any object in which it is found, it is called a concept and these factors too will be found in our thought.

Retention. When a former perception or sensation reappears in consciousness as an image and is recognized as due to the original experience some explanation of the return of the image must be invented. This can be due only to some effect or trace left in the cortex by the original impression. The period of its retention is the period of its absence. Many theories have been conceived at different times, each one as accurate as the knowledge of brain physiology of those times permitted. For a considerable period it was assumed that the nerves are hollow tubes filled with a fluid (animal spirits) and, that when we come in contact with an object, the fluid is pushed inward and makes literally an "impression" or dent in the substance of the brain. Hence comes our word, impression. Plato likened mental images to doves in a dove cote, whose possessor could reach into it and bring forth any one that he needed. 

From such a conception, no doubt, we have such words as "comprehend," "apprehend" or "grasp" a meaning. This would explain also why we often cannot recall the idea we want.

The modern conception of retention implies, for example, that the visual perception of an object results in the discharge of nervous impulses through a great number of cortical neurons. Thereafter, there is a tendency for the impulses to pass more readily through these neurons again. This tendency is the physiological ground of retention. When impulses again pass along these neurons, the result is a recalled image of the object originally seen. All retention and recall are of this nature. The investigations of Sherrington have shown that the chief resistance

to the passage of nerve impulses is in the synapses, where the branches (collaterals) of one nerve fiber or axon arborize with the dendrites of a second neuron. If impulses have passed repeatedly from one neuron to another, the resistance of that synapse is reduced or its permeability increased. Repeated recall, then, increases the permeability of the synapses. But attention also facilitates recall. So the effort of attention in trying to recall a past thought is probably the effort necessary to reduce the resistance of synapses.

Reproduction or Recall.-The various conditions under which the recall of past experiences takes place must be discussed in connection with memory and association. 

EXERCISES 

1. Mentally spell a long word backwards or recite the alphabet backwards. Were images present in the process? 

2. By what method only can mental images be studied? 

3. In reading a fine description of scenes and events can you supply mental imagery for it equal in vividness to a moving picture? 

4. What type of imagery is most common in your thought? 5. 

Give an account of "imageless thought." 

6. Give further differences between sensations and images. 

7. Is every part of your visual image of all six sides of a room equally clear? If not, which portions are least clear? Can this be changed by attention? 

8. When the word, saxophone, is uttered do you hear the sound or see the instrument with your mind's eye?

CHAPTER XIII IMAGINATION 

Imagination is said to consist of two types, reproductive imagination and creative or inventive imagination. 

When the combinations of creative imagination are more or less lawless or purposeless it is called fancy. 

In reproductive imagination the images of objects, persons and situations recur to consciousness somewhat as they were in perception, i. e., apart from slight decay of parts of the images due to lapse of time and the filling of these slight gaps by invention, the images are true copies of the earlier percepts. In fact, Titchener finds that the imagination images are especially stable, permanent and unchanging. Even if there is some decay of parts of the image it is quite unnoticed for an image may stand for a percept somewhat as a word stands for an object. The image is much more of a literal copy than the word but it need not be a perfect copy. 

Evidently the work of reproductive imagination has been adequately described in the account of imagery and thought. If that account is true the march of images in their mutual relationships constitutes a large part of our ordinary thought.

Creative Imagination.-While one who had never seen red could not imagine such a color and one who had heard no tones could have no images like them, it has been shown that any one familiar with the color red or with a number of tones could in imagination fill gaps in a series of reds or of tones correctly, even though he had had no sensations

corresponding to the filled-in images. So much, no doubt, inventive imagination can accomplish and among the scientists who today are puzzling over the structure of the atom a more refined work of imagination is going on. In the latter case the conceiving is from effects to their only possible causes. While this may at present be called the work of conception, who can doubt that eventually the physicists will exhibit models of the structure of atoms and with so great a wealth of evidence as to carry conviction of their substantial correctness. All this imagining, however, will be by analogy with the behavior of particles, tones and colors already experienced by sense. While we cannot imagine new sense qualities, therefore, we can imagine new analogous attributes and, due to this, we may ascribe a great deal of creative work to imagination. By far the greater part of its work consists, however, in the discovery of novel relations. 

Creative imagination involves, first of all, a ready dissociation or separation of the parts of a complex in order that they may be combined in a new way. Preceding and presiding over the separation, however, there is always an anticipatory notion of the place the part is to fill in the new combination. It is not, therefore, mere dissociation but dissociation for a purpose. It is selection and selection for the building of a new creation. Even the creations of our dreams are not mere congeries of thoughts and parts of thoughts in chance assemblage. Our habits of thought are selective, so while dreams are lawless, they cannot, it seems, entirely escape the thrall of the habits of our waking hours. They may be due to chance oxidation of brain paths but are never quite free from the pull of a more permanent path which represents a purpose and gives them a

IMAGINATION 

421 twist toward a unitary structure. Consequently some dreams are quite consistent constructions. 

The invention of the sewing machine depended entirely on the dissociation of the eye of the needle from its head and its relocation in the point. Yet all the time the idea of the aim to be attained was pulling the inventor's thought toward this method of making the needle push instead of pull the thread. This element of selection is said to distinguish even the most faithful portrait from a photograph in which no human factor abides. 

The more primitive the imagination the grosser the parts which it selects. A lion's body and the face of a woman make the Sphinx and similarly for Pegasus or a mermaid. As knowledge grows the most subtle relationships and elementary parts are selected for recombination as well as the grosser ones. If the claim, often made, that graduates of technical schools invent less than untrained observers is true, it may be because analysis has carried them to the elements of things and consequently the combinations of grosser parts which can be made successfully are quite overlooked. If this explanation be the true one it is a beautiful example of apperception. Perhaps, however, the claim made for the untrained observer is exaggerated.

Whether primitive or refined, imagination is the same process. "It consists of the selection of parts of perceptual experiences and their recombination under the influence of resemblance or analogy, or knowledge of cause and effect." 

In mechanical contrivance imagination seems to have made much recent progress. This is due, however, to increase of knowledge and to ever further reaching analysis. The airplane and the horseless carriage are the result of a

newly developed powerful motor, not to newly developed imagination.

A mere outline of the intellectual work of imagination is thus found to present nothing unusual, though its product is everywhere hailed as magnificent and wonderful. 

True, "the painter, the sculptor, the architect and the inventor must have seen forms in order to construct forms. 

Musician and poet must have experienced much in order to bring their hearers under the spell of their tones and words. Delicacy and sharpness of perception and depth of experience are essential, of course, to productive activity of imagination." Yet if we are to find in the power of imagination something to correspond to the marvelous character of its works something more must be sought than the intellectual skeleton of the process. 

Its investigators show "that the greater and more significant the creations of imagination the less does the conscious will influence its work." By this it is not meant that an artist cannot supply the work of his genius to fill an "order" from a patron, though some have found that irksome indeed. It is also admitted that in all great works of imagination the will plays a part in the execution of the plan. But it is claimed that those states of consciousness out of which is born the plan of a great work of imagination, the moments of conception, cannot be voluntarily produced. The artist may, indeed, influence this process to a certain degree but he does not thereby bring about the power to produce but only favorable conditions under which such power may express itself, and he can never be sure that production will make its appearance at the moment when he wills it. Thus the highest manifestations of the intellect do not spring from conscious volition. 

Instead we speak of the "inspiration" of the genius, a term

IMAGINATION 

423 which strictly means possession and direction of the human spirit by a supernatural power. In speaking of the origin of his Zarathustra, Nietzsche said, "The conception is a revelation in the sense that suddenly with indescribable certainty and fineness something becomes visible and audible, which shakes and upsets one to the very depths of his being. One hears, but does not seek, one takes but does not ask who gives. All this happens as under strong compulsion from without and yet as in a very storm of freedom, of the unconditioned, of power, of Godlikeness." If it be objected that this is the introspection of a madman it may be replied that "genius is to madness near allied,” and we cannot ignore an observation merely because it was not made in a laboratory.

The above seems to be the state of mind and emotion when creative ability is at its best. "What is lacking, then, when in spite of the best will to achieve, creative work is impossible?" The artist replies, "I was not in the mood," and we shall see later that the total emotional state or mood at any time is capable of influencing the course of ideas, and even before they come to consciousness. It seems to become a member of the train of organic events. 

It may thus co-operate to bring about frightful visions in dreams or, in waking life and when coupled with talent, it creates the achievements of art and science. 

Like all emotional conditions this heightened mood is something of a mystery. "It may be ushered in in a purely bodily way as an intensification and heightening of the whole life of feeling. But when this happens the feelings discharge themselves in a heightened activity of imagination. Physiologically it would seem that the waves of excitement corresponding to the heightened feeling overflow wide realms of the cortex and change the place of greatest

potential energy into a region of genuine activity. On the other hand the heightened emotion may be called forth by the stimulating effect of particular imaginative ideas by which the whole course of thought is changed in direction." In other words, our mood often changes our ideas but quite as often our ideas change our mood. 

The emotional state favors the arousal of ideas related to it and puts even the realms of the unconscious under tribute to summon into consciousness material for selection. In this material the ideas appropriate to the mood gain all the interest and attention. Yet in order to be creative imagination rather than fancy the selection must be presided over by a "goal idea" which often takes on the dignity of an ideal, æsthetic, ethical or scientific. Imagination produces ever new ideas to satisfy the ideal, these ideas in turn intensify and prolong the emotional state, which again acts reflexly to increase the activity of the imagination, though the ideal is never quite reached. It is this endless chain of activities, it is thought, which lies at the basis of progress both in the individual and the race. No doubt this is true if we admit that the ideal is' reached continually and overpassed but before this is done a finer, higher, ideal has been conceived as a result of all this inward striving. Thus progress follows a will-o'-thewisp forever but a glance backward shows it to have been a true guide.

Before completing our account we must admit a close connection between bodily conditions and activity of imagination. No doubt the explanation of this connection will be a work of future physiology and psychology, but we cannot deny its existence.

The influence of puberty on imagination in both sexes is well known. Puberty is a time of daydreams, of ro-

IMAGINATION 

425 mance and of active though perhaps chimerical fancy. We know that the change of voice and the growth of the beard in a boy are due to a hormone not present before the onset of puberty. A collateral effect of its working might be a new stimulus to the imagination, and to other mental powers. 

Second, narcotic drugs such as hashish and opium produce the most vivid and original visions.

Third, a great deal of creative work has been done by minds, either at the time of their productiveness or soon afterwards, attacked by mental disease or a prey to narcotic drugs. Comte, Poe and Nietzsche may be mentioned as patent examples. One physician believed he could trace the progress of de Maupassant's psychosis in his writings. 

And Dr. Farrar in discussing the hopes of the eugenist to prevent mental aberration by suitable marriages says: "But he can afford to pause now and then and season his ambition with the reflection that had the generations gone produced only children of assured mental health and balance the names of Socrates, Petrarch, Dostoiewsky, Schumann, Coleridge, Napoleon, Cowper, Newton, Tasso, Ruskin, Southey, Mohammed, Keats, de Musset, Byron, George 

Sand, Manzoni, Manzoni, Burns, Swift, Flaubert, Beethoven, Luther, Carlyle, Comte, DeQuincey, Fechner, Poe, Saint- 

Pierre, Joan of Arc, Cromwell, James Thompson, Savonarola, Lamb, de Maupassant, Cellini, Baudelaire, Shelley, Schopenhauer, Goethe, would be missing from the world's hall of fame."

No doubt the list is too long in the sense that in some cases the achievement was quite independent of the psychopathic condition, yet there is evidence enough to show that there is some obscure relationship between the bodily 1913. 

White & Jelliffe, Modern Treatment of Nervous Diseases, Vol. 1, p. 587,

and the mental facts. This should be the subject of investigation. It should be unnecessary to remark that, however long the list may be, it is a list of exceptions for whose compilation all history has been examined with care. In general, mental aberration is ruination and the wrecks have left no names to be recorded. Only the unwisest youth in Christendom could believe that mental idiosyncrasy is an augury of success or fame. For ordinary mortals inspiration is the result of prolonged, willed attention.

At What Age Does Creative Ability Appear?—While all men possess creative imagination to some extent, famous creative ability is, as we say, a gift, originated by chance variation, the sport of nature, and often transmitted by heredity. Perhaps nothing shows this native, hereditary character of the gift better than the age at which fame-giving work has been done. Thanks to Ribot we can give the following examples of the precocity of genius:

In Music, Mozart composed at the age of three; Mendelssohn at five; Hayden at four; Handel at twelve; Schubert at eleven; Cherubini at thirteen. Beethoven and

Wagner developed later and the average age of creation in music is regarded as twelve or thirteen. In the plastic arts, the average age is fourteen. Giotto and Van Dyck began creative work at ten, Raphael, Greuze, and Guerchin at eight, Michaelangelo at thirteen, Dürer at fifteen, while Rubens and Jordaens were also precocious.

In poetry, Schiller and Byron began to write at sixteen, while the abstract imagination required in science and mathematics rarely develops before twenty, though 

Comte, Gauss, Leibniz, Pascal and Newton gave evidence of it before that age.2 "For many further examples see "Youthful Achievements of Great Scientists," by George. P. Meade, The Scientific Monthly, November, 1925.

IMAGINATION 

427 Imagination in Myths. The age of myths has been called the golden age of the imagination. This is doubtless true and imagination seems to be the highest power exercised by primitive man, for the faculties of conception, judgment, and reason, which are regarded as the highest, depend for their exercise upon analysis and upon knowledge, especially upon knowledge of some of the laws of nature. 

The primitive mind thinks by analogy and the chief analogy of myths consists in ascribing human traits and feelings to all sorts of objects, animate and inanimate. 

The savage finds the human in everything. Inanimate objects have the power and desire to do him good or ill. "The Indian traversing the Montana never feels himself alone. Legions of beings accompany him. All of the nature to whom he owes his soul speaks to him through the voice of the wind, in the roaring of the waterfall. The insect like the bird-everything even to the bending twig wet with dew-for him has language, distinct personality. 

The forest is alive in its depths, has caprices, periods of anger; it avoids the thicket under the tread of the huntsman, or again presses him more closely, drags him into infected swamps, into closed bogs, where miserable goblins exhaust all their witchcraft upon him, drink his blood by attaching their lips to the wounds made by briers. The 

Indian knows all that; he knows these dread genii by name." (Monnier, Des Andes au Para, p. 300, quoted by 

Ribot.) Given this animistic conception of human dangers and human ills and misfortunes it gives rise to a large part of mythology, to exorcism, propitiation and magic. 

If the tribe advances toward civilization these analogies become unreal. They are no longer believed but they persist now as personifications, similes, and metaphors. The primitive man employs a figurative language, and finally

invention occurs for its own sake and fiction and romance result. Consequently it is claimed that "literature is a decadent and rationalized mythology." The next stage is, no doubt, the hero worship of human beings, of great leaders, and evidently that period too is decadent among the most intelligent peoples of today.

Given this animistic and personifying account of the world how could analysis ever arise? How could science take the place of magic? I think that accident gave the new direction to human thought. A tree fallen across the stream suggests an artificial bridge. A campfire kindled on rich ore melts out some of the useful metal. 

The effect of fire suggests the use of fire, etc. Such accidents must have happened many times on many different parts of the earth, and they must have turned the minds of men from personal to impersonal explanation, toward analysis and science.

With children of civilized people analogy is much abridged. Dolls and hobbyhorses exist but their reality diminishes. The Santa Claus myth is taken lightly by most children. Due to the influence of environment the modern child thinks rather by similarity than analogy. 

One called the cork of a bottle a "door," another called a small coin a "baby dollar," and still a third called a folding pocket corkscrew "bad scissors." Even the second example involved no personification.

Ribot in Summary.-The following outline from Ribot conforms to the account of imagination in its higher forms, which I have given, and furnishes an excellent summary:

"The idea excites attention and takes a fixed character. 

The period of brooding begins. For Newton it lasted seventeen years, and at the time of definitely establishing his discovery by calculation he was so overcome with emotion that he had to assign to another the task of completing it. The mathematician, Hamilton, tells us that his method of quaternions burst upon him one day, completely finished, while he was near a bridge in Dublin. 'In that moment I had the result of fifteen years' labor.' With that the work is virtually or really ended."
