CHAPTER XIV  

Up to this point I have described the recurrence of past ideas, thoughts and images of various sorts and some of the relations between them. But the mere recurrence of a former thought or the thought of a former object is not commonly termed memory. As Dürr remarks, one does not say he remembers the appearance of ancient

Rome though, if he were a historian, he might have built up a pretty definite image of it from his study and investigation. Imagery may have reference to past time and yet not constitute a memory. Instead, it might be called a part of our knowledge, as I have already suggested, namely that part of it which no longer has a personal reference and when recalled does not return as consciously familiar. It seems to be habitual and impersonal rather than familiar, or if it still be popularly called familiar, its familiarity is below the threshold of consciousness, due no doubt to too frequent repetition. Our purpose thus far has been to describe this neutral, impersonal, habitual thought but not to deny that within it there often arise ideas which, as we say, "strike us as familiar, or are strikingly familiar." Probably these phrases are well suited to emphasize the contrast between the neutral character of habitual thought and that which emerges in consciousness with reminiscent force. Not reference to the past in general, therefore, but the presence or absence of familiarity with the idea is to distinguish the remembered idea from

that of ordinary habitual thinking, and from the novel combinations of creative endeavor. 

Titchener (T. B., p. 413) states the difference concisely when he says, "An idea comes to us as remembered only if it comes to us as consciously familiar." "An idea is a memory if it is accompanied by the feeling of familiarity; and an idea is specifically remembered if it is placed and dated by the organic reaction and by associated ideas." In the concise terms employed by Katzaroff (Arch. de Psych., XI, 41, 1911), this means that an idea is a memory if accompanied by immediate recognition and is specifically remembered if it is accompanied also by mediate recognition. We shall learn in a moment what these terms mean. Meanwhile it seems to me that at least one word of popular language has kept the necessary distinction. Memory involves reminiscence, or it is reminiscence more or less complete.

While recognition is usually described as the essential feature of memory it should not be forgotten that it occurs also in perception (perhaps even more commonly than in thought) and is the same process in both. In the former case we recognize an idea, in the latter a perceptible object. 

However, it was pointed out that imagery and meaning, knowledge about the object presented is the characteristic feature of perception. 

Recognition. On page 358 we saw that past impressions may be so thoroughly effaced that no images of their objects can recur unless the objects themselves are again present to our senses, i. e., a second perception must occur, but when it occurs it is not a new perception. No feeling of novelty attaches to it but instead the consciousness that we have had the experience before. This is generally described as the feeling of familiarity, le sentiment de déjà

vu, l'impression de déjà veçu, de déjà eprouvé, and is regarded as an emotional or affective state rather than an intellectual one. However that may be, our ability to recognize past experiences persists long after our ability to recall them has departed, or recognition seems to be the most stubbornly persistent element of memory. 

This mere arousal of the feeling of familiarity with the object or thought without the ability to name it, tell when we last had it in mind, or further identify it, has been called "immediate" or primary recognition. It is an interesting state of consciousness and for that reason it may have been emphasized too much, for it is rarer and less vivid than the feeling of strangeness or unfamiliarity in the presence of a novel object.

If we wish to get the feeling of familiarity in a somewhat pure state it is best to employ the sense of smell. 

When a number of small vials containing common liquids like coffee, vanilla, kerosene, alcohol, etc., are passed around among a group of persons, some will be unable to name the substance but they will be perfectly certain that they have smelled it before and there will be a haunting desire to name it and complete the recognition. A similar experience occurs when a certain few strains of music are similar or identical with a passage of some piece we have heard much earlier. In this case we are likely, sooner or later, to be able to hum the original tune. The fragment has enabled us to recall its early associates. 

When the identification has become more complete in this fashion recognition is mediate or secondary and it is now much more of an intellectual performance. We can say that the thought or object is identical with a former experience, or is similar to it and we can name the object or describe the similarity. This is due to our being able

to summon the associates of the original experience and to identify certain elements within it. Mediate recognition (as well as the immediate type) may be due, therefore, either to identity of the present object or thought with a past one, or to similarity between the two. When a botanist identifies a new plant as belonging to a certain species he does so by recognition of its similarities with the known plants of that species. Thus secondary recognition is often a matter of expert knowledge; recognition of an object by knowing the features of the class to which it belongs. 

Returning once more to the immediate feeling of familiarity which is aroused by objects and thoughts no longer novel, we must admit that the feeling occurs in different degrees of intensity. When the rather dim feeling overcomes a certain inward tension and mounts to full and clear recognition it becomes very strong. But with every repetition of the impression or thought the feeling becomes weaker until it is almost unnoticeable. To prove that it is present, however, we have only to observe how differently we are affected by persons and objects which are familiar and on the other hand by those which are strange. 

Two interesting physiological theories have been proposed to account for the feelings of familiarity and strangeness. The latter, says Meumann, is a sensation of being brought to a standstill and startled (des Stockens und des Stutzens) which has something of the character of a weak affective state, perhaps of a very weak fright. 

This is accompanied by motor inhibition, innervation of antagonistic muscles; head and body are stiff and upright; there is stoppage or hesitation of speech. The course of ideas is stopped or broken, there is a momentary consciousness of a void or emptiness. The novel object arouses no associates.

In the presence of the familiar none of these "symptoms" occurs; there is an easier flow of psychic processes; speech is ready instead of hesitant; the familiar object is quickly apprehended; there is no inhibition to overcome; relaxation rather than tension of muscles is present, and the affective state is one of mild pleasure. 

Titchener (T. B., p. 408) seems to hold a similar opinion: "Recognition, as such, seems to be wholly a matter of the feeling. What then is this feeling? In experiments upon recognition it is variously reported as a glow of warmth, a sense of ownership, a feeling of intimacy, a feeling of ease, a comfortable feeling. It is a feeling in the narrower sense, pleasurable in its affective quality, diffusively organic in its sensory character. That is all that analysis can tell us about it. If we allow ourselves to speculate, we may go further, and find a genetic sanction for its peculiar warmth and diffusion; we may suppose that it is a weakened survival of the emotion of relief, of fear unfulfilled. To an animal so defenseless as was primitive man, the strange must always have been cause for anxiety; 'fear' is, by its etymology, the emotion of the 'farer,' of the traveller away from home. The bodily attitude which expresses recognition is, on this view, still the attitude of relief from tension, of ease and confidence." 

By Meumann's account non-recognition in the presence of a strange experience is, or is accompanied, by a stopping or hesitation in the flow of psychic processes and, by both accounts, the affective state is one of tension, expectation, anxiety, or even fear of perhaps a gentle type. Recognition involves the smooth flow of mental processes, relief from tension, dread, or fear.

The reader should note that the description of even a mild feeling like that of familiarity or surprise is chiefly a

description of the bodily accompaniments or "symptoms" of the emotion.

Two writers, James and Claparéde, insist that our own past thoughts return to us clothed with a feeling of "warmth and intimacy" which new thoughts do not have. 

Familiar thoughts have our "brand" upon them. We mark our thoughts much as a newly painted surface would mark every one who touched it, etc. This is no doubt an observed fact. They explain the fact, however, by saying that our thoughts and perceptions cause widespread bodily adjustments in the continuous, steady sensations coming from our bodies, and which constitute the sense of our "self" or personality.

Thoughts and experiences which change at all this feeling tone of the body are thereafter marked by it as our own past thoughts and when they recur they bring "relief from tension," the feeling of familiarity and recognition, whereas on their first occurrence their strangeness caused us "to bristle up."

This theory, if true, shows how much our feelings, mood, temperament and disposition are dependent upon the condition of the body and the recent physiological work of Professor Cannon serves to give support to that opinion.

In summary, we may say that immediate recognition is an affair of feeling or affection only but mediate recognition is an affair of intelligence and involves associates and the identification of features and marks of the present object whereby it may even be classified. So experts must spend long years in education before they can diagnose a disease from its symptoms, or classify a plant or a mineral by its appearance. The surgeon who would operate from a

vague feeling of familiarity with a group of symptoms would not long be trusted. We cannot, therefore, agree that recognition seems to be wholly a matter of feeling, and recent researches point to the existence of both immediate and mediate recognition. 

False Recognition.-There may be false recognition of both the immediate and mediate types. Most people will testify that they often experience a strange feeling of having been before in exactly the present situation. They were speaking just these words to just these persons, etc. 

Or, with some there is a feeling that months before they had had in mind just the circumstances in which they now find themselves. This realization in fact of past imagery seems quite ominous and uncanny. The feeling almost never lasts long, is more frequent with young than with older people, and, if a stern attempt is made to examine it, it will usually be found that the past situation was so similar to the present one that the feeling of familiarity was aroused and clung to the present situation or this situation fulfills our past prophetic thought. The experience has been described as a feeling of having lived in another existence. In David Copperfield, Dickens mentions it as "a feeling that comes over us occasionally, of what we are saying and doing having been said and done before, in a remote time, of our having been surrounded dim ages ago, by the same faces, objects and circumstances." In normal psychology it has been named paramnesia, or perversion of memory, but that term should be kept for other uses. It is false recognition of the immediate type. 

Heymans has found that this experience is most frequent in those persons of strong and variable emotions who are inclined to revery and irregularity in work, and who have small talent for mathematical studies. It is least fre-

quent in those of mild and uniform emotions, who are not inclined to revery but to steady mental activity and who have small talent for linguistic studies. The two types are fairly well marked. 

False recognition of the mediate or intellectual type is far more important in practical life. Let us mention two examples. In one, several witnesses of a murderous affray between two Mexicans had testified that the guilty aggressor had worn a red necktie and they now pointed him out in the court-room by that same distinguishing mark. At the close of the testimony the defendant's attorney asked the man so identified to sign his name and it was found that he was not named in the indictment. Thus the attorney cleared his client. It was learned later that the guilty man had worn a red tie during the assault and the lawyer had caused the aggressor's cousin, who resembled him, to wear this tie in the court-room. The trick was perfectly successful in bringing about the desired false recognition.

Again, one of my students, when applying for a visitor's license for his motor car, found a well-dressed, excited woman assuring the judge in a most dramatic manner that she could identify the man who had robbed her home. The judge asked her to step into the adjoining room where, he said, an officer would bring before her the various prisoners. He then asked the student whether he would object to being used as a prisoner for this purpose. No objection being offered, he and six others, each in turn donning a brown chauffeur's coat, cap and gloves, were separately led before the woman by a stalwart police officer and six of the seven men were identified as the robber. These cases of false recognition are typical of thousands of others, and along with errors of memory and perception, they invalidate a great deal of human testimony.

Memory Image Versus Imagination Image.—We have learned that the prime difference between memory and imagination lies in the fact that recognition is present in memory and absent from imagination. Since the memory image returns with the vividness of familiarity it was long supposed to be a stable, definite, unchanging image, while the image of imagination was thought to be especially changeable and shifting. Titchener (T. B., pp. 416 ff.), however, finds just the reverse to be the fact. As a general rule memory images are unstable, imagination images very stable. Memory images are described as "filmy and vaporous, have almost no difference of light and shade, are often colorless and lack relief. They also develop slowly and last but a short time. In remembering an object by its class name the image may disappear entirely and only the name and 'absolute impression' remain.' 99 Imagination images are implied to be just the reverse of all this, to develop more rapidly, run a different temporal course, be more substantial, accurate and detailed; and finally we are more likely to read ourselves and our feelings into the imagination image than into the memory image. Even different neural functioning is assumed for the two types, cortical or peripheral or both. 

This difference is accounted for by the presence of recognition in memory. "The image is, after all, made into a memory image by the feeling of familiarity." (T. B., p. 

419.) (Titchener seems not to credit the existence of mediate recognition which Katzaroff describes so well.)

Hence the memory image may represent its object as a symbol represents an object, a process, or an operation. It need only mean that object or process. It need not be a copy, but the imagination image, lacking this element of familiarity must be a fairly literal copy. This, then, is the

difference between the typical images of memory and imagination, but intermediate forms occur which contain the elements of both.

We may mention this distinction of Professor Titchener's and no doubt it constitutes a subordinate or subsidiary difference between memory and imagination. Since artists and sculptors must have models, however, to which they refer at every moment we must not place too much reliance on the stability and definiteness of even the typical imagination image. There is a great deal of fading or decay of the image and its filling in with new construction. 

Definition. After our account of recognition we have no need to revise Professor James' definition of memory. "Memory is the knowledge of an event or fact, of which meantime we have not been thinking with the additional consciousness that we have thought or experienced it before." This additional consciousness may be only a feeling, as in immediate recognition, or it may be a more complete and intellectual identification of the present knowledge with the past, as in mediate recognition.

This definition states the primary or primitive function of memory which, as some one has said, is to cause the psychic yesterday to become today. We must admit, however, that in popular usage and in experimental pedagogy the term, memory, is used loosely for the ability to learn and sometimes for the correlative or result of learning.

Thus memory becomes a name for the ability to recall earlier experiences without a repetition of their outer causes.

The three phases or partial phases of memory are (1) the reception of the impression, (2) an unconscious interval of retention or period of latency, and (3) the appear-

ance of the after effect, reproduction or recall, and its recognition.

Retention. The reception of impressions from without is, of course, a matter of sensation and perception. Moreover, retention as having its basis in the ability of the brain to receive and retain impressions has already been discussed in the account of images and their relations. 

Doubtless some day physiology may tell us by what delicate process brain cells change their structure or connections so as to keep for years an impression of something we have seen or heard. That day, however, is surely far off.

Chemistry and physics must both help physiology with knowledge they have yet to acquire before this can be done. Meanwhile, we can speak only of the permanent "set" of cortical cells, due to a first impression, or we talk of a lowered resistance to the passage of the nervous impulse across the synapses, due to its earlier discharge along the same path, or of a disposition to recall, etc. This ground or basis of retention we would gladly know much more about. Our duty at present is, however, to mention certain types of retentiveness and certain practical considerations concerning retention.

Let us ask first, what is the relation of retention to the impression? Based on individual experience there was long a belief that the permanency of retention depends on the "depth" of the impression. But it was believed that the impression is somehow deepened by repetitions, so that permanency of retention seemed to be roughly proportional to the number of repetitions, or to the time and effort given to study. Meumann has abundantly proved this belief to be true and James had earlier incorporated it into his main law of association. Moreover, since the brain is a material thing and retention somehow a physi-

cal process it is difficult to see how it could escape the influence of physical law. It was long ago pointed out, I think by Hering, that matter, having once yielded to a force, yields in the same way much more easily a second time. Our coat sleeve falls into the same set of folds no matter how thoroughly we press them out, scar tissue is more easily abraded a second time, a dislocated limb easily falls a second time out of its socket, etc., with innumerable examples. James makes this property of matter the fundamental ground of habit which binds man more firmly than fate and easily overcomes the struggles of his boasted, "unconquerable soul." If this be the fact, and I think no one has ever doubted it in the face of the evidence, we should expect that frequent repetition would mean prolonged retention, and that few or hasty repetitions would mean but brief retention, and just this has been proved by experiments.

Since nonsense syllables form fewer associations than meaningful material we believe we get a better knowledge of impression and retention by using such material in experiments in memorizing. They are better learned if presented rather slowly and if a subjective rhythm is employed. After the first few readings there is fairly steady improvement, as if each reading deepened the impression, but the first ones met some internal resistance which appeared to require time to overcome. But the interval between repetitions is also important. There is what has been called "settling in memory." "It is better to distribute 24 readings in pairs to 12 days than to take them in fours on 6 days; and it is, again, better to do this than to take them in eights on 3 days." That is, a repetition strengthens an impression or an association made hours before more than one just recently made. Hence the school

boy who partly fixes his lesson in the evening and reviews it the following morning is following a sound method of learning, for fixing both the static and the associative impressions. Thus repetitions not only deepen impressions but there is a certain interval between repetitions which fixes the impression most firmly with a smaller number of repetitions. This must be due to the nature of the brain substance.

In the light of this evidence that, as elsewhere in the material world, the amount of work accomplished is dependent on the time and the effort expended, it is curious that the fact is thoroughly negatived in the minds of most students by the emphatic statement in the text-books of a piece of statistical psychology. Thorndike (1910, pp. 

183 and 184) found that the individuals who learn words more quickly than the average also remember more of them after the lapse of forty days. Hence it is disproved that the quick learner is the poor rememberer. Meumann obtained results just the reverse of Thorndike's and much work on the motor memory of mammals and birds confirms Meumann. We may, therefore, hold judgment in reserve when science is thus bounded by state lines. Nevertheless, it has become almost customary in American textbooks to insist that the quick learner retains as well, if not much better, than the slow learner. From this it is deduced that cramming is an excellent mode of study and almost implied that thoroughness in learning and possibly in other pursuits is a serious defect. In the case of Lord 

Macaulay it is said that one reading sufficed to fix whole pages in his memory. Here again is quick learning and long retention. But why should we draw conclusions from Macaulay's memory and the statistics of quick learners and say that quick learning is best retained when each

of us knows that for his own mind this is not the case? 

The practical question to ask is, "Given the type of mind I possess what acquisitions are best retained, those I have repeated many times and thought over much, or those I have crammed hastily for an examination?" Plainly the former acquisitions stick best. Laboratory work in general means that an enormous amount of time is to be given to fixing impressions and that the whole of the reflex arc shall be impressed by our manipulation of the apparatus. 

The evidence that impressions are deepened by repetitions, by thinking them over, by forming ever new associate impressions, by doing repeatedly the thing which we wish to learn to do well is perfectly clear in psychology. 

Of course there is nothing in all this to deny that if one wishes to enter a pursuit in which he lives by his wits instead of by his stock of information such pursuits are open to him, and there is a direct antagonism between living by one's wits and by one's knowledge. If a man must be sure his reply is true it will not be ready on the instant and hence not instantly effective. In this day of demand for experts, however, the "chances of survival" seem far greater for the mind possessed of expert knowledge by prolonged and systematic study, than for one deficient in knowledge but adept in cramming in moments of extreme need. In any event there is little reason to use the results of statistical psychology to contradict the results of all individual learning, especially when all the records are not in full agreement.

Native Retentiveness. What the statistical records and, indeed, the careful comparison of individual memories do bring to light is that memory involves two factors, (1) impressibility and (2) retentiveness and that individuals differ in both. Some memories are easily impressed and

yet tenacious to retain the impressions, while others forget readily even after painstaking learning. Probably even a greater number are fairly slow to be impressed but once an impression is made it is well retained. This at any rate is the condition in children. They require for learning more repetitions than adults, but, as we know, many of the impressions made in childhood are never effaced. 

Meumann found that youths of 18-20 years could immediately reproduce one and a half times as many syllables or words as children of 8-10 years. No doubt a part of this difference must, however, be credited to a difference in attention. The relative impressibility of childhood, middle, and old age is indicated by the fact that adults reproduced on the average 9 figures after hearing them once, a thirteen-year-old boy 6, a woman of eighty-eight years only 4. 

Not a ready impressibility but tenacious retentiveness characterizes the mind of the child. The memory of adults is not so tenacious but it is readily impressed, so that learning is rapid if not so permanent as in childhood. 

In extreme old age the threshold of impressibility rises once more. The aged person does not recall recent events and finally he may recite the same story he has told you a few minutes before and yet be quite unaware that he is repeating. In a woman of 89 years Elsenhans observed three repetitions of the same anecdote with pauses of only one to three minutes between. She was quite unconscious of the recital just past. There was one change of detail and some details added with successive repetitions. Elsen- 'hans thinks that once the old cortical set is re-aroused it leads to a sort of perseveration. This is important since perseveration occurs in fatigue and old age is regarded as a sort of permanent fatigue. 

In old age, therefore, the memory for recent events,

unless they are of especial interest, is very weak indeed, while events long past, especially if they are concerned with the welfare of the individual or his former companions, are retained with remarkable tenacity. Space memory seems especially to suffer in old age. The aged woman, mentioned above, who could recite but four of the numbers once read to her, had to learn the door of a particular room from among six which opened on the same hall. This she was able to do only after about 64 repetitions, and even afterward she made many mistakes. One experience would have fixed the impression for a normal adult. 

Both impressibility and retentiveness are diminished in hours of fatigue and are at their best when our minds and bodies are refreshed. Immediate memory, mentioned on p. 453, seems to be an affair chiefly of ready impressibility, permanent memory of native retentiveness. 

Professor James, noting how much retentiveness is influenced by age and fatigue, in short by the physiological condition of the brain, raised the question whether an individual's retentiveness can be improved by practice. On the basis of experiments with very ambiguous results and which were influenced by the factor of fatigue James decided that each individual's native retentiveness is unchangeable and the apparent improvement of memory by training is due chiefly to better methods of memorizing.

This conclusion seems to contradict ordinary experience and it also contradicts most of the recent experiments on the training of memory. Since I cannot rehearse the results of the wide range of experiments designed to answer the question, let me give dogmatically the conclusion to which, I think, all the more careful experiments point. 

One's native retentiveness may be unchangeable, perhaps, but only in the sense that one's touch sensitivity is

unchangeable. If one becomes blind his ability to make discriminations by the sense of touch increases many fold. 

This increase is one of the marvels of psychology. Yet the increase is due to attention and training. It is probably due to the development of the cortical centers alone. No one imagines that the touch points or nerve endings in the fingertips are increased beyond their original number. In this sense only has the blind man not increased his native sensitivity. His native equipment was inherited at birth but it would never have been developed to full capacity except under stress of his blindness. The rigorous training put him in possession of his full power. Without blindness he would have had no need of his marvelous touch discrimination.

The case of native retentiveness seems to me exactly like that of touch. Born with a certain type of cortex there is no doubt a limit beyond which we cannot go in retention. But none of us develops that power to anywhere near its full capacity because our needs do not force such development upon us. We do develop memory until it meets practically all the demands made upon it. The famous "lightning calculator" Rückle, could, when first tested, recite twenty-five figures which were read to him as five place numbers. After four years of almost continuous practice in such work he could recite sixty figures. In his earlier tests he could learn a square of twenty-five figures shown to him in fifteen to twenty-four seconds. In his later tests, after years of practice, he could learn such a square in twelve to fourteen seconds. In short, it may be stated roughly that by four years of rigorous practice Rückle doubled the power of his memory for numbers. He had a phenomenal number memory to begin with but it is probable that a man of average retentiveness could double the

number of data which he could learn and recite in a given time exactly as Rückle did. Plainly retentiveness can then be developed to almost any desired degree. The fact that there is probably a physiological limit in each of us beyond which we could not go is meaningless for the practical problems of life.

There is also evidence of the opposite kind that the impressibility and retentiveness of the brain can be increased by exercise. The laborer who does not tax his memory may have a first rate mind but soon he is limited to a small stock of images and memories which he cannot later in- The lack of exercise causes a natively good memory to decay. Apparently exercise or training is necessary to growth in retentiveness much as exercise is necessary to the development of a muscle. crease. 

Indirect Effect of Training.-While no one has denied that if one practises remembering names, numbers, prices, or prose, or poetry his ability to remember that particular class of data would improve greatly, whether by an improvement of his method of learning or otherwise, it has been denied that training with one of these types of subject-matter would have any influence on memory of the other types. Recently, however, it has been shown that practice in memorizing poetry improved the ability to learn prose. Memorizing series of letters led to an improvement in logical or substance memory, though the letters were but meaningless data, and so we might go on. The extremely long and severe training in number-memory to which Rückle subjected himself seemed finally to lead him to make a poorer record when memorizing color names, consonants and nonsense syllables. Thus there was a negative transfer of the effect of arduous training. Ordinary training in one type of subject-matter, seems to improve

the ability to remember other types. Since this has been proved now by an adequate number of careful experiments it is hardly correct to say that we have as many special memories as there are data to be remembered and that the exercise of one of these special memories has no influence on the rest. As soon as psychologists learned to make their experiments on groups of subjects so selected that the memory ability of both groups was equal as determined by a preliminary test, transfer of the effects of learning or training was consistently found. This is not in agreement with the opinion that there is a multitude of independent memory functions each of which must be trained specifically if it is to be exercised at all. There is some spread of the effect of practice, some indirect effect of training. Just as the success of intelligence tests indicates that there is some general ability which we may call intelligence, so the results of experiments on memory, such as the experiments of Winch, tend to show that there is a somewhat general ability of memory rather than a host of independent functions each of which must be practised separately. Of course, practice on one type of subject-matter results in the greatest improvement in learning that type of data but there is also improvement for related types. 

This improvement in mental processes related to the one practised is called "transfer of training” and its discussion belongs chiefly to educational psychology. A theory of transfer is held, however, which, if proved, would constitute a general law of the mind. This is the theory of identical elements and briefly stated it is to the effect that practice or training in the exercise of one mental process will improve another just so far as the two are identical or have identical elements. Immediately this is stated, we need examples of identical elements. The identical

element was at first defined as an "idea" common to both the practice series and the test series or the identical element consisted of sensations, images, and movements, which are alike in both series, or later by identical elements were meant "mental processes which have the same cell action in the brain as their physical correlates." Thus stated the theory of identical elements could hardly fail to be true but we need to know what brain processes are partly identical and possibly at this point introspective psychology gives the only hint. When the words, Sir Walter Raleigh, suggest the name, Sir Walter Scott, as they may to those who have noticed the similarity between the two names, is it not because the brain processes are partly identical as symbolized thus: 

Sir Walter

Raleigh 

Scott 

To prove or disprove this will require future investigation for neurology has as yet few methods which can be applied to the study of associations or connections above those of the peripheral nerves.

Instead of such examples, the standard illustration of identical elements has been the partial identity of processes in addition and multiplication. The theory assumes that improvement due to practise in addition will improve multiplication so far as there is addition in multiplication, and improvement due to practise in subtraction will transfer to division by a similar amount. This claim is definite and can be tested by experiment. As usual, the experiment results in modification of the theory rather than in complete verification of it.

At first eight students were divided into two groups of approximately equal ability by means of preliminary tests,

their scores on an intelligence test, and their scholastic records. The first group of four practised addition for five periods of forty minutes each on successive days, the second group practised subtraction. Both groups were then tested on addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. The experiment was then repeated with nine students in each group with results unchanged. It will be seen that the group practised in addition made no gain but a loss in the test in multiplication. The group practised in subtraction improved very much in both accuracy and speed in addition, but they made no gain in accuracy in division. The writer shared in one of the experiments as a subject. It seems plain that having added 18+8=26 repeatedly and then changed to subtrac-

tion, that the difference 26-8-18 is instantly known.

Since combinations made familiar by the practice in addition recur very frequently, we seem to have a reason for the improvement in subtraction due to practice in addition and conversely. The similarity or partial identity between addition and subtraction is subjective identity and it completely overcomes the objective identity between addition and multiplication, on the one hand, and that between subtraction and division on the other.

We seem to gain something of value for general psychology from this experiment. We cannot look simply at the objective world, our environment, and say the mind is a mirror of that; we need only to look at the world about us to discover the laws of mind. Nor can we observe human behavior and say it is produced only by the objective stimuli; there is no mind or consciousness co-operating or, if there is, it is without influence. Nor can we look at ani mal learning and say that human learning is exactly the same, except that it is speeded up considerably. These assumptions are not true. So-called objective psychology is by far the easiest to write and to "invent" and it looks plausible at first glance. But after discrimination and experiment it is evidently far more plausible than true. 

The mind remains a center of initiative and activity and the laws of that activity must be discovered and understood. They cannot be subsumed under a general belief that the mind is a mirror of the environment and human behavior nothing but reactions determined alone by the same environment. This belief itself is based on the mind's tendency to detect and respond to similarities and, due to that very tendency, human beings transform the environment, perhaps more than they are influenced by it in the direct mirroring and responding way. The environment

is often no more than the very raw material of stimulation and discrimination, which challenge us to make profound changes in external things and affairs.

Types of Memory Process.-Two important and different kinds of memory are (1) immediate memory and (2) permanent or enduring memory. Immediate memory is due to a single perception of the impressions. There is only a brief interval between perception and recital, so that the impressions are not replaced by others in consciousness. 

The chief condition of immediate memory is intense and uniform concentration of attention upon what is to be recalled. These two types of memory are different hereditary gifts. There are persons with good enduring memory and less ability for immediate memory and the reverse. This is what we should expect, since immediate memory depends on impressibility, permanent memory on retentiveness, and we have found these to be partially independent brain conditions. Permanent or enduring memory needs little description, since it is known to mean the fixing of impressions by repeated acts of attention and by forming associations between them, so that they can be recalled at a much later time. (3) Mechanical memory includes the retention of numbers, words, etc., in a desultory way and with little associative connection between them, somewhat as a phonograph record has impressions recorded upon it mechanically. Many almost imbecile minds have remarkable mechanical memory for numbers and simple music, while nor mal minds depend much more upon meaning. (4) Logical or substance memory depends upon the recognition of the meaning and logical connections of the data to be remembered. So great an investigator as Helmholtz complained of a poor mechanical memory, whereas the number of facts he must have retained, because of their relations one to an-

other, must have been enormous. (5) The so-called memory systems which are so often offered for sale are exam ples of ingenious methods of memorizing. A number alphabet is used to suggest dates in history. The number of days in each of the months or the forms of deductive reasoning are arranged in rhyme and so on. Probably the most useful of these devices is illustrated in those systems of stenography in which only the consonants are written, the vowels being indicated by the position of the consonant characters. The systems offered for sale often burden the memory more than they aid it, because so much of the "system" must be remembered. In one instance a young woman had purchased a book which detailed an ingenious method. For two weeks she followed it and was making famous progress when she mislaid the book and, despite every effort, she could not remember what she had done with it. This exemplifies the value of many such devices. 

The only genuine rule is to think over, review, and find as many associates as possible for the acquisitions which we wish to make permanent. When this is done regularly it seems to develop ability.

Extent, Permanence, and Fidelity of Memory.—The ex tent to which memoriter learning can be carried seems almost boundless. Men master several languages each of whose words includes a number of associations. The Cardinal Mezzofanti is said by Barth to have understood sixtysix languages, of which he spoke thirty-six perfectly, eleven less perfectly, seven imperfectly, and read twelve. If tradition may be believed, many citizens of Athens knew by heart the whole of the Iliad and the Odyssey, all the laws of Athens and its history, besides knowing a very great number of their fellow-citizens by name. The apparent inefficiency of modern memory may be due to the invention

of printing and the wide use of written memoranda. This has decreased the use of memory and at the same time increased records beyond the power of any memory to recall any fair portion of them. A language, for example, before the art of printing could not be voluminous. 

Permanence of retention varies from immediate forgetting to faithful retention for many years. Ebbinghaus learned many stanzas of Byron's Don Juan and did not review them for twenty-two years. In relearning the poem after that time he found that it required 7% fewer repetitions to relearn the stanzas formerly mastered than to learn others anew.

For fidelity of memory probably the wonderful performance of the young Mozart has never been equaled. At fourteen years of age he wrote down alomst exactly the score of the Miserere after a single hearing and completed the copy perfectly after a second hearing, though parts of the composition require nine voices. Fidelity is, however, no trait of the average memory. Stern found that 6% of all statements were false, when persons were asked to state what they had seen in a picture, exposed for one or two minutes, and 33% of all their statements, made in answer to questions, were false. The persons tested included both children and adults. Under the most favorable conditions 

10% of adults' statements and 25% of those of children were false. Obviously legal procedure should take such facts into account. Lipmann has reinvestigated the whole question with adults and finds that certain suggestive questions are highly productive of false answers, the Nonne questions perhaps most of all. The latter fact has to do with impressibility rather than retentiveness. 

Memory and Ideational Type.-I have already pointed out (p. 404) that it seems well-nigh impossible for a vocal

motor imaginer to learn by visualizing. It is believed that some pupils represent to themselves the data to be learned in the concrete form of things and situations, while others "think in words." No doubt the former are mainly visualizers. Imaginal type thus has an important influence on learning. The plain result for pedagogy is that subjectmatter to be learned should be presented to all the senses whenever such presentation is possible. As already stated, the presence of laboratories for teaching and manual training schools shows that many things can be properly learned only if the whole nervous circuit is engaged in the work. 

The child who moves his lips in learning testifies to the same important fact.

Finally interest, attention, and freedom from discouragement or depression are all subjective conditions which favor the work of memory. 

Disorders of Memory.-Any account of disorders of mind belongs, of course, to abnormal psychology rather than to a discussion of the normal functioning of the human mind. Certain types of loss of memory, however, are so common that they perhaps deserve brief mention even in an introductory course.

The more common disorders of memory and their relationship may be seen in the following outline: General.. 

1. Amnesia... temporary periodic progressive congenital 

Partial-i. e., loss of one group or type of memories 

2. Hypermnesia, abnormal exaltations of memory

3. Paramnesia, any one of several types of falsification of memory The time during which memory may be lost in temporary general amnesia may be brief or it may extend over years. A former student of mine was engaged in a friendly scuffle in a fellow-student's room. In falling his head struck an iron bedstead and this rendered him either unconscious or dazed for a short time. When he recovered he did not remember having gone to his friend's room, the scuffle, nor events preceding it for ten or twelve hours. 

He could recall attending a German class at 8 a. m. of the preceding day. The first event to be remembered after the accident, occurred some twelve hours after it. Thus his amnesia covered a period of about twenty-four hours. 

In such cases as this, one is tempted to believe some of the cortical neurons are disconnected at their synapses by the blow on the head. The period of amnesia may last but a few minutes. Epileptics usually lose all remembrance of what happens during the attack.

Periodic amnesia involves the loss of memory of one's personal history while consciousness of the present is undisturbed. Memory of this consciousness may then disappear for a time and be replaced by the former normal memories. Thus the individual develops two personalities, or, as it is often called, a "double personality." In the simplest case of this the first personality remembers its own experiences exclusively and the second remembers events of the second personality, though often the situation is more complicated than this. This change from one consciousness to the other may be due to hypnotism or to hysteria. The individual changes periodically from one state to the other.

Progressive Amnesia.-Progressive amnesia is well il-

lustrated in the loss of memory due to old age. This progresses in some cases until only a few of childhood's memories remain. It also occurs in diseases, as fevers. 

An Italian physician who visited this country during an epidemic of yellow fever was attacked by the disease. At the outset of the malady he spoke English, as the disease heightened he spoke French in his delirium, and later, as he succumbed, he spoke only his native language, Italian. 

This illustrates a curious law of the decay of memory, namely, that recent acquisitions disappear first, and the order of loss is just reverse of that of acquisition.2 

An aunt of one of my students lived in Quebec until she was eight years old. During that time she heard and spoke only French. Removing to the United States she forgot all her French because she no longer heard nor used it. Yet, when she came to her last illness, she spoke in her delirium only French. This case and the thousands like it show how firm and deep are the impressions of childhood. 

Men who have been almost drowned or who have been in any other imminent peril of death say that in a single moment they recalled all the events of their past lives. 

One young man, who fell seventy feet in a mine shaft, assures me that he seemed to recall his whole past life in that brief interval. Such exaltations of memory are called hypermnesia.

CHAPTER XV  

The amount of material that can be memorized in a given time and the number of errors made in reciting it can all be measured or counted and, if the experiment is continued for some time, a curve of improvement or curve of learning can be plotted from the results. While memorizing thus lends itself readily to experiment and measurement, it is a rather low form of learning, a sort of cerebral habit formation. In fact, the better a passage has been memorized, the less thought it requires to repeat it and the less meaning attaches to it. Some of the laws of memorizing and of intelligent learning are the same; some are not identical. For the sake of clearness, therefore, we shall make a distinction between memorizing and the higher forms of learning, which depend upon meaning, association, setting, interest, thinking, and logical relationships. Far less experimental work has been done on this type, though more practical importance attaches to it. Of course, these two forms of learning overlap considerably. When one studies to get the meaning of a difficult passage, he learns many of the words used but, because he has mastered the meaning, he is not dependent on the words. The meaning also becomes material for further thought and application. A thoroughly memorized passage remains unchanged and rather unattached to other meanings. We can also memorize senseless material, though there is nothing to be learned. 

This distinction between motor and ideational learning

reveals itself in one of the earliest and most important studies of learning, namely, that of Bryan and Harter on learning telegraphic language. The figure shows the curve of progress in sending and receiving over a period of thirtysix weeks. Bryan's remark on this fact deserves attention. He says, "Two of the curves show a fact which usually appears at a period of the learner's development later than that shown in these curves, namely, that the receiving rate finally exceeds the sending rate. This is almost the universal rule. A receiving operator with a typewriter can practically take his ease in taking the most rapid press work." (Psych. Rev., Vol. IV, 1897, p. 48.) In view of the very slow progress in receiving, which continues for many weeks, this statement of Bryan's is surprising, unless we

have before us two nervous processes which are at least partly different in kind. The explanation seems to be that learning to receive telegraphic language is ideational learning. For a long time it progresses very slowly indeed. 

Then, when finally a stock of associations has been formed, anticipatory ideas run ahead of the dots and dashes. After a few of the words are recorded, the meaning precedes the symbols and the operator can practically take his ease. 

This is characteristic of ideational learning. The mind finally outstrips the rate of the sender. Its foresights of meanings can precede the symbols and go far in advance of them.¹ This has required prolonged and intense effort. 

Something of the same kind appears in reading. No sooner do we read "more" than we expect "than," etc. It is possible to learn to read without knowing the alphabet at all. 

The curves of progress in the figure seem, therefore, to beckon us to recognize that motor learning and ideational learning are partly different processes, proceeding at different rates in the beginning of learning and ending at different levels of permanent achievement. Curiously enough, this difference has been almost completely ignored, except in the original paper. Learning to send telegraphically is acquiring a motor habit, a type of behavior. Receiving is the effortful acquisition of meanings, and many telegraphers could never get far above the slowest main line rate because of the intense effort involved. Many others could not even attain the main line rate in receiving. The sending is motor memorizing. Reciting words or nonsense syllables is the same thing save that lips

While this is possible, the fluctuations of attention cause errors when it is done. The expert telegrapher, therefore, does just the opposite. He does not look forward but lets the message outstrip his receiving. He even delays his transcribing by six to ten words behind the instrument. Since each letter of each word is composed of several dots and dashes, it is plain that the telegrapher hardly pays attention to the separate symbols. Probably words and phrases alone are the units to which he attends.

instead of the hands are used. Unless the curves of this classical experiment are contradicted, we shall do well to distinguish memorizing and motor learning in general from ideational learning, though behaviorists regard them as the same and will admit no factor of meaning. A further reason for the distinction is found in idiots savants. 

Some of them can memorize figures, melodies, names, with the greatest ease and rapidity but they are too unintelligent to learn meaningful or sensible material. They stop far short of acquiring ideas or mastering logical relations. 

Conditions Which Influence Memorizing. Everyone who has endeavored to memorize either meaningful material or senseless material, such as nonsense syllables or figures, or even a list of words in order, recognizes at once that his success in learning depends primarily on (1) the number of repetitions of the material to be learned. The repetitions gradually or rapidly break down resistance at the synapses and recall finally becomes rapid, sure, and automatic. Nonsense syllables, which usually consist of a vowel between two consonants, e. g., baf, lin, gif, form so few associations that learning them depends almost alone on repetitions (aside from the grade of attention). The number of repetitions required was, therefore, supposed to measure the native impressibility of different brains, and the number of syllables retained after a long interval was believed to measure native retentiveness. Ebbinghaus, who invented nonsense syllables for his investigation of memory, repeated a series of ten or twelve syllables until he could recite them once without an error. He found that for every time he read through a series of sixteen syllables, approximately twelve seconds per syllable were saved in learning them the following day. Other conditions equal, the readiness and certainty of recall seems to be almost

proportional to the number of times the learner has attentively repeated the recitation. Because of this fact the recitation of lessons in school is necessary and industry sometimes succeeds better than native facility in learning. 

But reviews are also needed because of (2) Jost's law, "When two associations are of like strength but of unlike age, repetition increases the strength of the older more than of the younger association. When two associations are of equal strength but unlike age, the younger fades more rapidly than does the older." Plainly, therefore, a review of material, which would otherwise soon be forgotten, reinstates it in memory for months or perhaps for years. The second half of the law shows why repetitions should be frequent at first, and later the intervals between successive repetitions may be more and more prolonged. (3) A certain pupil in the sixth grade, when she has been assigned a selection to memorize, very soon appeals to her mother to help her by "holding the book," while she recites. The child has discovered a method for economy of time in learning. Gates has measured the effect of this method. He compares the results of spending 100% of the time in reading with 20%, 40%, 60% and 80% of it spent in reciting. If only 20% of the time is devoted to reading and 80% to reciting, more than twice as many nonsense syllables can be recalled immediately after the learning, and more than three times as many after four hours. Thus 20% of the time given to reading and 80% to reciting is far more effective than reading alone. For material with meaning, 60% of the time should be devoted to reciting to obtain the best results. This gives a gain of about 27% in learning time.

The example is perhaps an extreme one, but Kuhn found in one instance that after 40 readings, 17 additional recitations were required to learn. 25 12 99 99 

99 

99 99 99 99 "9 5 99 99 99 2 

Nonsense syllables were employed in this experiment; in this instance too many readings proved to be an obstacle to memorizing. Plainly, when we study for the sake of reciting, the best plan is to begin to recite as soon as possible. This is what we really do when we study seriously. The tendency to recite on the part of Gate's subjects was "well-nigh irresistible." "The advantage of recitation differs considerably according to the kind of material being studied; the more senseless and less connected the material, the greater the advantage of recitation over reading." (Gates, 1917.) The value of reciting is greater when introduced after six readings, than when introduced after eleven or sixteen readings. Perhaps a good rule for such learning is to spend about 20% to 25% of the time estimated as necessary for the mastery of the material, in the first period of study, one half of this period being devoted to reading and the other half to recitation. 

In reading there is, as everyone knows, a tendency to relax and become inattentive. Thus we may read a whole page and fail to recall a single idea there stated. In recitation there is more activity and alertness. Because of this, it has been claimed that more energy is expended in reciting. Yet Gates found that reading consumed more energy than reciting. Fatigue was greater after reading, etc. As suggested elsewhere, the present writer believes that, because the whole reflex arc is employed when one is reciting, the learning goes on more rapidly than with reading alone. It is perhaps surprising that those be-

haviorists, who regard the individual as nothing more than a bundle of reflex arcs to be conditioned, should not have offered this observation as a law of conditioning. 

Learning by reciting was far more satisfying to Gates' subjects; there was consciousness of greater success. The work was more of a pleasure and less of a bore. Finally, there appeared to be a difference in method between visualizers and auditory-verbal-motor thinkers. The latter were more dependent on recitation than the former, though all were greatly helped by it. 

Rhythm. Almost everyone has observed that poetry is more rapidly and easily memorized than prose, because it has both rhythm and rhyme. Even in learning nonsense syllables, a subjective rhythm is introduced by every learner. Some cannot memorize at all without its aid. Ebbinghaus could learn poetry nine or ten times as fast as his syllables. Sherrington finds that the rhythm of the final common path must be equal to that of the higher neurons when they discharge into it. The ubiquity of music and poetry is evidence of rhythm in nervous impulses but we know little about its nature. (5) I am not aware of experiments on learning by means of writing the data to be learned. Nevertheless, the habit, grown up in many public schools, of handing in great numbers of papers in all classes, has bred a race of students who feel that the only method of learning lies in making abstracts and outlines. This is so slow a process that only a very scant amount of information is gained by means of it. That the habit is fixed immutably by certain school systems cannot be denied. (6) Spaced Study.-This peculiar term is becoming attached to the method of studying with time intervals between the intervals of study or groups of repetitions.

With nonsense syllables, Ebbinghaus found that 68 repetitions which followed in immediate successions, were less effective than 38 distributed over three days. Jost found eight readings per day for three days far less effective than six readings per day for four days. The latter, in turn, were less effective than two readings per day for twelve days. While these results were obtained in memorizing syllables, part of the effect holds good for meaningful material. The boy who goes over his Latin lesson to five-sixths or seven-eighths of mastery, then reviews it next morning, is saving some time over an attempt at complete mastery in one period of study. Intervals between periods of study reduce the number of repetitions required for mastery. This is partly expressed in Jost's law. There is a fixing of associations in the brain between the periods of study, a set acquired by the first efforts. We do not know the brain conditions underlying the process but we do know that no inorganic mechanism ever acts in a similar way and we should remember this fact when we speak of mechanisms of the nervous system. They are very different from non-living mechanisms. In Meumann's experiments all of his subjects retained better after 24 hours than after 8 hours, a result ascribed partly to fatigue but partly to this latent effect of practise which, for the lack of a better term, has been called "settling in memory." 

(7) Whole and Part Methods.-Is it better to study a selection to be learned through from beginning to end, the whole method, or to learn it part by part and then proceed to join the parts into a whole? Quite generally pupils who have to learn poetry or prose repeat a stanza or paragraph at a time until it is learned. The result of such repetition is to stamp in an associative connection between the end of a paragraph and its beginning, instead of one between

the end of each paragraph and the beginning of the next. 

The result is that in "putting together" the parts the former connection must be unlearned and the latter established. This it appears wastes time, so that Meumann found the whole method of learning to be superior to the part method in most instances.

By the whole method the selection to be learned is read through each time from beginning to end, and it proves to be economical of time and effort, but more economical for adults than for children, and more economical in logical than in mechanical memorizing. Of course, if some parts are very difficult, others very easy to learn, the whole method leads to too many repetitions of the easier portions in order to master the more difficult ones. It is a curious fact, though observed by everyone, that attention to a middle of a series is never so good as at its beginning and end. 

This is a defect of the whole-method once more. To meet the difficulty Meumann employs a third method composite of both. The material to be learned is divided into parts and the divisions marked for the recognition of the learner, but the parts are read through consecutively with brief pauses at the points of division. This aids attention and at the same time avoids the false associations of the part method.

In case the learner wishes to commit new matter to memory as quickly as possible the part method seems to be the best. The whole method demands more repetitions but leads to more permanent retention and to greater certainty of reproduction. For the quickest learning of new subjectmatter and average retention the composite method is best. 

(8) Working Against Time.-Industrial psycholo gists are well aware that piece work is more efficient than work by the day or hour. Immediately the worker finds

that he is to be paid by the number of pieces of work completed, he begins to try to finish more work in the given time. His work becomes stimulating. He counts up the number of finished pieces, perhaps every hour, and tries to complete as many or even more in the hours to come. In the same way, it is found that persons, who try to learn as much as possible in a given time, learn considerably more than those who pay no attention to the passing of time. 

In an emergency, an actress is said to have learned a long and difficult part in a play in two hours because that was all the time at her disposal. In this case the brief time was a part of the stimulus to rapid learning. (9) The choice of a period of study which is neither too long nor too short is another aid to memorizing. This must be determined by each individual but the period may be extended after practice. The period for logical learning is longer than that for memorizing because the topic changes and develops. One must not suppose that the first moment of decreased learning limits the period. At first there is the initial "spurt," when learning is rapid. A period of slower progress then sets in in which achievement improves for some time. Fatigue and slow progress begin later. There is, however, an optimum period for study. By adhering to it more is accomplished than by choosing either a longer or a shorter period. The healthy adult is adaptable, however, within wide limits in the matter of the period of study. The time of day at which study goes best seems to be entirely a matter of habit. All of the above conditions and methods, and perhaps many more, yet undiscovered, tend to reduce the time for learning either meaningless or meaningful material. If memory were a mere mechanism or a number of mechanisms, as some psychologists claim, we could add together the sav-

ings of time made by the use of all these methods and thus determine the total advantage of these devices over learning in the usual haphazard manner or by means of repetition alone. Gates has done this in the following words: "To learn a series of symbols frequently used in laboratory studies by the somewhat crude methods we are likely to adopt without tuition requires, let us say, one hundred minutes. If the average learner adopts the single device of working against time, he will realize a saving of twenty per cent. of the learning time. The single device of studying the material as a whole instead of parts brings a saving of fifteen per cent.; the single device of recalling instead of re-reading yields a saving of thirty per cent.; the single device of employing a learning period of optimum length saves fifteen per cent.; the single device of an optimum interval between repetitions saves twenty per cent.; the single effect of certain subtle means of relating the items saves ten per cent. of the time. Add these single savings together and the child learns the lesson not in one hundred minutes but in ten minutes less than no time at all." (Gates, A. I., J. of Ed. Psychology, Vol. 19, 1928, p. 386.)

Two conclusions at least may be derived from this striking quotation: (1) We cannot apply statistics uncritically to mental precesses. Gates wrote the above lines to warn us against this. (2) Even in the most mechanical learning, that of learning senseless material, memory does not work like a mechanism. There is perhaps competition by different parts of the brain for the energy available at the moment. The permeability of pathways for nervous impulses in the cortex varies continually, as witness our inability to recall some familiar fact or name at one moment and our perfectly easy remembrance of it twenty

minutes later. There are fluctuations of attention. Attention must be brought back to the matter in hand, to the emphasis of items which have escaped our grasp. All this is not at all like a mechanism but like a very delicate and complex organic structure. It will be long indeed before scientific analysis and imagination will penetrate to the physical conditions which may underly its processes. Introspection alone gives us the nearest approach to explanation that we can attain. To turn to a premature mechanomorphism is only to confess that the machine age, in which we live, has unduly impressed the naive psychologist. The human brain and its connections cannot be described as if they differ but little from those of a telephone system. By following the methods named above we may improve our rate of learning and improve it a great deal, but we can achieve no such result as that obtained by adding the savings together. 

Forgetting.—After learning nonsense syllables so as to recite the list perfectly once, they are quickly forgotten because they form few associations. Often we find a curve of forgetting plotted on the basis of Ebbinghaus's results. 

The table below shows, however, that such a curve is very misleading. The rate of forgetting was quite different for two different learners and it is quite probable that others would show still different rates. In all probability we should again encounter "the fallacy of the average," if we should attempt to plot a curve of forgetting. One's rate of forgetting seems to be a factor of his personality. 

Ebbinghaus found that immediately after learning or "stamping in" the impression of the syllables forgetting is very rapid, then slower, and at last it proceeds very slowly indeed. He thought that the amount forgotten is not proportional to the time elapsed but to the logarithm of the

time. Meumann found the first forgetting proportional to time. Then it proceeded even more rapidly, then very slowly. The several per cents. forgotten as found by the two investigators are tabulated below, with E. for the results of Ebbinghaus, M. for those of Meumann:
