Ideational Learning. Many of the methods of memorizing outlined above apply also to learning logical material. 

They are therefore valuable for this more important type of learning but other conditions still apply to this process. (1) He learns best or most permanently who weaves the material to be learned into patterns of association by thinking it over, by "turning it over in his mind” until its implications are thought of and all sorts of connections are discovered. Each of the associations thus becomes a cue or suggestion by which the memory of the data may be aroused. The student, who does not think a matter over until he understands it, will have little chance of recalling it and if he does happen to recall it, he will apply it to the wrong situation or use it to answer the wrong question.

This is often to be found in the examination papers of memorizers. As a palliative for this, recognition questions have been devised, in answer to which the student

merely decides whether statements are true or false. Since we can recognize far more than we can understandingly remember and apply, this puts a great premium on merely recognizing. Certain subjects of study can be presented in the forms of problems to be solved. They must be thought over and they are, therefore, stimulating. But many facts must be learned which will be useful in the solution of future problems. They too must be thoughtfully studied so that their implications will be understood. 

To learn ideationally is, therefore, to learn understandingly, to acquire a stock of meanings; as Cameron remarks, “A world of meanings is constructed that supplements and corrects perceptual experience." These meanings sometimes refute our very senses. We no longer believe that the sun moves. We interpret the apparent movement quite differently as our knowledge grows. Science furnishes innumerable similar examples in which our vision is by the mind's eye. (2) Do we learn better when studying in a class or group or by individual study? Elkine tested forty children and found that they retained more of a list of words and of a list of figures which they had studied in class than of a similar list which they had studied alone. The superiority of classwork varied around thirty per cent. for the several tests. He points out that the individual is a different person when he enters a social group. Emulation, rivalry, imitation, and still subtler motives influence him. We need further investigations of the social influence on learning. For older students, no doubt, habits of study already formed would be a factor. With children Elkine found only five who did better work alone than in the class. This should at least make us optimistic relative to the value of classwork.

(3) The Will to Remember.-Things which are na tively interesting are easily learned. They arouse spontaneous attention. But attention must be given to many studies because of their future value or for some mediate or secondary value which they possess; secondary to some main purpose. How little is remembered without the will to remember is shown by Cameron's observation: "A number of experimenters have reported, for example, that they have repeated a series of nonsense syllables to a learner a sufficient number of times for the latter to memorize them, and then the same series again to a second learner, and still a third, without being able to remember the series themselves." This could happen with material full of meaning only to a less degree. But the absence of an intention to remember goes far toward preventing all learning. Hence we find the whole theory of motivation. 

Unless the student finds reasons and motives for attentive effort until his interest is aroused, he will not succeed in learning. Fortunately, most material, which involves important meaning, soon arouses interest in fertile minds. 

Numerous experiments could be described showing that the will to remember is the most essential factor in learning. Peterson tested the memory of students for lists of words. In the first test they were not aware that they would be required to recite the lists. In the second, they knew this requirement and studied with the purpose to remember. Purposive study averaged 22.4% more effective than the less purposive for immediate recall, and 

49.7% more effective for delayed recall. Miss Mulhall attained quite as decisive results for purposive and nonpurposive study. The effectiveness of the former was greater for material rich in associations than for nonsense syllables.

Allowing students to know their scores in learning and practice and urging them to outdo their previous scores, was found by Book and Norvell to result in great improvement. A control group, which was directed to pay no attention to their past scores, did not improve so much and the improvement of the first group was shared in by all its members. The practical conclusion to draw is that students be informed of results of their efforts in study. 

Experiment shows that trying to improve one's past achievement results in improvement whether the task is mental or physical. We meet here a general psychological condition. 

(4) Encouragement and Discouragement.-Everyone knows how difficult it is to work when discouraged and this applies with increased force to the work of learning. 

Two questionnaire reports indicate that praise is more effective than blame in stimulating to increased effort in study. We know little about what may be called social discouragement except that it is a potent cause of failure.

The student who learns slowly and with difficulty often compares his partial failures with the greater success of his mates and a permanent mood of discouragement may result. A similar condition arises when a student attempts more work than he can possibly do well. It is depressing to rob one's self of the feeling of satisfaction which arises from creditable achievement. Surpassing our previous records ministers to this satisfaction. It is probable that a certain psychological theory has introduced something in the nature of despair in regard to study. By the theory of mental discipline, the student might be encouraged by the belief that he would certainly gain better mastery and control of his powers by effort and exercise, than by letting them decay for lack of exercise. The vigor with which the

theory of discipline was attacked tended to deny that mental exercise is of any value whatever. But it is of value, whatever we may think of the transfer of the effects of exercise. The following remarks by Professor James are as true today as when they were written. "Let no youth have any anxiety about the upshot of his education, whatever the line of it may be. If he keeps faithfully busy each hour of the working day, he may safely leave the final result to itself. He can with perfect certainty count on waking up some fine morning to find himself one of the competent ones of his generation in whatever pursuit he may have singled out. Silently, between all the details of his business, the power of judging in all that class of matter will have built itself up within him as a possession that will never pass away. Young people should know this truth in advance. The ignorance of it has probably engendered more discouragement and faint-heartedness in youths embarking on arduous careers than all other causes put together." This is not meant to counsel to carelessness in choosing a career but it is true that devotion to it will develop secure ability even in men of limited powers. 

Plateaus in Learning.-In their investigation of the learning of telegraphy, Bryan and Harter found that there were long periods in learning to receive messages during which there was very slight improvement or none at all. 

The curve of progress flattened out for a time. Hence it has been called a "plateau" in the learning curve. Plateaus in learning to send messages were not common. A study of the curve of receiving showed that there was improvement in receiving letters and words, and, only when this had reached almost its limit, did marked improvement in connected discourse begin again. Thus practice in receiving smaller units led finally to better reception

of combinations, reception of a higher order. Anyone who has practised computation for a considerable time or studied a foreign language, recognizes by introspection that mastery of higher combinations finally occurs and a great step in progress has then been made. The plateau in telegraphy indicated only an apparent lack of progress. 

The efforts on words and letters were a necessary preliminary to distinguishing higher combinations with facility. First, words which were frequently used, then others came to be recognized with less attention required for the letters. Meaning thus began to triumph over mere symbols. This is characteristic of ideational learning. In learning a language, for months the words of foreigners sound like a "broth of syllables." Gradually the meanings of the words most used shed light on those uttered along with them and a long plateau in learning is passed. 

Plateaus have been otherwise explained as due to lack of interest, becoming bored with a task, etc. No doubt flattening of learning curves may occur from these causes but increased effort and attention can at once result in a greater rate of progress. These are not periods of preparation for learning of a higher order as were the plateaus in learning to receive telegraphic messages. 

Probably the chief distinction between memorizing and ideational learning is the fact that in the latter we are able to make these higher combinations, due to our attention to meanings. New relationships suddenly arise which were never thought of before. Finally we come to proceed confidently at a mere hint. (5) A fifth method of learning is, therefore, the giving of attention to meanings rather than to symbols. As already pointed out, the meaning or sense of a passage being memorized diminishes with

successive readings. The number of mental images which arise also diminish in this experiment. (6) Attention and Distractions. - Enough has been said in the present topic and in the chapter on attention to show that giving attention, setting one's mind to the task, the will to learn, is the chief condition of learning and all the methods suggested are chiefly aids to giving attention. We need not go over this again but efforts to measure the degree or intensity of attention by measuring the amount of distraction overcome, have often been made. But we soon become adapted to external distraction and it ceases to be a distraction. It occurred to the writer that in learning to read a foreign language, distractions continue for a long time and they are internal distractions, or belong to the subject-matter to be mastered. Words must be continually looked up and fitted into the meaning of the text. The grammar must be consulted, etc. Do these distractions interfere with getting the meaning of the text? Miss Freund, with the aid of sixteen students who had had a year's study of German or of French, or four years' study of Latin, gained an answer to this question. Eleven of the sixteen subjects of the experiment retained more ideas from the foreign reading than from reading a very similar passage in English, i. e., a translation into English of the immediately succeeding foreign text. The excess of ideas retained for the three foreign languages over English, stated in per cents., was as follows:

French German

Latin 5.8% 4.7% 0.3%

It seems evident that the added difficulty of reading the foreign language was a help in recalling ideas of the

text 24 and 48 hours after the reading. Of course more time was required for the foreign reading. The writer recalls more facts which are read in German than in English. This experiment confirms others in which added distraction or difficulties seemed only to increase attention and further the recall of ideas. Further experimentation is needed to learn how wide the application of these results may be. It can safely be said, however, that the ordinary hum of activity in a school room is no obstacle to effective study. There should probably be one class reciting while another is engaged in study. It may be, also, that we have here a confirmation of the wide-spread belief that the study of language has an educative value beyond that of, say, typewriting, though enormous statistical tables are claimed to prove the contrary. 

Learning in General. If we try to survey the whole field of human and animal learning in the broadest sense of the term, only four ways of learning have been found. 

1. Trial and error

Learning by 

2.

Being put through the act to be learned 

3. Imitation 4. Means of ideas 

Learning by Trial and Error.—If a very hungry cat is placed in a cage, with a door fastened by a button, and food is placed outside the cage, the cat struggles to escape and reach the food. In this struggle a chance stroke of its paw depresses the button and the animal is fed. If returned to the cage for a second trial, the animal escapes, on the average, in about half the time required in the first trial. After this the cat slowly decreases the time for opening the door until it finally depresses the button in a few seconds. This is trial and error learning. It seems to be merely the slow formation of a habit; the cat can know

nothing of the mechanics of such boxes. It cannot, therefore, have the slightest insight into the situation. Its very slow learning led at first to the hypothesis that the animal could have no ideas at all. More recently, Woodworth regards the animal as responding to visual cues and he seems to imply that it has a memory of the place at which to claw, in order to escape from the puzzle box. Certainly there is no more than this. Anyone who watches such an animal learning to escape will feel sure that he is observing the slow coupling together of nervous connections into a habit of direct instead of random clawing; almost pure behavior whose conscious accompaniments are intense hunger, the excitement of the attempt to escape, and possibly the factor of place memory mentioned by 

Woodworth. 

Now human beings learn certain acts and acquire certain skills by this method of trial and error. Perhaps learning to play golf is a present example. Only slowly and by much trial and error does facility increase, except in the young. Only those, who have begun practice in games of skill when the lower nervous system is plastic, show any surprising mastery. The old and the new brain have different periods of development and reach maturity at different times. No matter how mechanical the performance, which a man is learning to execute, he gains ideas of better ways to do the thing. New insights develop.

So it is difficult to frame a conception of the bareness of the cat's or of the rat's learning by trial and error in mazes and puzzle boxes. Repetition with slight accidental increase in facility appears to be all there is of it. 

The criticism should be recognized, however, that mazes and puzzle boxes have been devised on the basis of man's own intelligence and are so foreign to the animal's nature

and abilities that the experiments could reveal no more than they do. In certain natural situations the animals seem to show a sagacity which our experiments do not probe. Perhaps in the course of time we shall find that the animals have abilities so different from those of man that at present we are setting only clumsy experiments. 

The discovery of trial and error learning by Thorndike was a distinct addition to psychological knowledge. But it also brought to light a feature of human psychology. For a considerable time after the discovery the claim was made that human learning also is of the trial and error type, just as the claim is now made that learning is nothing but "conditioning." The latter claim is due to Pavlov's discoveries. Plainly, this enthusiasm for extending a new discovery to cover everything is a distinct error of judg. ment. Cameron states a much wiser position in the fol lowing words: "But while man's kinship with the lower animals cannot be questioned, and the significance of his life activities cannot be understood unless this relationship is taken into account, it is a grave mistake to minimize the importance of the great gulf between man's nature and that of the most highly developed of the lower animals. 

In no respect are these differences more marked than in the various forms of learning." (Cameron, Educational 

Psychology, pp. 6 and 7.)

Learning from Being Put Through the Act to be Learned. -In his experiments with cats in a puzzle box, Thorndike tried repeatedly to see if the animals could learn to release a latch or turn a button by being put through the act. 

They all failed to profit by this help. He concluded that the animals had no ideas to associate and their learning consisted only of coupling motor impulses into a complex habit, motor learning only. They could learn only by in-

nervating their own muscles. The present writer worked with raccoons. These animals live in a wild environment and may be supposed to have keener wits or greater intelligence than the house cat.

Our first observation was that a hungry raccoon, which has been lifted into a box from which he escaped and was fed, would rush quickly back into the box, apparently for the purpose of again escaping and obtaining food. Later we arranged a box very difficult for the animals to learn. 

The door was secured by five fastenings, all of which must be released before the door would open. Because of the difficulty, the animals failed to escape by their own efforts. 

A typical result may be quoted. After failing, raccoon 

No. 3 was put through the acts six times. He then succeeded eighteen times consecutively by his own efforts. 

The next morning he failed after twenty-five minutes to pull one of the loops. Two hours later he failed after eleven minutes of steady trying. Put through ten times, he succeeded in forty seconds, then in twenty-nine and so on. In addition to this, we tried two raccoons on nine different puzzle boxes by putting them through the acts and two brothers of these two animals were allowed to learn the same boxes by trial and error. The average time of the first unaided escape from the boxes for those put through the act was 41.6 seconds; for those not put through, 90.2 seconds. There can be no doubt that raccoons profit in learning by being put through the act to be learned. They need not innervate their own muscles. They are capable of something more than motor learning. Cats are not.

Another observation may be added to these. When the four raccoons were received, they were the size of squirrels and were fed milk from a bottle fitted with a nipple. In order, as we supposed, to conceal the bottle, we set it on

top of a barrel out of sight of the animals. Instantly one of them scaled the side of the barrel and, before we could stop him, he had taken hold of the nipple and had drunk half of the milk. All of the raccoons would climb up the barrel, though they had only seen the bottle disappear over its edge. This appears to be place memory. It is much more definite than the place memory of cats. This behavior of raccoons seems to approach the insight which Köhler proved that chimpanzees possess in a considerable degree. We can no longer say, therefore, that all animals learn only by trial and error and only by innervating their own muscles. No doubt, if we had enough crucial experiments, we should find various grades of intelligence or ability to learn among them, exactly as we know that their eyesight varies from vague and ill-defined to acute and definite.

Learning by Imitation.-As stated on an earlier page, very little evidence of imitation has been found in monkeys and no evidence at all in the higher vertebrates below the monkeys. When we come to the chimpanzees, Köhler has observed instances of imitation but these animals have no instinct of imitation. "Imitation is almost as difficult for apes and as rare in them as it is in the lower vertebrates." (Psychologies of 1925, p. 156.) Nevertheless we may quote two examples from Köhler. "On the playground a man has painted a wooden pole in white color. After the work is done he goes away leaving behind a pot of white paint and a beautiful brush. I observe the only chimpanzee who is present, hiding my face behind my hands, as if I were not paying attention to him. The ape for a while gives much attention to me before approaching the brush and the paint because he has learned that misuse of our things may have serious consequences. But very soon, encour-

aged by my attitude, he takes the brush, puts it into the pot of color and paints a big stone which happens to be in the place a beautiful white." (Ibid., 157.)

Again, when an ape had failed for hours to get food which hung from the top of the cage but out of reach, Köhler "took a box, put it under the food, climbed up and touched the food." Then he stepped down and threw the box several yards away. In less than a minute the ape got the box and thus reached the food. This is plainly learning by imitation, yet Köhler thinks the animals learn in this way only if they get a true insight into the act. It is really ideational learning or, as we should say of human beings, it is conscious imitation. 

In human beings it is only necessary to reflect on fashions in clothes and manners, on the learning of language, and on the spread of stammering from a single stammerer, to recognize the influence of imitation as a means of learning. 

Learning by Means of Ideas.-Ideational learning is so important in human beings that probably nine-tenths of school time is devoted to it. The history of civilization is, in fact, little more than the history of the development and influence of ideas. By means of them behavior due to the new brain replaces the impulsive behavior of the old, though the conquest is very slow. As we have seen, trial and error learning was for a long time believed to be the only form of animal learning and the conception was so attractive to some that it was believed by them to include all human learning as well. There were few experiments at that time which indicated any other form of learning in animals. Now the situation is quite different. Apes have been found suddenly to acquire insight whereby they solve problems almost instantly and not by trial and error

at all. This addition to psychological knowledge must be stated briefly, since we are now trying to give an account of learning in general. Between the insight of apes and the trial and error learning of cats we may interpolate the quick success of the raccoon in performing an act after he has been put through it, though he failed completely of his own efforts. Is this the dawn of insight which is perfectly clear in the apes?

Köhler buried some fruit in the sand too far away from the chimpanzee's cage for him to reach it though he watched the burying with interest. When Köhler came near the cage the chimpanzee "seized my arm and tried to push it in the direction of the hidden food as he would do whenever he could not find a method of approach to it himself." After waiting three quarters of an hour Köhler "threw a stick into the cage on the opposite side from the fruit. The ape accustomed to the use of sticks as instruments, instantly took it, went to the bars nearest the place of the food, began to scratch away the sand exactly in the right spot, and pulled the food toward him. Repetitions of the experiment with other positions of the food had the same result."

Again, when an ape had seen a stick put up under the roof of a cage, out of his sight and next morning found bananas too far outside the cage to be reached, he looked about, as if looking for a stick. "After some seconds, however, his eyes went up to the place where the stick was hidden the evening before. He could not see it, but he climbed at once in the shortest possible way up to that part of the ceiling where the stick was hidden, came down with it, and scratched the food toward him." All the other chimpanzees who had seen the stick hidden did the same thing. This is very similar to the raccoon's climbing

to the top of a barrel to get the milk bottle which was out of sight but apparently not out of memory. In this case, however, there was not a long interval between hiding the bottle and their climbing to get it. Unprejudiced readers will see in this behavior of the chimpanzees a clear case of the employment of memory in solving a problem. 

Not only do these animals use memory but they also solve problems which require a novel act, never before performed by them. In Köhler's term, they show "insight" into the problem. One of the chimpanzees, who had often used sticks in order to draw bits of food within reach, when it had been placed outside the cage, was completely baffled for a time, when two pieces of bamboo were given him instead of one longer piece. He gave up the task for a time. Then suddenly he fitted the end of the smaller piece into that of the larger one and drew the food within reach. 

When the stick thus made fell apart, he again combined the two parts. This abrupt change of method is something entirely different from the behavior of cats and can be accounted for only by insight, as if the ape suddenly gained an idea of how the thing could be done. Yerkes observed similar abrupt learning in the orang-utan with no errors after the mastery of the situation.

As perhaps everyone now knows, these famous apes of Köhler's would bring a box from some distance to a point underneath food, which was hanging from the roof of the cage. When the food could not be reached by standing on one box, another was placed on top of it and finally four boxes were thus put, one on top of another, though they were never in stable equilibrium but ready to topple over. 

The ape has, therefore, no insight into how to build a stable column of boxes but he did devise a novel method of getting food which was hung far above his reach.

If intelligence is defined as ability to learn above the level of trial and error or to deal with a novel situation, the psychologist certainly confronts simple intelligence in the behavior of these chimpanzees. It is, no doubt, only the beginning of intelligence that he sees. Abyssmal stupidity is also shown by these animals. Their intelligence could never become human, yet they have something more than the ability to form habits. 

Is Learning Nothing But Conditioning?-Pavlov's famous experiment of measuring the amount of saliva secreted by a dog, which has been fed repeatedly at a given signal, has been described under the title, "the conditioned reflex." 

This is the name which he has given to the reaction. The saliva appears whenever the signal is given after the dog has become habituated and if he is hungry. When hunger is appeased the reflex secretion is entirely inhibited and Boldyreff has shown that the amount of saliva diminishes with repeated feedings and diminishes day after day, if the same food is continued, notwithstanding the presence of hunger. When an unpleasant stimulus, dilute hydrochloric acid, was forcibly placed in the dog's mouth, the flow of saliva was increased for days, and with increased strength of the stimulus rage appeared. These are evidently protective reactions. From these observations there is evidently some difference between glandular reactions and muscular reactions, the diminution of saliva, though hunger continues is especially to be noted. The two laws of the conditioned reflex derived by Boldyreff are so different from those deduced by the psychologists from the same experiment that we may wonder which one should be accepted.

The psychologists, who have derived laws of learning from the reflex, are disposed to say that learning is nothing

but conditioning. It seems to me rather that conditioning is one form of learning, one type of learning. After several or many repetitions of the signal followed by feeding, the dog expects food and his salivary glands begin secretion before the food is in his mouth. It is, as Boldyreff says, a cerebral reflex. If the dog has memory he has learned by repetition to anticipate food. As a matter of learning, this does not seem widely different from a dog's learning to come to be fed when he is called. He merely recognizes the familiar call, and his muscles respond. In 

Pavlov's experiments the dog's salivary glands respond and the method of testing responses by salivary secretions is entirely novel and original. This is the unique feature of Pavlov's work. 

As Woodworth points out, the word, "conditioning," is awkward. The sense in which it is used is exceptional. 

The dog does promptly form a glandular habit, a simple form of learning, but the claim that there are not higher forms of learning than this is hardly warranted by the facts.

CHAPTER XVI ASSOCIATION 

Since Plato remarked that the sight of a lover suggests the lyre, because the two were usually seen together, it has been a matter of common observation that ideas suggest one another, whether our thought is creative or merely reproductive. Consciousness, we say, is in ceaseless change; consciousness is a process; images pass before the mind's eye; we possess a stream of thought or consciousness. Since consciousness is a process or a streaming phenomenon, we must sooner or later try to discover the conditions of its proceeding or streaming, how its momentary states or fields are forever shifting in focus and margin, some parts dying away, others suggesting new associates until, in a few moments, we say we are no longer thinking of the same thing. In other words, we must in our study alternately give attention to two questions: 

What are the contents of consciousness? and since consciousness is a process, How do the contents proceed? i. e.,

How do the momentary states change one into another, until we have a right to say that consciousness is in ceaseless change? It is this question which concerns us now. 

Under the influence of attention our thoughts are forced steadily toward some goal very much as gravity forces a stream to ever lower levels. In spite of its twisting and turning due to temporary obstacles, there is, therefore, a very distinct difference between voluntary and involuntary trains of thought. At present we shall neglect the factor of voluntary attention and consider only the

ASSOCIATION 

491 undirected or involuntary thought which is usually termed revery.

Again, we must not overlook the fact of interruptions of our thought from without. Someone speaks to us. The telephone rings. An urgent letter is received. Some matter of importance must be attended to at once, etc. Thus our thought is constantly being given a new direction by external influences. Each of these influences may become the starting point of a new train of thought, but more often they are interruptions which must be "recovered from" and which we must consequently omit from consideration in discussing the transitions of consciousness from one state to another.

The investigation of association first took the form of observing the connection between the thought just vanishing from consciousness and the idea which comes to take its focal place. Aside from the remark of Plato, already referred to, such observation began with Aristotle and finally reached its most extensive consideration in the writings of Hume, who likened the influence of association in psychology to that of gravitation in physics. Our first task, however, is not to state the importance of association, but to ascertain the conditions under which one idea suggests another or serves to recall another. The statements of these conditions are often called the laws of association.

Association by Frequency of Repetition. From what we have learned of the nervous system and its synapses, it would seem evident that, when a given area of the cortex is active, nervous impulses tend to discharge from it into any other center which has before been active along with the first. Also, when one of two ideas or memories, which were acquired at the same time or which have been fre-

quently repeated together, is present in consciousness it tends to suggest the other. The strength of the tendency is proportional to the number of repetitions. When subjects in an experiment are asked to respond to stimulus words with the first word which comes to mind, most of them will respond to the word "man" with the word "woman." Boy-girl, house-barn, hot-cold, are similarly paired because they have been frequently repeated together by every one. If two ideas have frequently been in mind at the same time, one, on recurring, will tend to re-arouse the other. Even in association by similarity the influence of frequency can usually be found to be present. 

Before the art of printing influenced human thought so much, it was natural to say that, if two things were often seen together, the idea of one would recall that of the other. But, if two things are seen together, they are contiguous. Hence the early name for the law of frequency was the law of contiguity. This phrase is still widely used and it accounts for the statement that, if one were gifted with a perfect memory, it would be a complete mirror of the world about him. His imagery would mirror the surrounding world. This was probably truer of the mind before men had to recall and associate so many meanings, words, and abstract symbols and consequently gave more attention to natural scenes which can be recalled in imagery.

The law of association by frequency or contiguity in space or time underlies man's knowledge of cause and effect. Primitive man, hearing the roar of the wind in the forest and feeling its strong pressure against his own body, and then witnessing the fall of a great tree, would have no difficulty in deciding that the wind was the cause, because the gust of wind and the fall of the tree occurred

ASSOCIATION 

493 at the same moment. Had they been separated by weeks or months, he might never have made the correct inference. 

Having arrived at this example of cause and effect, the savage might pass to a conception of other causes. Of course, he might add a god of the wind as a more remote cause, but this was merely because he thought all causes must be personal and like himself. Introspection gave him his first knowledge of causes or agencies. Contiguity probably gave him the first hint of an immediate, impersonal cause. The long search for such causes has produced the science of today. 

Association by frequent repetitions lies at the basis of learning. The young child soon learns his own name because he is frequently addressed by it. Only much later does he learn his family name because he does not so often hear it. He learns the alphabet and other matter to be recited verbatim by dint of many repetitions. As he grows older, fewer repetitions are required for learning but the learning is not so permanent. Some psychologists believe that learning, and especially learning by repetition, is identical with the formation of habits. It would be better to say that the two are similar, for we shall find certain differences between them.

Association by Similarity.-If the order of our ideas were governed solely by repetition, our thought would be humdrum and commonplace indeed, like the recital of a well prepared lesson. One condition which prevents this is the similarity between many of our experiences. When, on hearing a story, a man utters the inevitable, "That reminds me," he means, not that the teller of the story has recited one of his experiences, but one more or less like an incident of his own life. This he can hardly refrain from relating. In a recent novel, no sooner was the tragedy re-

vealed, than readers said, "Yes, that plot was used years ago in a short story by de Maupassant." The similarity here amounted to almost complete identity. Similarity is usually partial indentity. 

While the similarities most useful in our thought are commonly likenesses between situations, meanings and relations, examples of such thoughts would be too long for description in a text-book. Let us take similarities between words recalled just as we are about to write or speak them. I wished to recall the name of a student, June Ashley. Instead, I first recalled the name, June Downey. 

Why? Had these names ever before been associated in my mind? Never. Could the law of repetition influence the recall at all, then? No. Plainly the similarities between the two names accounted for the recall, first, of the one I was not seeking, then of the correct one. The number of syllables, the accent, the rhythm, the beginning and the end of both these words were the same. Because of this partial identity the memory of one led to the recall of the other.

If we wish to imagine the probable brain action in the recall, we need only resort to the same sort of diagram by which we explained the erroneous recalls, also influenced by similarity, which, when spoken or written, are called lapses (p. 171). Ashl- June ey Down Here, since both the beginning and the end of both names are the same, we need only imagine partly common brain paths for them. Thus the cortical patterns of the discharge of impulses for the two names are partly identi-

ASSOCIATION 

495 cal, so the two patterns are interconnected. The interconnection alone would account for the association of the two names. The same type of pattern of discharge which leads to a false recall (a lapse) may also lead to a correct one.

One difference between lapses and correct recalls lies in the fact that the final common path functions in lapses, while only the paths common to two cortical patterns need function in recall due to similarity. 

Of course, this is a theory of cortical action in association by similarity. There must be some theory of such action and the conception here proposed has important evidence in its favor. (1) It is only an extension of Sherrington's theory of the final common path and he fully proved that theory by neurological experiments. The nervous system cannot work in one way in its final paths and in a totally different way in the cortical centers. (2) Without some such conception as that stated above, association by similarity is absurd. An idea which I cannot now recall but which, I feel sure, will come to mind in a few seconds cannot be similar to one already present in consciousness. "There cannot be similarity until both things are there." "Similarity is a relation perceived after the fact and cannot be an agent of anything." There is no disputing this absurdity as long as we speak only of ideas. But association by similarity is a fact, observed by everyone. It furnishes one of the very best of the intelligence tests. So, instead of denying the fact, we must formulate a theory in harmony with it. Cortical patterns with partly common paths can account for the fact. Activity in such patterns can be an agent or cause of recall of one similar by another just as such activity is the cause of all other types of recall. 

In association by repetition the connection between neu-

rons is assumed to be serial. In association by similarity we assume the connections to be of the pattern variety.¹

We have seen in the account of imagination that its creations are due to association by similarity. Wit and poetry, of course, depend upon it. There are surely similar rhythm patterns for similar strains of music, etc. Since all creative thought, except that due to the cause and effect relation, seems to depend on association by similarity, we have had to give some space to its description, using for examples only the very simplest of this type of association. 

Recency. In considering memory we found that nonsense syllables are forgotten very quickly indeed. Even material with meaning is much easier to recall if it has just recently been learned. Recency of a few minutes or a few hours is thus a condition favoring recall. This fact has given us the distinction between immediate and permanent memory. In the former, the stimulus or impression is given but once and recall must occur immediately. 

In the latter, time elapses between impression and recall, and the idea is fixed in mind by associations and repetitions. Immediate and permanent memory are found to be quite different abilities in the sense that the same person may be very efficient in the exercise of one and inefficient in the other. We all know men who have an enormous stock of information but to whom we would not turn to hear of the day's events. They have excellent associative memories, poor immediate memory. 

It seems doubtful whether recency is of much help, therefore, in associative memory. Connections due to recency fade too quickly. Consequently, while text-books state 

Koffka's words defining association by similarity fit such patterns as I have drawn so well that it may be asked whether such patterns do not furnish an almost complete neural explanation of the Gestalt theory. See Helson, "Psychology of Gestalt," American Journal of Psychology, July, 1925, pp. 354 and 355.

ASSOCIATION 

497 that recency is a cause of recall, it is doubtful whether it is an aid in association to the degree of the other conditions which we are considering. It would be truer to say that recency has great effect on the recall of disconnected or dissociated facts; little influence on association. 

Immediate memory has an important function besides the recall of disconnected recent events. It serves to usher in the permanent memory of the child. Teachers of young children must observe the condition of recency. Recitations must follow soon after instruction or they will not follow at all. Very soon the child's time-span of memory increases. Instead of disconnected items he forms associations and permanent memory has been enthroned. 

In colleges the student who crams for an examination the night before it is to be given is trusting to recency of impressions. Unless there have been previous repetitions he is likely to find the essential connections gone when he most needs them. In this dilemma he makes many substantive statements one of which, he hopes, may answer the question and be credited by the reader. In the socalled objective type of examination he is asked not to answer any question, but merely whether he can recognize the correct answer among others. Here recency works better than in the essay type of quiz.

Perhaps an example of recency appears in the peculiar cyclical character of the conversation in a commonplace community, each cycle or topic lasting about two months. 

With student communities, the series is likely to be football, basketball, baseball, and plans for vacation, interspersed with mention of the weather, whose sole claim to interest is that it has always recently changed. 

Vividness. Certain ideas have a connection with our deepest interests. They concern the self. Such ideas or

memories are vivid. There may be no instinct of self-preservation, but dangerous experiences give vivid memories. 

Anyone who has witnessed an earthquake, an avalanche or some very terrible accident will find it difficult to rid his mind of its image. The knowledge of personal guilt is sometimes vivid, so the popular psychologist proclaims, "You are not the boss of your forgetter." This truth applies to all very vivid ideas. We forget reading this very morning of someone's losing his fortune, but let the news come that we, ourselves, have suffered complete loss. The idea will then be vivid and unforgettable. Intensity of the impression has nothing to do with vividness. A wisp of smoke or its odor, far less intense than would be emitted by a single cigarette, will make a most vivid impression if it suggests that the floor below is on fire and all avenue of escape is cut off. Such an impression will be remembered, though we ignore far more intense ones and forget them instantly. 

In teaching, methods are continually being devised and sold whose vividness, it is claimed, removes all need for the drudgery of learning and repetition. They are short-lived and of doubtful value. If the teacher can convince the pupil that knowledge may further his interests in the future, so that he begins working for a permanent goal, all his acquisitions will be better remembered.

Besides the above type of vividness, it is probable that novel experiences are vivid and easily recalled, because they appeal to curiosity, the fundamental intellectual impulse. They must, however, find some association or connection with knowledge which we already possess. Without this they are not recalled because they are not understood. It is quite possible that the novelty of the child's

ASSOCIATION 

499 world and the consequent vividness of his experiences contribute a large part to the happiness of childhood. 

Harmony With Our Mood.—The man who expresses an opinion which we do not like to hear is promptly called a pessimist. Like and dislike are feelings. We thus charge the pessimist with speaking from his feelings, rather than from facts and reasons, when it may be our own optimism which prevents us from entertaining any belief in his forebodings. The courtier and politician recognize the influence of feeling as so great that they are more likely to state what is welcome than what is true. If we do not like even to hear opinions stated that are unwelcome to our feelings, we certainly do not recall ideas which are out of harmony with our mood. The egotist likes to dwell in his thought and conversation on himself and his achievements. He is scarcely less unwelcome than the pessimist. 

If reproved, however, he replies that modesty is an extreme form of egotism and proceeds with his theme. When our mood is less hopeful and changes to depression, only gloomy thoughts come to mind. 

The war may furnish an example of the influence of feelings on the train of ideas. A mother in a neutral country writes to one in a country at war, "I do not see how you can bear to send your son to the front." The reply was, "I could not bear not to have him go. We are fighting for principle and our very life." The imagery in the minds of the two mothers was doubtless much the same, but in the latter they were clothed with feelings of patriotism and self-sacrifice, which led to entirely different thought and action. Again, interest is a mild intellectual feeling. Yet without this feeling even the best intellects accomplish nothing. 

The old doctrine of temperaments, caused by humors

in the blood, which divided men into phlegmatic, choleric, sanguine and melancholic, according to their predominant mood, was no more than a recognition that feeling influences the train of thought, that ideas harmonize with emotional states. It was also a recognition that bodily conditions have great influence on our feelings. It is curious, indeed, that modern knowledge concerning hormones, supplied by glands to the blood stream, and some of which are closely related to emotional states, is so similar to the doctrine of humors in the blood, which were believed to determine mood and temperament. Our future knowledge of hormones and their effects will form a most interesting chapter in physiology and psychology. 

The moment we recognize the influence of feelings on association and thought we have passed beyond the association of ideas to a wider view. Ideas are associated with each other, but they are also associated with feelings and with impulses to acts. In the following schema, I stands for idea, F for feeling, and W for an impulse of the will to action. The following combinations may then be set down:

II 

IF

FF IW FW WW But it is the combination IFW which causes action rather than one of the combinations of the table. 

Should we consider such combinations, we should have passed far beyond the connections between ideas considered by pairs, and we should really be trying to describe some of the complications of association as it occurs in human experience. This we had better leave to the introspection and imagination of the novelist. If an idea is both recent and vivid, oft-repeated, and similar to other interesting ideas,

ASSOCIATION 

501 and if, in addition, it agrees with our mood, it will not only be recalled, but it may be hard to get rid of it when we may wish to do so. Possibly the "fixed ideas" of certain insane patients have most or all of these conditions in favor of their keeping a focal place in consciousness. 

Association in Practical Psychology.-In schools condi tions are arranged as far as possible so as to be favorable to a mood for study. The teacher knows, also, that if objects of instruction are presented in the relation of similarity, of contrast, of cause and effect, of sign and thing signified, or in numerous other relations, and the relationship made clear and emphasized, the data are remembered with almost no necessity for repetitions, while disconnected facts give the drudgery of learning. Therefore, the more and not the fewer the relations which the teacher can discover and point out, the more easily learning proceeds. It should be our duty to discover all the relationships which make learning easier and more permanent. 

If, in an attempt to determine how many times a list of nonsense syllables must be repeated in order to be learned, one or more of the syllables is recognized as similar to some word we know one glance serves to fix it for years.. 

In one instance, a professor of psychology offered the nonsense word "ergin" and gave it the meaning "work." But an erg is a unit of work in physics and instead of offering a difficulty in learning, the nonsense word could not be forgotten because of this association. It is next to impossible to defeat the mind in this relation-finding tendency. Almost any nonsense syllable will suggest some word which we already know or will link with another of the syllables, often in such a way as to give a meaning. 

Dissociated facts are remembered only after many repetitions; associated facts often after a single presentation.

If the emphasizing of connections is important to the teacher it is doubly so for the advertiser, who wishes his every statement to make some impression and their sum total to contribute largely to the permanent reputation of his business. For the same effect, advertisements may appear less frequently in proportion as they are better written, yet the aim of many a national advertiser seems to be that there shall be no one who has not seen his announcement recently, frequently and often in vivid electric signs.

Difference Between Learning and Habit Formation.—The process of learning makes use of all the laws of association stated above and really of many more. Similarity, for example, may be similarity in any feature, in any respect or in any relation that a given mind may detect. Besides these innumerable relations, learning depends upon mean. ing. Habit, of course, does not. It depends upon repetition and learning also demands repetition when the data to be learned have almost no associations, as in the case of nonsense syllables, disconnected symbols, etc. This seems to be the chief point of likeness between learning and the formation of a habit.

Again, men use entirely different language in describing learning and habit. We say we cannot "break” a habit, but do we ever say that we cannot break the remembrance of the dates and events of history, the facts of psychology or the technicalities of the law of property? No. We very readily forget them. Habits are few in number in each individual and they are permanent. The connections on which memory depends are numerous and impermanent. 

Once more, we learn much more rapidly than we form habits. I think these differences depend partly on the different neural conditions of the two processes. Habits de-

ASSOCIATION 

503 pend on the use of some final common path. Every repetition makes closer the connection of the final path with the numerous neurons of the next higher order to all of which it is common. The pattern is like that of a river which receives at its head innumerable smaller streams, every freshet in which deepens their channels at the entrance to the river. In learning, the discharges from various patterns do not use a single final path. A pattern due to learning may today be connected with another, but tomorrow with a quite different one according to temporary conditions of recency, vividness or a change of interest. 

Habit presents no such fluctuations. Its pattern of connections is different from cortical patterns. In fact the hair-trigger connections of the cortex, so quickly formed and so momentary at times, have been described as the means whereby it adapts us to a varying environment. The more permanent connections of lower centers adjust us very well to a fixed environment. Habit and memory, habit formation and learning seem, therefore, to be fundamentally different. Because of this it seems quite false to teach that habit in animals and learning in human beings are one and the same process, both governed only by frequency of repetition, and to ignore completely association by similarity. This teaching is itself insisting on the similarity between human and animal learning, when the difference is far more apparent and more important to emphasize. 

Surely the similarity between two things should not be employed to assert that there is no association by similarity. 

The assertion is not openly made. Instead such association is simply not mentioned in several recent text-books of psychology, so the beginning student would never know that such associations occur unless he made the discovery unaided. Professor McDougall gives further evidence of

the difference between habit and memory. Until his evidence is refuted, which seems improbable, we need not ignore these differences.

Mediate Association. First, let us take some typical examples. A list of nonsense syllables is being read to a bright student and to each syllable she is to respond with the first word which comes to mind. Among the syllables occurs "yag." Instantly there arises the picture of a masked man with a dark lantern and a jimmy, and considerably later the word, yeggman, comes to consciousness. Here the similarity of yag and yegg must have been, the student felt sure, the link between the stimulus-syllable and the mental image of the masked man, but the word, yegg, did not at once come to mind. The unconscious brain condition must have been the link between the syllable and the visual image. The intermediary was purely physiological. 

Again, while passing through a street in Leipzig and busied with reflections concerning his affairs, a German business man was surprised by the sudden arousal of images of localities in London with which he had been familiar many years before. A moment or two later he perceived the odor of an English tobacco, which had been smoked by many in those London localities, and with which he had become familiar during his residence there. Then he perceived a man several paces in front of him who was smoking this tobacco. The odor of the tobacco had evidently aroused the imagery of London without itself being perceived until later. Perhaps the odor would have remained unperceived had not the remembrance led to attention being given to its cause. 

The classical example of mediate association is that of Sir William Hamilton, who, after thinking of Loch Lomond, found himself thinking over the Prussian system of

ASSOCIATION 

505 education and later discovered that a Prussian officer, who had conversed with him on that subject when he had visited the lake, was the connecting link between the two series of thoughts.

If we accept the notion of brain patterns, which I have mentioned, it seems entirely reasonable that some element of a pattern might have no counterpart in consciousness, and yet, when active, it might serve to connect two other elements both of which do result in states of consciousness. 

This is the usual explanation offered by Scripture and others, while still other psychologists, as Münsterberg and Titchener, refuse to accept it. The latter believes that association requires attention. This might imply that there is no such thing as an involuntary train of thought, such as I am attempting to describe in this chapter. 

The experiences, of course, are not doubted, but only the explanation offered. The dispute is influenced also by each psychologist's opinion of subconscious and unconscious states and their possible influence on consciousness. 

The frequency of occurrence of mediate associations is also a matter of discussion. One writer thinks that they constitute 4% of all associations; others that they are so rare as to be almost negligible. 

Freely Arising Ideas and Perseveration.-Closely related to the question of mediate association is the further question, Can an idea arise freely and independent of any association or connection with the ideas already "before the footlights of consciousness"? Wundt believes that in all probability there is no reproduction without association, but he greatly broadens the concept of association. 

Herbart, on the contrary, thought that an idea would emerge in consciousness whenever it was not repressed or inhibited by ideas already there. It could, as it were,

bound into consciousness of its own elasticity whenever the inhibitions were removed. Herbart's psychology was finally rejected, though it furnished the basis of the "amusement doctrine" of education in America. 

Meanwhile, and quite independent of a priori theory, ideas do sometimes seem to arise spontaneously. A man suddenly thinks of a distant friend or of the debt that he owes, though such thoughts break all the bonds of association. A particular word is used repeatedly as a response in an association test, though the subject of the experiment is unconscious of the repetition. Doggerel verse or scraps of melody recur hauntingly and there are "fixed ideas" of the insane.

Two explanations are offered for this: (1) the associative links are unconscious or unnoticed and, if this be the case, we may have nothing more than examples of mediate association once more; (2) the idea arises of its own strength. The advocates of the latter view ascribe to the recurring idea a "perseverative tendency." This is no more than a name for the fact of recurrence. It explains nothing and reminds us of the famous explanation, that opium produces sleep because it has dormative powers, yet no doubt the fact should be named while we await its explanation. 

Besides all the above conditions, it has been suggested that the bizarre associations of many dreams may be due to brain conditions alone. The nervous impulses discharge through the pathways of greatest permeability, "like sparks in burnt up paper," to use Lowell's phrase.

The consciousness would then correspond to these random discharges. This hypothesis would, indeed, account for the lawless character of many dreams. 

The Direction of Association.-Under the alternate in-

ASSOCIATION 

507 fluence of one or another of these conditions our thought would surely zigzag in a most erratic way. This our involuntary thought seems to do save for certain causes which are said to influence its direction. It is pointed out for example that b follows a only if we are thinking alphabetically; e follows a if we are thinking of the vowels; a' or a" might follow it if our task was mathematical, etc. So when speaking French we do not think of German words, etc. Embarked on a given task (see pp. 510 ff.), the preceding associations determine with cumulative influence those which are next to come. In reciting one poem, for instance, we are never deceived into introducing a line from another, however similar the two may be. 

Each associative system remains pure and uninfluenced by other systems. Altogether, this is but saying that a cortical habit formed at one time will not interfere with one formed at another time in our personal history. I can see no more in this than the law of contiguity with which we started, on a somewhat wider scale. 

Our feelings also give direction to thought as I have already described, but perhaps interest is so influential in this particular that it deserves special mention. Listening for half an hour to the conversation of a group of men will often show how their interests influence the direction of their associations, and many believe that by such observation they can pick out the teacher, the merchant, the engineer, or the salesman by this revelation of their permanent interests. The fact is of importance for it shows the influence of environment on the human mind. 

Once a man has chosen a pursuit and devoted himself to it for some years his profession becomes his environment. Unconsciously his associations and opinions are warped and molded by the environment which hems them

in. Thousands of disagreements between individuals are accounted for by this fact alone. That we agree politically well enough to hold a great republic together is on the whole surprising, and due perhaps to the simple environment of an undeveloped country which gave us all somewhat similar experiences. It is to be noted that, in the cases mentioned, our habits have produced our interests rather than the reverse. The influence of our habitual stock of associations on any incoming new idea has frequently been named apperception, and under that title I wish in a succeeding paragraph to give examples of its effect, for it is of the utmost importance to both social psychology and progress. For the present we see that what 

I have called "systems of associations," feelings and especially interest operate to give direction to our involuntary trains of thought somewhat as a purpose or goal idea influences the direction and result of our voluntary thinking. Thus our reveries are perhaps saved from utter chaos.

Apperception and Prejudice. If the mere choice of a profession so shapes our associations as to produce misunderstandings what shall we say of the more powerful influence of earlier social environment? Surely nothing less than to point to the growing conviction of statesmen that boundary lines in Europe should be drawn in accordance with racial unity, i. e., that a people with a similar stock of ideas and associations should constitute a nation. In a word, until a given mind's associations are formed it can suit itself to any environment, whether on Earth or Mars; thereafter to only one environment and other social surroundings result in insuperable antagonisms.

The one thing that breaks into an established environment and threatens it most with change, is a new idea.

ASSOCIATION 

509 The stock of ideas born of that environment resists the acceptance of the new. To show the final power of association we have only to point to the strength of this resistance against certain new discoveries and this will show that association results in a social force of the first magnitude. 

Galileo lost his professorship, because he dared to dispute the authority of Aristotle. In fact so great was the influence of their stock of ideas on his colleagues that, when the different weights which he dropped from the tower of Pisa struck the earth at the same instant, they refused to believe the evidence of their senses. 

Daguerre was regarded by his friends as insane and they actually placed him in an asylum for a time because of his declaration that he could cause sunlight to make a picture on a plate of tin. Galvani was ridiculed by his friends and dubbed "the frog's dancing master" because of his pioneer discoveries in electricity. Franklin's paper on lightning conductors was considered foolish and refused publication by the British Royal Society, and, finally, when certain scientific pioneers in Europe resolved to extract nitrogen from the air on a commercial scale they found that they dare employ only young chemists in their work. The older chemists knew altogether too many reasons why the attempts were foredoomed to failure. In fact it is claimed that long technical training sometimes destroys originality by substituting scientific scruples for the more hopeful assurance of success.

Thus we find the reason for Professor James' statement that finally each of us must inevitably become an old fogy. 

With the stock of ideas and associations once fixed no further progress is possible. 

Voluntary Thought.—The founders of the associationist

school thought that the association of ideas, as they termed it, would account for every variety of thought. Yet the formula never quite covered the facts, for in their writings there occur examples of judgments based on experience and other illustrations of attentive, effortful thought. 

We may surely say, then, that voluntary thought differs from the passive flow of ideas in being governed by a purpose or goal idea. Ideas which promise to realize this goal are selected, detained and dwelt upon. Those which are irrelevant to our purpose are rejected, or in many cases almost completely suppressed, so that they hardly enter consciousness at all. This repression of certain thoughts by the task in hand, or Aufgabe, is an interesting discovery in the study of association and judgment. For instance 

Külpe found that if he instructed his subjects to direct their attention to the color of certain letters which he exposed quickly with a tachistoscope, the letters themselves were unnoticed. If attention was directed to the letters, their colors and arrangement were unnoticed. 

Again two Englishmen, who were masters of the German language, were responding to German stimulus words in a long association test. At the outset each had thought to himself, "I must not respond in English." As a result

English words rarely came to consciousness at all. In similar fashion, when one is asked to respond to nouns with adjectives other nouns are repressed, with co-ordinate words subordinates are suppressed, etc. Perhaps the most interesting feature of this is that the idea of the task may soon lapse from consciousness entirely and yet the responses are in complete harmony with it. The instructions, with which an association-test began, are forgotten yet they are obeyed implicitly, as if one by setting his mind to a task closed the door to intruding or distracting

ASSOCIATION 

511 thoughts. This fact was long ago observed and described in introspective psychology. It has recently been investigated and verified by experimental methods. Moreover, its investigators insist that in this influence of the task or purpose we have nothing less than the influence of the will in our thought. The fundamental difference between ordinary or "springing reproduction" (to use Ziehen's term), and judgment lies in the fact that in judgment the association must be meant, willed, or at the very least, recognized as suitable.

Nor need it be said that these results are the artificial product of the laboratory. Their truth is supported by daily experience. The increase of divorce is due to the fact that during the "task” of married life every thought of divorce is not repressed, so that it never comes to consciousness. Under the teachings of the times separation is present in consciousness as a possible alternative. Conversely, the steady payment by so many thousands of men of life insurance premiums for a term of at least twenty years, though accompanied by sacrifice and deprivation, is carried out faithfully just because the Aufgabe, from the very outset, permits not even a thought of the neglect of this duty. Only an era of speculation breaks down, in some minds, the instructions self-given at the outset. 

Voluntary thought is characterized further by a feeling of activity, and sometimes of very distinct effort, which is absent from revery. In the latter we often feel ourselves to be passive onlookers, in the former active participants or the agents of the whole process. The effort is that of voluntary attention as distinguished from the spontaneous variety. Judgment, reasoning, discrimination, study, active synthesis of ideas as distinguished from passive connection, etc., are the subdivisions or varieties of

the voluntary thought which results in productive work.

Experimental Results.-Experimental tests of associa tion have usually taken the form of pronouncing to the subject of the experiment a particular word to which he is to respond with the first word suggested to him by the stimulus-word. Or again, the stimulus-words may be presented visually, or objects, or pictures of objects may be presented. The tests have had various aims, to ascertain association-time, the various kinds of association, the occurrence of mediate associations, and to ascertain the particular realm of experience whence the associations come. 

Association-times vary considerably from person to person so their measurement really belongs to individual psychology, and average times would seem to be of value only as standards with which to compare individual variations if, indeed, their use for such a purpose may not be questioned. Wundt gives times ranging from 341 sigma for common associations, as Sturm-Wind, to 1190 sigma for less common ones, as Staub-Sand. The average reproduction-time is set down as 600-620 sigma, with the average for the most common associations as 300-450 sigma.

These figures are obtained by subtracting from the total time the recognition time of 100—130 sigma and the simple reaction-time. Ach has quite reasonably protested against such subtraction as arbitrary, and Henmon with equal reason in the case of discrimination time. The assumption that average reaction and recognition-times may be subtracted must be experimentally reviewed.

Irreversibility of Successive Association.—It is a matter of common observation that the learning of a series of items in one order is of almost no help if we wish to recite them in the reverse order. It is generally a hindrance to learning them in the opposite order. There are many series of such items, the letters of the alphabet, the days of the week, the months of the year, the number series, a poem or speech learned by heart, and so on.

The repro- duction of such a series can take place readily only in the direction in which it was practised, therefore, learning to read a foreign language is of almost no help toward learning to speak it. For mastery, practice must take place in both directions, e. g., English-Deutsch and Deutsch- 

English. Even when we attempt to recite the alphabet backward we really do not do so, but visualize to ourselves YZ, then XY, etc. Thus the best evidence of visual

imagination is found in the ability to spell ordinary words backward with some facility.

It has even been found that the same figures in the same order are added less rapidly and more accurately, when the adding proceeds downward instead of upward, if the person was originally trained to add upward. This difference in rate and accuracy is much more pronounced if the order of the figures is also reversed, and one professor of mathematics was fond of saying that he could never give the product of seven times eight until he repeated it as eight times seven. All this irreversibility must be due to brain conditions and to the direction of discharge of nervous impulses. The permeability of a synapse seems to be reduced for an impulse passing in one direction and heightened for one going in the opposite direction.

The Term, Association. The earlier discussions of association were carried on under the title, "association of ideas" (Ideenassoziation), and this usage is continued in the fairly recent writings of Ziehen. The present conception insists that the association is the connection, which must be assumed, between traces or impressions in the brain as the basis of future reproductions. If Messer² is to be credited, this is the most general usage of the term. 

If that be the case it will seem that an attempt to conceive the possible brain conditions in association by similarity is important, since that type of association is observed almost as frequently as association by frequency of repetition.

CHAPTER XVII DISCRIMINATION AND CONCEPTION 

Discrimination consists of noting the difference or differences between two objects of thought. Repeated acts of discrimination result in analysis and a great store of knowledge is the product of analysis. The ancients discriminated earth, air, fire, and water as the elements. 

Modern science has subdivided these into ninety-two elements, a few of which are seen by the mind's eye alone. 

But each of these substances, in turn, is composed of molecules, the molecules of atoms, and each atom of electrons, but long ago Franklin, who correctly forecast the existence of such "particles," divided them into two classes, positive and negative. The status of a race or a generation of men can be defined by the point it has reached in scientific analysis. 

The babe soon discriminates the people about him. A little later he can tell different kinds of food and he shows a preference for one and rejects the other. Perhaps such brain patterns as were suggested for association by similarity also lie at the basis of this, since they have paths which are not common, which might give the experience of difference as well as the common paths would give identity.

As McDougall suggests, the child's world is discriminated for him in large part by the race. To each separate thing a name is given and the very learning of the things with their names constitutes a practical analysis of the world. This is a social inheritance of the highest value.

DISCRIMINATION AND CONCEPTION 

517 The separate names bring to his attention differences which the race may have been long in discovering. Thus to differences directly perceived, others inferred, and still others, singled out in compounds we may add differences anticipated to exist between objects which have different names. Some names are not fully adequate, so definitions must be employed. The clearness of Professor Millikan, the winner of the Nobel prize, lies partly in his ability to state very exact definitions at the very borders of his abstruse science. Apparently because of this habit of keen discrimination and exact definition, he can arrange the most refined and illuminating experiments. Anyone who reflects on the use of separate names and the value of exact definitions in learning and teaching will hardly underrate the importance of the process of discrimination. The prevalence of tests of discrimination in intelligence tests shows that it is a large factor in general mental ability. To be called undiscriminating is a serious reproach. The college student who inquired, "What are Keats?" illustrates an inability to make a discrimination on the basis of names already applied by the race, but this is the type of exception which tends to prove McDougall's claim. The same author's statement, "If a human mind were developed by means of a perfect series of discriminations, under the guidance of a perfect language, it would achieve a (mental) structure which would be a perfect microcosm or mirror of the world" (p. 336), comes near describing the wide use of discrimination in a single sentence.

Conception. It is vitally important to note differences between pairs of ideas or their objects, but it is equally important to note and name likenesses. When a child says, "That isn't fair," he has already begun to form the abstract idea of justice and he has named it "being fair."

He has seen certain actions which were alike in being fair and certain others alike in the absence of that quality. The paradox, "Who taught you justice? The unjust," has much truth in it. The notion of a quality apart from the objects in which it is found is called an abstract concept. 

A mere list of some of the names of abstracts suggests their importance for thought. Energy, velocity, attraction, justice, virtue, integrity, courage, efficiency, and thoroughness are random examples. Since it is plain that these notions are formed by noting similarities between concrete instances, it seems probable that conception may be due to the activity of the common paths of brain patterns. It is claimed that if you continue to think intently of an abstract or general notion a particular concrete example will arise, i. e., impulses begin to discharge from the common into the non-common pathways of the brain patterns concerned.

General Concepts.-Abstract concepts are, of course, more general in their application than the concrete experiences from which they were derived, so they are often called general concepts. More exactly, however, general concepts are ideas or notions of classes. Liquids and gases may be termed fluids when we are thinking of their common properties. The term fruit includes everything which has pulp and seeds and is the outcome of vegetable growth. 

Without such general terms and ideas language would be hopelessly clumsy. Some Indians are said to have words for four species of oak but none for oak in general, and another tribe has thirty words for specific acts of washing but none for washing in general. (McDougall, p. 385.)

Problematic Concepts. When the mathematician sets down x as the answer to his problem, when he shall have solved it, he is helped by the device. The x is known only

DISCRIMINATION AND CONCEPTION 

519 by its relations. Until the problem is solved the x is problematic. The concept of the ether explains many phenomena but as long as it does not explain all, so that there is a rival explanation in the field, it is a problematic conception. Problematics are perhaps the most useful ideas for discovery. The scientist first does the experiment in his mind, then in his laboratory to test the truth of the problematic, and progress results. 

Race progress has been defined as due to bringing the work of genius within the reach and comprehension of the common people. The most useful works of geniuses are their inventions of abstract and general ideas; for example, the use of zero as a symbol of nothing and which gives place and value to the other digits. This was so abstract an idea that some fourteen centuries elapsed, after simple counting began, before its invention. Innumerable examples of the usefulness of abstract and general ideas could be given, but here we are concerned only to remark that the grade of pursuit or profession in which a man can succeed is determined largely by the point to which he can follow the genius in his abstractions and generalizations. 

If he can go far up the scale, a long list of pursuits is open to him which are closed to those who cannot follow so far. "Vocational guides" should recognize this fact. This shows also why intelligence tests are so valuable in the field of guidance. They too proceed to more and more refined discrimination and difficult abstraction. In this they approximate a reduced copy of a career.
