CHAPTER XVIII  

Habitual Associations. When considering perception we found that objects of thought suggest meanings. The whistle which I hear may suggest an oncoming motor car which, as a pedestrian, I must avoid, or, because their signals are similar, it may suggest an approaching interurban car, which I must strive to reach if I would begin my journey. My safety depends also on my not confusing these two meanings of similar whistles and giving to one the response which "belongs" to the other. These meanings are, as it were, agreed upon by the community, so they constitute nothing more than associations of ideas fixed by habitual experience. 

The higher animals seem to form such associations. 

The dog, for example, detects a threatening tone of his master's voice and slinks away, while a friendly call of the same voice makes him approach with every appearance of satisfaction or joy. Even fishes have been proved to approach the usual feeding place whenever they sensed the footsteps of their keeper. Under the influence of habit and repetition, therefore, animals with but rudimentary development of higher brain centers seem to associate a stimulus with a hurtful or beneficial experience. The meanings of certain stimuli are fixed by repetition and remain associated with their usual effects so long as exceptions do not occur.

Magic and Science. So much may be said for the meanings which objects may have. No animal, however, looks

for meanings which objects by their nature and relations must have. Primitive man, on the contrary, seems always to have believed in a connection between things and this belief led first to magic, then to the beginnings of science. 

Magic believed that one object can influence another. Rain might be started by sprinkling the ground or by incantations. "If you would have yams grow well in your garden, put a stone there that looks like a yam. If you wished to injure an enemy, you should either make an image of him or get some of his hair or other belongings, or get his name written. Injuring the substitute you thus made him suffer correspondingly. What made things act was the mysterious energy in them, and the more awful they were, the more of this mana they possessed. Common things needed no special explanation, remarkable things alone, odd things, especially deaths, calamities, diseases, called for it." 

As late as 1630 a French nobleman made the valuable discovery that branches of the alder and the willow could be used for the discovery of subterranean veins of water. 

Before the year 1692 the scientific world had no special interest in the matter. In that year, however, the divining rod was used to lead its bearer to the house of a man, who, on this evidence, was convicted of murder and actually executed. It was believed that thieves and murderers, as well as precious metals and veins of water could be discovered by the divining rod. Lehmann, from whose book I have taken the above account, thinks that "the divining rod is the last link in the great magical apparatus." "The learned world lost interest in the divining rod. But the belief in it still lives among ignorant folk." 

This history of the divining rod is one of the best ex- 

¹James, Wm., Some Problems of Philosophy, p. 17.

amples of the human belief in a connection between objects. It is curious that the belief should have existed so long before real connections were found to any important extent. However it originated, the belief that objects are connected or influence each other seems to be the human trait which lies at the basis of reasoning. Not only connection, but necessary connection, between objects is now a postulate of logic. This postulate is called the law of totality and says "that our knowledge is capable of arrangement in a self-consistent and harmonious system, which moreover in its content and form faithfully represents objective reality."

Doubtless this so-called law is still in need of complete proof, yet when we reflect that many objects of thought are material objects, whose behavior obeys material laws, that many other mental objects are forms between whose parts geometrical relations subsist, and finally that any quantity may be found if we know its relations, we have accounted for an enormous amount of connection between objects by the laws of physics and mathematics alone, not to mention the interrelations of these two sciences. Some add to this that a great deal of human behavior can be predicted en masse by means of statistics. It seems evident from all this that the primitive belief in a connection between things has, with fair warrant, become the law of totality in logic. The exceptions may be of the kind which increased knowledge will show to be only apparent ones. 

However, whether the law is universal in its application, or merely covers a wide range of instances, is of little practical importance. Every triumph of reason at least increases our confidence that objects are related and that judgment and reason can find these relations and their results.

The belief that objects are related and influence each other is probably due to the fact that human beings must deal with the future. The only guide for such dealings is the past. We observe the drift of past events and decide that the immediate future will show a similar array. If a bank has shown for several years past a steady increase of deposits and loans we decide that it will continue prosperous though we do not know the exact causes of its prosperity. Similarly with the securities of "seasoned" corporations. Having withstood the vicissitudes of years we decide by analogy with the past that they will continue to do so, though, for aught we know, destructive factors may be at work at the very moment of our decision. Tables of mortality and of prices furnish further examples. But such tables are statistics. We simply compare the facts of the present and the immediate past and, if our information goes no deeper than that, we decide that the future must be approximately similar. In recent years we are very likely to plot our statistics in the form of a curve. 

Such a graphic representation presented to the eye seems to simplify matters and make inference easier or more certain.

This inference by analogy of the future with the recent past seems to be the simplest form of inductive reasoning, yet there is a method less certain perhaps than that. Often we cannot collect all the facts which ought to appear in our statistics or graphs. Then we resort to sampling. We take typical prices and of their average we make an “index," or "barometer." Or the mining engineer "grabs" samples at many spots on the surface of the new body of ore and, having analyzed the samples, infers that the ore body must have a similar average value for its whole extent. This is called the method of incomplete enumera-

tion, but psychologically it is still the method of analogy. 

In both cases there is great risk that our conclusions will prove to be false.

Enumeration or statistics frequently enables us to reach conclusions of more than analogical certainty. If in a certain city one-fourth of the babies die in families whose income is $450 per year, one-sixth when the income is $450- $850, one-eighth when it reaches $850-1050, while only onesixteenth die before the close of the first year, when the income is $1050 or more, we are warranted in inferring that poverty is the chief cause of infant mortality in that city and in suspecting it to be a cause elsewhere. This detection of causes (or effects) as a result of the analysis of conditions and the discovery of general characteristics from the study of particular ones seems to be the chief work of genuine or highly developed inductive reasoning. 

The mental process is more complicated and the conclusion far more certain than in inferences of the simpler type. 

The Methods of Induction.-If the examples above are typical the following outline suggests the methods of induction: by similarity of conditions or characters analogy partial 

Methods of 

Induction with or by enumeration without exceptions complete scientific analysis We must not regard these methods as separate, however, in actual reasoning. A stroke of one is often followed instantly by a stroke of the other. Analogical insight may detect a true cause which is verified by analysis, etc.

Analogy. In the examples of analogy which I have given we infer a set of conditions because we detect no factor capable of changing in a new way the present status of affairs. The change, if there be any, must be like the changes of the recent past. Psychologically this is a sort of analogy by negation.

In positive analogy there is a trifle more of analytical insight. We associate together and consequently form classes of objects which are similar in some respect. Then we are led to infer that the behavior of one object will be like that of another to which it is similar. As Bosanquet says, "in analogy we weigh the instances rather than count them," and, as already stated, detecting analogies in some respect is an important preliminary to many discoveries. 

Darwin saw the analogy between a breeder's selection of stock to breed from and nature's selection of the "fittest" to survive. Newton detected the analogy between a falling object and the motions of the moon; Hargreave, between an overturned spinning wheel which continued its motion, and the spinning jenny of many spindles, etc.

The method of enumeration often ends in analogy. 

Having noted all the instances we can, we decide that those we have not observed, being analogous, will follow the same rule. For example, having found some fact to be true of the chlorides of sodium and potassium we may suspect that it will hold true also of the chlorides of lithium and ammonium. 

Professor Hibben says, "Analogy should never be regarded as having more weight than extremely high probability. Its true function is suggestive, leading to hypothesis and experiment, and it needs this supplementary proof. 

A child might conclude that oil would put out fire, because it so closely resembles water."

The Method of Enumeration.-Does the character x al ways and invariably belong to the complex y? Are all swans white? Do all flying birds have their large bones hollow and full of air cells? Here we are seeking for a similar character in all the instances of the complex. By the method of enumeration we count the instances in which the character x is present. But in some cases we cannot examine all the instances. The conclusion cannot be certain and we consequently call the statement an empirical law. If no exception has been found, however, we have great confidence that the law is likely to include new instances.

In other cases we can enumerate all the instances of the occurrence of x with y, or we can be certain that those we have enumerated are exactly like those we have not observed. This is complete enumeration as distinguished from the partial enumeration of the preceding paragraph. 

In complete enumeration, if there are no exceptions we are said to have made a perfect induction. All the planets can be observed to move around the sun. Certain statements can be made of the whole class of triangles though we cannot have observed them all.

In both partial and complete enumeration we often find exceptions and consciously or unconsciously we note the proportion of exceptions to the total number of instances. On this basis we calculate our chances of success in adopting a given course. Most or many ships complete their voyages, so we embark on this one. Many men are honest so we loan a small sum to an applicant though he is a partial stranger.

Our lives are filled with the taking of such risks on the basis of empirical laws and a more or less rapid calculation of the chances for success. If the calculation is

more rapid the number of correct decisions is decreased enormously. The executive who decides rapidly decides wrongly. If there is wisdom in counsel it is because all the probable results of a course of action are likely to come under review if we listen to the opinions of many unprejudiced men, while an oligarchy is almost always in error. The deliberate method whereby Benjamin Franklin assured attention to all the reasons, both for and against a course of action, is described on page 578. 

Professor James seems to think that impulsive natures may retrieve their mistakes. Thus they substitute a sort of experiment for deliberation. Like a child, they must be burned before they will dread the fire. A census of their successes and failures would doubtless compare very unfavorably with those of the deliberate type, however brilliant and unexpected their fewer successes may be. 

But the deliberate type is much more reliable, since reversing decisions is a far less frequent method of procedure with them.

Much of the dramatic quality of life would be absent had we not so often to decide under the guidance of empirical laws and the calculation of chances. Yet increase of knowledge removes each year many important concerns from the realm of chance and probability to that of certainty, as science is substituted for empiricism. It must not be denied, however, that in many of our decisions we must be guided by analogy, by enumeration complete or partial and in most cases exceptions are numerous. Even with such data, reason would work well and give us a strong probability of success were it not that conditions are forever changing. What was true yesterday is not true today, so that the business man was wise who, when asked his opinion, replied, "We cannot be sure. You see these

changes always happen in the night." He understood the vicissitudes of his hazardous business, which so often baffle human forecasting. 

Yet to the man with a "head for risks," who stakes his future on analogy and slender evidence and wins, society responds by saying, "Now take what reward you will.”

This is regarded in some quarters as a serious social injustice since often what "happens in the night" favors venturesome forecasts and thus success becomes a matter of chance. He who protests against this social psychology, however, will find himself flying in the face of an ageold habit of the race, born when he who successfully led a forlorn hope became the king and ruler of the people. 

The Method of Scientific Analysis. This is the search for causal connection. We need a greater certainty for our forecast than that given by analogy and enumeration. 

This can be gained only if we can isolate the essential factors from their irrelevant concomitants. Let us take some examples. The statistics of infant mortality mentioned above point straight to poverty as the cause of the slaughter of the innocents. If with this factor in the focus of our attention we study other cases of a high death rate for babes we can determine whether it is a chief cause. 

Archimedes was set the problem of finding whether the gold supplied to make a crown had been alloyed with baser metal by the goldsmith. This was to be done without injuring the crown. Reflecting on this problem, he noticed, while in his bath, that his body was buoyed up by the water and with that his problem was solved. 

Whether the story is true or not it illustrates ideally the work of reason. If Archimedes at once decided that a body placed in a fluid is buoyed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced, he had discovered the law

of specific gravity or density. Probably his first analogical insight did not penetrate so deeply as that. More probably he guessed at a constant support for each type of substance and verified that hypothesis by weighing various objects in air and in water. One of the objects must have been some pure gold. No doubt the attempt at verification led to the discovery of the exact relationship. 

This discovery of the relation between the weight of a body and that of a fluid displaced by it illustrates the work of analytical, inductive reasoning. Nor will the thoughtful reader miss the fact that the discovery resulted from an experiment, though it was an experiment unconsciously set. "Diamonds, rubies and sapphires are now tested by floating to prove their genuineness. The liquid used has five times the density of water. 

The tests are rapidly made, as all stones of the same nature have the same specific gravity, while none of the bogus ones have the same weight as those they are made to imitate." (Hibben.)

This is simply a modern application of Archimedes' principle, a deduction from the law he discovered. That gold is 19.36 times as heavy as the same volume of water and diamond 3.53 times as heavy are now essential elements of the concepts of gold and diamond. These elements were discovered by analysis, notwithstanding that the analysis had to be verified and given an exact statement by experiment. The first process of inductive reasoning, after the collecting of the facts, is, therefore, penetrating analysis. 

Simple qualities suggest their relations and consequences much more clearly and certainly than the compounds in which they occur. Consequently the sciences, which are pre-eminently the work of reasoning, are due to more and more refined abstraction.

Moreover reason seems to be baffled only when analysis cannot isolate the abstract necessary to the solution of the problem, as the following example shows. It was long known that fevers abound in the neighborhood of swamps, that they were prevalent in new countries where swamps had to be drained before farms could be established. In truth the term miasma, or swamp-gas, was used as a name for a disease-producing exhalation of the swamp, which was supposed to cause fevers. Darwin had even written the following lines, "In all unhealthy countries the greatest risk of fever is run by sleeping on shore. Is this owing to the state of the body during sleep, or to a greater abundance of miasma at such times? It appears certain that those who stay on board a vessel, though anchored at only a short distance from the coast, generally suffer less than those actually on shore." (Voyage of a Naturalist, quoted by Hibben.) This remark shows that the fertile mind of

Darwin had already gone part way toward isolating the cause of the disease. He asked the question but could not answer it. Perhaps he was blinded by the very word, miasma, which named the current theory of the cause of fever. Thus it remained for Carroll and other medical men to infer that fevers are due to mosquitoes, then to a germ carried by mosquitoes, and to prove their inference correct. Doubtless the discoveries of Pasteur taught the later investigators what to look for while analysis could proceed no further in Darwin's time. Yet their reasoning led to the banishment of yellow fever and the control of malaria with the consequent prolonging of life and the making habitable for white men of great regions which were deadly before. Finally, this conquest of medical knowledge made possible the digging of the Panama Canal,

Because of such achievenments the work of reason is prized more highly than that of any other human faculty. 

The Procedures of Scientific Analysis. We have seen that what I have called genuine or typical inductive reasoning always involves analysis and is usually a search for the causes of phenomena. A careful comparison of the procedures employed in many cases of discovery led John 

Stuart Mill to describe what he termed the "Four Experimental Methods," though there are in fact five procedures.

Whenever a number of observations can be assembled as Mill describes, the mind is likely to hit upon the true cause of the fact observed but by virtue of association by similarity the mind is also likely to group together just those instances which have at least one element or factor in common. Thus we see that association by similarity is a fundamental factor in reasoning and a statement of the "four methods" seems to be no more than a description of the mental processes which occur in all successful induction. These processes are named as follows: 

(1) The method of agreement. 

(2) The method of difference. 

(3) The joint method of agreement and difference. (4) The method of concomitant variations. (5) The method of residues.

The Method of Agreement.-Mill used the capital letters as symbols of antecedents, the small letters to designate consequents. Thus, if with ABC we find ayz and with ADE we find ast and with AOP occurs aqr etc. etc. we are led to the inference that A is the cause of a. 

Of course the criticism is true that nature's instances

of complexes are by no means so simple, so sharply differenced, nor so easily factorable as these cases represented by symbols. It may be replied that only after such reflection and discrimination by the reasoner as brings the elements to almost this degree of sharpness is a discovery likely to be made. Nature does not sharply differentiate the elements. The successful reasoner does so. The average observer might notice hundreds of times that the air grows warmer when the snow begins to fall without being able to hit upon the single factor on which the increase in temperature depends. The good reasoner would isolate the cause very quickly. Similarly, it is easy to observe that an increase in temperature is followed by the expansion of any ordinary metal but such observation provokes in the reasoner the invention of the molecular theory. The method of agreement, therefore, may suggest a cause. It does not guarantee its discovery. The remembering and collection of similar instances is thus a preliminary to successful analysis. It cannot be denied, however, that if one event uniformly follows another we have a strong tendency to believe the first to be the cause of the second, even when analysis cannot penetrate to explanation. At present the method of agreement finds a wide application in statistics.

Besides the fact that it may not be easy to find the common element in the antecedents, this element may prove to be a mere accompaniment and not essential to the production of the effect. Again, the cause to which the method points may not be the only cause, and, once more, the cause may be present and yet produce no effect because of the presence of counteracting influences. All this amounts to saying that the method gives only more or less probability, not certainty, and that it must be used as an aid to

analysis, not as a substitute for it. As already remarked, however, human beings must act on probabilities in many of the affairs of life in which certainty with regard to the outcome is not attainable.

The rule for the method of agreement is stated by Professor Hibben as follows: "If two or more instances of the phenomenon under investigation have only one circumstance in common, the circumstance in which alone all the instances agree is the probable cause (or effect) of the given phenomenon or sustains some causal relation to it." 

The Method of Difference.-"If an instance in which the phenomenon under investigation occurs and an instance in which it does not occur have every circumstance save one in common, that one occurring only in the former, the circumstance in which alone the two instances differ is the effect, or it may be the cause, or a necessary part of the cause of the phenomenon."

Permitting two men to sleep on the Roman Campagna unprotected from mosquitoes and two others to sleep there perfectly protected from them is an instance of the application of this method. Only the former two contracted fever. It is plain that mosquitoes must be suspected as the cause, or bearers of the cause of fever, before such an experiment would be devised. Thus the four methods are often methods of verification, sometimes aids in suggesting hypotheses. 

Sir Robert Boyle in 1670 observed that an acid turns extract of litmus red. The acid was believed to be the cause since experience is continually showing that litmus untouched by acid or oxygen remains blue.

Obviously the method of difference may be used to confirm the method of agreement. Elements suspected of being causal may be withdrawn or re-introduced at will in

experiments. There are of course precautions to be observed in applying the method but they need not be discussed here.

The Joint Method of Agreement and Difference.—The method of difference deals usually with only two instances. 

Since withdrawing the suspected cause might destroy the phenomenon itself or might be impossible by known methods and, since it might also be impossible to neutralize the effect of the supposed cause, it is customary to select other phenomena as much as possible like the one in question, except that the causal element is absent.

For example, we may wish to know whether the power of shrimps and similar animals to maintain a normal position in the water is due to the eyes or to the statocyst organs? Or are the statocysts organs of hearing? The eyes may be painted over or, because they are located on stalk-like projections, they may be cut off and the experimenter may wait for shock effects to pass away. One or more statocysts may be removed or the statoliths may be washed out of the open statocysts, or the shrimp, which has shed its skin, may not be allowed to form new statoliths or it may be allowed to form statoliths of iron filings on which a magnet would act as gravity acts on natural statoliths. If the equilibration of the animal is altered by every one of these experiments on the statocysts and the statoliths and is not altered by interfering with its vision and if, moreover, its hearing is unchanged by the experiments on the statocysts or statoliths we may be sure that the latter organs taken together are exclusively organs of equilibration and that the animal has a true, special, static sense.

Whether alcohol is a cause of crime, whether coffee interferes with sleep, etc., may be learned by this method, if

the method of difference alone does not give convincing results. 

The rule or canon of this method is stated thus: "If several instances in which the phenomenon occurs have only one circumstance in common, while several in which it does not occur have nothing in common save the absence of that circumstance, the circumstance in which alone the two sets of instances differ is the effect, or cause, or a necessary part of the cause of the phenomenon." 

The Method of Concomitant Variations. Professor Hibben states the canon of this method as follows: "What ever phenomenon varies in any manner, whenever another phenomenon varies in some particular, is either a cause or an effect of that phenomenon, or is connected with it through some fact of causation."

The steady increase in the volume of a metal with rising temperature, presents perhaps the simplest example of the method of concomitant variations, and the observation led to the invention of the ordinary thermometer. Yet temperature is not the sole cause of a change of volume unless the pressure remains constant.

The increase in the number of particles in solution with the degree of dissociation of certain chemical salts furnishes another illustration of concomitant variations. 

It is especially in the use of this method of discovery or proof that we are led to plot curves to show the relation of the two variables. If distances along a base line were made to represent degrees of temperature and distances along ordinates to represent the height of a column of mercury, a curve could be drawn which would give the height of the mercury column for every temperature. Such curves, or the tables from which they are plotted, are of great convenience as standards of reference, whenever

the values have been determined with scientific accuracy. 

It would be a great error, however, to plot a few points on a curve and then to extend it according to the few observations already made. The relationship discovered might hold true for only a short distance along the curve. Water, for example, contracts on cooling generally, but it expands from 39° F. to the freezing point. Almost innumerable instances could be given of a change in the relationship between the two variables even though they still vary con comitantly.

The method of concomitant variations and the plotting of results obtained by it are of very wide application. It was found that there is an increase in the number of deaths from grippe with every marked increase in humidity merely by plotting the chart of humidity and comparing it with the death rate from that disease. The U. S. Treasury is said to discover a curious relationship between the lowering of temperature in autumn and the amount of burned paper money sent in for redemption. Beginning at the north of the country the burned money comes in from farther and farther south as the onset of cool weather proceeds southward. The only conclusion is that people use heating stoves in summer in which to conceal sums of money and forget its presence there when fires are lighted in the autumn. The prevalence of the custom would hardly be suspected if the money were not sent to one place for redemption. The calculation of coefficients of correlation seems to be only an extension and refinement of the method of concomitant variations.

The Method of Residues. The rule of this method is, "Subduct from any phenomenon such part as is known by previous inductions to be the effect of certain antecedents,

and the residue of the phenomenon is the effect of the remaining antecedents."

By the use of this method the planet Neptune was discovered by Adams and Le Verrier, who were working on the problem independently and who yet reached the same result. "These astronomers had observed certain perturbations in the planet Uranus. It did not keep its proper orbit as determined by their mathematical calculations based upon the presence of the known stellar bodies. It behaved as though beyond its orbit was an outer planet, whose presence alone could account for the observed perturbations. 

Adams and Le Verrier then proceeded to calculate the exact position of such a disturbing body as determined by the nature and magnitude of the perturbations of Uranus. The telescope was then pointed to the exact point in the heavens, as thus indicated, and the planet Neptune was revealed to the eye according to the determination of farreaching prophecy, which confidently asserted that it must be there." (Hibben.)

The method of residues has been used abundantly to detect the difference between theory and fact in just this fashion. In the above example the difference was so great that a new world was required-and found-to account for it.²

Darwin especially employed this method of residues in his reasoning. His son said of him, "There was one quality of mind which seemed to be of special and extreme advantage in leading him to make discoveries. It was the power of never letting exceptions pass unnoticed. Everybody notices a fact as an exception when it is striking or frequent, but he had a special instinct for arresting an exception. A point apparently slight and unconnected with his 

Note that most of the evidences for the Einstein theory are of this nature.

present work is passed over by many a man almost unconsciously with some half-considered explanation, which is in fact no explanation. It was just these things that he seized upon to make a start from. In a certain sense there is nothing special in this procedure, many discoveries being made by means of it. I only mention it because, as I watched him at his work, the value of this power to an experimenter was so strongly impressed upon me.” 

I make this quotation because the habit of studying exceptions especially is now ascribed to almost all great scientists. Every distinguished physical chemist is said to have said, "Where you find an exception or deviation from law, there begin your investigation." Franklin's method of balancing reasons for and against a given course, and of acting as the remainder indicated, is after all a use of the method of residues applied to judgment instead of reasoning.

These methods of induction should be studied because they are the methods of successful thinking in life and in business as well as in science, discovery, and invention. 

Whether the thinker consciously knows it or not, he does follow one or another of these methods in thinking if he thinks effectively. Many young men in laboratories now pick up a hint of the methods by imitation and piecemeal. 

They would master the uses of all of them more quickly and use them more certainly if, in addition to imitation, they should learn the names and rules of the methods and some of the discoveries which have been made by means of them.

Mill, it is true, described the methods in his logic, but it is admitted that in describing them he had simply crystallized "the principles and practices of the scientific investigators who had caught and reflected the spirit of mod-

ern research." These methods are grounded in turn on association by similarity and contrast. They are methods of comparison and contrast and the mental process is the same whether similarities are noticed more or less formally. Psychology must give some account of the associative processes of constructive thought as well as of those of the passive flow of ideas.

Pure Belief and Control Experiments.-Anyone, who has framed a hypothesis or a theory which seems reasonable, is likely to have arise within him a firm belief that his theory is indubitably true. Unconsciously he becomes a partisan of his opinion and criticism of it arouses within him antagonism, resistance, and feeling instead of openminded reconsideration. Facts which speak definitely against his theory are dismissed rather than considered, or he replies to them plausibly rather than with disproof. Every human belief or theory seems to struggle vigorously for selfpreservation. This attitude is unscientific. A theory is a thing to be tested and verified, not a thing to be fought for like a social or political reform. In the account of magic we have seen what absurd beliefs the human mind can hold without questioning them in the least and in spite of facts to the contrary. The witchcraft delusion may be added to the list there given, a genuine delusion held by sane minds. 

The strong tendency to distort facts to conform to a theory seems to be a vestige of this ancient, strong devotion to pure beliefs. To correct this tendency, so-called, “control experiments" should be employed wherever they are possible.

It is not sufficient that, if a drug has been administered to an animal, its condition should be ascribed to the action of the drug unless another animal under exactly the same conditions, except the absence of the drug, presents a different state of health. Otherwise it is pure assumption

to believe that the drug was the sole cause of the first animal's symptoms. It is difficult to believe that such control precautions should be taken in every case, but experience has abundantly proved the need of them. Control experiments are examples of the method of difference. We are concerned here, however, with the fact that, unless a control is employed, the investigator presents merely evidence and sincere belief instead of the clearest obtainable proof. 

If someone else tests his theory by experiment and finds it false, he finds it hard indeed to correct his opinions. 

Many examples could be given from present-day science, or pseudo-science. Years have been wasted in this fruitless struggle to maintain false theories. It requires enormous force of character on the part of an investigator to admit that the very method by which he made his announced discovery was faulty and "uncontrolled." Very few men possess that degree of candor, and sometimes it seems as if control experiments were omitted for the very purpose of permitting audacious theories to be announced and to provoke wide discussion before they provoke rigorous experimental tests. Such procedure immediately redounds to practical advantage but it delays the advent of the truth.

Genuine Induction. Following current opinion I have regarded the analytical method as necessary to complete or genuine induction and analogy and enumeration as partial or preliminary processes. If current opinion is correct no improvement can be made upon Professor James' definition of reasoning as "the substitution of parts and their implications or consequences for wholes." we can isolate the effective factor, whose consequences we know, great certainty results. Nevertheless, conclusions must often be drawn and action be taken on the basis of If

a similarity of the present situation with the past ones with which we are familiar. In other words much of our reasoning is of the probable type.

Accident and Experiment in Discovery.-Intentional and systematic experiments are now a regular aid to analysis and verification. Yet the history of discovery and invention shows, I think, that the earliest experiments were accidental ones, like that of Archimedes. A swinging chandelier suggests the invention of the pendulum, a falling apple the attraction between the planets, and it can hardly be doubted that some campfire burning above an ore melted out some of the metal it contained. Thenceforth the concept of an ore included a content of one or another metal. In this case the accident led not only to analysis but to a method of extracting metals, which could hardly have been hit upon by thought alone. No doubt accident still aids discovery for, while the result of experiment often disproves one theory, it gives hints toward another truer one. Accident is never an aid to discovery, however, unless it happens to the "prepared mind."

Deduction. Whether the text be English or German, tradition seems to demand that an account of deduction begin with the time-worn syllogism, Alle Menschen sind sterblich,

Sokrates ist ein Mensch, Also ist Sokrates sterblich. 

It has been wisely enough remarked that anyone who doubted the mortality of Socrates would doubt the first statement or major premise, and, in turn, if that premise were doubted the death of Socrates might also be in doubt. 

Plainly the fact is that reasoning, in order to be of value, must bring to light new truth.

The relation of deduction to induction is better shown

in the following example, which resulted in the discovery of antiseptic and asceptic methods. "In simple fracture of the ribs, if the lung be punctured by a fragment, the blood effused into the pleural cavity, though freely mixed with air, undergoes no decomposition. Why air introduced into the pleural cavity through a wounded lung should have such wholly different effects from that entering directly through a wound in the chest was to me a complete mystery until I heard of the germ theory of putrefaction, when it at once occurred to me that it was only natural that air should be filtered of germs by the air passages, one of whose offices is to arrest inhaled particles of dust and prevent them from entering the air cells." (Professor Lister.)

In this instance, while the method of difference was not effective in leading to the discovery of the cause, Professor Lister could at once deduce the cause from the germtheory of putrefaction.

In natural science induction and deduction will usually be found as closely interwoven as in this instance. A stroke of one prepares the way for a stroke of the other. 

The general principle and the abstract quality suggest their implications and consequences much more readily than do concrete instances which may include a host of irrelevant particulars. 

The student who has mastered geometry has practised deduction or the application of general principles to particular instances in the realm of forms, where the use of deductive processes is peculiarly clear and uncomplicated. 

No better examples of deduction could be given.

EXERCISES 

1. A class in college was given an intelligence test. At the end of a term it was found that of the quarter of the class ranking highest in intelligence 8% had failed; in the next quarter 13%; in the third quarter 29%; and in the quarter of lowest intelligence scores 57% failed. To what extent is intelligence a cause of success in college studies? Is it the sole cause? What method of reasoning do these facts illustrate? 

2. If the student with the highest rank in intelligence had held the highest place in scholarship and all others had kept the same relative place in both series of scores: (a) What place could be assigned to intelligence as a cause of success? (b) How would the conclusion be affected if some students carried 10 hours, others 15? 

3. Name all the causes of success in studies whose effects you think could be reliably measured. Those whose effects cannot be measured. 

4. To what extent can success or failure be predicted in this field? 

5. Give worthwhile examples of the use of each of the methods of induction. 

6. If a culture of typhoid bacilli stands for months beside a similar vessel of once sterilized beef tea, both covered with gauze, but the air freely accessible to both, what will be the result? How would this affect the miasma theory of infection?

CHAPTER XIX 

ATTENTION Bodily Accompaniments of Attention. It is less difficult to give a behavioristic account of attention than to analyze the psychological process. A French phrase for listening intently is tendre l'oreille, and my friend with a highpowered motor car says he cannot drive fast without leaning forward. From this bodily adjustment attention has been named. Men not only lean forward toward any object which they wish to perceive more clearly, but both men and animals turn the head and body toward a stimulus to which they are attentive. Men converge the eyes upon it and accommodation takes place. The eyes may be half closed. The body becomes motionless. There is tension of the muscles. Breathing stops momentarily and, when it begins again, attention is diminished. If attention is more prolonged, the breathing is shallow. The heartbeat is changed and becomes slower in rapt attention. There may be decrease in the volume of the arm, indicating that blood has been withdrawn to the brain from the rest of the body. The pulse rate and blood pressure change.

Nowhere is this immobility and breathless attention seen more clearly than in wild animals. Their very life often depends upon the alertness of their attention, and the consequent promptness and correctness of their reactions. When such animals have been half-tamed, their keen attention to the trainer or keeper often leads to muscle reading, which he does not suspect. Probably, there-

fore, the animals give us examples of the most intense attention, though its scope may be quite narrow. 

If attention is to be given to some intellectual object, instead of to an external one, the bodily conditions are no less marked but they are quite different from those of the latter case. The eye muscles are relaxed. The stare becomes fixed but aimless. The brow may be wrinkled, the fists clenched and the whole play of the features is characteristically different from that in sensorial attention.

The bodily movements serve two purposes and are of two kinds: (1) movements of adjustment for the clearer reception of the stimulus or for the clearer grasp of the idea, (2) movements of inhibition or movements which tend to exclude other stimuli from the sensory field and which help to prevent other ideas from entering the field of consciousness. Consequently, when attentive, we are like a delicate optical instrument, adjusted for the objects which lie in a single plane, but that very adjustment makes the objects which lie in other planes obscure and ill-defined. This is Meumann's conception of the effect of bodily adjustment in attention. So far as the body is concerned attention is an activity, a vigorous and sometimes a violent adjustment of the whole organism to the reception of the stimulus. Our activity in making such adjustment has much to do with the clearness of the idea or sensation to which the adjustment has been made. Thus attention seems to be partly a bodily process. Even Professor Titchener, who holds that the word "active," when applied to attention, is a misnomer, says, "We may assume that attention in its beginnings was a definitely determined reaction of the whole organism-sensory, affective, motor-upon a single stimulus." (T. B., p. 281.)

ATTENTION 

547 

The Character of the Stimulus.-While we may conven iently name the characters of the stimuli which arouse human attention, no one should imagine that the stimulus as such arouses attention. Only its relation to the human mind and nervous system makes it stimulating at all. 

Some stimuli which are intense when applied to men are not stimuli for animals at all. Some are stimulating to both. Strictly, therefore, the conditions of attention are all subjective conditions. If nothing within us responds, the stimulus might discharge energy forever and yet receive no attention. The stimuli which do arouse attention are determined, no doubt, by natural selection in the development of the nervous system of each animal. By describing the stimuli we may, if we are thoughtful, gain some knowledge of the mental and emotional nature of the individual and the race.

A stimulus which is intense or novel or unexpected or in strong contrast with present impressions or ideas instantly provokes attention. Any one of these characters or all of them taken together may be depended upon if we wish to attract attention. They are employed for this purpose in the business of advertising. If a headline is especially large or clear we say it is "striking." But if the statement is novel or unexpected the same result is attained.¹ The use of colors and of types of various sizes involves contrast and the skillful use of margins and of wide interlinear spaces seems to depend upon the same psychic factor. Pictures are more stimulating than words, apparently because the printed word came into the environment of the race but yesterday. But this is also connected with the fact that we say an advertisement must be "attractive," For example "The berth of a nation," for Simmons beds, or "From the engaging age of six to the engagement age of twenty," we have gowns, etc.

i. e., if a stimulus or an object gives pleasure it arouses and sustains attention.

Again if a statement or object or an example of behavior is mysterious or secret or baffles expectation or explanation, attention is sharply stimulated by it. Students of psychology today are interested in hypnotism, the subconscious, double or divided personality, telepathy and theories of dreams quite as much as their ancestors were interested in magic and witchcraft. An enigma, puzzle or riddle rarely fails to provoke attention. This interest in the mysterious or the occult begins earlier in life than we think. A child of seven had read to her for the first time the opening chapter of a story with an element of the mysterious. She demanded that the first instalment be re-read four times. Then she read it twice more herself and the magazines containing the denouement of the plot had to be purchased. As long as the mystery deepened the interest was sustained. This interest in what is not understood is the germ of scientific curiosity. 

Bright objects, moving things, most animals, strange persons and the doings of all the persons we see about us appear to be instinctively interesting. Apparently these objects appeal to interests which have become ingrained during the history of the race because attention to them has always contributed to self-preservation.

The sexes differ somewhat in these interests. If a child is led along a village street hardly a woman will fail to notice its presence and no man will do so. 

Professor James gives a brilliant list of the activities which instinctively arouse our attention. "With the child life is all play and fairy tales and learning the external properties of things; with the youth it is bodily exercises of a more systematic sort, novels of the real world, boon-

ATTENTION 549 fellowship and song, friendship and love, nature, travel and adventure, science and philosophy; with the man, ambition and policy, acquisitiveness, responsibility to others and the selfish zest of the battle of life." Most of the objects of these interests arouse spontaneous attention at the periods mentioned. Spontaneous attention is said to be more passive than the intellectual, voluntary variety. 

This statement must be discussed later. 

In order to be attended to for any considerable length of time a stimulus must change but it must not change too quickly. The unchanging object soon wearies attention. 

The instantly disappearing or constantly changing object escapes it. Perhaps the latter statement is illustrated at present by cinema pictures. One changes in to another so swiftly that very few of the spectators retain anything of what has passed. This fact should be considered by those who expect moving pictures to become a means of education. Note how little is told of what has been seen on the screen. A certain amount of time is necessary to bring attention to its full effect.

Again, what appeals to but one sense is less likely to arouse sustained attention than an object of two or more senses. Reading aloud maintains attention more readily than silent reading. An object which is both seen and handled receives prolonged attention. Drawing and modeling are perennial sources of interest in the child as well as means of discovery of "the external properties of things." The importance of all sorts of Arbeitschulen, insisted on by modern pedagogy, finds its psychological ground in these facts. We shall find that the effort of voluntary attention arises when there is a conflict between two interests. Different senses either antagonize or re-enforce each other hence the ease with which we give atten-

tion to any manual performance which enlists at least two senses. It is an example of the simultaneous summation of stimuli. Yet when the measurement of attention has been perfected I think it will be found that less attention is required for manual than for mental work. Hence brain workers find gardening or carpentering a source of relaxation.

Intellectual Attention.-From the statements just made it is evident that we can name the kinds and qualities of stimuli which arouses spontaneous attention in all normal human beings. The reason for this is the fact that human beings have instincts in common which determine spontaneous attention. The instincts are inherited and, therefore, the attention. Aside from this common inheritance each of us varies from his neighbor in the objects to which he gives his attention. First, no doubt, due to individual gifts and later, due to experience, training or investigation, we acquire certain stocks of ideas. The presence of these leads us to notice and remember all similar instances which by the laws of association group themselves with the original stock and seem to increase its attractive force. Thus we acquire permanent interests which end by shaping our intellectual lives. All facts and experiences which have a relation to these interests instantly attract and sustain attention while irrelevant facts are neglected or forgotten.

Anticipatory Images and Ideas. It seems desirable to attempt to describe a little further this chief subjective factor of attention. Let us take a simple but perhaps a common example, namely, the experience of one who for the first time attempts to use a microscope of high power. Under direction he has carefully prepared, cut, and stained a thin section of tissue. He places it under the object glass

ATTENTION 551 and, try as he will, he sees just nothing at all but a conglomerate blur of color which is perhaps not quite homogeneous throughout. He sees nothing definite. At this point in his discouragement the expert instructor comes to his assistance, who asks whether this or that structure is distinguished and the answer is an emphatic No. Then the instructor sketches the field. "Now in the upper left quadrant do you see a black cone-shaped structure with its apex at the surface of the tissue?" Then in a few moments the answer is Yes. "And extending downward and inward toward the center of the field do you see a very fine black line which finally divides into these two even finer branches?" (As he draws.) Thus seeing the sketch and looking for its duplicate in the field the student does see the parts not long after they are drawn for him. "Well, that is a sense cell with its fibre stained black with an iron stain." The instructor and his sketch have merely supplied to the student's mind an anticipatory image without which selection and discriminatory vision were quite impossible. The moment he acquires such an image attention becomes easier. He sees the nucleus and nucleolus of the cell because he suspects them to be there and by careful sketching himself he discriminates related structures which he either understands or concerning which he must be instructed. Sometimes an artifact will seem to be of the utmost importance until he learns that such accidental objects are not uncommon and how he may expect to distinguish them. 

Effort was at first baffled and discouraged until a hint of what to look for was given. Then genuine attention began and continued with success. Then the field became clear and intensely interesting, but was not this clearness a result of the anticipatory images? I think the expe-

rienced reader will admit that the clearness of the object observed was the effect of the idea of what to look for.² Certainly the clearness does not "set in" until that idea is present.

If an anticipatory image is necessary how were discoveries made in the first place? The answer is, by men who had already formed a notion (perhaps quite incorrect) of what to look for, by those with a theory of how the thing might appear, and who were looking for confirmation or refutation of their theory. True, they might find the object different from their preconceived notion. One productive scientist says that only once in all his investigations did the facts discovered fufill his opinion exactly. 

Generally, however, the discovery is not absolutely remote and different from the anticipation, else it is discovered by someone whose expectation is nearer the fact, or by accident. In view of this fact psychologists have recently turned about the old adage and read it, believing is seeing, instead of the reverse. We really observe and discover what our previous training fits us to discover. 

Possibly the best evidence of this anticipatory factor in attention lies in the fact that the preconceived idea or theory blinds men so often to facts which contradict their ideas. They see only what they expect to see. Innumerable examples of this could be given.

It is by virtue of this inner factor that attention becomes selection. Selection would be hard to describe without the presence of some such factor. One does not select in a general way and with reference to nothing. He selects and rejects one anticipatory idea after another until one The Gestaltpsychologie calls this a "readiness to reach in a certain way" but emphasizes its anticipatory character. Thus, if asked to state which of two grays is the lighter the observer judges lighter or darker even when the grays are the same. Thus the expectation given by the instructions determines the response.

ATTENTION 553 is found which finally leads to the solution of his problem. 

This shows why so much of our attentive study and investigation is painful groping. 

Any serious student who begins very difficult microscopic work without preliminary training, and then receives expert instruction, will be convinced at the end of a few weeks that his eyesight must have improved physically in sharpness and acuity, so much has he gained in ability to discriminate and identify. But he will not note the change except when using the microscope. Since the time is too brief for a physical change, even if that were possible at all, the increased clearness must be due to a knowledge of what to look for, due to his weeks of effort and instruction. For us, therefore, until contrary evidence is more decisive, clearness shall be the result of attention, rather than attention itself. Attention consists of those adjustments to sensations and ideas which serve to make them clearer, to give them a higher grade of consciousness, and in proportion as one idea becomes clear, all other items of consciousness become obscure or vanish altogether. No doubt the bodily adjustments should be included, but I mean to emphasize especially the influence of anticipatory images which cause mental adjustment or rearrangement of ideas. With each pulse of attention the ideational pattern changes. In all probability attention is also a concentration of energy upon objects and ideas. 

Recent physiological work tends to confirm this opinion and if Ach may speak authoritatively of “an energetic act of will," we may surely speak of an energetic act of at tention. Comparison of many descriptions of attention seems to show that this is the opinion most widely held. 

The definition of Elsenhans is typical. I translate it as follows: "We understand by attention not indeed exclu-

sively a process of the will, but a state of consciousness, in which, under the guidance of the will and under participation of other psychic factors, of ideation, of a feeling of activity, and of certain bodily sensations of tension, together with their feeling tones, there occurs a clear and distinct apprehension of certain objects and a simultaneous obscurity of others." (P. 347.)

We now see why attention is called "focusing of consciousness" and why, at the same time, it is called an "exploratory reaction." The groping is quite characteristic in intellectual effort. We should also recognize why most, if not all, intelligence tests contain tests of mental alertness, which endeavor to measure the quickness with which a student can summon the right anticipatory images for the solution of a problem or the answer to a difficult question. Mental alertness is quickly productive attention.

Even when specific tests of alertness are not included, the intelligence test is timed, which again tests alertness.

Therefore, attention seems to be a large factor of intelligence.

Some of these

Degrees of Clearness in Attention. 

ways presents a certain pattern of items. are clear or vivid, others hazy or obscure. The latter are said to be in the margin of the field of consciousness; the clear items in the focus. The sensations or ideas which receive or attract attention are decidedly clearer than the marginal items, of which we are but vaguely conscious. 

Yet the marginal idea of a moment ago may become the focal one now. It then becomes vivid and definite. Sensations change from focus to margin in the same way.

Muscular reactions apparently do not occupy the focus at the moment of their execution. If we wish to acquire a skilful act we must "keep our eye on the ball," not on the

ATTENTION 555 way we are to strike it, or if shooting, on the target. Reflecting on the cause of our failures finally leads to improvement in the reaction, but at the crucial moment the reaction must be reflex rather than clearly conscious. If muscular responses were as amenable to attention as sensations and ideas, the golf player would improve his stroke more rapidly than he does.

Formerly it was believed that, besides the very high clearness of the focus, there are grades of less and less clearness down to the complete obscurity of the unconscious. Common language much more often refers merely to the clear and the obscure and psychology seems now to conform to the ordinary belief. The following diagram from Titchener, modified by Major, seems to represent the
