Titchener, T. B.) facts. The dotted lines represent degrees of focal clearness, the solid line marginal obscurity. No doubt the focus of consciousness does vary in degree of clearness in the same mind at different times. It may reach only one of the lower levels at the beginning of study and the highest level after longer effort and habituation. It is even more likely that some of the lower, dotted, cross lines represent the maximal attention or mental alertness of certain slow-moving minds. They seem never to have very

clear ideas.

This seems to be their chief defect of intelligence. 

In rare cases the margin disappears altogether. Soldiers have been wounded in battle without being aware of it until the excitement of the struggle was past. The anecdote of Archimedes' rapt attention to his circles represents a similar degree of absorption in intellectual attention, which is so rare as to have become historic. It seems possible, therefore, that at times the marginal items sink entirely below the threshold of consciousness.

If The clearness of a sensation must not be confused with its intensity. The clearness is due to a reaction of the mind itself. In listening for a very faint tone or overtone, it may be clear but it cannot be said to be intense. the overtone cannot be heard apart from its accompanying tones, we may hear it if we sound that note separately, so that we have an immediate memory of its pitch and character, and thus know what to look for in the combination of tones. Many qualities which are clear for the expert are obscure indeed for the untrained observer. 

Promptly detecting the cause of a new sound in the engine of a motor car is the commonest example today of the value of previous attentive experience.

Distraction and Distractibility of Attention. There is always a conflict between attention to instinctive and sensorial stimuli and intellectual attention. The latter must often be sustained by great effort. The telephone bell rings and instantly focus and margin have changed places.

The important and valuable idea has vanished, at least for the moment. Some investigators have tried to use this fact as a means of measuring attention. If certain selected distractions could diminish clearness by fixed amounts, so that it would subside through the levels represented by

ATTENTION 557 the dotted, cross-lines in Figure 48, the use of different distractors might lead us to a measure of attention. The obstacle to this lies in the fact that we quickly become adapted to each distraction. The disturbing effect of every stimulus disappears either quickly or gradually. Habituation to the distraction is established and its effect is lost. 

Anyone who has seen men composedly carrying on their work amid the clatter of telegraph instruments will see the force of this difficulty. This psychological fact also delays the adoption of noiseless typewriters.

Even before adaptation occurs there is a much more surprising effect of distraction. We actually attend best to our work and accomplish more under the influence of slight distraction. We make more of an effort, close our minds to the disturbing influence and the result is an increase instead of a decrease in the clearness of our ideas. 

As a somewhat humorous application of this fact, Colvin insists that there should be no easy chair in a study. Too much comfort and quiet are not conducive to good intellectual work. That students who earn part of their way through college often do better work than those who have no such need may be a further application of this law. 

Notwithstanding this ability to give better attention under distraction, there is in most of us a persistent tendency of the focus of consciousness to admit intruders irrelevant to our purpose. It seems difficult to force them into marginal obscurity, yet, if they are admitted, clearness fades to the dead level of distributed attention, as in revery. In fatigued states this tendency is very much increased. It then results in "flight of ideas." One idea displaces another from the focus and is in turn displaced before either can gain even a fair degree of clearness. This is distractibility and the extreme of this condition is seen

in chronic nervous exhaustion, or neurasthenia. The patient loses all capacity for mental work. He cannot make even the simplest computations. Ideas cannot be retained nor new associations formed. Among normal persons the degree of distractibility or concentration varies enormously. Some can keep a steady level of attention for hours. Others get their mental work done amid the intervals of their mind wanderings.

Kinds or Forms of Attention. We have seen that certain stimuli arouse spontaneous attention even in young children (p. 548). This seems to be accompanied by little or no effort, though it is quite possible that the cortical cells would show evidence of fatigue if they could be examined by methods sufficiently delicate. Because of the apparent absence of effort, this kind of attention is called passive and involuntary. The whole business of advertising depends on this type of attention. 

We all find at certain times that attention demands effort. The ideas to which we wish to attend are crowded out of the focus or, more often, altogether out of consciousness by others with a stronger emotional tone. Our anxieties, for example, obstruct the presence of the ideas to which we purpose to attend. We cannot dismiss our worries and turn to productive thought and, if we finally do so, effort is required. This final success in spite of obstacles is called voluntary attention. Usually repeated efforts are necessary before the emotionally toned ideas are forced into the margin of consciousness. Voluntary attention occurs when there is a conflict of one train of thought with another. It has been claimed that it occurs only when there is such a conflict. We shall consider this claim in a moment.

With children the conflict most often occurs between

ATTENTION 

559 sensorial stimuli and the object to which teacher or parent wishes them to attend. Only by having their efforts recalled many times to their lessons or other duties do they finally acquire some power of voluntary attention. Formerly it was believed that this discipline was of the utmost value to the child and gave him a certain self-mastery and reliability. 

Does voluntary attention arise only when there is conflict between two competing systems of ideas or between sensations and ideas? Effort may be great also when the facts or other items to be mastered are unfamiliar and at the same time complex and abstract, when, as we say, we cannot understand them, or they do not find associations with ideas we already have in mind. Every student knows how difficult it is to master the first principles of a science, which may later become intensely interesting. 

The mind may be quite fresh and unfatigued. It may be free from anxiety and concern, yet discrimination may be so difficult and the ideas to be mastered so novel that every effort must be summoned to our aid. Here the effort seems rather to overcome the inherent difficulties of the task and to summon the right ideas than to be expended in banishing irrelevant ideas. Since in this case the difficulty seems to be of a different nature and the effort to have a different direction it seems that conflict is not the conditio sine qua non of voluntary attention. Of course irrelevant ideas tend to displace the relevant ones when mental work is difficult. In this sense there is conflict. 

But such ideas have none of the energy of emotionallytoned thoughts which drive our very purpose out of mind. 

It seems fair to conclude that voluntary attention is required (1) when there is conflict and (2) when subjectmatter is very difficult of mastery.

As a result of prolonged and repeated attention to some subject or pursuit we gain a multitude of ideas about it. 

Because of this and because a habit of attending to such ideas has also been acquired, attention becomes less and less difficult and what was at first voluntary and effortful attention becomes practically passive once more. Our attention is now carried along by our acquired interest. This passive attention as result of earlier efforts of voluntary attention is called secondary passive attention. Thus there are three forms of attention: (1) involuntary, passive or spontaneous attention, due to native interests, (2) voluntary attention accompanied by effort, due to conflict or difficulty, and finally (3) secondary passive attention due to acquired interests and habits and partial or complete mastery of the subject.

It should be emphasized that the period of voluntary attention is a period of education, of difficult but profitable acquisition, of the forming of new interests and new associations, while the later passive attention may be a period of greater and easier acquisition and perhaps of greater clearness of the objects of thought to which we attend. This leads to a conception of education which is often overlooked. When the student can proceed with a subject by means of secondary passive attention, it is probably time for him to drop that subject and turn to a new study. He will then have at graduation a partial mastery of a half dozen fields of endeavor, to any one of which he may later turn for a life pursuit. Then the sooner he attains complete mastery and most of his work becomes routine, the more efficient he will be. Thus men use secondary passive attention in life, but much more voluntary attention during the period of training.

The Goal Idea. The idea or complex of ideas to which

ATTENTION 

561 we attend stands at every moment in the very center of consciousness. All our ideas center about this complex. It forms innumerable associations and determines among the ideas those which shall be accepted and those which shall be rejected. Thus it determines the whole course of psychic life until, after years of attention to one pursuit, the individual ends by becoming a different person. Facts and ideas which belong to his pursuit accumulate in consciousness and cluster like grapes to their stems. The ideas attended to remain fixed in consciousness or rather recur again and again. They arouse their former associates as well as feelings and will. With this central idea we identify our very self. For the moment it is the I, and our chief interest clings to it. It is the thing which we will. 

It drafts off to itself all the energy at our disposal and thus, through the adjustment or concentration of attention, it gains the position of a monarch in consciousness and guarantees the unity and inner connection of mental life for the time during which we attend. This is the goal idea which determines to a large extent the character of the individual.

In some ambitious minds the goal idea becomes much more than this. It is the permanent image of what we wish to achieve or become. Our every effort is directed toward that end. Ideas unrelated to this idea either gain no entrance to consciousness or, if they do enter, are quickly expelled or forgotten. The adoption of a goal idea and the persistence with which we try to realize it determines our fate. Without it we are likely to be prey to the momentary influences of the environment, as a derelict is a prey to changing winds. It drifts across the trade routes but it never stays in them. Because of this effect of the goal idea, society has changed its character. It has found itself

better served by specialists and experts, so it no longer favors a frequent change of goal. The youth is fortunate who early becomes possessed of a permanent purpose, which guides all his efforts. Thoughtful and successful men are convinced that an idea, which thus takes possession of a man's mind and action, ends by converting itself into a realized fact. How it does so may be something of a mystery but the fact can hardly be denied. Almost every worthy achievement seems to depend on this law of attention. On the other hand, the evil effects of an ever-changing goal idea are in no danger of overstatement. 

Fixed Ideas. If there is ever to be a science of mental hygiene, psychology must give at least a glance at disorders of attention. While blunting of attention and consequent utter indifference to the surroundings, as in forms of dementia, is perhaps the most common disorder of attention in diseased minds, there is often what appears to be a pathological exaggeration of attention. Some single, haunting idea forever returns to bring with it worry and anxiety. Finally it disturbs even physical health. The fear of poverty or of persecution becomes the delusion of poverty or of persecution. The patient's thought centers in this matter of supreme concern and forever returns to it. No distraction will divert him. His words, if taken down by a stenographer, never depart far from his delusion. Even his answers to questions may twist toward it. 

His mind seems like the base-weighted toys of children which, no matter how you strike them down, return instantly to the upright position. There is an insistent return to the delusion.

If we compare this abnormal state with ordinary anxiety, we find it merely a heightened condition of the same sort. Fear coupled with fixed attention is anxiety. It

ATTENTION 

563 seems to introspection to involve an enormous expenditure of nervous energy and physiology fully confirms this belief. Here attention reaches too profound a degree of intensity. The expenditure of energy is so great that it often goes beyond the point of ready recuperation. The novelist who described fear as "disintegration of the very soul," meant the fear of anxiety as well. Had he called it a disintegration of cortical cells he would have stated a literal scientific truth. In the presence of anxiety or worry the thoughtless friend prescribes with the thoughtless formula, "Forget it." The popular psychologist replies with equal slang, "You are not the boss of your forgetter"; while the physician, knowing that certain cortical cells have been used to exhaustion, prescribes a change of environment in the hope that new scenes will permit once more a normal distractibility. For us it is enough to show that emotion may cause an intensity and persistence of attention which is entirely unhealthy.

The Span of Attention.-No account of attention is re garded as complete without the anecdote of the magician who made a contest of seeing whether he or his son could name the greater number of objects in a store window after having quickly passed by it. In the psychological laboratory the experiment is made by permitting a number of figures or characters or pictures to fall past an opening in a screen through which the observer is looking. The results may be stated briefly.

If the elements cannot be grouped in any way, the adult can apprehend at once six different elements. Meumann's researches give four to six. The six-year-old child is able to observe clearly two or three; the twelve-year-old three to four; the fourteen-year-old, on the average, five.

In the case of letters, which form a word fifteen or twenty

have been seen with certainty. Any grouping or meaning of the data to be attended to increases the number which a single wave of attention can include. As many simple groups can be apprehended simultaneously as separate letters or numbers.

The number grasped is the same if, instead of being simultaneous, the stimuli are successive. The adult perceives six (sometimes seven or eight), when all grouping and rhythm are excluded. For each individual there is one rate or tempo of beats which is more favorable than any other. If the rate be slower or faster than that he does not do so well. Yet Kraepelin believes that the successive links of a chain of ideas should follow one another at intervals of two seconds in order that each one should attain the maximal clearness.

If there is a different rate of apprehension for different persons, the public certainly recognizes the fact in its most common criticism of intelligence tests. It is insistently claimed that if the tests were not timed, many persons would show high intelligence, who make low scores on a timed test.

Duration of Attention. We often give attention to a book or a game for hours at a time. But this means that we experience a whole chain of shifting ideas which, by their novelty and associations, support our attention. 

Suppose it be a single, unchanging stimulus, how long can we give it attention? Or what is the period of fluctuations of attention which we all notice? When listening to the ticking of a watch at a considerable distance from the ear, it is heard for a few seconds, disappears for a similar period, then reappears again. Two investigations have found these fluctuations to be, on the average, 3.5 seconds, and one theory would have it that this is the

ATTENTION 565 average duration of the attention wave. From this estimate, opinions vary down to one second and up to two or three minutes. With such variety of opinion among investigators, we can only say that attention fluctuates and that the duration of attention to an unchanging stimulus is brief.

Probable Brain Action in Attention.-In terms of nervous activity a single explanation of behavior and thought is met with on all sides. "There is resistance at the synapses." It is overcome and the action or thought takes place. If "resistance is overcome" this clearly implies that there is energy to overcome it in the nervous impulses or that they are energy. While this has been stoutly denied, the discovery of Parker that an active nerve secretes or releases CO₂ amounts, I should think, to proof of it. 

Let us assume, then, that the resistance at synapses is overcome by the energy of nervous impulses. 

Then, in voluntary thought, attention (or will) is in control of this energy and the effort of attention is effort necessary to cause a discharge across certain synapses, resistant because not used repeatedly. There is expenditure of energy in attention because of the constant change of direction of the impulses into new pathways. The ease of routine and habitual thought is due to the use of old paths. When one must continually change the direction of nervous discharges energy is required. The executive who must continually face and decide new problems soon meets fatigue or exhaustion. He must turn his thought, as it were, through wide angles and the greater the angle the greater the expenditure of energy. Less energy is needed to turn from one topic to another related to it. Some of the connections are already formed. 

The "focusing" or concentration of attention is prob-

ably a true concentration of nervous impulses, and consequently of energy, in one direction or another, toward the visual apparatus when the stimulus is visual, toward the auditory region when there is an auditory stimulus, and away from both in intellectual attention. This conception offers a reason for the almost violent bodily adjustments which accompany a change of attention. Conceivably they help in the change of direction of nervous impulses. This is almost observably true in sensorial attention, when some of the accompaniments are adjustments of the sense organ. One of the widest changes of direction is from one sense realm to another. On this view, the difficulty of a new subject of study is due to the probability that many of the synaptic connections are being formed for the first time. Synapses, across which impulses have passed many times, soon cease to offer resistance, so secondary passive attention is soon established and goes on without effort. Synapses, which have closed to distracting influences, remain closed to them. This we have described as adaptation of attention. The intense and apparently effortless character of instinctive attention would be due to the fact that synapses on which instinct depends are among the oldest and closest of brain connections. They are inherited and are believed to lie in older portions of the brain than the newer cortical connections. Thus we share this type of attention with the higher animals. The exploratory character of attention would be due to an effort to send impulses, first into one, then into another cortical center. 

This opinion also accounts for our reading, perhaps a whole page, with no knowledge of what we have read. 

Reading as behavior can go on almost reflexly by the use of synaptic connections made long before. To read with

ATTENTION 

567 an understanding of meaning requires a constant change of direction of nervous impulses within the cortex. Again the conflict, which is said to accompany voluntary attention, would be accounted for by the tendency of neurons already active to continue their activity. In nervous fatigue, instead of a diminution of the energy, the nervous impulses seem to go even faster and to stick to the old paths. Thus anxiety and worry lead to sleeplessness rather than to final relaxation. In this, nervous fatigue appears to differ emphatically from muscular fatigue and exhaustion. On the basis of all the evidence it seems fair to conclude that attention involves a real expenditure of energy.

CHAPTER XX WILL 

Attention, either involuntary or voluntary, accompanies and directs all our thought processes. It is a general ability and influences or controls all others. It probably involves, especially in its voluntary form, an expenditure of energy toward the attainment of some goal or purpose of our thought. When a difficult problem must be solved, the very difficulty causes, apparently, a greater expenditure of energy in attention. Practically, this appears to me identical with an "energetic act of will" but the term, attention, describes voluntary thinking; the term, will, is used to describe voluntary action. The experience appears much the same whether I strive to solve this problem or to master this foreign language or whether I strive to gain skill in typewriting, to scale a difficult mountain ledge, or to change a firmly established habit. 

Again, a child's lawless, impulsive thought is believed gradually to come under the control of voluntary attention, very much as his impulsive acts gradually come under the sway of his will.

In typical acts of will the action contemplated has to do with the attainment of a remote goal or purpose and means of attainment must be devised. Shall I be better satisfied in the long run if I enter college or if I engage in business? The one pursuit demands one type of preparation, a series of acts extending over several years; the other demands quite different behavior. Having entered college, shall I engage in study or in "activities,” and, if

WILL in the former, have I sufficient force of character to resist temptations and attain my self-determined goal?

Here, as in moral decisions, we see that really the choice of a character is at stake as well as the choice of a career. 

The old phrase, "Sow an act and you reap a habit, sow a habit and you reap a character, sow a character and you reap destiny," is genuinely true. This is because an act repeated but comparatively few times becomes a habit. Inaction likewise becomes a habit and yielding to one type of motive rather than acting on its opposite soon becomes habitual as well. The volition is complete when action be- `gins. The die is then cast for better or worse. 

Attention may be defined as striving to attain a goal of thought, will as striving to attain a goal of action, or the transformation of a goal idea into action is a less accurate definition. "Purposive Striving."-McDougall (address at meeting of The British Association, 1924) is right, I believe, in describing all our life as "purposive striving" for the attainment of goals by thought and action and in spite of difficulties. If this were not the fundamental feature of human life, the explorer would not "tackle" the most terrible dangers and hardships in which at least some lives, he knows, will be lost. The pioneer would not delight to tell of the struggles of the early settlement and the hairbreadth escapes, nor would the student who "worked his way through" remember with a certain pride the exact sum of the scanty resources with which he started. In business, offerings of the securities of corporations would not recite that the business is under the same management that brought it to success from slender capital, unless we believe that the men who conquered great difficulties can now cope successfully with lesser ones. We seem, there-

fore, not only to find satisfaction in striving but to have a firm belief in the "striver." In fact striving is so fundamental a trait of our natures that we must arrange artificial difficulties where no natural ones exist, as in vigorous, struggling games. The football game with a minor opponent finds the team "stale" and off its guard. The contest between hitherto undefeated teams keys them both up for herculean efforts. It is very doubtful, however, whether overcoming artificial difficulties and attaining artificial goals has the invigorating effect of a natural struggle. Nature blows no whistle when the breath comes short.

Realizing that character itself is at stake in so many decisions and that yielding is itself decision, our forefathers practised much self-denial for its own sake; resistance to impulsive and instinctive desires as a valuable preparation for further resistance, should occasion for it arise. Their achievements seem to justify their psychological belief. Just now a very wealthy man seems to the tender-minded quite cruel to his grandchildren for, in creating a trust fund, he recites that it all may be given to charity as he regards wealth as damaging to the young. 

Why?-except that it cuts them off from the opportunity for serious, purposive striving. That is his reason and that he regards as sufficient. Lack of exercise of this trait results, he believes, in a weakness equivalent to paralysis of will.

How We Learn to Perform Purposive Acts. It would seem reasonable to suppose that a child endowed with body and limbs would have innate ideas of the movements his members are capable of making. This reasonable supposition deviates widely from the facts. We do not know the movements which we can make until we have hit upon them accidentally. The babe gurgles and babbles by the

WILL accidental passage of breath over its vocal cords. If it hears its babblings it becomes interested in repeating them, until it hears other interesting sounds from other lips, which it tries to imitate, and thus it becomes aware of the delicate movements of which tongue, lips, larynx, and palate are capable. It has acquired memories of the efforts necessary to pronounce words but, as we have said (p. 

411), these are not images. The images are the auditory ones supplied by the ear. If the child hears neither the sounds made by his own lips nor those made by others, he remains speechless throughout his life. A stock of memories of the efforts necessary to pronounce words is the prerequisite for voluntary speech. But a stock of memories of efforts for every other act is, apparently, equally necessary.

Woodworth shows that a babe can, of course, blow out its breath but several attempts are necessary before it can blow out a candle intentionally. The attempts give a memory of the necessary efforts. We must acquire knowledge of the movements we can make. Once we have control of our muscles and can execute the necessary complicated movements, action usually follows at once upon the presence of an idea to be realized by the act, the goal idea. 

It is stated that action follows also upon an idea or memory of how the act would feel in the muscles, tendons and joints which execute the deed, a motor or kinaesthetic image. This is called a resident idea because the feeling is resident in the parts affected. I think such an idea is almost never a motive for the will, beyond the first stages of learning a series of complicated movements, and then only in relatively few persons, after childhood is past. 

Meumann remarks, "The sight of an object to be grasped, or of a goal, or a decision to reach a goal, releases the ex-

ecuting movements. Ideas of movement enter in only darkly, and many men find not a trace of them before an action." (Intelligenz und Wille, p. 194.) In examples given by psychologists of voluntary or impulsive action I can find none in which the kinaesthetic idea "sets off" the action. The marksman must keep this attention on the target, not on an image of the "feel" of the gun in his hands. 

Even kinaesthetic sensations promptly subside into unconsciousness in most persons to the result that the immediate goal is the sole cause of action. While resident sensations guide and modify our acts, resident ideas are probably of minor influence on behavior, even in those persons who testify that they have kinaesthetic images. For most of us there is a clear distinction between motor and sensory memory. The former is habit.

Impulsive or Ideo-Motor Action. What mankind had always before called impulsive action James analyzed into what he termed ideo-motor action. This permits us to see the impulsive force of ideas, to see that most of our behavior is impulsive, and that voluntary acts occur only when one of two impelling ideas must be accepted (and the other rejected) before action can occur.

To illustrate ideo-motor action by a very common example, you are not now driving the automobile but you have often done so. Now you are sitting beside the driver.

Suddenly another car appears dangerously near. A crash is imminent. Instantly you find you are pressing your feet almost through the very floorboards in an attempt to depress a clutch and a brake which are not there. The crash avoided, you feel a trifle "foolish" because of your futile endeavor, but you repeat it on the next similar occasion. 

Did you will the act? Not at all. The mere idea of the crash and of possibly avoiding it produced instantly this

WILL somewhat complicated behavior. This prompt action immediately on the presence of an idea is ideo-motor action. 

We speak instantly the idea to be expressed occurs to us. 

The babe blows out the candle immediately it is presented, etc. Practically, ideo-motor action explains why so many secrets are not kept. Associations lead to the thought of the secret and ideo-motor action produces the revealing speech before we have time to recall our solemn promise never to mention the matter. Ideas, then, tend strongly to be expressed in both speech and action. Nerve currents, unless prevented by others, discharge into motor centers and thence into the final common paths for action. So most action is ideo-motor. It was called impulsive because the idea so promptly gets itself "enacted." Sometimes, however, other ideas inhibit the action for a time at least. Does this usher in the condition prerequisite for voluntary action? Not always. A unique experiment which James performed, not in his laboratory, but in his bed, throws so much light on the matter that we must give it in his own' words. "We know what it is to get out of bed on a freezing morning in a room without fire, and how the very vital principle within us protests against this ordeal. Probably most persons have lain on certain mornings for an hour at a time unable to brace themselves to the resolve. We think how late we shall be, how the duties of the day will suffer; we say, 'I must get up, this is ignominious,' etc.; but still the warm couch feels too delicious, the cold outside too cruel. And resolution faints away and postpones itself again and again just as it seemed on the verge of bursting the resistance and passing over into the decisive act. Now how do we ever get up under such circumstances? If I may generalize from my own experience, we more often than not get up without any struggle or decision at all. We

suddenly find that we have got up. A fortunate lapse of consciousness occurs; we forget both the warmth and the cold; we fall into some revery connected with the day's life, in the course of which the idea flashes across us, 'Hollo! I must lie here no longer'-—an idea which at that lucky instant awakens no contradictory or paralyzing suggestions, and consequently produces immediately its appropriate motor effects." At the moment the inhibiting idea of the cold was not present. "This case," he adds, "seems to contain in miniature the data for an entire psychology of volition." (James, Briefer Course, pp. 424425.) 

In such a case, when the inhibiting idea does not disappear from the focus of attention at the moment of deciding, we have the conditions for an act of will. 

Conflict of Motives.-If, in the instance of pushing on the floor of an automobile when a collision is imminent, society should decide that such behavior is a deep and lasting insult to the driver or a confession of contemptible weakness we would all promptly try to restrain our ideo-motor impulses. While this would result in a conflict of impulses at first, our decision for courtesy or courage, would finally triumph and we should remain impassive in the face of danger, much as soldiers for the ideal of honor might charge in the face of far greater peril. In their case the will has become dominant over the impulse of fear. Many conflicts of motives are between lower and higher impulses of this sort. Having determined to follow honor we are able to face danger to life itself. Decisions are often more complex but perhaps never more difficult than this. The overcoming of instinctive and habitual desires by more ideal considerations furnishes an intense conflict. 

Due to the narrowness of attention, motives must be

WILL considered by pairs. We weigh one goal idea against another until finally one is chosen. Then come the problems of means of attainment and these in turn can usually be considered in pairs.

Ways of Making Decisions.-Once ideo-motor action was made clear, there arose a tendency to separate it sharply from voluntary choice, as if the two kinds of action were quite distinct. This, I think, is erroneous. Ideomotor impulses are ready to supervene at any moment and to influence our decisions. I should divide decisions, therefore, into those that are partly ideo-motor and those which are more purely voluntary, in the sense that they arise from the influence of all the motives rather than from a single idea. There are doubtless many types of decision besides those in the outline below but the latter will serve to suggest them. (1) by predetermination (2) due to accidental advent of an idea from without (3) due to accident from within (4) due to change of mood 

Partly ideo-motor Decisions (1) the reasonable type

Voluntary.. 

(2) the intuitive type (3) the "wilful" type

Decision by Predetermination.-Ach found that, when two numbers were shown to an observer and he was told beforehand either to add or subtract them, the action came very promptly and it was, of course, in accordance with the instructions given. Consent by the observer determined the action. Such consent makes the decision ideo-motor. When the numbers were shown without previous instructions, the action was delayed and deliberate choice took place according to conditions which first had

to be considered. This is far more voluntary action. Similar experiments were made by Michotte and Prum.¹ 

It is surprising how many of our decisions are predetermined. The executive decides that a certain expenditure would overdraw the budget and decides against it, because long ago he determined against an overdraft. One executive had predetermined that all his decisions should be prompt and on the instant. Thus the actual merits of each case could receive only intuitive consideration in the time allowed. The result of this predetermination was less than one-half of correct decisions whereas decision by chance would have averaged one-half correct in the long run.

When a particular decision has been endorsed by society it becomes a law and predetermines the conduct of all future law-abiding citizens. Consequently we find our choices predetermined by laws made hundreds of years ago. To these are added rules and regulations without limit. We thus find predeterminations to govern us in many situations where otherwise judgment and will could be exercised.

Accidental Influence of an Idea. This type is not predetermined but determined by accident at some lucky or unlucky moment. Indecision is a type of thought which many impulsive natures cannot endure. Doubt and suspense are too distressing to be borne long. Decision brings relief even though we suspect the decision to be wrong. In such natures as cannot endure deliberation, decision often occurs before the evidence is all in or before it has been given any adequate attention. Some accidental circumstance "tips the beam." Some one idea, and that perhaps 

Archives de Psychologie, December, 1910.

WILL an unimportant one, gets attention and promptly forces a decision.

This type of decision is often capitalized by salesmanship. Some one remark of a salesman penetrates our attention and begets decision. The security he offers us is a first mortgage and therefore safe. We really act on this idea of a first mortgage and its safety quite unreflecting that a prior mortgage may be created by pledging the property of a subsidiary concern. This decision by an adventitious idea is surely ideo-motor behavior.

The distress of indecision is often great. This leads to the curious fact that after repeated visits by one salesman a competitor makes the sale because the "prospect's" resistance has been weakened by the first. The idea may be no more than that precious time is being wasted in deliberation and in being solicited and further interruption cannot be endured. This is of course quite incidental to the practical problem to be solved. If the idea "comes from within" the case is the same. All ideas come from the very focus of attention at the moment of deciding. The influence of emotional state or mood on our decisions need hardly be discussed. All values change with moods. What seemed vital yesterday is regarded as valueless today. When boys marched away to war the citizens assembled and tears readily filled their eyes. Had a memorial subscription been asked for then it would have been oversubscribed. 

Five years later memorial committees find only great reluctance. The mood has changed and with it the idea of the value.

Of the more voluntary decisions the first is called the judicious or reasonable type. This seems more valid and important than any of the preceding ones. In this we weigh the two alternatives against each other until delib-

eration is complete. Either willingly or wilfully we accept the state of suspense and indecision. Advantages and disadvantages are marshalled and considered. If the issue is a grave one the feeling and attention are intense and this intensity may cause us at any moment to break over into ideo-motor action. If this does occur we throw scruples to the wind and say, "This will I do, though the heavens fall." Here impulse overcomes deliberation, and choice and volition have no chance. But in the genuinely reasonable type we continue to weigh evidence. We curb impulse and endure suspense until finally deliberation brings the verdict that there is a clear preponderance of evidence for one course. Action then follows in that direction.

Fortunate the impulsive man, if he can follow the calculating and judicious method of Franklin, who said that if a decision was important, he carefully set down the reasons for and against it, balancing those of equal weight against each other. If, after that was done, there appeared a clear over-balance of weighty reasons for a given course he adopted that as his decision. No doubt the very act of picking up the pen gave acceptance to suspense and to "balancing" reasons. How rare this type of decision is may be inferred from my relating the method to an executive and his reply. He said, "I balance reasons in that way. Then I don't do it." That is, ideo-motor impulses broke over the dam and reasons were forgotten. No wonder psychologists say that ideas lead to action. "The end and purpose of all thought is action." Or, "Every pulse of feeling which we have is the correlate of some neural activity that is already on its way to instigate a movement. 

Our sensations and thoughts are but cross-sections, as it were, of currents whose essential consequence is motion, and which have no sooner run in at one nerve than they

WILL 

579 are ready to run out by another." (James, B. C., 426.)

Due either to a change in the nervous system or to an accumulated background of experience or perhaps due to both conditions, this avalanche tendency of impulses to break right over into action subsides to some extent after youth is past. The decisions of the middle-aged man are more judicious, more reasonable. He is more patient in weighing all the evidence, so, I believe, there is a maxim, "Oh, if the young could know and the old could do!" Conversely, in youth thought leads to action so precipitately that we call the action "ill-considered," and the "folly of youth" is proverbial.

Not only the differential psychology of youth and age begins here, but that of different races, as well as the psychology of personality. Members of one race "plump" into action. They have a "hair-trigger" organization.

Others are far slower to decide, have a higher breaking point, are more patient in weighing evidence. They have a greater internal resistance which can be overcome only by evidence and good reasons. They can stand intellectual suspense as the others cannot. Personalities, probably nervous systems, vary in the same way. The nervous and impulsive break into action before the judicious type has its first pair of reasons balanced one against the other. "Reptilian" and "simian" are the eloquent terms used by

James to describe how each of these types appears to the other.

The intuitive type of decision is closely related to the reasonable type. We cannot analyze the situation into its factors sufficiently to be certain that our action will be best. But the whole background of our experience and beliefs cooperates to give an intellectual "feeling" that this course will be the right one and we act in accordance

with this more or less vague feeling. It may be little more than a vague recognition of precedents which we could not possibly recall. Or in half-recalled similar cases such action has been satisfactory. Women are believed to decide in this fashion more often than men. Consequently they may give less satisfactory reasons for their decisions than men. But men also decide in this way at times and this dark background of feeling and past experience probably influences many of our decisions. The total evidence probably has weight in this type, not merely a focal idea. 

The Wilful Type. This kind of decision is almost a subdivision of the reasonable type, except that we seem to ourselves to be acting against all the most attractive reasons and motives. In the other forms of decision the rejected motives disappear in an almost instant "fade out," the moment decision is complete. In the wilful type all the advantages, joys, and delights which this decision will make us lose are vivid in consciousness at the moment of deciding to give them up. They have more weight with us and promise us far more than the thing we are going to do. By adding the weight of our will against them we manage to act in the opposite direction. It is really this form of behavior which seems to bring the force of will to light.

To illustrate with a simple case, one youth had a veritable passion for a military career. He had studied and striven to qualify for it for several years and finally by competitive examination he had won an appointment to West Point. His goal achieved, he had a few months to rejoice inwardly over his success and the future promise his staunch efforts had won for him. Then came the knowledge that, because of a parent's ill-health, all these fond hopes must be surrendered. Yet they could not be mini-

WILL 

581 mized. In choo the new course he knew that its end and every intervening of it would be unwelcome throughout the years. Yet shoulu fail to make the renunciation and act from the "nobler" motives he would probably be despised by all but those apologists who set about finding "what is good" in every abuse so that no wrong need be fought. Such a decision as this young man made exhibits the will, in its most genuine form. This is decision with effort. The innermost soul is searched for energy to combat the former fond hopes. 

Because of this type of decision and its consequent action James sets down the inequations, I per se <P

I+E > P in which I is the ideal impulse, P the propensity to act in a certain way and E the effort of attention or will. The second inequation is a true formula of the stresses in our psychic structure. Manhood is, of course, an entirely different thing from what it would be without this faculty for effort.

It may be added that a youth who had repressed hopes so fondly cherished as those illustrated above and had also repressed every expression of disappointment over their necessary surrender, should, by the Freudian psychology, have the "suppressed complex” forever thereafter making trouble in his mental and emotional life. Even a hurried observation of those who have made such choices shows them to be the most healthy-minded of all. 

Freedom of Will. This fundamental type of decision leads to the question, "Is the feeling that we are deciding by sheer effort of will and against the strongest motives an illusion?" Recent investigators of the will describe repeatedly an "energetic act of will" and they describe the

vercoming a strong or this form of decision. conditions under which it occurs 

Labio always gives occas

Since matter is ow well-nigh dissolved into energy, a human being may very well be a center of energy which he may quite possibly display in "wilful" decisions. The feeling of effort would not then be illusory at all. 

We are not at all concerned with the metaphysical question of freedom, but only with the practical, behavioristic one. Has the user of drugs, for example, who can no more help again resorting to the needle than a stone hurled from a precipice can help falling to the stream below, has such a man lost a power of resistance which he once possessed? Is his behavior different from that of his twin brother, who somehow feared the first offer of the drug and now has no appetite for it? The evidence for the possession of this practical freedom is, I think, the very ease with which it can be lost. It is lost by lack of exercise just as any other of our powers. We have seen (p. 

164) that Ach found the "habit equivalent of will" to be established by 120-150 repetitions of an act. After that our behavior is a matter of habit-dominance over the will and perhaps the number of repetitions required for such dominance is fewer for plastic brains than for mature ones. Habits formed early in life are rarely changed at all. It seems possible to lose entirely the power of effort of attention to certain ideas. They will not stay for an instant in the focus of consciousness and the behavior of such persons is quite different from that of their companions. This difference is an observable fact and it is all that need concern us here. The feeling of effort accompanies the expenditure of energy and this expenditure brings about the result. 

Action Versus Thought. From what has been said, ac-

WILL 

583 tion is the easiest and most natural behavior for any normal human being. Almost every idea at times seems to urge to immediate activity. To repress action is more difficult. To restrain action and deliberate is most difficult of all. This is a function of thought which leads us to correct decisions instead of to impulsive ones. Were thought less important so many thousand men would not be sitting at desks today. The scientist and the diplomat, the attorney and the physician must arrive at correct decisions, though in very different fields. After that, the action which follows may be relatively trivial, signing one's name or reaching for a telephone. Originally the man of action found the environment well suited to his inclinations. Now he finds it less so, even in time of war. 

Success depends far more on plans and preparation. The environment has been changed by the new brain and its cortex.

CHAPTER XXI MESMERISM, HYPNOTISM, SUGGESTION, AND PSYCHOANALYSIS 

The account of these related topics belongs, I believe, to the field of pathological psychology. Yet psychoanalysis has recently gained so widespread attention, because of its reference to sex and to magic, that concessions are being made to it even in introductory texts on psychology. 

Probably mesmerism was quite as hauntingly interesting in its time. If we are to consider psychoanalysis at all, we must recognize its historical antecedents. Not only the individual mind but that of the group must work according to laws of association. One discovery prepares the way for another. The practice of mesmerism (animal magnetism) led to that of hypnotism, the latter to suggestion, and this very naturally to psychoanalysis. 

There are hysterical patients who, after a few minutes of a dazed or unconscious condition, lose all memory of their past life and begin a second series of memories consistently connected with one another. In the secondary state these secondary memories are present. In the primary state its memories make up the personal history. 

Even the emotional disposition of such a patient may be changed in the second state. When memory and emotion are thus altered, one body really exhibits two different personalities at different times. We consequently speak of such a patient as having an alternating personality, a first and a second self. Sooner or later the second state disappears and the first self returns. This self owns as mem-

ories the experiences which have taken place in the first state and may know nothing of those of the secondary state. This is the usual condition. The second self may know nothing of the first one or it may recognize the existence of such a personality but regards it as foreign to itself. 

What becomes of the first personality while the second is present and of the second while the first holds the field? 

The first explanation was that the body of the patient was "possessed" by an evil spirit which must be exorcised, really a not unreasonable explanation when we consider the established beliefs of those times. Now we say simply that the self which no longer manifests itself in the patient has vanished for the time being from his consciousness. 

Some say, however, that it is in the unconscious or subconscious, a statement quite different from the one just preceding, since it personifies the unconscious as a sort of realm. In fact now and then a popular writer speaks of the "sub-cellar" of the mind. Then it is explicitly a realm to be explored. We can only plead that the "explorer" should be scientifically critical. When caution is relaxed there is a strong tendency to write psychologies of the unconscious on very meager evidence and to people the realm with all sorts of creations of fancy. The unconscious becomes consciousness over again. We forget that it is unconscious. Of course, when memories return which have been long absent, when a second self returns to a hysterical patient, or when complicated acts are performed, as walking in one's sleep, and apparently quite independent of consciousness, we must invoke unconscious brain action for the retention of the memories of the second self and unconscious nervous action of some sort to account for the automatic behavior. The hypothesis of the unconscious (or

MESMERISM, HYPNOTISM, SUGGESTION 

587 subconscious) cannot be dispensed with but it must not be overworked by the uncritical or the credulous. 

Even before this spontaneous change from one personality to another was recognized as characteristic of many cases, a secondary state was produced by the influence of one person on another. Aside from the early examples, regarded as instances of "possessions," Antoine Mesmer, b. 1734, was one of the first to produce this change. He employed a magnet, to which the patient's attention was directed, and at that time he believed in animal magnetism as the agent which produced the mental transformation. 

The magnet served to rivet the attention of the subject as a bright object does in hypnotism, or as a crystal may serve in crystal gazing with this type of person. Later Mesmer ceased to use a magnet and produced the hypnotic sleep and other secondary states by "passes," i. e., movements of the hands of the operator before the eyes of the patient. 

The charlatanism becoming apparent, two commissions were appointed of one of which Franklin was a member. 

Their report considered "imagination as the sole active agent" and certainly hysteria is at present a psychic disorder for which we do not know the nervous substratum. 

In giving up the use of a magnet Mesmer gave up, of course, his former theory of his cures and treatments. 

Henceforth the theoretical emphasis was to be laid on the somnolent or trance-like state produced by the operator on his subject. The latter was said to be hypnotized or in a state of hypnosis (from hypnos, sleep). This may be regarded as the second period of the practice. Some hysterical patients were cured of anesthesias, paralyses, amnesias, tics, etc., by the strong suggestion during hypnosis that they would on awaking find themselves healed. The disorder, being psychic, could be removed by psychic means.

This was a time, however, when reckless hypnotizers pro duced a double personality in many a patient who would not have developed it spontaneously. These patients also came very soon to depend upon the hypnotizer. One youth had to "hear his master's voice," at least over the telephone, before he could go to sleep at night. Another asked to be hypnotized to break the habit of biting his nails. 

Such patients obey the commands given them by the operator during the hypnotic state even after they have awakened from hypnosis. This is known as post-hypnotic suggestion. The large number of cases in which hysterical persons were really damaged by hypnosis and developed secondary and conflicting personalities led to the next stage of development.

It was found unnecessary to induce deep hypnotic sleep in these patients in order to have the operator's suggestions influence them profoundly. Shallow hypnosis, very slight somnolence or none at all was found favorable to suggestion. Almost as striking cures were exhibited as by hypnosis. Troublesome obsessions and fear of failure and disaster could often be readily banished by suggestion applied to the subject in his waking state. It was often found necessary, however, to find the nature and cause of the troublesome thoughts before the appropriate suggestion for their banishment could be given. This "finding out" is, of course, the beginning of psychoanalysis. If next it should be found in many cases, that the mere recital of the desire or ideas which caused emotional disturbance and the expression of the emotions aroused by the ideas would get rid of their disturbing influence, the essence of the practice and theory of psychoanalysis would have been discovered. 

This appears to be the history of its development. Some have thoughtlessly assumed that even the healthy-minded

MESMERISM, HYPNOTISM, SUGGESTION 

589 are subject to suppressed ideas which disturb their mental and emotional life. This is quite unwarranted by the facts. 

Until a careful record is kept we shall not know how much good or harm has been done to hystericals by psychoanalysis, suggestion or hypnotism. Assume, then, that it is not necessary to give positive suggestions in order that the disturbing conditions may disappear. The arousal of the repressed ideas from unconsciousness to clear, articulate consciousness, the recognition of them as causes of the disturbed emotional life, the natural expression of them and their associated emotions, instead of their repression, may bring about a cure. In fact, the repression is believed to be the cause of the disorder and the desires, motives, and ideas which are thus forced into the unconscious, are called "repressed complexes." Freud traces all these complexes to sex (more recently other primary desires as hunger have been added) and their repression is due to the demands of society, morality or some other imperative motive. Not all of his followers agree with Freud as to the sex origin of the complexes, nor do they all subscribe to his further claim that every dream is the psychic expression of an unfulfilled wish. By his opinion the effect of the subconscious is especially evident in dreams. They furnish the clues whereby the psychoanalyst ferrets out, feature by feature, the whole complex, which may have been due to some experience of infancy or early childhood. Disturbed mental and emotional conditions arise from these repressions. The patient knows nothing of them except their effect on his consciousness. The psychoanalyst must find the cause. He will be both wise and fortunate if he does not bring to the consciousness of the patient conceptions which were never there before and were never repressed. 

To avoid this it must be admitted that Freud, so far as

possible, leads the patient on a voyage of self-discovery of his repressions. But these suggestible persons might easily be led to believe that they were discovering past experiences when the discoveries are really new inventions of fancy under the influence of the psychoanalyst's questions. 

Surely science needs to know whether the beneficent effects of the analysis remain permanent. Effects of suggestion were often transitory.

Given these assumptions and we have before us much of the theory of the subconscious or unconscious and its so-called psychoanalysis. It is a method of mental healing on a par with hypnotism and suggestion. When great emphasis is placed upon dream experiences, it makes the theory one of the interpretation of dreams, an ancient art of the soothsayers. A supplementary claim is that we all tend to forget or ignore everything which is unpleasant. 

This we repress into the unconscious but, once repressed, it too may produce emotional disturbances in the subject. 

With this hint or glance at the place which psychoanalysis occupies we must be content. 

Something like this is possible with hysterical patients. 

Their personalities may, as we have seen, be divided, one being split off from the other entirely or the second personality may recognize the first but regard it as entirely dif ferent from the present self and as belonging to another. 

Such cases suggest the existence of something which may be called the subconscious and which is brought to consciousness by hypnosis. Thus the description of hypnotism, suggestion, and psychoanalysis is a chapter in the story of hysterical, borderline phenomena, rather than an account of healthy-minded human beings. Note the statement of Pierre Janet: "Despite the affirmations of certain authors we must confess that we have not succeeded in giv-

MESMERISM, HYPNOTISM, SUGGESTION 

591 ing suggestions to people of normal good health. (P. 269.)

And to speak of suggestion with sane persons one is obliged to consider quite different facts-effects of edu cation, habits, recollections, beliefs, etc. They are psychological facts which are apparently akin to suggestion, but the mechanism of which is quite different. Docile, obedient persons, disposed to think of others as having more intelligence than themselves, who on account of this easily believe what they are taught, are not suggestible persons. This complete and automatic development of an isolated idea of personality, in the fashion of a parasite, is not met with in the normal man." (Mental State of Hystericals, p. 270.) Janet also quotes M. Gilles de la Tourette who describes "the whole mental state of hysteria in the one word, suggestibility." (P. 227.)

From the whole history of the development of knowledge on this subject it seems evident that persons who have been subject to "possessions," who have proved amenable to animal magnetism, hypnotism and suggestion and who, presumably, have been helped by psychoanalysis have been predominantly hysterical subjects. 

The matter would perhaps be of little importance had not the doctrine of psychoanalysis been adopted as a psychological creed widely applicable and which instantly excuses all shortcomings. We are inefficient because we have an "inferiority complex." We forget disagreeable matters. Therefore we forget, avoid and ignore disagreeable duties. This seems to be the credo and apology of the unreliable and inefficient among the psychological intelligentsia. We "rationalize" our acts, i. e., we do what we desire to do, then we set about to find a plausible reason for our conduct. Asked for an explanation, we give the most plausible reason we can invent. Therefore we are

not constrained to be truthful even with ourselves. We never name our behavior stupid, unreliable, shifty or downright idleness. This taking over by certain types of persons of the psychology of hystericals as a pseudo-ethics of conduct is doing considerable harm. It breeds a weakness akin to that of their prototypes. Better far the vigorous Puritanism expressed by a popular writer in the words, "If you don't like it, do it." That breeds strength and best of all a strength sufficient to face the truth rather than to flinch from it.

CHAPTER XXII PSYCHIC TRAITS OF THE SEXES 

Personality seems to be a term which we use much and of whose meaning we know little. Professor Woodworth points out that personality is partly a matter of appearance or "looks," depends partly upon physique and "chemique" (hormones), partly upon the social instincts, and it is often partly confused with character. Since the term is so vague and all-inclusive of both physical and mental traits, it seems desirable to omit discussion of it and to undertake, instead, a step preliminary to the study of individual differences. The two sexes present certain marked differences of personality due to sex alone. In other words, personalities seem first to belong to two classes. They are masculine or feminine. Perhaps, then, "the riddle of personality" might sooner reach a solution if its investigators ceased to compare personalities indiscriminately and instead compared the traits of women with women, and of men with men. This preliminary step may not be necessary but it seems as if it might offer a better beginning for the analysis of individuals. In the following paragraphs we can make only some fragmentary statements concerning sex differences which seem to be generally accepted.

Differences in Instincts and Emotions.-It is often said that women lead more quiet and less eventful lives than men. They have to face fewer crises of their own making. 

Men are said to have greater initiative, to be more aggressive and more venturesome, and to take greater and more

frequent risks than women. These traits would certainly give them more eventful lives. Women, unless they be pampered, are said to be more docile, more conservative, more easily persuaded, and far less constructively critical than men. These are probably not intellectual differences, but temperamental ones due to differences of emotion and instinct.

If we may use the results of experiments on animals, the results of physiology, it seems probable that this difference between the sexes is one of "chemique," to employ again Woodworth's very apt term. It is well known that, if a young animal is unsexed, there presently appear almost all the characteristics of the opposite sex. The female becomes masculine, aggressive, active, and less docile and demure. While experiments are not numerous enough to assure any general explanation, it has been shown for some animals, that the internal secretions of female sex glands inhibit and prevent the development of male traits, and corresponding hormones of the male prevent the appearance of female traits. Removal of the glands permits the traits of the opposite sex to develop. It is as if nature provides the body with the traits of both sexes, but prevents the development of one set of them by biochemical means. While the operated female cannot attain the size of the male, because size is determined by the pituitary gland, the relative proportions of parts of the body may be changed by the operation. The facts must be more complicated than this, however, for a recently reported case indicates that disease of an adrenal gland may cause the appearance of masculine traits in a human female, and removal of the disease causes a return of feminine traits. The total result of our knowledge would warrant the conclusion that many male and female traits have a

PSYCHIC TRAITS OF THE SEXES 

595 biochemical cause and are therefore organic and funda. mental.

It is desirable to keep this in mind because we are so often asked whether the psychic differences between men and women are not entirely products of the environment and due to centuries of subordination of women to the so-called "lords of creation." While this may be partly true, the general statement seems quite improbable. A talented woman, who had succeeded fully in attaining a career and fame, said of it, "It satisfies my mind but not my heart." Since such a woman is a most competent witness and since we have other evidence we must admit the existence of sex differences which are independent of environmental causes. The most profound psychic differences are to be found in the old brain which seems especially to preside over instinct and emotion. In fact, the lack of confidence in her knowledge, no matter how accurate such knowledge may be, seems to me the most marked psychic difference between men and women.

The psychologists, who have studied most carefully the achievements of women, assure us that women have better memories than men.¹ They excel in general school knowledge, in zeal, perseverance, attendance upon classes, in duty, orderliness, and conscientiousness in study. In exactness in quantitative work, the two sexes were equal. 

In other traits men excelled, i. e., in criticism, in devotion to a special pursuit, in theoretical interest and in reasoning. But men excelled especially in confidence in the facts learned. Confidence in knowledge acquired, whether it is accurate or not, seems to be pre-eminently a masculine trait. It is a feeling rather than an intellectual trait, a permanent feeling tone of knowledge. It is this confidence 'On the basis of tests Pyle says that women have the same ability for retention as men.

which makes a man willing and eager to announce his theories and to try them. The trial may fail, and sometimes with disastrous results, but some trials must succeed and this makes progress. Because of his confidence he may become a great surgeon, an intrepid explorer, a daring investigator, a speculator, or one of those teachers far more interested in pointing the way to Utopia than in teaching how mankind has come thus far. As the knowledge of the race increases, more and more trials of it in actual life succeed. The knowledge may be just as truly a woman's possession. Her knowledge may be more extensive and reliable but she does not rely on it. She does not readily make trial of her beliefs nor is she generally so ready to do heroic battle to establish her theories. She does not often formulate theories. This is an intellectual difference but it is not so important as the difference between the two sexes in confidence in their knowledge. 

Many differences of behavior can be traced to this. Probably the historic forerunner of this confidence possessed by men was their confidence and reliance upon their bodily strength in former times, when bodily strength was the greatest source of victory and survival. Strength is due to metabolism. The confidence may be a by-product of the metabolism. Invalids and men completely exhausted lose all confidence and all hope. The athlete has a great deal of it. We have seen reason to believe that hormones influence imagination (p. 425) and nothing is more certain than that the bodies of men and women are different biochemical machines. The chemical differences affect instinct and emotion, even though they may have little effect on intelligence. What was originally the adventurous spirit of primitive man and a certain fierce delight in facing physical dangers has now been transformed into

PSYCHIC TRAITS OF THE SEXES 

599 all the faculties, i. e., of law, medicine, mathematicalnatural science, etc. In addition to this twelve per cent. more women than men stood high in professional examinations.

In America, intelligence tests have been administered to students, both men and women, boys and girls. The result has led Terman to remark that the discussion, as to whether men or women are the more intelligent, is as futile as the discussion whether the world is flat. He believes that no difference can be found. Porteus grants this only for the ability to learn. On the basis of a different group of tests, he says, "As regards tests of development involving the capacities of persistent effort, resistance to suggestibility, mental alertness and power to inhibit nervousness and emotion. males of every race are superior to females." He also believes that equality of intelligence in the two sexes is contrary to common observation, and points to the inadequacy of intelligence tests to determine the matter. It is notable that, aside from mental alertness, the traits tested by Porteus are rather traits of character than of intelligence. Judgment and Reasoning.—Tradition has long claimed that women arrive at decisions by the method of intuition (p. 579), while men analyze and weigh the evidence. There is evidence to support this tradition. It is also certain that women in general can be persuaded to decision and action more readily than men. They do not resist suggestion to the extent that men do. This is merely a corollary of the lack of confidence in their own knowledge as a basis for action. 

Perception. There is one striking difference between 'Porteus, S. D., "Temperament and Mentality in Maturity, Sex and Race."

Journal of Applied Psychology, Vol. VIII, No. 1, pp. 72-73, 1924.

men and women in perception. Women have a better sense of color, men of form. This fact is evident in almost any class in geometry and it has led to the elimination of that subject for girls in many high schools. On the other hand, women are superior as decorators wherever colors are involved. This may be correlated with the fact that women are almost never color-blind. Many women have become pre-eminently successful as decorators in recent years. 

Possibly it is because of this difference that the clothing of women includes colors in great variety while that of men does not for any prolonged period. The period of color for men, even in army uniforms, seems to have passed. 

Motor Reactions.-When subjected to tests, men showed greater quickness and accuracy of movement than women, but women were far superior in the co-ordination of fine movements. Possibly because of this difference, lace, tapestry, and embroidery have been the product of women's handiwork in times past and they are employed in stenography and typing in the present. It is notable in schools that girls are superior in penmanship to boys. 

The above statements give mere fragments of information, but they may serve to show the pronounced mental and emotional differences between the sexes. These differences are more marked than those between personalities of the same sex. We shall probably arrive at the differences between personalities more surely if we first distinguish them as masculine and feminine.
